knowledge_statements.title: Residual-System Solution Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential identities and local linearized systems for smooth finite-dimensional residual maps and nonlinear least-squares objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be twice continuously differentiable, let \(J(x)=F'(x)\), and define \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\). Then
\[
\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x),\qquad \nabla^2\phi(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m F_i(x)\nabla^2F_i(x).
\]
A Gauss--Newton step minimizes \(\lVert F(x)+J(x)p\rVert_2\), equivalently satisfying \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)p=-J(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x)\) when the normal matrix is nonsingular. If \(m=n\) and \(J(x)\) is nonsingular, the Newton root step instead satisfies \(J(x)p=-F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual sum of squares has an exact Jacobian-based gradient and a Hessian split into Gauss–Newton and residual-curvature terms; local steps solve the corresponding linearized residual systems.
assumptions_latex: For the stated Gauss--Newton normal-equation characterization, \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)\) is nonsingular.
For the Newton root step, \(m=n\) and \(J(x)\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(
abla\phi=J^{\mathsf T}F\), \(
abla^2\phi=J^{\mathsf T}J+\sum_i F_i
abla^2F_i\), with Gauss--Newton and Newton steps obtained from the displayed linearized systems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General smooth nonlinear constrained optimization model and local-solution algorithmic scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation of a finite-dimensional smooth nonlinear program together with the stated scope of the iterative algorithms under consideration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)\) subject to \(c_i(x)=0\) for \(i\in\mathcal E\) and \(c_i(x)\ge 0\) for \(i\in\mathcal I\), where \(\mathcal E\) and \(\mathcal I\) are finite and \(f\) and every \(c_i\) are smooth real-valued functions on a subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The algorithms considered for this model are iterative methods aimed at local solutions: they generate solution estimates \(x_k\), and some also generate estimates of the associated Lagrange multipliers; finding a global solution is excluded from the stated scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general smooth nonlinear program minimizes a smooth real-valued objective over finitely many smooth equality and inequality constraints. The algorithms considered are iterative methods for finding local solutions, producing successive solution estimates and, in some cases, multiplier estimates; global optimization is outside their stated scope.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E\) and \(\mathcal I\) are finite index sets.
\(f\) and \(c_i\) for all \(i\in\mathcal E\cup\mathcal I\) are smooth real-valued functions on a subset of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)\ \text{s.t.}\ c_i(x)=0\ (i\in\mathcal E),\ c_i(x)\ge0\ (i\in\mathcal I)\) is the operative model, and the stated algorithmic scope is iterative search for local, not global, solutions, with optional multiplier estimation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-problem geometric taxonomy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, let \(R:X\to\mathbb R^m\) be a residual map, and, when used, let \(G:X\to X\) be an iteration map and \(W\in\mathbb S_+^m\) a residual weight.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional residual systems; the definition classifies formulations and local solution geometry without imposing smoothness or an algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The residual problem generated by \(R\) is classified first by its solution object: a root problem has \(Z_R:=\{x\in X:R(x)=0\}\); a fixed-point problem has \(\operatorname{Fix}(G):=\{x\in X:G(x)=x\}\); and a least-squares problem has \(M_{R,W}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\tfrac12R(x)^TWR(x)\). A representation is exact when the designated solution sets coincide. A root \(x_*\in Z_R\) is isolated when some \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfies \(Z_R\cap B_\varepsilon(x_*)=\{x_*\}\), and nonisolated otherwise. When \(R\) is differentiable, a root is regular if \(DR(x_*)\) has maximal rank appropriate to the representation, and degenerate otherwise. The residual is consistent when \(Z_R\neq\varnothing\), and inconsistent when \(Z_R=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual problem is classified by whether its designated solutions are zeros of a residual, fixed points of a map, or minimizers of a weighted squared residual. Representations are exact when their solution sets agree. Roots are isolated or nonisolated according to whether they are locally unique, regular or degenerate according to the rank of the residual derivative, and the system is consistent exactly when its zero set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z_R=\{R=0\},\quad \operatorname{Fix}(G)=\{G=I\},\quad M_{R,W}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\tfrac12R(x)^TWR(x)\), with exact reformulation meaning equality of the relevant sets.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(W=I\), \(M_{R,I}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\).
If \(Z_R\neq\varnothing\) and \(W\succ0\), then \(Z_R=M_{R,W}\) exactly when every global least-squares minimizer has zero residual.
special_cases_latex: For a square smooth system, regularity means \(\det DR(x_*)\neq0\).
For \(m<n\), maximal-rank regularity commonly means full row rank \(\operatorname{rank}DR(x_*)=m\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every isolated regular square root is locally the only member of \(Z_R\).
An inconsistent residual system can still have a nonempty least-squares solution set.
boundary_notes: Maximal rank alone does not classify singular roots by multiplicity.
The taxonomy does not assert existence of roots, minimizers, or fixed points.

notation.meaning: zero set of the residual map

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Root and fixed-point representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(F:D\to\mathbb R^n\), and let \(G:D\to D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional square residual systems and self-maps; no contraction or convergence hypothesis is part of the representation itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The root representation of a nonlinear system is the problem of finding \(x_*\in D\) such that \(F(x_*)=0\), with solution set \(Z(F):=F^{-1}(\{0\})\). The fixed-point representation of a self-map \(G\) is the problem of finding \(x_*\in D\) such that \(G(x_*)=x_*\), with solution set \(\operatorname{Fix}(G)\). The pair \((F,G)\) is an exact root–fixed-point representation when \(Z(F)=\operatorname{Fix}(G)\). More generally, it is locally exact at \(x_*\) when some neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\) satisfies \(Z(F)\cap U=\operatorname{Fix}(G)\cap U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A root representation seeks a point where a square residual map vanishes. A fixed-point representation seeks a point left unchanged by a self-map. The two representations are exact when their solution sets are equal, and locally exact at a solution when those sets agree in a neighborhood of that solution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x_*\in\operatorname{Fix}(G)\iff (I-G)(x_*)=0\); hence every fixed-point problem is a root problem for \(F=I-G\).
If \(A(x)\) is nonsingular for every \(x\in D\) and \(G(x)=x-A(x)^{-1}F(x)\), then \(G(x)=x\iff F(x)=0\).
special_cases_latex: Newton's iteration map is \(G_N(x)=x-DF(x)^{-1}F(x)\) wherever \(DF(x)\) is nonsingular.
A stationary-point problem \(\nabla f(x)=0\) is a root problem with \(F=\nabla f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: An iteration \(x_{k+1}=G(x_k)\) targets the original root set only when the fixed-point reformulation is exact on the relevant domain.
boundary_notes: Equality \(G(x_*)=x_*\) does not by itself imply that iteration from nearby points converges to \(x_*\).
For rectangular residuals \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) with \(m\ne n\), a square self-map requires an additional construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Square Nonlinear Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square nonlinear system has equally many scalar equations and unknowns; its solutions are zeros of a map from a subset of n-space to n-space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A square nonlinear system is a root problem for a mapping \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\): find \(x^\star\in D\) such that \[F(x^\star)=0.\] It is square because the number of scalar equations equals the number of unknowns. If \(F\) is differentiable at \(x\), its Jacobian \(J_F(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is square; nonsingularity of \(J_F(x^\star)\) is an additional regularity condition, not part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\text{ solves the system}\iff x^\star\in D\text{ and }F(x^\star)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real square residual systems.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of F at x when it exists

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Reformulations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting an invertibly scaled residual from the current point produces a fixed-point map whose fixed points are exactly the residual roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(M:D\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be such that \(M(x)\) is nonsingular for every \(x\in D\). Define \(T:D\to\mathbb{R}^n\) by \[T(x)=x-M(x)F(x).\] Whenever \(T(D)\subseteq D\), the residual and fixed-point formulations have exactly the same solutions: \[F(x^\star)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T(x^\star)=x^\star.\] Thus an iteration \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) targets the original roots, although equivalence alone does not guarantee convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(M(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\text{ is nonsingular for all }x\in D\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reformulation of a square residual equation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact fixed-point reformulation of a residual equation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(F:D\to\mathbb R^n\), and let \(A:D\to\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) satisfy \(\det A(x)\ne0\) for every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square finite-dimensional systems with a pointwise invertible scaling or model matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The preconditioned fixed-point reformulation of \(F(x)=0\) induced by \(A\) is the self-map \(G_A:D\to\mathbb R^n\) defined by \(G_A(x):=x-A(x)^{-1}F(x)\), restricted to any subset on which \(G_A(x)\in D\). It is exact because, for every \(x\in D\), \(G_A(x)=x\) if and only if \(A(x)^{-1}F(x)=0\), equivalently \(F(x)=0\). Thus \(\operatorname{Fix}(G_A)=Z(F)\). A general self-map \(G:D\to D\) is called an exact fixed-point reformulation of \(F(x)=0\) when this equality of solution sets holds, whether or not \(G\) has the displayed preconditioned form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible matrix-valued scaling turns a square residual equation into the fixed-point map obtained by subtracting the scaled residual from the current point. Because the scaling is invertible, a point is fixed exactly when its residual is zero. More generally, any self-map with precisely the same solutions as the residual equation is an exact fixed-point reformulation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The fixed-point residual is \(x-G_A(x)=A(x)^{-1}F(x)\).
For a given self-map \(G\), the equation \(G(x)=x\) is exactly the residual equation \((I-G)(x)=0\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(A(x)=DF(x)\) yields the Newton fixed-point map wherever \(DF(x)\) is nonsingular.
Taking \(A(x)=\alpha^{-1}I\) yields \(G(x)=x-\alpha F(x)\) for \(\alpha\ne0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Spurious fixed points cannot occur under pointwise invertibility of \(A(x)\).
A singular or generalized inverse in place of \(A(x)^{-1}\) may destroy the equivalence.
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert that \(G_A\) maps all of \(D\) into itself.
Exactness of solution sets is separate from stability or contractivity of the iteration map.

notation.meaning: fixed-point map induced by the invertible scaling A

knowledge_statements.title: Overdetermined Equation Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An overdetermined system has more scalar equations than unknowns. Exact roots may not exist, so least squares is often used as a surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An overdetermined nonlinear equation system is specified by \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) with \(m>n\), and asks for \(x^\star\in D\) satisfying \[F(x^\star)=0.\] The system is consistent precisely when \(0\in F(D)\). If no root exists, minimizing \(\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\) defines a nonlinear least-squares surrogate, but a stationary point or minimizer of that surrogate is an exact solution only when its residual value is zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual systems with more equations than unknowns.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Over-determined Systems p. 110

knowledge_statements.title: Underdetermined Equation Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An underdetermined system has fewer equations than unknowns. This inequality does not guarantee a solution, but at a full-row-rank root of a continuously differentiable map on an open domain, the nearby solutions form a smooth manifold of dimension n minus m.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An underdetermined nonlinear equation system is specified by a mapping \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), where \(m<n\), and asks for \(x^\star\in U\) satisfying \[F(x^\star)=0.\] The dimension inequality alone neither guarantees consistency nor determines the local solution geometry. If \(U\) is open, \(F\in C^1(U;\mathbb{R}^m)\), and \(J_F(x^\star)\) has row rank \(m\), then the root set near \(x^\star\) is an embedded \(C^1\) submanifold of dimension \(n-m\). Rank loss may instead permit singular or branching geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\text{ solves the system}\iff x^\star\in U\text{ and }F(x^\star)=0\); moreover, if \(F\in C^1(U;\mathbb{R}^m)\) and \(\operatorname{rank}J_F(x^\star)=m\), then \(F^{-1}(0)\) is locally an embedded \(C^1\) submanifold of dimension \(n-m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional residual systems with fewer equations than unknowns, on an open domain when local differential geometry is asserted.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consistency and local geometry of a residual solution set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(R:X\to\mathbb R^m\). Define \(Z:=\{x\in X:R(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact residual equations; differentiability is needed only for the rank-based subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The residual system \(R(x)=0\) is consistent when \(Z\ne\varnothing\) and inconsistent when \(Z=\varnothing\). For \(x_*\in Z\), the solution is isolated when there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(Z\cap B_\varepsilon(x_*)=\{x_*\}\); otherwise it is nonisolated. If \(R\) is differentiable at \(x_*\), the local linearized solution directions form \(\ker DR(x_*)\). A regular solution is one at which \(DR(x_*)\) has the maximal rank required by the system regime; a solution failing that rank condition is degenerate. The local consistency geometry is the collection of these properties together with the local set germ \(Z\cap U\) for neighborhoods \(U\) of \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual equation is consistent exactly when it has at least one zero. At a zero, local geometry distinguishes a locally unique solution from one accumulated by other solutions. For differentiable residuals, the null space of the Jacobian gives the linearized solution directions, while maximal-rank and rank-deficient points are called regular and degenerate, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x)=0\text{ is consistent}\iff Z\ne\varnothing\), and \(x_*\text{ is isolated}\iff \exists\varepsilon>0:\ Z\cap B_\varepsilon(x_*)=\{x_*\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x_*\) is nonisolated if and only if every neighborhood of \(x_*\) contains some \(z\in Z\setminus\{x_*\}\).
In Euclidean space, nonisolation is equivalent to the existence of a sequence \(z_k\in Z\setminus\{x_*\}\) with \(z_k\to x_*\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=n\), a regular root has nonsingular Jacobian \(DR(x_*)\).
For an underdetermined system \(m<n\), full row rank gives \(\dim\ker DR(x_*)=n-m\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonisolated root cannot be locally unique.
Consistency is independent of whether a particular numerical method finds a root.
boundary_notes: A rank-deficient root may be isolated or nonisolated; degeneracy alone does not decide isolation.
The definition does not assign multiplicity to a singular root.

notation.meaning: solution or zero set of R

knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Regular Roots
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular root has an invertible Jacobian. For a square continuously differentiable system, such a root is locally unique and therefore isolated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable on an open set. A root \(x^\star\in U\) is regular when \[F(x^\star)=0\quad\text{and}\quad \det J_F(x^\star)\ne0.\] It is isolated when some \(r>0\) satisfies \[F^{-1}(0)\cap B_r(x^\star)=\{x^\star\}.\] By local invertibility, every regular root is isolated; equivalently, sufficiently near \(x^\star\), the equation \(F(x)=0\) has the unique solution \(x=x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity and isolation for square continuously differentiable systems.

notation.meaning: open Euclidean ball of radius r

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition and local-isolation conclusion are mathematically standard and correctly scoped to square C1 systems, and the definition kind fits the container. No citation is supplied for the inverse-function-theorem implication that a regular root is isolated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Isolated degenerate root
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^n\) be differentiable, and let \(x_*\in U\) satisfy \(F(x_*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth square finite-dimensional nonlinear systems; degeneracy is Jacobian singularity, not an assigned algebraic multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The point \(x_*\) is an isolated degenerate root of \(F\) when both \(\det DF(x_*)=0\) and local uniqueness hold: there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(B_\varepsilon(x_*)\subset U\) such that \(F^{-1}(\{0\})\cap B_\varepsilon(x_*)=\{x_*\}\). Equivalently, \(x_*\) is an isolated point of the zero set while the first-order linearization \(DF(x_*)s=0\) has a nonzero solution direction. The definition records the coexistence of nonlinear isolation and failure of first-order invertibility; it does not require that nearby linearized null directions integrate into actual solution curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isolated degenerate root is a locally unique zero of a differentiable square system whose Jacobian at that zero is singular. Thus the nonlinear equation has no other nearby solutions even though its linearization possesses a nonzero null direction. The term does not by itself specify multiplicity or the order of the first nonvanishing higher derivative.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a square matrix, \(\det DF(x_*)=0\iff \ker DF(x_*)\ne\{0\}\).
Isolation is equivalent to the absence of a sequence of distinct roots converging to \(x_*\).
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the conditions become \(F(x_*)=0\), \(F'(x_*)=0\), and local uniqueness of the zero.
The scalar function \(F(x)=(x-x_*)^q\) with integer \(q\ge2\) has an isolated degenerate root at \(x_*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The inverse function theorem cannot certify local invertibility at an isolated degenerate root.
Standard nonsingular-Jacobian Newton theory does not apply without modification.
boundary_notes: A singular Jacobian does not imply isolation; a continuum of roots may also be singular.
Multiplicity, semiregularity, and deflation structure require additional definitions.

notation.meaning: Jacobian matrix of F at the root

review_flags: The inspected nonlinear-equations sources treat regular roots but do not provide a precise locator for this combined isolated-and-degenerate definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolated degenerate root
Isolated Singular Roots
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isolated singular root is locally the only root despite having a rank-deficient Jacobian. Singularity and isolation are logically distinct conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable at a root \(x^\star\). The point \(x^\star\) is an isolated singular root when \[F(x^\star)=0,\qquad \operatorname{rank}J_F(x^\star)<n,\] and there exists \(r>0\) such that \[F^{-1}(0)\cap B_r(x^\star)=\{x^\star\}.\] Singularity records failure of first-order local invertibility, whereas isolation records local uniqueness; neither condition implies the other without further hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\text{ is isolated singular}\iff F(x^\star)=0,\ \operatorname{rank}J_F(x^\star)<n,\ \exists r>0:\ F^{-1}(0)\cap B_r(x^\star)=\{x^\star\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isolated roots with rank-deficient square Jacobian.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The displayed conditions correctly define an isolated singular root and fit the terminal container. An authoritative singular-root locator is absent. The phrase about failure of first-order local invertibility should be supported or understood specifically as failure of the Jacobian nonsingularity criterion, since a singular derivative does not by itself preclude a locally invertible map.

knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Multiple Roots
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an isolated analytic root, multiplicity is the dimension of the local analytic quotient algebra. Dimension one means simple; larger finite dimension means multiple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)\) be analytic near an isolated root \(x^\star\in\mathbb{C}^n\). Write \(\mathcal O_{x^\star}\) for the local ring of analytic germs at \(x^\star\), and let \(I_F=\langle f_1,\ldots,f_n\rangle\). The multiplicity of the isolated root is \[\mu(F,x^\star)=\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(\mathcal O_{x^\star}/I_F\bigr).\] The root is multiple when \(\mu(F,x^\star)>1\), and simple when \(\mu(F,x^\star)=1\). Isolation ensures this quotient has finite complex dimension.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic multiplicity for isolated analytic square-system roots.

notation.meaning: local ring of analytic germs at the root
ideal generated by the component germs of F

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The local-quotient-algebra definition is appropriate for isolated complex-analytic square-system roots, and isolation yields finite local-algebra dimension under this convention. Because the convention is specialized and no source is cited, an authoritative definition or theorem locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity–Singularity Interactions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an isolated analytic square-system root, multiplicity one is equivalent to an invertible Jacobian; hence isolated multiple roots are exactly the singular ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C}^n\) be analytic near an isolated root \(x^\star\), and let \(\mu(F,x^\star)\) denote its local algebraic multiplicity. Then \[\mu(F,x^\star)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \det J_F(x^\star)\ne0.\] Consequently, every isolated multiple root satisfies \(\det J_F(x^\star)=0\). Conversely, for an isolated root of an analytic square system, Jacobian singularity implies multiplicity greater than one. Isolation is essential because the finite local-algebra multiplicity used here need not be defined for a positive-dimensional root set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of simplicity and Jacobian nonsingularity for isolated analytic roots.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: For an isolated complex-analytic square-system root with the stated local-algebra multiplicity, simplicity is equivalent to Jacobian nonsingularity, so the mathematical interaction is correctly stated and the property kind fits the container. No authoritative source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonisolated residual solution and regular solution manifold
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(R:U\to\mathbb R^m\), and let \(Z:=R^{-1}(\{0\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The topological definition needs no smoothness; the manifold specialization assumes continuous differentiability and locally constant full row rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A root \(x_*\in Z\) is nonisolated when every \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(B_\varepsilon(x_*)\subset U\) contains a distinct root, that is, \((Z\setminus\{x_*\})\cap B_\varepsilon(x_*)\ne\varnothing\). If \(R\) is continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), \(m<n\), and \(DR(x_*)\) has full row rank \(m\), then the corresponding regular nonisolated geometry is locally a solution manifold of dimension \(n-m\), with tangent space \(T_{x_*}Z=\ker DR(x_*)\). In this regime an algorithm may converge to a nearby member of \(Z\) depending on its initial point rather than to a preselected root.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A root is nonisolated when every neighborhood contains another root. For an underdetermined continuously differentiable system with full row-rank Jacobian, the regular local model is a solution manifold whose dimension is the number of variables minus the number of equations and whose tangent space is the Jacobian null space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*\text{ nonisolated}\iff \forall\varepsilon>0,\ (Z\setminus\{x_*\})\cap B_\varepsilon(x_*)\ne\varnothing\); under full row rank, \(\dim_{x_*}Z=n-m\) and \(T_{x_*}Z=\ker DR(x_*)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: In Euclidean space, nonisolation is equivalent to distinct \(z_k\in Z\) satisfying \(z_k\to x_*\).
For full row rank, \(\dim\ker DR(x_*)=n-m>0\).
special_cases_latex: For a scalar equation in two variables with nonzero gradient, the local zero set is a curve.
For \(R(x)=Ax-b\) with consistent full-row-rank \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(Z=x_0+\ker A\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Local uniqueness fails at every point of a positive-dimensional regular solution manifold.
A minimum-norm or other selection rule is additional structure, not part of the equation \(R(x)=0\).
boundary_notes: A nonisolated zero set need not be a smooth manifold at rank-deficient points.
The manifold assertion is local and does not determine global topology or connectedness.

notation.meaning: tangent space to the regular zero set at x_*

source_refs.locator: §2.4.3, zero set Z, underdetermined discussion, and Theorem 2.4.2, pp. 26–27

review_flags: The cited source explicitly supports convergence to an initial-point-dependent member of a nonunique zero set; the local manifold dimension uses the standard full-row-rank interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated Root Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A root is nonisolated when arbitrarily close distinct roots exist. This accumulation condition alone imposes no smoothness, tangent, or dimension structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a mapping \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(Z=F^{-1}(0)\). A root \(x^\star\in Z\) is nonisolated when every neighborhood of \(x^\star\) contains another root. Equivalently, \[\forall r>0,\qquad \bigl(Z\cap B_r(x^\star)\bigr)\setminus\{x^\star\}\ne\varnothing.\] The root set is locally nonisolated at \(x^\star\) under this condition. Nonisolation alone does not imply that \(Z\) is a manifold, has a unique tangent space, or possesses a fixed local dimension.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local accumulation geometry of residual roots.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The neighborhood and ball formulations correctly express nonisolation, and the cautions about manifold, tangent, and dimension structure are not overstated. The definition fits the terminal container, but the record supplies no source or explicit standard-field rationale.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Solution Manifolds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a full-row-rank root of an underdetermined smooth system, the nearby solutions form a smooth manifold whose tangent space is the Jacobian nullspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(F\in C^1(U;\mathbb{R}^m)\) with \(m<n\). If \(F(x^\star)=0\) and \(J_F(x^\star)\) has row rank \(m\), then there exists a neighborhood \(V\subseteq U\) of \(x^\star\) such that \[F^{-1}(0)\cap V\] is an embedded \(C^1\) submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) of dimension \(n-m\). Its tangent space at \(x^\star\) is \[T_{x^\star}F^{-1}(0)=\ker J_F(x^\star).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{-1}(0)\text{ is locally an embedded }C^1\text{ manifold of dimension }n-m\text{ with }T_{x^\star}F^{-1}(0)=\ker J_F(x^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-level-set form for underdetermined residual systems.

notation.meaning: tangent space to the local solution manifold
neighborhood on which the manifold description holds

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The hypotheses and conclusion correctly state the local regular-level-set theorem, including dimension and tangent space, and theorem is the proper content kind. No authoritative theorem, section, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Solution Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero set of y squared minus x squared consists of two crossing lines, showing how rank loss can create nonmanifold branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Full-rank regular-level geometry can fail at a rank-deficient root. For example, define \(F:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) by \[F(x,y)=y^2-x^2.\] Its zero set is \[F^{-1}(0)=\{(x,y):y=x\}\cup\{(x,y):y=-x\}.\] The origin is nonisolated and satisfies \(J_F(0,0)=(0,0)\). Two smooth one-dimensional branches meet there with distinct tangent lines, so no neighborhood of the origin in the zero set is an embedded one-dimensional manifold. Thus Jacobian rank loss allows branching, although it does not force branching in every system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{-1}(0)\text{ has two branches crossing at }(0,0)\text{ and is not locally an embedded one-dimensional manifold there}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank loss permits intersecting branches rather than a manifold.

notation.meaning: Jacobian row at the branching root

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The crossing-lines example is correct: the origin is rank deficient, nonisolated, and not locally an embedded one-dimensional manifold. It appropriately records a branching failure boundary without claiming rank loss always forces branching. No source or standard-field rationale is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact, inconsistent, and positive-residual regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, let \(R:X\to\mathbb R^m\), and define \(f(x):=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\) and \(f_*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean residual minimization; attainment is stated separately from the infimum classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The residual problem is exactly consistent when there exists \(x\in X\) with \(R(x)=0\), equivalently when the least-squares minimum is attained with value zero. It is inconsistent when no such point exists. An attained least-squares problem is a zero-residual problem when every global minimizer \(x_*\) has \(R(x_*)=0\), and a positive-residual problem when its attained optimal value satisfies \(f_*>0\). A merely asymptotically consistent problem has \(f_*=0\) but no root and no zero-residual minimizer. The informal labels small-residual and large-residual are comparative regimes based on the size of \(\|R(x_*)\|\) relative to derivative scales; unlike zero residual, they have no invariant threshold without a specified scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A system is exactly consistent if a zero residual is attained and inconsistent otherwise. An attained least-squares problem is zero-residual when its optimal residual vanishes and positive-residual when its optimal value is strictly positive. A separate nonattainment case occurs when residuals approach zero but no root exists. Small and large residual are scale-dependent descriptions rather than absolute mathematical categories.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z_R\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow f_*=0\); if the infimum is attained, \(Z_R\ne\varnothing\iff f_*=0\), while \(f_*>0\) is the positive-residual regime.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Exact consistency is \(0\in R(X)\); asymptotic consistency is \(0\in\overline{R(X)}\).
special_cases_latex: For continuous \(R\) on compact \(X\), \(f_*\) is attained, so \(f_*=0\) implies exact consistency.
In data fitting, zero residual means every observation is fit exactly.
immediate_consequences_latex: A positive-residual least-squares minimizer is not a root of \(R\).
Zero residual eliminates the residual-weighted second-order term in the least-squares Hessian.
boundary_notes: The implication \(f_*=0\Rightarrow Z_R\ne\varnothing\) can fail without attainment.
Small versus large residual requires a declared normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Consistent Residual Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual system is consistent exactly when its residual map attains zero, so at least one exact solution exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be a residual mapping, and define its solution set by \[Z=\{x\in D:F(x)=0\}=F^{-1}(0).\] The residual system is consistent when \(Z\ne\varnothing\), equivalently when \(0\in F(D)\). It is inconsistent when \(Z=\varnothing\). Consistency asserts existence of at least one exact zero-residual point; it does not imply uniqueness, regularity, isolation, or numerical attainability by a specified algorithm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact solvability of a general residual equation.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6 Sums of Squares and Nonlinear Equations p. 110

knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent Residual Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual system is inconsistent when no feasible point has zero residual; its best residual need not be positive unless the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(r:X\to\mathbb{R}^m\). The residual system \(r(x)=0\) is inconsistent on \(X\) precisely when its zero set is empty: \[Z:=\{x\in X:r(x)=0\}=\varnothing.\] If a norm \(\|\cdot\|\) is fixed, inconsistency does not by itself imply \(\inf_{x\in X}\|r(x)\|>0\); that strict inequality follows when the residual norm attains its infimum, for example when \(X\) is compact and \(r\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional residual equations with no exact root on the feasible domain.

notation.meaning: zero set of the residual mapping on the feasible domain

knowledge_statements.title: Consistency Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuous residuals on a compact domain, consistency is equivalent to a zero minimum residual, and transitions occur only on the consistency-set boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be compact, let \(\Lambda\) be a metric space, and let \(r:X\times\Lambda\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuous. Define \(v(\lambda):=\min_{x\in X}\|r(x,\lambda)\|\) and \(C:=\{\lambda\in\Lambda:v(\lambda)=0\}\). Then \(v\) is continuous, \(C\) is closed, and the residual system at \(\lambda\) is consistent exactly when \(\lambda\in C\). A consistency transition can occur only at a boundary point of \(C\), equivalently where arbitrarily nearby parameters exhibit different zero-set status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{\lambda:\exists x\in X,\ r(x,\lambda)=0\}=v^{-1}(\{0\})\) is closed, and transitions lie in \(\partial C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-dependent transition between nonempty and empty residual zero sets.

notation.meaning: minimum residual norm at parameter lambda
set of parameters producing consistent systems

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The compact-domain value function and closed consistency-set claims are mathematically plausible and correctly scoped, but no source is supplied for the parameterized minimum-value continuity result or the boundary characterization of transitions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonlinear least-squares problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and let \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:X\to\mathbb R^m\) be nonlinear in at least one decision variable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained ordinary nonlinear least squares in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces; constrained, weighted, and robust variants are separate specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ordinary nonlinear least-squares problem generated by \(R\) is \(\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in X} f(x)\), where \(f(x):=\tfrac12R(x)^TR(x)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2\). Its solution set is \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\). A zero-residual solution is a minimizer \(x_*\) satisfying \(R(x_*)=0\); such a point is automatically a global minimizer because \(f\ge0\). A stationary least-squares point, when \(R\) is differentiable and \(x_*\) is interior to \(X\), satisfies \(J(x_*)^TR(x_*)=0\), where \(J=DR\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear least squares minimizes one half of the sum of squared component residuals. Its solutions are global minimizers of that scalar objective. A root of the residual is a zero-residual global solution, while an interior differentiable stationary point satisfies the normal-equation condition that the Jacobian transpose times the residual is zero.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Minimizing \(f\) is equivalent to minimizing \(\|R(x)\|_2\) because squaring and multiplication by \(1/2\) preserve the ordering of nonnegative values.
For data \((t_i,y_i)\) and model \(q(x,t)\), take \(r_i(x)=q(x,t_i)-y_i\).
special_cases_latex: If every \(r_i\) is affine, the problem is linear least squares.
When \(m=n\) and a root exists, solving \(R(x)=0\) is included as the zero-residual special case.
immediate_consequences_latex: At an exact fit, the least-squares objective has value zero.
The residual vector, Jacobian, and their product \(J^TR\) provide the basic first-order structure.
boundary_notes: A stationary point with nonzero residual need not be a local or global minimizer.
Nonlinear refers to the residual dependence on the parameters, not to the squaring operation alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Nonlinear Least Squares
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary nonlinear least squares minimizes the unweighted sum of squared residual components; any feasible exact root is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m):X\to\mathbb{R}^m\). Ordinary nonlinear least squares is the optimization problem \[\min_{x\in X} f(x),\qquad f(x):=\frac12\|r(x)\|_2^2=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2.\] Any global solution belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\|r(x)\|_2\). If the residual system is consistent, every feasible root is a global minimizer with objective value zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted Euclidean least-squares formulation for a nonlinear residual mapping.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted and generalized nonlinear least squares
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and let \(W\in\mathbb S_+^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear residuals with a fixed symmetric positive-semidefinite weight; statistical generalized least squares typically uses a positive-definite inverse covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The weighted nonlinear least-squares problem is \(\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in X} f_W(x)\), where \(f_W(x):=\tfrac12R(x)^TWR(x)\). If \(W=L^TL\), then \(f_W(x)=\tfrac12\|LR(x)\|_2^2\), so weighting is ordinary least squares applied to the transformed residual \(LR\). Generalized least squares is the case \(W=\Sigma^{-1}\) for a symmetric positive-definite residual covariance matrix \(\Sigma\); equivalently, for \(\Sigma=CC^T\), it minimizes \(\tfrac12\|C^{-1}R(x)\|_2^2\). Diagonal \(W=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,\ldots,w_m)\) gives \(f_W(x)=\tfrac12\sum_iw_ir_i(x)^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted nonlinear least squares minimizes a quadratic form in the residual. Factoring the weight turns it into ordinary least squares for a transformed residual. Generalized least squares uses the inverse residual covariance, which whitens correlated or unequally scaled errors. Positive diagonal weights recover the familiar sum of individually weighted squared residuals.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(W=\Sigma^{-1}\succ0\) and \(\Sigma=CC^T\), \(R^TWR=\|C^{-1}R\|_2^2\).
For diagonal positive weights, replace each residual \(r_i\) by \(\sqrt{w_i}r_i\).
special_cases_latex: \(W=I\) is ordinary nonlinear least squares.
A singular \(W\succeq0\) defines a seminorm and ignores residual components in \(\ker W\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(W\succ0\), then \(f_W(x)=0\iff R(x)=0\).
If \(W\) is singular, a zero weighted objective need not imply a zero residual.
boundary_notes: Parameter-dependent weights define a different objective and require derivative terms from the weight map.
A covariance interpretation requires \(\Sigma\succ0\); merely semidefinite weights need not correspond to invertible whitening.

notation.meaning: symmetric positive-semidefinite m by m matrices

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Nonlinear Least Squares
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted nonlinear least squares scales each squared residual by a positive weight and equals ordinary least squares after residual rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r:X\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and let \(w_i>0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Weighted nonlinear least squares is \[\min_{x\in X} f_W(x),\qquad f_W(x):=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m w_i r_i(x)^2=\frac12 r(x)^{\mathsf T}Wr(x),\] where \(W:=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,\ldots,w_m)\succ0\). Equivalently, it is ordinary least squares for the transformed residual \(W^{1/2}r(x)\). Positive weights preserve the residual zero set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal positive weighting of nonlinear residual components.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal positive-weight formulation, transformed-residual representation, and zero-set preservation claim are mathematically correct and fit the definition leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Nonlinear Least Squares
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized nonlinear least squares measures residuals using a full positive-definite inverse covariance and is ordinary least squares after whitening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r:X\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and let \(\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be symmetric positive definite. Generalized nonlinear least squares is \[\min_{x\in X} f_{\Sigma}(x),\qquad f_{\Sigma}(x):=\frac12 r(x)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}r(x).\] If \(L\) is any nonsingular factor satisfying \(L^{\mathsf T}L=\Sigma^{-1}\), then \(f_{\Sigma}(x)=\frac12\|Lr(x)\|_2^2\). Thus generalized least squares is ordinary least squares applied to a whitened residual and allows correlated residual components.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear least squares in a full positive-definite residual metric.

notation.meaning: positive-definite residual covariance or scale matrix

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The positive-definite residual-metric formulation and whitening identity are coherent and appropriate for generalized nonlinear least squares, but no source or precise locator supports the convention that Sigma is the residual covariance or scale matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighting Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite weight creates an ellipsoidal residual norm, and stationarity makes the residual orthogonal to feasible linearized residual changes in that metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(W=W^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), define \(\langle u,v\rangle_W:=u^{\mathsf T}Wv\) and \(\|u\|_W:=\sqrt{u^{\mathsf T}Wu}\). The objective \(f_W(x)=\frac12\|r(x)\|_W^2\) measures the residual image in ellipsoidal geometry: its level set \(\{u:u^{\mathsf T}Wu=c\}\) is an ellipsoid for \(c>0\). If \(r\) is differentiable, then \(\nabla f_W(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}Wr(x)\); hence unconstrained stationarity means that \(r(x)\) is \(W\)-orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}J(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f_W(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}Wr(x)\), so \(\nabla f_W(x)=0\iff \langle r(x),J(x)d\rangle_W=0\) for all \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric effect of a positive-definite residual metric on distance and stationarity.

notation.meaning: inner product induced by the weight matrix

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The induced inner product, ellipsoidal level sets, weighted gradient, and orthogonality condition are mathematically correct and the property kind fits the geometry leaf. However, the cited locator is generic and the record itself flags that a locator supporting the weighted extension is still pending.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Nonlinear Least Squares
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust nonlinear least squares replaces squared residuals with losses whose growth or derivative limits the influence of large standardized residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m):X\to\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(s_i>0\), and let \(\rho_i:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)\) satisfy \(\rho_i(0)=0\). Robust nonlinear least squares is \[\min_{x\in X} F(x),\qquad F(x):=\sum_{i=1}^m \rho_i\!\left(\frac{r_i(x)}{s_i}\right).\] When each \(\rho_i(t)=t^2/2\), this reduces to scaled weighted least squares. Bounded or subquadratic derivatives of \(\rho_i\) limit the marginal influence of large standardized residuals.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise loss formulation reducing the influence of large residuals.

notation.meaning: loss applied to the i-th standardized residual

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The separable-loss formulation is a reasonable definition of robust nonlinear least squares, but no source is supplied. The final influence claim also requires a precise authoritative formulation because bounded derivative and subquadratic growth are distinct conditions and do not express identical influence guarantees.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robust nonlinear residual fitting
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(s_i>0\), and let \(\rho_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R_+\) be loss functions with \(\rho_i(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable robust nonlinear fitting; losses may be smooth, nonsmooth, convex, or nonconvex, and those choices define distinct subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A separable robust nonlinear least-squares problem is \(\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in X}\Phi(x)\), where \(\Phi(x):=\sum_{i=1}^m\rho_i(r_i(x)/s_i)\). It is robustified relative to ordinary least squares when the loss grows more slowly than \(t^2\) for large \(|t|\), thereby limiting the objective contribution of large standardized residuals. The Huber subclass uses \(\rho_\delta(t)=\tfrac12t^2\) for \(|t|\le\delta\) and \(\rho_\delta(t)=\delta|t|-\tfrac12\delta^2\) for \(|t|>\delta\). Its influence score is \(\psi_\delta(t)=\rho_\delta'(t)=\operatorname{clip}(t,-\delta,\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust nonlinear least squares replaces each squared standardized residual by a chosen loss and sums those losses. A robustifying loss grows less rapidly than a square for large residuals, reducing their leverage. The Huber loss is quadratic near zero and linear in magnitude outside a threshold, with a bounded derivative.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Where \(r_i\ne0\), \(\rho_i(r_i)=\tfrac12w_i(r_i)r_i^2\) with \(w_i(t):=2\rho_i(t)/t^2\), giving an objective-level reweighted-square representation.
If all \(\rho_i(t)=\tfrac12t^2\), the formulation reduces to scaled ordinary nonlinear least squares.
special_cases_latex: The absolute loss \(\rho(t)=|t|\) yields nonlinear \(\ell_1\) fitting.
Huber loss is convex and continuously differentiable but is not twice differentiable at \(|t|=\delta\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For differentiable losses and residuals, \(\nabla\Phi(x)=\sum_i\psi_i(r_i(x)/s_i)\nabla r_i(x)/s_i\).
Bounded \(\psi_i\) limits the first-order contribution of a single large residual.
boundary_notes: Robust nonlinear least squares is not the same as worst-case robust optimization over uncertain data.
A redescending nonconvex loss may introduce additional stationary points.

notation.meaning: loss applied to the ith standardized residual

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal Distance Regression
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal distance regression fits a model while minimizing weighted corrections to both observed predictors and responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given observations \((a_i,y_i)\in\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q\), a model \(g:\mathbb{R}^p\times\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^q\), and positive-definite matrices \(W_i\) and \(V_i\), orthogonal distance regression solves \[\min_{\theta\in\Theta,\,\delta_i,\,\varepsilon_i}\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N\left(\delta_i^{\mathsf T}W_i\delta_i+\varepsilon_i^{\mathsf T}V_i\varepsilon_i\right)\quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i+\varepsilon_i=g(a_i+\delta_i;\theta).\] It therefore fits the model by correcting both predictor and response coordinates rather than treating predictors as exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\theta,\delta,\varepsilon)\) minimizes total weighted coordinate correction subject to the corrected observations lying on the model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Errors-in-variables fitting by minimizing corrections to observed predictors and responses.

notation.meaning: correction to the i-th predictor observation
correction to the i-th response observation

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The errors-in-variables constrained formulation is coherent and fits the orthogonal-distance-regression leaf, but sign, weighting, and coordinate-correction conventions vary across sources. An authoritative source with a specific section or page is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted orthogonal distance regression as nonlinear least squares
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation for nonlinear errors-in-variables regression when both the input ordinates and observed responses may be perturbed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observations $(t_j,y_j)$, a model $\phi(x;t)$, and prescribed weights $w_j,d_j$, introduce perturbations $\delta_j,\epsilon_j$ satisfying
\[
y_j=\phi(x;t_j+\delta_j)+\epsilon_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
\]
The weighted orthogonal-distance problem is
\[
\min_{x,\delta,\epsilon}\frac12\sum_{j=1}^m\left(w_j^2\epsilon_j^2+d_j^2\delta_j^2\right)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad y_j=\phi(x;t_j+\delta_j)+\epsilon_j.
\]
Eliminating $\epsilon_j$ yields
\[
\min_{x,\delta}F(x,\delta)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^m\left(w_j^2[y_j-\phi(x;t_j+\delta_j)]^2+d_j^2\delta_j^2\right),
\]
which is an unconstrained nonlinear least-squares problem in the model parameters and ordinate perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal distance regression accounts for errors in both the input ordinates and observed responses. Introducing an input perturbation and a response error for each observation gives a weighted constrained least-squares formulation; eliminating the response errors produces an unconstrained nonlinear least-squares problem in the model parameters and input perturbations.
assumptions_latex: \phi(x;t_j+\delta_j)\text{ is defined for the considered }x\text{ and }\delta_j

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First- and second-order least-squares model structure
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:U\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice continuously differentiable, and set \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained ordinary nonlinear least squares in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The least-squares stationarity model structure consists of \(J(x):=DR(x)\), \(g(x):=
abla f(x)=J(x)^TR(x)\), and \(H(x):=
abla^2f(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+S(x)\), where \(S(x):=\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)
abla^2r_i(x)\). A stationary point is any \(x_*\in U\) satisfying \(g(x_*)=J(x_*)^TR(x_*)=0\). The quadratic Taylor model at \(x\) is \(q_x(s)=f(x)+g(x)^Ts+	frac12s^TH(x)s\). The Gauss–Newton model replaces \(H(x)\) by \(J(x)^TJ(x)\), equivalently using the squared norm of the affine residual model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice differentiable squared-residual objective, the gradient is the Jacobian transpose times the residual. The Hessian splits into a positive-semidefinite Gauss–Newton term and a residual-weighted sum of component Hessians. Stationarity means the residual is orthogonal to every column of the Jacobian. The full Taylor model uses both Hessian terms, whereas the Gauss–Newton model keeps only the first.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(J(x_*)^TR(x_*)=0\iff R(x_*)\perp\operatorname{range}J(x_*)\).
The Gauss–Newton model is \(m_x(s)=\tfrac12\|R(x)+J(x)s\|_2^2\).
special_cases_latex: At a zero-residual point, \(S(x_*)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(x_*)=J(x_*)^TJ(x_*)\).
If every residual is affine, \(S(x)=0\) for all \(x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every root is stationary.
A stationary nonroot can occur when a nonzero residual is orthogonal to the Jacobian range.
boundary_notes: For constrained least squares, stationarity requires normal-cone or multiplier terms.
For nonsmooth residuals or losses, generalized derivatives replace these formulas.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient and Hessian structure of nonlinear least squares
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the residual-vector and Jacobian representations of the gradient and Hessian, including the exact residual-curvature term excluded from the Gauss–Newton component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
r(x)=(r_1(x),\ldots,r_m(x))^T,\qquad f(x)=\frac12\|r(x)\|_2^2,
\]
where each $r_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is twice continuously differentiable, and define
\[
J(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla r_1(x)^T\\ \vdots\\ \nabla r_m(x)^T\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}.
\]
Then
\[
\nabla f(x)=J(x)^Tr(x)
\]
and
\[
\nabla^2f(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m r_j(x)\nabla^2r_j(x).
\]
The term $J(x)^TJ(x)$ requires only first derivatives of the residuals. The correction term is zero when the residuals are affine and may be relatively small when the residual values or residual curvatures are relatively small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonlinear least-squares objective, the gradient is J transpose r and the Hessian is J transpose J plus the residual-weighted sum of the residual Hessians. The J transpose J term uses only first residual derivatives. The correction vanishes for affine residuals and may be relatively small for small residuals or small residual curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Stationarity Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Least-squares stationarity is the normal-equation condition that the residual is orthogonal to all linearized residual changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and define \(f(x):=\frac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\). If \(J(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is the Jacobian of \(r\), then \[\nabla f(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}r(x).\] Consequently, \(x\) is a first-order stationary point exactly when \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}r(x)=0\), equivalently when the residual vector is orthogonal to every linearized residual variation \(J(x)d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}r(x)\), and \(x\) is stationary iff \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}r(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity for unconstrained smooth nonlinear least squares.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual orthogonality characterization of stationarity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable on an open set and let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order structure for smooth unconstrained nonlinear least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The residual stationarity map is \(g_R:U\to\mathbb R^n\) defined by \(g_R(x):=J(x)^TR(x)\), where \(J(x)=DR(x)\). A point \(x_*\in U\) is residual-stationary when \(g_R(x_*)=0\). Equivalently, the residual vector is orthogonal to the linearized residual range: \(R(x_*)\in\ker J(x_*)^T=(\operatorname{range}J(x_*))^\perp\). This condition includes every root but can also hold at a nonroot. The stationarity residual \(\|J(x)^TR(x)\|\) measures first-order criticality of the scalar least-squares objective, whereas \(\|R(x)\|\) measures violation of the original equation; the two measures are not interchangeable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual stationarity is the vanishing of the Jacobian-transposed residual. Geometrically, the current residual is orthogonal to every first-order residual change available through a parameter perturbation. Every exact root is stationary, but a nonzero residual can also be stationary. Consequently, a small gradient does not necessarily mean that the original equations are nearly solved.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), residual stationarity is \(R(x_*)^TJ(x_*)d=0\).
It is exactly the unconstrained first-order condition \(\nabla(\tfrac12\|R\|^2)(x_*)=0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(J(x_*)\) has full row rank, then \(\ker J(x_*)^T=\{0\}\), so stationarity implies \(R(x_*)=0\).
If \(m>n\), a nonzero vector can lie in \((\operatorname{range}J)^\perp\), allowing stationary nonroots.
immediate_consequences_latex: Root tests and stationarity tests answer different questions.
A least-squares solver may terminate at a stationary nonroot when the system is inconsistent.
boundary_notes: Stationarity is necessary but not sufficient for local minimality.
At boundary-constrained points, projected or normal-cone stationarity is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauss–Newton Model Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gauss–Newton model squares the linearized residual, producing a positive-semidefinite approximate Hessian and linear least-squares step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\frac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\) with differentiable \(r\), the Gauss–Newton model at \(x\) is \[m_x(d):=\frac12\|r(x)+J(x)d\|_2^2=f(x)+d^{\mathsf T}J(x)^{\mathsf T}r(x)+\frac12d^{\mathsf T}J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)d.\] Its Hessian approximation is \(B_{\mathrm{GN}}(x):=J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)\succeq0\). An unconstrained model minimizer satisfies the normal equations \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)d=-J(x)^{\mathsf T}r(x)\), whenever they are solvable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic model obtained by linearizing the residual and squaring its norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton local model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be differentiable, let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\), and fix \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth ordinary nonlinear least squares; this defines the local model and step, not a globalized algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Gauss–Newton model at \(x\) is the squared norm of the affine residual approximation, \(m_x^{GN}(s):=\tfrac12\|R(x)+J(x)s\|_2^2\). Expanded as a quadratic, it is \(f(x)+[J(x)^TR(x)]^Ts+\tfrac12s^TJ(x)^TJ(x)s\). A Gauss–Newton step is any minimizer of this linear least-squares model. It therefore satisfies the normal equations \(J(x)^TJ(x)s=-J(x)^TR(x)\). If \(J(x)\) has full column rank, the step is unique and equals \(-[J(x)^TJ(x)]^{-1}J(x)^TR(x)\); otherwise a designated minimum-norm step is \(-J(x)^\dagger R(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gauss–Newton model squares the affine approximation of the residual. Its gradient term matches the true least-squares gradient, while its curvature matrix is the positive-semidefinite matrix formed from the Jacobian. A Gauss–Newton step minimizes this linearized residual norm. Full column rank makes the step unique; otherwise a pseudoinverse can select the minimum-norm step.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(s_{GN}\) solves \(J^TJs=-J^TR\).
When \(J\) has full column rank, \(s_{GN}=-(J^TJ)^{-1}J^TR\).
special_cases_latex: For a square nonsingular \(J\), \(s_{GN}=-J^{-1}R\), the Newton step for the residual equation.
For affine \(R\), one Gauss–Newton model is the exact least-squares objective up to the step parameterization.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Gauss–Newton curvature \(J^TJ\) is always positive semidefinite.
At zero residual, the Gauss–Newton curvature equals the exact least-squares Hessian.
boundary_notes: Normal equations can worsen numerical conditioning and need not be the preferred computational representation.
Without rank or regularization, the model minimizer may be nonunique.

notation.meaning: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the residual Jacobian

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Univariate Reduction of the Euclidean Regularized Residual Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduces the Euclidean auxiliary Gauss–Newton model to scalar convex optimization and reconstructs its minimizing step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lVert x\rVert^2=\langle B_1x,x\rangle\) and \(\lVert u\rVert^2=\langle B_2u,u\rangle\), where \(B_1=B_1^*\succ0\) and \(B_2=B_2^*\succ0\), and let \(M>0\). Put \(g:=F'(x)^*B_2F(x)\). Then the regularized linearized-residual value satisfies \[f_M(x)=\min_{\tau\geq0}\left\{\tau+\frac{\lVert F(x)\rVert^2}{\tau}-\left\langle[\tau F'(x)^*B_2F'(x)+\tau^2MB_1]^{-1}g,g\right\rangle\right\},\] where the displayed expression is evaluated for \(\tau>0\) and any admissible \(\tau=0\) boundary value is understood by its limiting extension. If \(\tau^*\) is optimal, a minimizing step is \[h^*=-[F'(x)^*B_2F'(x)+\tau^*MB_1]^{-1}F'(x)^*B_2F(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive-definite Euclidean metrics, the regularized linearized-residual subproblem reduces to a one-dimensional convex minimization in tau. An optimal tau determines the primal step through one shifted normal-equation solve.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic accuracy of the composite Gauss–Newton model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the difference between the merit objective and its affine-residual composite model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(y)=\phi(F(y)) and \psi(x;y)=\phi\bigl(F(x)+F'(x)(y-x)\bigr). Assume the sharp merit function and smoothness hypotheses used to define these functions, including an L-Lipschitz derivative of F on \mathcal F. Then, for every x,y\in\mathcal F, \bigl|f(y)-\psi(x;y)\bigr|\le \tfrac12L\|y-x\|^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated sharp-merit and Lipschitz-derivative assumptions, the composite Gauss–Newton model approximates the true merit objective with an error bounded quadratically in the step length.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Form of the Regularized Linearized-Residual Subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A primal-dual representation of the auxiliary model used by the modified Gauss–Newton scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\) and \(M>0\), and define \(f_M(x):=\min_{h\in\mathbb E_1}\{\lVert F(x)+F'(x)h\rVert+\tfrac12M\lVert h\rVert^2\}\). With the dual norm on \(\mathbb E_2^*\) and the adjoint \(F'(x)^*\), this value has the representation \[f_M(x)=\max_{\substack{s\in\mathbb E_2^*\\ \lVert s\rVert_*\leq1}}\left\{\langle s,F(x)\rangle-\frac{1}{2M}\lVert F'(x)^*s\rVert_*^2\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularized linearized-residual subproblem equals a maximization over the dual unit ball of the residual pairing minus a quadratic adjoint penalty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal and Dual Nondegeneracy of a Linear Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions based respectively on the smallest singular values of an operator and its adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2$ be linear between finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let $A^*:\mathbb E_2\to\mathbb E_1$ be its adjoint, and define $\sigma_{\min}(B):=\min_{\|x\|=1}\|Bx\|$ over the domain of $B$. The operator $A$ is primal nondegenerate if $\sigma_{\min}(A)>0$ and dual nondegenerate if $\sigma_{\min}(A^*)>0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear operator is primal nondegenerate when its smallest singular value is positive and dual nondegenerate when the smallest singular value of its adjoint is positive.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E_1,\mathbb E_2\text{ are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces}
A^*:\mathbb E_2\to\mathbb E_1\text{ is the adjoint of }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is primal nondegenerate}\iff\sigma_{\min}(A)>0,\qquad A\text{ is dual nondegenerate}\iff\sigma_{\min}(A^*)>0

knowledge_statements.title: Full Second-Order Residual Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact least-squares Hessian equals the Gauss–Newton matrix plus a residual-weighted curvature term, which vanishes at exact roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each \(r_i:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable and let \(f(x):= rac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2\). Then the exact Hessian decomposes as \[
abla^2 f(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)
abla^2 r_i(x).\] The first term is the Gauss–Newton matrix; the second is the residual-curvature correction. At every exact root \(r(x)=0\), the correction vanishes and \(
abla^2 f(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)\succeq0\).
assumptions_latex: \(r_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice continuously differentiable for each \(i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Hessian decomposition for twice-differentiable nonlinear least squares.

notation.meaning: Hessian of the i-th scalar residual

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact second-order decomposition for squared residuals
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice continuously differentiable and \(f(x)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Twice-smooth ordinary nonlinear least squares in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The full second-order residual structure at \(x\in U\) is the exact Hessian decomposition \(
abla^2f(x)=G(x)+S(x)\), where \(G(x):=J(x)^TJ(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m
abla r_i(x)
abla r_i(x)^T\) is the Gauss–Newton term and \(S(x):=\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)
abla^2r_i(x)\) is the residual-weighted curvature term. The full Newton quadratic model is \(q_x(s)=f(x)+[J(x)^TR(x)]^Ts+	frac12s^T[G(x)+S(x)]s\). This structure separates curvature arising from first-order variation of the residuals from curvature arising from their component nonlinearities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact Hessian of a squared-residual objective is the sum of the Jacobian Gram matrix and a residual-weighted sum of the individual residual Hessians. The first term is always positive semidefinite. The second carries the omitted nonlinear curvature and can be indefinite. Full Newton modeling retains both terms.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every direction \(d\), \(d^T\nabla^2f(x)d=\|J(x)d\|_2^2+\sum_i r_i(x)d^T\nabla^2r_i(x)d\).
The Gauss–Newton approximation is obtained by setting \(S(x)=0\) in the exact model.
special_cases_latex: If all residual components are affine, then \(S(x)=0\) everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: Unlike \(J^TJ\), the full Hessian need not be positive semidefinite away from a minimizer.
Large residual or strongly curved components can make the correction \(S(x)\) significant.
boundary_notes: For weighted least squares with constant \(W\), the analogous formulas contain \(W\); parameter-dependent weights add further derivatives.
Twice differentiability is essential for this classical Hessian formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Roots versus Stationary Nonroots
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every exact root is stationary and globally optimal, but a stationary point may retain nonzero residual unless the Jacobian has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For differentiable \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(f(x)=\frac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\), every root \(r(x)=0\) is stationary and is a global minimizer with \(f(x)=0\). The converse need not hold: a stationary nonroot satisfies \[r(x)\ne0,\qquad J(x)^{\mathsf T}r(x)=0.\] Such a point can occur only when the nonzero residual lies in \(\ker J(x)^{\mathsf T}\). In particular, if \(J(x)\) has full row rank, stationarity at \(x\) implies \(r(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between exact residual roots and nonzero stationary least-squares points.

notation.meaning: left nullspace of the residual Jacobian

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Root and stationary-nonroot partition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable and let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained nonlinear least squares; the classification concerns first-order stationary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A root is a point \(x_*\in U\) with \(R(x_*)=0\). A stationary nonroot is a point \(x_*\in U\) satisfying \(J(x_*)^TR(x_*)=0\) and \(R(x_*)\ne0\). Hence the stationary set \(\mathcal S:=\{x\in U:J(x)^TR(x)=0\}\) is the disjoint union \(\mathcal S=Z\,\dot\cup\,N\), where \(Z:=\{x:R(x)=0\}\) and \(N:=\{x:J(x)^TR(x)=0,\ R(x)\ne0\}\). At a stationary nonroot, the nonzero residual lies in \(\ker J(x_*)^T\), so no infinitesimal parameter displacement decreases the objective to first order even though the original equations remain unsatisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Roots have zero residual and are automatically stationary for the squared-residual objective. Stationary nonroots have a nonzero residual that is orthogonal to the Jacobian range. The stationary set therefore splits into exact roots and nonroot critical points. This distinction prevents a small least-squares gradient from being misread as a small equation residual.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x_*\in N\iff 0\ne R(x_*)\in(\operatorname{range}J(x_*))^\perp\).
If \(J(x_*)\) has full row rank, then stationarity implies root status, so \(N\) is empty locally at such points.
special_cases_latex: In an inconsistent overdetermined fit, a least-squares minimizer is typically a stationary nonroot.
At a zero-residual solution, both the equation residual and stationarity residual vanish.
immediate_consequences_latex: Stopping solely on \(\|J^TR\|\) certifies stationarity, not equation satisfaction.
A root is a global least-squares minimizer, whereas a stationary nonroot may be a minimum, saddle, or maximum.
boundary_notes: The partition excludes constrained stationary conditions at the boundary of a feasible set.
Nonsmooth robust losses require a different stationarity mapping.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual dimension and Jacobian-rank regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be differentiable and let \(J(x)=DR(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares and residual equations classified pointwise by dimensions and Jacobian rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The residual-dimension regime is overdetermined when \(m>n\), square when \(m=n\), and underdetermined when \(m<n\). At a point \(x\), the Jacobian is maximal rank when \(\operatorname{rank}J(x)=\min\{m,n\}\), and rank deficient otherwise. Thus maximal rank means full column rank in the overdetermined case, nonsingularity in the square case, and full row rank in the underdetermined case. The Gauss–Newton matrix \(J(x)^TJ(x)\) is positive definite exactly when \(J(x)\) has full column rank; consequently an unregularized Gauss–Newton step is uniquely determined by the normal equations in the overdetermined full-column-rank regime, but not generally in an underdetermined regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual systems are overdetermined, square, or underdetermined according to the number of residuals relative to the number of variables. Maximal Jacobian rank means full column rank, nonsingularity, or full row rank in those three cases. Rank deficiency changes local identifiability and whether the Gauss–Newton normal equations determine a unique step.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(J\) has full column rank \(\iff J^TJ\succ0\).
\(J\) has full row rank \(\iff JJ^T\succ0\).
special_cases_latex: At a square maximal-rank root, \(J^{-1}\) exists.
For \(m<n\) and full row rank, \(\dim\ker J=n-m\), giving undetermined linearized directions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Rank deficiency makes \(J^TJ\) singular.
In an overdetermined system, full column rank does not imply that a zero residual exists.
boundary_notes: The rank regime is pointwise and may change with \(x\).
Numerical rank requires a tolerance and can differ from exact algebraic rank.
Residual magnitude and Jacobian rank are independent classifications.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-magnitude regimes at least-squares stationary points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be a residual map, let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\), and let \(S=\{x\in D:J(x)^Tr(x)=0\}\), where \(J(x)=Dr(x)\). Fix a scale \(s>0\) and dimensionless thresholds \(0\leq\tau_0<\tau_1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a finite-dimensional classification by the scaled residual norm at a stationary point. It does not assert that the thresholds are universal or that residual magnitude alone determines conditioning or convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[S_0=\{x\in S:\|r(x)\|_2=0\},\qquad S_{\mathrm{small}}=\{x\in S:0<\|r(x)\|_2/s\leq\tau_0\},\qquad S_{\mathrm{moderate}}=\{x\in S:\tau_0<\|r(x)\|_2/s\leq\tau_1\},\qquad S_{\mathrm{large}}=\{x\in S:\|r(x)\|_2/s>\tau_1\}.\] The residual-magnitude regime family is the threshold-indexed partition \(\mathcal R(s,\tau_0,\tau_1)=\{S_0,S_{\mathrm{small}},S_{\mathrm{moderate}},S_{\mathrm{large}}\}\), after empty members are discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonlinear least-squares residual, choose a positive residual scale and two ordered dimensionless thresholds. Stationary points are classified as zero-, small-, moderate-, or large-residual points according to the scaled Euclidean norm of their residual. The family consists of the resulting threshold-indexed classes, with empty classes omitted.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(r:D\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(r\) is differentiable at every point being classified.
Only stationary points satisfying \(J(x)^Tr(x)=0\) belong to the classified set \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(\rho(x)=\|r(x)\|_2/s\), the four regimes are respectively \(\rho=0\), \(0<\rho\leq\tau_0\), \(\tau_0<\rho\leq\tau_1\), and \(\rho>\tau_1\).
special_cases_latex: If data and residuals are already dimensionless, one may take \(s=1\).
For an exact-fit solution \(x_*\), \(r(x_*)=0\), so \(x_*\in S_0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing \(s\) or either threshold can change a point's regime without changing the least-squares problem.
Every classified stationary point has exactly one regime because the defining scalar intervals are disjoint and exhaustive.
boundary_notes: There is no problem-independent numerical boundary separating small from large residuals; the scale and thresholds are part of this definition.
Residual magnitude is distinct from Jacobian rank, parameter identifiability, and the size of the second-order term \(\sum_i r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x)\).

notation.meaning: Positive reference scale for residual magnitude.

review_flags: No inspected authoritative source was available for the threshold-based regime terminology or its precise normalization.
The thresholds are explicitly definition parameters rather than claimed universal constants.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-magnitude regimes at least-squares stationary points
Zero-Residual Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero-residual regime consists of exact fits. Every exact fit globally minimizes the sum of squares; if the residual map is differentiable on a neighborhood of the point, the objective gradient is zero there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, let \(r:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^m\), and define \(F(x)=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)\rVert_2^2\). A point \(x_*\in\mathcal D\) is in the zero-residual regime precisely when \(r(x_*)=0\). Consequently, \(F(x_*)=0=\inf_{x\in\mathcal D}F(x)\), so \(x_*\) is a global least-squares minimizer. If \(\mathcal D\) contains an open neighborhood of \(x_*\) and \(r\) is differentiable at \(x_*\), then \(\nabla F(x_*)=J(x_*)^{\mathsf T}r(x_*)=0\), independently of the rank of \(J(x_*)\).
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and \(x_*\in\mathcal D\).
For the gradient conclusion, \(\mathcal D\) contains an open neighborhood of \(x_*\) and \(r\) is differentiable at \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r(x_*)=0\Longrightarrow F(x_*)=0=\inf_{x\in\mathcal D}F(x)\), and the stated differentiability assumptions imply \(\nabla F(x_*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-fit regime for a finite-dimensional nonlinear least-squares problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual is small only relative to a declared scale and tolerance. When the residual components are twice differentiable, the displayed estimate bounds the absolute error in the Gauss–Newton Hessian approximation; relative accuracy requires additional comparison with the Gauss–Newton term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(x\in\mathcal D\), define \(F(x)=	frac12\lVert r(x)Vert_2^2\), choose a residual scale \(ho>0\), and fix a dimensionless tolerance \(0<\varepsilon<1\). The point \(x\) lies in the \((\varepsilon,ho)\)-small-residual regime when \(0<\lVert r(x)Vert_2\leq\varepsilonho\). If \(\mathcal D\) contains an open neighborhood of \(x\) and \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)\) is twice differentiable at \(x\), then \(
abla^2F(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)
