abla^2F(x)-J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x) igrVert_2\leq\varepsilonho igl(\sum_{i=1}^m\lVert
abla^2r_i(x)Vert_2^2 igr)^{1/2}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Regime Transition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual-regime transition is a boundary parameter where a continuous normalized residual leaves zero or takes values on both sides of one explicitly declared regime threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\subseteq\mathbb R\) be an interval, let \(r:\mathcal D\times T\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(x:T\to\mathcal D\) be continuous, let \(\rho:T\to(0,\infty)\) be continuous, and define \(q(t)=\lVert r(x(t),t)\rVert_2/\rho(t)\). Fix thresholds \(0<\varepsilon_s<\varepsilon_\ell\). A zero-to-nonzero transition occurs at \(t_0\in T\) when \(q(t_0)=0\) and every neighborhood of \(t_0\) in \(T\) contains a point \(t\) with \(q(t)>0\). For \(\tau\in\{\varepsilon_s,\varepsilon_\ell\}\), a threshold-crossing transition occurs at \(t_0\) when \(q(t_0)=\tau\) and every neighborhood of \(t_0\) in \(T\) contains points \(t_-\) and \(t_+\) such that \(q(t_-)<\tau<q(t_+)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A transition point lies on the boundary of \(\{t:q(t)=0\}\) or is a crossing point of a level set \(\{t:q(t)=\tau\}\) for some \(\tau\in\{\varepsilon_s,\varepsilon_\ell\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary crossings along a continuous family of residual problems or iterates.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: regime boundaries are defined by normalized residual level sets

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Residual Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual is large relative to a declared scale. In this regime, residual-weighted second derivatives may materially affect the least-squares Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)\rVert_2^2\), choose a scale \(\rho>0\), and fix a threshold \(\varepsilon_\ell>0\). A point \(x\in\mathcal D\) lies in the \((\varepsilon_\ell,\rho)\)-large-residual regime when \(\lVert r(x)\rVert_2\geq\varepsilon_\ell\rho\). If \(r\) is twice differentiable, then \(\nabla^2F(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)+S(x)\), where \(S(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x)\). Residual magnitude alone supplies no bound making \(S(x)\) negligible relative to \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)\); such a conclusion requires additional curvature information.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is twice differentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert r(x)\rVert_2\geq\varepsilon_\ell\rho\), and neglect of \(S(x)\) is not justified by residual magnitude alone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-relative regime where residual-weighted curvature cannot generally be neglected.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Large-residual nonlinear least-squares regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice differentiable near a stationary point \(x_*\) of \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\). Let \(J=Dr\), choose a residual scale \(s>0\), and fix a dimensionless threshold \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns residual magnitude at a specified stationary point in finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares. It does not by itself impose Jacobian rank or second-order sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[x_*\text{ is in the large-residual regime relative to }(s,\tau)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad J(x_*)^Tr(x_*)=0\ \text{ and }\ \|r(x_*)\|_2>\tau s.\] The corresponding regime set is \(S_{\mathrm L}(s,\tau)=\{x\in D:J(x)^Tr(x)=0,\ \|r(x)\|_2>\tau s\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary point of a nonlinear least-squares objective is in the large-residual regime, relative to a declared positive scale and threshold, exactly when its residual norm exceeds the threshold times that scale. The regime set contains all and only stationary points satisfying this strict inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) is differentiable at each classified point so that \(J(x)^Tr(x)\) is defined.
\(s>0\) is expressed in the same units as \(\|r(x)\|_2\), and \(\tau>0\) is dimensionless.
The designation is made only after the stationary-point condition \(J(x_*)^Tr(x_*)=0\) has been imposed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(\rho(x)=\|r(x)\|_2/s\), the large-residual condition is \(\rho(x_*)>\tau\).
special_cases_latex: For \(s=1\), the condition reduces to \(\|r(x_*)\|_2>\tau\).
An exact-fit stationary point with \(r(x_*)=0\) never belongs to \(S_{\mathrm L}(s,\tau)\) for \(s,\tau>0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The large-residual regime is monotone in the threshold: if \(0<\tau_1\leq\tau_2\), then \(S_{\mathrm L}(s,\tau_2)\subseteq S_{\mathrm L}(s,\tau_1)\).
Multiplying both \(r\) and \(s\) by the same positive scalar leaves the classification unchanged.
boundary_notes: A large residual need not imply that \(J(x_*)\) is rank deficient or that \(x_*\) is not a local minimizer.
The strict boundary \(\|r(x_*)\|_2=\tau s\) is excluded; another convention must be declared if boundary points are to be included.

notation.meaning: Set of stationary points classified as large residual.

review_flags: No inspected source established a canonical numerical threshold for the phrase large residual.
The record therefore makes the scale and threshold explicit parameters of the definition.

Residual magnitude alone supplies no bound making \(S(x)\) negligible relative to \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)\); such a conclusion requires additional curvature information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual is large relative to a declared scale. In this regime, residual-weighted second derivatives may materially affect the least-squares Hessian.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is twice differentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert r(x)\rVert_2\geq\varepsilon_\ell\rho\), and neglect of \(S(x)\) is not justified by residual magnitude alone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobian-rank regimes of a residual map
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be differentiable and let \(J(x)=Dr(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Let \(S\subseteq D\) be the set of points under consideration, such as the stationary points of \(\tfrac12\|r\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a pointwise finite-dimensional rank classification. Numerical rank based on singular-value tolerances is a separate, implementation-dependent variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[S_k=\{x\in S:\operatorname{rank}J(x)=k\},\qquad 0\leq k\leq\min\{m,n\}.\] The Jacobian rank regime family is \(\mathcal J(S)=\{S_k:0\leq k\leq\min(m,n)\}\). Its named subfamilies are the full-column-rank regime \(S_n\) when \(m\geq n\), the full-row-rank regime \(S_m\) when \(m\leq n\), and the rank-deficient regime \(S_{\mathrm{def}}=\{x\in S:\operatorname{rank}J(x)<\min(m,n)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Jacobian-rank regime family partitions a chosen set of residual-map points by the exact algebraic rank of the Jacobian. Full column rank, full row rank, and rank deficiency are named unions or members of this rank-indexed family, depending on the dimensions of the residual and parameter spaces.
assumptions_latex: The dimensions \(m\) and \(n\) are finite and fixed.
Rank means exact linear-algebraic rank, not a floating-point estimate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in S_k\) if and only if \(J(x)\) has exactly \(k\) positive singular values.
For \(m\geq n\), \(x\in S_n\) if and only if \(J(x)^TJ(x)\) is positive definite.
For \(m\leq n\), \(x\in S_m\) if and only if \(J(x)J(x)^T\) is positive definite.
special_cases_latex: For a square residual system \(m=n\), full row rank and full column rank both mean that \(J(x)\) is nonsingular.
If \(J(x)=0\), then \(x\in S_0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: At a full-column-rank point, \(J(x)^TJ(x)\) is invertible.
At a rank-deficient point, at least one nonzero parameter direction lies in \(\ker J(x)\) when \(\operatorname{rank}J(x)<n\).
boundary_notes: Exact rank regimes can be unstable under perturbations near a small nonzero singular value.
Rank classification alone neither establishes local identifiability nor determines the residual-magnitude regime.

notation.meaning: Points whose residual Jacobian has rank exactly k.
Jacobian rank regime family on S.

knowledge_statements.title: Jacobian-rank regimes of a residual map
Full-Rank Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is full rank when its Jacobian has independent columns. Its Gauss–Newton matrix is then positive definite and its step is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable residual map \(r:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) with \(m\geq n\), the model is full rank at \(x\in\mathcal D\) when \(\operatorname{rank}J(x)=n\), equivalently \(\ker J(x)=\{0\}\). Then \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)\) is symmetric positive definite, the Gauss--Newton equation \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)p=-J(x)^{\mathsf T}r(x)\) has a unique solution, and the linearized residual model has no nonzero parameter direction invisible to first order.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is differentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}J(x)=n\Longleftrightarrow J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)\succ0\), yielding a unique Gauss--Newton step.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-column-rank residual Jacobians in overdetermined or square least squares.

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.1 Least-Squares Problems p. 68

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-deficient model has nonzero parameter directions invisible to the linearized residual; its Gauss–Newton matrix is singular and ordinary normal-equation steps are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable residual map \(r:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), the model is column-rank deficient at \(x\in\mathcal D\) when \(\operatorname{rank}J(x)<n\), equivalently when some \(d\neq0\) satisfies \(J(x)d=0\). In that case \(J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)\) is positive semidefinite and singular. If the Gauss--Newton normal equations are consistent, their solutions are nonunique up to addition of vectors in \(\ker J(x)\); the Moore--Penrose solution \(p=-J(x)^\dagger r(x)\) is the unique solution of minimum Euclidean norm.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is differentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual models possessing first-order invisible parameter directions.

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 Linear Least-Squares Problems p. 106

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Loss Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank loss occurs where the smallest singular value reaches zero at the boundary of full rank, causing the Gauss–Newton system to become singular or ill-conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J:T\to\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be continuous with \(m\geq n\). A parameter \(t_0\in T\) is a rank-loss transition when \(\operatorname{rank}J(t_0)<n\) and every neighborhood of \(t_0\) contains some \(t\) with \(\operatorname{rank}J(t)=n\). Equivalently, \(\sigma_{\min}(J(t_0))=0\) while arbitrarily nearby full-rank points have \(\sigma_{\min}(J(t))>0\). Along any sequence of such full-rank points converging to \(t_0\), the condition number of \(J(t)^{\mathsf T}J(t)\) diverges whenever \(\sigma_{\max}(J(t))\) stays bounded away from zero.
assumptions_latex: \(J:T\to\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is continuous and \(m\geq n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where a continuously varying residual Jacobian loses column rank.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local and infinitesimal parameter-identifiability regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a parameter domain and let \(M:P\to\mathcal Y\) be a model-output map into a metric observation space \(\mathcal Y\). For data \(y\), a residual representation may be \(r(x)=M(x)-y\) when \(\mathcal Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The principal notion is deterministic local structural identifiability. Statistical identifiability of probability laws and practical identifiability under noisy finite data are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[x_*\text{ is locally identifiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists\text{ a neighborhood }U\subseteq P\text{ of }x_*:\ M^{-1}(M(x_*))\cap U=\{x_*\}.\] It is locally nonidentifiable when every neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\) contains some \(x\neq x_*\) with \(M(x)=M(x_*)\). If \(M\) is differentiable, \(x_*\) is infinitesimally identifiable when \(\ker DM(x_*)=\{0\}\). These three predicates form the local, nonidentifiable, and differential regimes of the parameter-identifiability family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter is locally identifiable when no distinct nearby parameter produces exactly the same model output. It is locally nonidentifiable when observationally equivalent parameters occur arbitrarily close to it. For differentiable models, infinitesimal identifiability means that the model derivative has no nonzero null direction.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) carries the relative Euclidean topology.
Equality in \(\mathcal Y\) represents exact observational equivalence.
The infinitesimal regime is used only when \(M\) is differentiable at \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal I_{\mathrm{loc}}=\{x_*\in P:\exists U\ni x_*,\ M^{-1}(M(x_*))\cap U=\{x_*\}\},\qquad \mathcal I_{\mathrm{inf}}=\{x_*\in P:\ker DM(x_*)=\{0\}\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Local identifiability is equivalent to the restriction of \(M\) to some neighborhood of \(x_*\) having singleton fiber at \(M(x_*)\).
For \(M:P\to\mathbb R^m\), infinitesimal identifiability is equivalent to \(DM(x_*)\) having full column rank \(n\).
special_cases_latex: If \(M\) is injective on all of \(P\), every parameter is locally identifiable.
For a linear model \(M(x)=Ax\), all parameters are identifiable exactly when \(\ker A=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonzero vector in \(\ker DM(x_*)\) is an infinitesimally unobservable parameter direction.
Local identifiability depends on the model-output map and parameter domain, not on a particular optimization algorithm.
boundary_notes: Full column rank is not asserted here to be equivalent to local identifiability without additional regularity and dimension hypotheses.
Discrete symmetries can destroy global identifiability while preserving local identifiability away from symmetry-fixed points.
review_flags: No inspected source supported the exact three-regime taxonomy.
The distinction between local structural and infinitesimal identifiability requires source verification.
knowledge_statements.title: Local and infinitesimal parameter-identifiability regimes
Identifiable Parameterizations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameters are locally identifiable when no distinct nearby parameter gives the same residual map value. Full column rank is a sufficient local differential condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r:\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\). A parameterization is locally identifiable at \(\theta_*\in\Theta\) when there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\theta_*\) such that \(r(\theta)=r(\theta_*)\) and \(\theta\in U\) imply \(\theta=\theta_*\). It is globally identifiable on \(\Theta\) when this implication holds for every pair in \(\Theta\). If \(r\) is continuously differentiable near \(\theta_*\) and \(J(\theta_*)\) has full column rank, then the parameterization is locally identifiable at \(\theta_*\).
assumptions_latex: For the rank criterion, \(r\) is continuously differentiable near \(\theta_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local structural identifiability from the residual or prediction map.

An identifiability-specific source with a definition or theorem locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonidentifiable Parameterizations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterization is locally nonidentifiable when distinct, arbitrarily nearby parameters produce the same residual. Exact symmetry curves necessarily create Jacobian null directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r:\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\). The parameterization is locally nonidentifiable at \(\theta_*\in\Theta\) when every neighborhood \(U\) of \(\theta_*\) contains some \(\theta\neq\theta_*\) satisfying \(r(\theta)=r(\theta_*)\). If a differentiable curve \(\gamma:(-\delta,\delta)\to\Theta\) satisfies \(\gamma(0)=\theta_*\), \(\gamma'(0)\neq0\), and \(r(\gamma(s))=r(\theta_*)\) for all \(s\), then the parameterization is locally nonidentifiable and \(J(\theta_*)\gamma'(0)=0\). Thus exact parameter symmetries generate Jacobian null directions.
assumptions_latex: For the curve criterion, \(r\) and \(\gamma\) are differentiable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local nonuniqueness of parameters producing the same residual or prediction.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition and symmetry-curve implication are mathematically plausible and internally consistent, but the cited generic least-squares chapter has not been shown to support local nonidentifiability or the exact-symmetry criterion. Supply an identifiability-specific definition or theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Identifiability Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An identifiability transition occurs when the parameter-to-residual Jacobian loses full column rank. This removes a sufficient local criterion but does not alone prove nonidentifiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_t:\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable in \(\theta\), and let \(\theta:T\to\Theta\) be continuous. Write \(J(t)=D_\theta r_t(\theta(t))\). A differential-identifiability transition occurs at \(t_0\) when \(\operatorname{rank}J(t_0)<n\) and every neighborhood of \(t_0\) contains a \(t\) with \(\operatorname{rank}J(t)=n\). Equivalently, the smallest singular value reaches zero at \(t_0\) from positive nearby values. This marks loss of the full-rank sufficient condition for local identifiability, but does not by itself establish structural nonidentifiability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\min}(J(t_0))=0\) at the boundary of the full-column-rank regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential-identifiability boundary along a parameterized family of residual maps.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The record carefully limits the claim to loss of a differential sufficient condition and correctly avoids inferring structural nonidentifiability. However, the cited linear least-squares section has not been shown to support the interpretation as an identifiability transition. A source connecting Jacobian rank to differential identifiability, with a specific locator, is needed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structured factorization of a residual map
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(r:D\to\mathbb R^m\), and choose intermediate spaces \(Z_i\), parameter-extraction maps \(E_i:D\to Z_i\), and component maps \(\rho_i:Z_i\to\mathbb R^{m_i}\), where \(\sum_{i=1}^q m_i=m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition records an exact mathematical factorization of a residual. It covers separability, block dependence, shared features, and composed operators, but it does not prescribe storage or an evaluation algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[r(x)=\bigl(\rho_1(E_1x),\ldots,\rho_q(E_qx)\bigr),\qquad x\in D.\] A structured residual parameterization is the tuple \(\mathfrak P=(\{Z_i,E_i,\rho_i\}_{i=1}^q,\Pi)\), where \(\Pi\) is a fixed assembly map identifying \(\prod_i\mathbb R^{m_i}\) with \(\mathbb R^m\), such that \(r=\Pi\circ(\rho_1\circ E_1,\ldots,\rho_q\circ E_q)\) on all of \(D\). The structure is nontrivial when at least one \(E_i\) omits a parameter direction or two components share a declared intermediate quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual has a structured parameterization when it is represented exactly as an assembly of component residuals, each acting on a declared extraction or feature map of the full parameter. The parameterization includes the intermediate spaces, extraction maps, component maps, and assembly rule; it is not merely an informal observation about the formula.
assumptions_latex: Every composition \(\rho_i\circ E_i\) is defined on \(D\).
The assembly map \(\Pi\) and all dependencies are fixed as part of the representation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(E(x)=(E_1x,\ldots,E_qx)\) and \(\rho(z_1,\ldots,z_q)=\Pi(\rho_1(z_1),\ldots,\rho_q(z_q))\), the representation is \(r=\rho\circ E\).
special_cases_latex: If each \(E_i\) selects a coordinate block, the parameterization is block structured.
If \(r(x)=A(\alpha)c-b\) with \(x=(\alpha,c)\), the residual separates nonlinear parameters \(\alpha\) from linear parameters \(c\).
immediate_consequences_latex: When differentiable, the Jacobian factors componentwise as \(D(\rho_i\circ E_i)(x)=D\rho_i(E_ix)DE_i(x)\).
The declared dependency maps determine which parameter directions can influence each residual block.
boundary_notes: An arbitrary identity factorization \(r=r\circ I\) is formally valid but is excluded by the stated nontriviality convention.
Approximate low-rank, surrogate, or compressed representations are not exact structured parameterizations unless their approximation status is added explicitly.

notation.meaning: Parameter extraction or feature map for component i.

knowledge_statements.title: Separable Nonlinear Least Squares
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear parameters can be eliminated exactly by least squares, leaving a reduced nonlinear problem whose residual is the projection of the data onto the orthogonal complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A separable nonlinear least-squares problem has the form \(\min_{a\in\mathbb R^p,\,y\in Y}\tfrac12\lVert A(y)a-b\rVert_2^2\), where dependence on \(a\) is linear and dependence on \(y\) may be nonlinear. For each \(y\), the minimum-norm linear least-squares solution is \(a(y)=A(y)^\dagger b\). Eliminating \(a\) gives the reduced problem \(\min_{y\in Y}\tfrac12\lVert (I-A(y)A(y)^\dagger)b\rVert_2^2\). If \(A(y)\) has locally constant rank, then the projector and reduced residual vary continuously; under suitable smoothness they are differentiable.
assumptions_latex: For regularity of the reduced map, \(A\) is smooth and has locally constant rank.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-projection representation with linear and nonlinear parameter blocks.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The elimination formula, pseudoinverse solution, reduced projector residual, and constant-rank regularity qualification are mathematically appropriate for separable nonlinear least squares. The cited general projections section has not been shown to cover variable projection or the stated regularity claim; a separable nonlinear least-squares or variable-projection source with a precise locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separable nonlinear least-squares problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^{m\times q}\) be a matrix-valued nonlinear map, let \(b:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R^m\), and let the unknown be \((\alpha,c)\in\mathcal A\times\mathbb R^q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is unconstrained finite-dimensional separable nonlinear least squares with parameters \(c\) entering linearly and parameters \(\alpha\) entering nonlinearly. Constraints or regularizers require a modified inner problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\min_{\alpha\in\mathcal A,\ c\in\mathbb R^q}\Phi(\alpha,c),\qquad \Phi(\alpha,c)=\tfrac12\|A(\alpha)c-b(\alpha)\|_2^2.\] The problem is separable nonlinear least squares because, for each fixed \(\alpha\), the inner minimization over \(c\) is linear least squares. Its reduced value function and coefficient solution set are \[\phi(\alpha)=\min_c\Phi(\alpha,c),\qquad C(\alpha)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathbb R^q}\|A(\alpha)c-b(\alpha)\|_2^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear least-squares problem is separable when its unknowns split into nonlinear parameters and linear coefficients, and the residual is affine in the linear coefficients for every fixed nonlinear parameter. Eliminating the linear coefficients defines a reduced objective over the nonlinear parameters and a possibly set-valued inner least-squares solution map.
assumptions_latex: \(A(\alpha)\in\mathbb R^{m\times q}\) and \(b(\alpha)\in\mathbb R^m\) are defined for every \(\alpha\in\mathcal A\).
The coefficient domain is \(\mathbb R^q\), so the inner problem is ordinary unconstrained linear least squares.
No uniqueness of \(C(\alpha)\) is assumed unless \(A(\alpha)\) has full column rank.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the Moore–Penrose inverse, \(C(\alpha)=A(\alpha)^\dagger b(\alpha)+\ker A(\alpha)\).
The reduced value is \(\phi(\alpha)=\tfrac12\|(I-A(\alpha)A(\alpha)^\dagger)b(\alpha)\|_2^2\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A(\alpha)\) has full column rank, the unique inner solution is \(c(\alpha)=(A(\alpha)^TA(\alpha))^{-1}A(\alpha)^Tb(\alpha)\).
A sum of exponentials fitted with unknown amplitudes and nonlinear decay rates has this form when the amplitudes comprise \(c\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Any global minimizer \((\alpha_*,c_*)\) satisfies \(c_*\in C(\alpha_*)\).
Rank loss in \(A(\alpha)\) can make the coefficient solution map set-valued even though the reduced value remains well defined.
boundary_notes: If both parameter blocks enter nonlinearly, the problem is not separable in this sense.
Penalized or constrained coefficients lead to a generalized variable-elimination model rather than the unmodified linear least-squares inner problem.

notation.meaning: Reduced least-squares value after eliminating c.

review_flags: The formulation is standard, but the supplied source hints were not inspected and therefore cannot support a citation.
The pseudoinverse formulations require locator-level verification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse block-dependency representation of residual systems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Partition \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\) with \(x_j\in\mathbb R^{n_j}\), and partition \(r(x)=(r_1(x),\ldots,r_q(x))\) with \(r_i(x)\in\mathbb R^{m_i}\). Let \(G\subseteq\{1,\ldots,q\}\times\{1,\ldots,p\}\) be a bipartite dependency relation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns exact structural block sparsity of a finite-dimensional residual and its Jacobian. Accidental numerical zeros at an individual evaluation point do not define the structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[r_i(x)=\widehat r_i\bigl((x_j)_{j\in N(i)}\bigr),\qquad N(i)=\{j:(i,j)\in G\}.\] The tuple \((\{x_j\},\{r_i\},G,\{\widehat r_i\})\) is a sparse block-structure representation when this equality holds for every \(x\) in the domain and \(|G|<pq\). If the component maps are differentiable, the structural condition is \[\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial x_j}(x)=0\quad\text{for every }x\text{ whenever }(i,j)\notin G.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual has a sparse block-structure representation when its parameters and residuals are partitioned into blocks and each residual block depends only on a declared proper subset of parameter blocks. The bipartite dependency graph is part of the representation, and missing edges require identically zero cross-block derivatives wherever differentiability holds.
assumptions_latex: The parameter and residual block partitions are fixed and cover all coordinates.
Each local map \(\widehat r_i\) is defined on the product of the parameter blocks indexed by \(N(i)\).
Sparsity means \(|G|<pq\); the complete bipartite dependency graph is excluded.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The dependency graph \(G\) is the structural block-sparsity pattern of the Jacobian.
For coordinate-sized blocks, the definition reduces to a structurally sparse scalar Jacobian pattern.
special_cases_latex: If each \(N(i)\) contains one parameter-block index, the residual is block separable.
A banded dependency graph gives a block-banded Jacobian.
immediate_consequences_latex: The normal-equation block \((J^TJ)_{jk}\) can be nonzero only if some residual block is adjacent to both \(j\) and \(k\).
Permuting parameter or residual blocks relabels \(G\) without changing the represented dependency structure.
boundary_notes: A derivative block that vanishes only at isolated points is not structurally absent.
Sparse residual dependence does not guarantee that \(J^TJ\) has a comparably sparse factorization because fill may occur.

notation.meaning: Parameter-block neighborhood of residual block i.
Jacobian block from parameter block j to residual block i.

review_flags: No inspected source supported the precise graph-based definition and all stated consequences.
The distinction between structural and pointwise numerical sparsity needs locator-level evidence.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse block-dependency representation of residual systems
Sparse Residual Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual map is structurally sparse when each residual component depends on only a small subset of variables, forcing corresponding Jacobian entries to vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m):\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^m\). The residual map is structurally sparse when, for each \(i\), there is an index set \(S_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \(r_i(x)\) depends only on \((x_j)_{j\in S_i}\), with most \(S_i\) small relative to \(n\). Wherever \(r\) is differentiable, \(j\notin S_i\) implies \(\partial r_i(x)/\partial x_j=0\); hence the Jacobian sparsity pattern is contained in \(\{(i,j):j\in S_i\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) has component functions \(r_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual maps whose components depend on restricted parameter subsets.

notation.meaning: variables on which residual component i depends
structural nonzero pattern of the Jacobian

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Structured Residual Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-structured residual comprises equation blocks, each depending only on a specified subset of variable blocks, which induces zero blocks in its Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the variable space be decomposed as \(\mathbb R^n=\prod_{j=1}^q\mathbb R^{n_j}\) and the residual space as \(\mathbb R^m=\prod_{i=1}^p\mathbb R^{m_i}\). A block-structured residual map has the representation \[R(x)=\bigl(R_1(x_{N_1}),\ldots,R_p(x_{N_p})\bigr),\] where \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_q)\), each incidence set \(N_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,q\}\), and \(R_i:\prod_{j\in N_i}\mathbb R^{n_j}\to\mathbb R^{m_i}\). If \(R\) is differentiable, its Jacobian block \(J_{ij}(x)=\partial R_i(x)/\partial x_j\) vanishes whenever \(j\notin N_i\).
assumptions_latex: R_i\text{ is differentiable when Jacobian structure is asserted}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional residual maps partitioned by variable and equation blocks.

notation.meaning: Variable-block incidence set for residual block i.
Jacobian block mapping perturbations of variable block j to residual block i.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The representation and its induced zero Jacobian blocks are mathematically coherent and fit the representation leaf, but the record cites no inspectable source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity–Block Interactions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block incidence determines which Jacobian blocks may be nonzero; additional sparsity can occur inside permitted blocks, and both levels contribute to structured products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable block residual \(R=(R_i)_{i=1}^p\) with variable blocks \((x_j)_{j=1}^q\), define the block incidence graph by an edge \((i,j)\) precisely when \(R_i\) may depend on \(x_j\). Then \[DR(x)v=\left(\sum_{j\in N_i}J_{ij}(x)v_j\right)_{i=1}^p.\] Hence block incidence supplies a structural sparsity envelope: \(j\notin N_i\) implies \(J_{ij}(x)=0\), while an edge permits but does not require nonzero scalar entries. Consequently, block sparsity and within-block sparsity are distinct and may be exploited simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interaction between block incidence and scalar or block Jacobian sparsity.

notation.meaning: Variable blocks incident to residual block i.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Residual Operators
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-free residual implementation returns residual values and Jacobian or adjoint-Jacobian products without explicitly assembling the Jacobian matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be differentiable. A matrix-free residual operator is an implementation that, at each admissible \(x\), evaluates \(R(x)\) and provides the actions \[v\longmapsto DR(x)v\quad\text{and, when required,}\quad w\longmapsto DR(x)^{\mathsf T}w\] without forming or storing the matrix \(DR(x)\). The returned actions must equal the corresponding exact derivative products, or be accompanied by a declared approximation rule and error tolerance. Thus Newton–Krylov and least-squares iterations can access the required linear operators using storage determined by the evaluation procedure rather than by all Jacobian entries.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle representation of residuals and derivative actions without assembled Jacobians.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the matrix-free operator topic, but the exact-or-declared-approximation requirement and storage claim are implementation semantics requiring an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix-free first-order residual-operator interface
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), and let \(r:D\subseteq X\to Y\) be differentiable. Equip \(X\) and \(Y\) with Euclidean inner products, so the adjoint of \(J(x)=Dr(x)\) is \(J(x)^T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free is an access model for residual and derivative actions, not a different residual equation. Exact and approximate oracle variants must be distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix-free residual operator is a tuple \(\mathcal O=(\mathcal R,\mathcal J,\mathcal J^*)\) satisfying, for every admissible \(x\in D\), \(v\in X\), and \(w\in Y\), \[\mathcal R(x)=r(x),\qquad \mathcal J(x;v)=J(x)v,\qquad \mathcal J^*(x;w)=J(x)^Tw,\] while the interface neither requires nor returns the assembled matrix \(J(x)\). An exact matrix-free interface satisfies these identities algebraically; an \((\varepsilon_R,\varepsilon_J,\varepsilon_{J^*})\)-inexact interface replaces them by declared norm-error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-free residual operator supplies residual values, Jacobian-vector products, and adjoint-Jacobian-vector products as operator actions without requiring an assembled Jacobian matrix. Exactness means that all returned actions equal the corresponding mathematical quantities; an approximate implementation is matrix-free only with separately declared action-error tolerances.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) is differentiable at every point at which derivative actions are requested.
The domain and codomain inner products are fixed, determining the adjoint action.
The operator accepts arbitrary admissible directions \(v\) and covectors represented by \(w\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The gradient of \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\) is available matrix-free as \(\nabla f(x)=\mathcal J^*(x;\mathcal R(x))\).
A Gauss–Newton normal-operator action is \(v\mapsto\mathcal J^*(x;\mathcal J(x;v))=J(x)^TJ(x)v\).
special_cases_latex: A directional automatic-differentiation routine can realize \(\mathcal J(x;v)\).
For a square nonlinear equation, an implementation may provide only \(\mathcal R\) and \(\mathcal J\) when no adjoint action is needed.
immediate_consequences_latex: First-order residual and normal-operator products can be evaluated without storing all \(mn\) Jacobian entries.
The definition is invariant under the internal method used to compute each action.
boundary_notes: Finite-difference directional products are inexact unless their approximation error is explicitly set to zero by assumption.
A routine that evaluates only \(r(x)\) is not a complete first-order matrix-free interface under this definition.
review_flags: The operational definition and exact oracle scope were not verified against an inspected source.
Whether the node requires both forward and adjoint actions is source-dependent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local parameterized solvability-and-attraction model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be normed spaces, let \(P\) be a parameter space, and let \(F:D\subseteq X\times P\to Y\). For each \(p\), let \(T_p\) be an iteration map defined near a reference solution \((x_*,p_*)\) satisfying \(F(x_*,p_*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition packages local existence, local uniqueness, parameter stability, and attraction. It does not specify Newton, secant, or least-squares iterations and does not claim a particular convergence order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((F,\{T_p\})\) has a local solvability-convergence structure at \((x_*,p_*)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(P_0\ni p_*\) and \(U\ni x_*\), a map \(s:P_0\to U\), and attraction neighborhoods \(V_p\subseteq U\) such that \[F(s(p),p)=0,\qquad \{x\in U:F(x,p)=0\}=\{s(p)\},\qquad T_p(V_p)\subseteq V_p,\qquad \lim_{k\to\infty}T_p^k(x_0)=s(p)\] for every \(p\in P_0\) and every \(x_0\in V_p\). The structure is well posed when \(s\) is continuous at \(p_*\), and Lipschitz well posed when \(s\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual family and iteration possess a local solvability-convergence structure when nearby parameter values have a unique nearby solution, those solutions form a stable local solution map, and each nearby solution attracts all iterates started in a declared invariant neighborhood. This definition does not select an algorithm or prescribe a rate.
assumptions_latex: Every iteration map \(T_p\) is defined on its declared attraction neighborhood \(V_p\).
Uniqueness is local to the common neighborhood \(U\), not necessarily global in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall p\in P_0\ \exists!\,s(p)\in U:F(s(p),p)=0,\qquad \forall x_0\in V_p:\ T_p^k(x_0)\to s(p).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The solution relation \(F^{-1}(0)\cap(U\times P_0)\) is the graph \(\{(s(p),p):p\in P_0\}\), and each graph point has a declared basin \(V_p\).
special_cases_latex: With no parameter variation, \(P_0=\{p_*\}\), the definition reduces to a locally unique root with a local attraction neighborhood.
For fixed-point residuals \(F(x,p)=x-T_p(x)\), solutions and fixed points coincide.
immediate_consequences_latex: The definition separates the solution neighborhood \(U\) from the possibly smaller attraction neighborhood \(V_p\).
Continuity or Lipschitz continuity of \(s\) quantifies stability with respect to parameter perturbations.
boundary_notes: Existence without uniqueness, or convergence to an unspecified member of a solution set, is outside this definition.
Semilocal results based only on data at an initial point are a distinct certification regime.
review_flags: The node is broad and no inspected source identified this packaged definition as canonical.
The precise inclusion of parameterized stability versus fixed-problem convergence requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.title: Local parameterized solvability-and-attraction model

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quantitative local well-posedness and attraction certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be normed spaces, let \(F:D\subseteq X\to Y\), let \(x_*\in D\) satisfy \(F(x_*)=0\), and let \(T:D_T\subseteq X\to X\) satisfy \(T(x_*)=x_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unlike the parameterized parent notion, this definition concerns one fixed residual equation and supplies quantitative error and contraction bounds on a specified neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local well-posedness-attraction certificate for \((F,T,x_*)\) is a tuple \((U,V,\kappa,q)\) with neighborhoods \(V\subseteq U\) of \(x_*\), \(\kappa>0\), and \(0\leq q<1\), such that \[\|x-x_*\|\leq\kappa\|F(x)\|\quad(x\in U),\qquad T(V)\subseteq V,\qquad \|T(x)-x_*\|\leq q\|x-x_*\|\quad(x\in V).\] The first inequality is the local residual error bound; the latter two conditions define local attraction with contraction factor \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local well-posedness-attraction certificate consists of a neighborhood where distance to the root is bounded by residual size and a possibly smaller invariant neighborhood where one iteration contracts distance to that root by a uniform factor below one. The neighborhoods and constants are part of the certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(V\subseteq U\subseteq D\cap D_T\) are neighborhoods of \(x_*\).
\(\kappa>0\) and \(q\in[0,1)\) are uniform over their respective neighborhoods.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The error bound is equivalently \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(0)\cap U)\leq\kappa\|F(x)\|\) because the localized zero set is a singleton.
The attraction inequality states that \(x_*\) is a uniformly linearly attracting fixed point on \(V\).
special_cases_latex: If \(q=0\), one iteration maps every point of \(V\) to \(x_*\).
For \(F(x)=x-T(x)\), both parts of the certificate concern the same fixed-point equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: The residual error bound excludes a second zero of \(F\) in \(U\).
The contraction estimate supplies a geometric distance bound for every orbit beginning in \(V\).
boundary_notes: A derivative-based nonsingularity condition can imply such bounds but is not part of this definition.
Convergence from points outside \(V\), superlinear rates, and robustness to inexact iteration are not covered.
review_flags: No inspected source established this combined error-bound and attraction certificate as the canonical definition.
The displayed geometric consequence should be checked against a supporting fixed-point source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local inverse and implicit solution-map correspondence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), and let \(G:U\subseteq X\times Y\to\mathbb R^n\) satisfy \(G(x_*,y_*)=0\). For the inverse specialization, let \(H:X\to X\) and set \(G(x,y)=H(x)-y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition records the local graph objects related by inverse and implicit formulations. Existence and differentiability under derivative nonsingularity are theorem-level guarantees, not assumed consequences here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inverse-implicit function correspondence at \((x_*,y_*)\) is a pair of neighborhoods \(U_x\ni x_*\), \(U_y\ni y_*\) and a single-valued map \(\varphi:U_y\to U_x\) such that \[G(x,y)=0\text{ with }(x,y)\in U_x\times U_y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=\varphi(y).\] In the specialization \(G(x,y)=H(x)-y\), the same map is a local inverse of \(H\): \[H(\varphi(y))=y\quad(y\in U_y),\qquad \varphi(H(x))=x\quad(x\in U_x),\] after shrinking the neighborhoods so that \(H(U_x)\subseteq U_y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inverse-implicit correspondence is a local solution graph of an equation in which the solved-for variable is a single-valued function of the remaining variable. When the equation is obtained by writing a map as its output minus a target value, that implicit solution map is exactly a local inverse of the original map.
assumptions_latex: The neighborhoods and solution map satisfy the displayed graph equivalence; their existence is part of the defined object.
For the inverse specialization, \(G(x,y)=H(x)-y\) and \(H(U_x)\subseteq U_y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{(x,y)\in U_x\times U_y:G(x,y)=0\}=\{(\varphi(y),y):y\in U_y\},\] and for \(G(x,y)=H(x)-y\), \(\varphi=H^{-1}\) locally.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The local zero set of \(G\) is the graph of \(\varphi\).
A local inverse of \(H\) is the implicit solution map for \(H(x)-y=0\).
special_cases_latex: For scalar \(H:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), the correspondence is the usual local inverse relation.
For a parameterized residual \(F(x,p)=0\), take \(y=p\) and \(G=F\) to obtain a local parameter-to-solution map.
immediate_consequences_latex: The graph condition gives local uniqueness of the solved-for variable \(x\) for each \(y\in U_y\).
In the inverse specialization, both compositions are identities on their declared neighborhoods.
boundary_notes: A set-valued solution relation is not an inverse-implicit correspondence under this single-valued definition.
Derivative formulas such as \(D\varphi(y_*)=-D_xG(x_*,y_*)^{-1}D_yG(x_*,y_*)\) require additional differentiability and nonsingularity hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Equation map defining the local solution relation.
Local implicit solution map or local inverse.
Map used in the inverse-function specialization.

review_flags: A relevant source hint was supplied but not inspected, so no locator can be cited.
The record intentionally defines the correspondence without asserting inverse- or implicit-function existence theorems.
knowledge_statements.title: Local inverse and implicit solution-map correspondence
Inverse-Function Principle
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable square map with nonsingular derivative is locally invertible, with a continuously differentiable inverse and locally unique solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(x_*\in U\). If \(DF(x_*)\) is nonsingular, then there exist open neighborhoods \(V\subseteq U\) of \(x_*\) and \(W\) of \(F(x_*)\) such that \(F|_V:V\to W\) is bijective. Its inverse \(G:W\to V\) is continuously differentiable and satisfies \[DG(y)=DF(G(y))^{-1}\quad\text{for every }y\in W.\] In particular, the local residual equation \(F(x)=y\) has exactly one solution in \(V\) for every \(y\in W\).
assumptions_latex: U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is open and }x_*\in U
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists V,W:\ F|_V:V\to W\text{ is a }C^1\text{ bijection and }DG(y)=DF(G(y))^{-1}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional continuously differentiable inverse-function theorem.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard and properly scoped finite-dimensional inverse-function theorem, but no theorem, section, or page citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Function Principle
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the derivative with respect to the solution variables is nonsingular, nearby residual zeros form a unique continuously differentiable function of the parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\) be open and let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable. Suppose \(F(x_*,y_*)=0\) and the partial derivative \(D_yF(x_*,y_*)\) is nonsingular. Then there are neighborhoods \(X\) of \(x_*\) and \(Y\) of \(y_*\), and a unique continuously differentiable map \(g:X\to Y\), such that \[F(x,g(x))=0\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Moreover, every zero of \(F\) in \(X\times Y\) has \(y=g(x)\), and \[Dg(x)=-D_yF(x,g(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,g(x)).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional parameterized residual equation.

notation.meaning: Partial derivatives with respect to parameter and solution variables.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The statement is a standard finite-dimensional implicit-function theorem and the theorem kind fits the leaf, but it lacks an inspectable authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a singular derivative, local inverses may lose differentiability and residual zero sets may branch, so classical inverse or implicit conclusions can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonsingularity cannot generally be removed from the classical inverse and implicit principles. The map \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(F(x)=x^3\), is smooth and bijective, but \(F'(0)=0\) and its inverse \(F^{-1}(y)=y^{1/3}\) is not differentiable or locally Lipschitz at \(0\). Likewise, the smooth residual \(H(x,y)=y^2-x\) satisfies \(H(0,0)=0\) and \(D_yH(0,0)=0\); its nearby zero set consists of \(y=\pm\sqrt{x}\) for \(x\geq0\), so it is not the graph of a unique continuously differentiable function \(y=g(x)\) on any neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'(0)=0,\quad D_yH(0,0)=0,\quad C^1\text{ local inverse or implicit uniqueness fails}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of classical inverse and implicit conclusions at singular derivatives.

notation.meaning: Residual exhibiting a branched zero set.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Both examples correctly exhibit failures at singular derivatives and fit a failure-boundary leaf, but directly checkable examples still require registered evidence under the common contract.

knowledge_statements.title: Contraction-Mapping Principle
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction on a closed subset of a complete metric space has one fixed point, and iteration from any point in the subset converges to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a complete metric space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(T:C\to C\). If there exists \(q\in[0,1)\) such that \(d(Tx,Ty)\leq qd(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\), then \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x_*\in C\). For every \(x_0\in C\), the iteration \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) converges to \(x_*\), and \[d(x_k,x_*)\leq \frac{q^k}{1-q}d(x_1,x_0).\] Thus rewriting a residual equation as \(x=T(x)\) yields existence, uniqueness, and convergence whenever an invariant contraction domain is established.
assumptions_latex: (X,d)\text{ is complete and }\varnothing\ne C\subseteq X\text{ is closed}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach fixed-point theorem with an a posteriori distance estimate.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The contraction theorem and a posteriori estimate are standard and internally consistent, but the record provides no authoritative theorem or page locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Certified contraction domain for fixed-point iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a complete metric space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(T:C\to X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition isolates the hypotheses of the Banach contraction framework and the associated iteration certificate. It is global on \(C\), although \(C\) may itself be a local neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A contraction-mapping certificate for \(T\) on \(C\) is a constant \(q\in[0,1)\) such that \[T(C)\subseteq C,\qquad d(Tx,Ty)\leq q\,d(x,y)\quad\text{for every }x,y\in C.\] The pair \((C,q)\) is called a certified contraction domain. For a designated center \(x_0\) and radius \(R\), a ball certificate additionally requires \(C=\overline B(x_0,R)\) and \(d(Tx_0,x_0)\leq(1-q)R\), which ensures the stated self-map condition from the center bound and contraction inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified contraction domain is a nonempty closed subset of a complete metric space that is mapped into itself by an iteration whose Lipschitz factor is uniformly below one. A ball certificate records a center, radius, contraction factor, and center displacement sufficient to express invariance of that ball.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and closed, hence complete with the induced metric.
\(T\) is defined on all of \(C\), maps \(C\) into itself, and has a uniform factor \(q<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(C,q)\text{ is a certified contraction domain}\iff T(C)\subseteq C\ \wedge\ \operatorname{Lip}(T|_C)\leq q<1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The contraction inequality is \(\sup_{x\neq y\in C}d(Tx,Ty)/d(x,y)\leq q<1\).
For differentiable \(T\) on a convex subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), the sufficient derivative form is \(\sup_{x\in C}\|DT(x)\|\leq q<1\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\overline B(x_0,R)\), the center-displacement condition \(d(Tx_0,x_0)\leq(1-q)R\) is a standard ball-invariance certificate.
For an affine iteration \(T(x)=Ax+b\), any induced norm satisfying \(\|A\|<1\) supplies a contraction factor.
immediate_consequences_latex: The declared factor \(q\) quantifies the strongest uniform linear contraction asserted by the certificate.
Closedness of \(C\) is needed so that limit points of Cauchy iteration sequences remain in \(C\).
boundary_notes: A nonexpansive map with \(q=1\) is not a contraction under this definition.
Local derivative contraction at one point does not establish a certified contraction domain without a uniform neighborhood bound and invariance.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz modulus of T restricted to C.

review_flags: No fixed-point source passage was inspected, so the standard certificate and ball specialization lack citation support.
The node title suggests a theorem, but the immutable slot requests a definition; this record therefore defines its hypothesis certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Newton–Kantorovich certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, let \(D\subseteq X\) be open and convex, let \(F:D\to Y\) be continuously Fréchet differentiable, and choose \(x_0\in D\) such that \(F'(x_0)\) is boundedly invertible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the classical Lipschitz-derivative, semilocal certificate normalized by the derivative at the initial point. It defines the certifying data and radii, not a convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Newton–Kantorovich certificate at \(x_0\) is a pair \((\beta,L)\) with \(\beta\geq0\), \(L>0\), and \(h=\beta L\leq\tfrac12\), satisfying \[\|F'(x_0)^{-1}F(x_0)\|\leq\beta,\qquad \|F'(x_0)^{-1}(F'(x)-F'(y))\|\leq L\|x-y\|\quad(x,y\in D_0),\] where \(D_0\subseteq D\) contains the closed ball of radius \[t_* =\frac{1-\sqrt{1-2h}}{L}\] about \(x_0\). The associated scalar majorant is \(m(t)=\beta-t+\tfrac L2t^2\), whose smaller nonnegative zero is \(t_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A classical Newton–Kantorovich certificate consists of a normalized initial Newton-step bound and a normalized Lipschitz bound for the derivative. Their product must not exceed one half, the prescribed domain must contain the resulting closed ball, and the smaller zero of the associated quadratic majorant defines the certified radius.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Banach spaces, and \(D\) is open and convex.
\(F\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable on \(D\), and \(F'(x_0)^{-1}\) exists and is bounded.
The normalized derivative Lipschitz inequality holds throughout \(D_0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The discriminant condition for the quadratic majorant is \(1-2\beta L\geq0\).
The larger majorant zero is \(t^{**}=(1+\sqrt{1-2\beta L})/L\).
special_cases_latex: At the limiting value \(h=\tfrac12\), the two majorant zeros coincide at \(1/L\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The certificate depends only on data anchored at \(x_0\) and bounds over a containing domain, rather than prior knowledge of a root.
The normalized inequalities are unchanged if the equation is premultiplied by a boundedly invertible linear operator.
boundary_notes: Variants using an unnormalized Lipschitz bound, Hölder derivatives, generalized equations, or alternative majorants are not identical to this certificate.
The convergence and uniqueness conclusions associated with the certificate require an independently sourced theorem statement.

notation.meaning: Upper bound on the initial normalized Newton step.

review_flags: No Newton–Kantorovich source was inspected for the exact normalization, domain assumptions, and constants.
The source hints primarily concern local Newton convergence and do not independently support this semilocal certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Newton–Kantorovich certificate
Semilocal Convergence Domains
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kantorovich bounds define explicit nested radii: Newton iterates converge to a zero in the smaller ball, which is unique in the larger ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq X\to Y\) be continuously Fréchet differentiable between Banach spaces, with \(D\) open and convex. Suppose \(F'(x_0)\) is invertible, \(\|F'(x_0)^{-1}F(x_0)\|\leq\beta\), and \(\|F'(x_0)^{-1}(F'(x)-F'(y))\|\leq\gamma\|x-y\|\) on \(D\). Set \(h=\beta\gamma\) and \(r_\pm=(1\pm\sqrt{1-2h})/\gamma\). If \(h\leq1/2\) and \(\overline B(x_0,r_+)\subseteq D\), Newton's iterates are well defined, remain in \(\overline B(x_0,r_-)\), and converge to a zero \(x_*\) there. If \(h<1/2\), that zero is unique in \(B(x_0,r_+)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k\to x_*\in\overline B(x_0,r_-),\quad F(x_*)=0;\quad h<\tfrac12\Longrightarrow x_*\text{ unique in }B(x_0,r_+)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Lipschitz-derivative Newton–Kantorovich domain in Banach spaces.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The stated radii and larger-ball uniqueness convention depend on a particular Newton–Kantorovich variant and require full-text verification. The formulas also divide by gamma without explicitly assuming gamma>0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semilocal Newton domain generated by a quadratic majorant
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq X\to Y\) satisfy a Newton–Kantorovich certificate at \(x_0\) with constants \(\beta\geq0\), \(L>0\), \(h=\beta L\leq\tfrac12\), and majorant \(m(t)=\beta-t+\tfrac L2t^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The domain is semilocal because it is constructed from an initial point and neighborhood bounds, without assuming that the location of a solution is known beforehand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The associated closed semilocal convergence domain is \[\mathcal D_{\mathrm{semi}}(x_0;\beta,L)=\overline B(x_0,t_*),\qquad t_*=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-2\beta L}}{L},\] provided \(\overline B(x_0,t_*)\subseteq D\) and the certifying normalized derivative bound holds on a set containing this ball. The associated uniqueness-comparison radius is \[t^{**}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-2\beta L}}{L},\] when the larger ball required by the applicable theorem lies in the certifying domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic-majorant semilocal domain is the closed ball centered at the initial Newton point whose radius is the smaller nonnegative zero of the Kantorovich majorant. It is admissible only when the residual map and normalized derivative bound are valid on a set containing that ball. The larger zero supplies a separate comparison radius when additional domain conditions hold.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(t_*\) is the least nonnegative solution of \(\beta-t+\tfrac L2t^2=0\).
For \(h>0\), \(t_*=2\beta/(1+\sqrt{1-2h})\), which avoids subtractive cancellation.
special_cases_latex: If \(\beta=0\), the semilocal ball degenerates to \(\{x_0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Increasing \(\beta\) or \(L\) while retaining \(\beta L\leq\tfrac12\) changes the certified radius through the majorant roots.
The definition distinguishes the smaller convergence radius \(t_*\) from the larger comparison radius \(t^{**}\).
boundary_notes: The ball is not claimed to be a maximal basin of attraction.
No convergence conclusion is asserted unless the full hypotheses of a sourced Newton–Kantorovich theorem are satisfied.

notation.meaning: Closed semilocal domain centered at the initial point.
Smaller zero of the quadratic majorant.
Larger zero of the quadratic majorant.

review_flags: No inspected source supported the exact semilocal-radius convention and larger-root interpretation.
The term convergence domain may require a theorem rather than only this certificate definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Localized well-posed zero of a residual equation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be normed spaces, let \(F:D\subseteq X\to Y\), and let \(x_*\in D\) satisfy \(F(x_*)=0\). Let \(U\subseteq D\) be a neighborhood of \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a metric localization of existence, uniqueness, and residual stability for one zero. Differentiability is not required by the definition, although derivative conditions may certify it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero \(x_*\) is well posed relative to \(U\) with modulus \(\kappa>0\) when \[F^{-1}(0)\cap U=\{x_*\},\qquad \|x-x_*\|\leq\kappa\|F(x)\|\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\] A well-posedness localization is a pair \((U,\kappa)\) satisfying these conditions. The maximal localization family is \[\mathfrak W(x_*)=\{(U,\kappa):U\ni x_*,\ U\subseteq D,\ \kappa>0,\text{ and the displayed conditions hold}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A well-posedness localization is a neighborhood containing exactly one zero together with a uniform constant that bounds distance to that zero by residual size. The definition records the neighborhood and modulus explicitly, and the localization family consists of every pair satisfying those requirements.
assumptions_latex: The same finite constant \(\kappa>0\) applies to every \(x\in U\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because the localized zero set is a singleton, the stability inequality is \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(0)\cap U)\leq\kappa\|F(x)\|\).
The least admissible modulus for fixed \(U\) is \(\kappa_U=\sup_{x\in U\setminus\{x_*\}}\|x-x_*\|/\|F(x)\|\), when this supremum is finite.
special_cases_latex: For an invertible linear map \(F(x)=A(x-x_*)\), one may take \(U=X\) and \(\kappa=\|A^{-1}\|\).
If \(F\) is continuously differentiable and \(F'(x_*)\) is boundedly invertible, sufficiently small neighborhoods are candidates for localization.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any pair in \(\mathfrak W(x_*)\) excludes other zeros from \(U\).
If \(U'\subseteq U\) is also a neighborhood of \(x_*\), then \((U',\kappa)\in\mathfrak W(x_*)\).
boundary_notes: Uniqueness without a finite residual-error modulus is not well posed under this definition.
This definition does not quantify perturbations in an external parameter or right-hand side.

notation.meaning: Family of well-posedness localizations at the zero.

review_flags: No inspected source established this residual-error-bound formulation as the intended localization notion.
The derivative-based special case is only identified as a candidate and requires theorem-level sourcing.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized well-posed zero of a residual equation
Existence Localization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smaller Kantorovich radius encloses the Newton trajectory and at least one zero of the residual map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the Newton–Kantorovich assumptions \(\|F'(x_0)^{-1}F(x_0)\|\leq\beta\), \(\|F'(x_0)^{-1}(F'(x)-F'(y))\|\leq\gamma\|x-y\|\), and \(h=\beta\gamma\leq1/2\), define \[r_- = \frac{1-\sqrt{1-2h}}{\gamma}.\] If the required derivative bound holds on a convex domain containing \(\overline B(x_0,r_-)\), then Newton's sequence starting at \(x_0\) remains in that ball and converges to some \(x_*\in\overline B(x_0,r_-)\) satisfying \(F(x_*)=0\). Thus the smaller root of the scalar Kantorovich majorant localizes existence of a residual-system solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence ball furnished by the classical Kantorovich quadratic majorant.

notation.meaning: Product beta gamma controlling the majorant discriminant.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The smaller-root localization is plausible, but the standalone record does not introduce the Banach spaces, the map and its domain, or the Newton iteration completely, and it divides by gamma without stating gamma>0. An authoritative Kantorovich locator is needed to settle the exact hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness Localization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the Kantorovich product is strictly below one half, the converged zero is unique throughout the ball determined by the larger majorant root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the Newton–Kantorovich hypotheses with \(h=\beta\gamma<1/2\), define \[r_+ = \frac{1+\sqrt{1-2h}}{\gamma}.\] If the preconditioned derivative Lipschitz bound is valid throughout a convex domain containing \(\overline B(x_0,r_+)\), then the zero \(x_*\) reached by Newton's method is the only solution of \(F(x)=0\) in \(B(x_0,r_+)\). The larger majorant root therefore gives a uniqueness neighborhood, whereas the smaller radius \(r_-\) localizes the Newton trajectory and existence. At the boundary \(h=1/2\), this strict larger-ball uniqueness formulation requires separate treatment.
assumptions_latex: \overline B(x_0,r_+)\text{ lies in the convex derivative-control domain}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness ball associated with the larger Kantorovich majorant root.

notation.meaning: Zero obtained from the Newton–Kantorovich convergence conclusion.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The larger-root uniqueness claim is variant-sensitive and lacks a source. The statement also relies on F, x0, beta, gamma, and the previously obtained zero without fully introducing their domains, and r+ requires gamma>0.

knowledge_statements.title: Localization-Radius Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As the residual bound increases, the existence radius expands and the uniqueness radius contracts; both become infinitely sensitive near the Kantorovich threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\gamma>0\) and let \(0<\beta\gamma<1/2\). For \[r_\pm(\beta,\gamma)=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1-2\beta\gamma}}{\gamma},\] differentiation with respect to \(\beta\) gives \[\frac{\partial r_-}{\partial\beta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2\beta\gamma}},\qquad \frac{\partial r_+}{\partial\beta}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2\beta\gamma}}.\] Hence increasing the initial residual bound enlarges the existence radius \(r_-\), shrinks the uniqueness radius \(r_+\), and drives both toward \(1/\gamma\). Their sensitivities diverge as \(\beta\gamma\uparrow1/2\), identifying the discriminant boundary as an ill-conditioned localization regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of classical Kantorovich radii to the residual-size bound.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The derivative calculations and limiting sensitivity are algebraically correct and fit a property leaf, but the interpretation as localization-radius sensitivity has no registered source or locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-invariant majorant certificate family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, let \(D\subseteq X\) be open and convex, let \(F:D\to Y\) be continuously Fréchet differentiable, and let \(x_0\in D\) have boundedly invertible derivative \(F'(x_0)\). Fix \(R>0\) with \(B(x_0,R)\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition describes scalar-majorant certificates normalized by the initial derivative. It includes the quadratic Kantorovich majorant as a special case but allows nonquadratic majorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An affine-invariant majorant certificate at \(x_0\) is a differentiable scalar function \(f:[0,R)\to\mathbb R\) such that \[f(0)>0,\qquad f'(0)=-1,\qquad f'\text{ is convex and strictly increasing},\qquad \|F'(x_0)^{-1}F(x_0)\|\leq f(0),\] and, whenever \(x,y\in B(x_0,R)\) with \(\|x-x_0\|+\|y-x\|<R\), \[\|F'(x_0)^{-1}(F'(y)-F'(x))\|\leq f'(\|x-x_0\|+\|y-x\|)-f'(\|x-x_0\|).\] The majorant-affine-invariant variant family is the set of all such certificates, together with the scalar Newton map \(n_f(t)=t-f(t)/f'(t)\) wherever \(f'(t)\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine-invariant majorant certificate bounds normalized changes in the derivative of a nonlinear residual by increments of the derivative of a scalar majorant. The majorant has a positive initial value, normalized initial slope minus one, and an increasing convex derivative. Each admissible majorant and its scalar Newton map define one member of the variant family.
assumptions_latex: The displayed normalized derivative comparison holds for every admissible pair \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak M(F,x_0,R)=\{f:\ f\text{ satisfies all displayed scalar and normalized derivative conditions}\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The derivative comparison uses only \(F'(x_0)^{-1}F\) and is therefore invariant under replacing \(F\) by \(AF\) for any boundedly invertible linear map \(A:Y\to Y\).
For \(f(t)=\beta-t+\tfrac L2t^2\), the comparison reduces to \(\|F'(x_0)^{-1}(F'(y)-F'(x))\|\leq L\|y-x\|\).
special_cases_latex: The quadratic majorant yields the classical Lipschitz-derivative Newton–Kantorovich certificate.
Nonquadratic choices of \(f\) can encode derivative growth that is not represented sharply by one global Lipschitz constant.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different valid majorants for the same residual define different scalar comparison models and potentially different certified radii.
Premultiplication of the residual equation by an invertible linear operator does not change the normalized comparison quantities.
boundary_notes: Existence of a positive zero of \(f\), invariance of a Newton ball, and convergence of either scalar or operator Newton iterates require additional hypotheses and a sourced theorem.
Majorants for Hölder or generalized derivatives may require altered regularity conditions and are not silently included.

notation.meaning: Scalar Newton map associated with the majorant.

review_flags: No inspected source supported the precise majorant regularity and comparison inequality.
The affine-invariance statement and quadratic specialization require locator-level verification.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-invariant majorant certificate family
Majorant Variants
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar function can dominate derivative variation and Newton step lengths; changing this function yields Lipschitz, Hölder, analytic, or problem-specific convergence variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalar majorant for a residual map \(F\) at \(x_0\) is a differentiable function \(f:[0,R)\to\mathbb R\) whose derivative increments dominate the preconditioned derivative increments of \(F\): \[\|F'(x_0)^{-1}(F'(y)-F'(x))\|\leq f'(\|x-x_0\|+\|y-x\|)-f'(\|x-x_0\|)\] whenever the displayed arguments lie in \([0,R)\). With compatible initial bounds, the scalar Newton sequence \(t_{k+1}=t_k-f(t_k)/f'(t_k)\) majorizes the step lengths of the operator Newton sequence. The Lipschitz variant uses \(f(t)=\beta-t+\gamma t^2/2\); alternative majorants encode Hölder, analytic, or problem-specific derivative growth.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ satisfies the stated derivative-increment domination}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t_{k+1}=t_k-\frac{f(t_k)}{f'(t_k)}\text{ controls the corresponding operator Newton steps}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar majorant representation underlying classical and generalized Newton bounds.

notation.meaning: Radius over which the majorant comparison is imposed.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The scalar-majorant representation fits the leaf, but derivative domination alone does not establish the asserted Newton-step majorization. The phrase 'with compatible initial bounds' leaves essential hypotheses unstated, and the exact conditions vary across majorant theorems; a specific authoritative source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Invariant Variants
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton iterates commute with invertible affine coordinate changes and residual scalings; normalized derivative-variation conditions remain unchanged when the norms are transported consistently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\subset X\to Y\) be continuously Fréchet differentiable between Banach spaces, and let \(F'(x_0)\) be invertible. For invertible affine coordinate maps \(x=Tz+a\) and invertible residual scaling \(S:Y\to Y\), define \(G(z)=SF(Tz+a)\). Newton iterates correspond exactly: if \(x_k=Tz_k+a\), then \(x_{k+1}=x_k-F'(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\) if and only if \(z_{k+1}=z_k-G'(z_k)^{-1}G(z_k)\). Consequently, Kantorovich hypotheses expressed through normalized operators such as \(F'(x_0)^{-1}[F'(x)-F'(y)]\), using transported norms, are invariant under these transformations.
assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) and \(S:Y\to Y\) are bounded linear isomorphisms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k=Tz_k+a\) for corresponding Newton sequences, and normalized Kantorovich conditions are transformation invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine covariance and normalized derivative variation in Newton–Kantorovich analysis.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The affine covariance statement is mathematically plausible and fits the property container, but no source or inspectable locator supports the transported-norm invariance claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raw inverse-Jacobian, residual, and Lipschitz constants depend on scaling, although their dimensionless products and the Newton correction are invariant under scalar residual scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F'(x_0)\) be invertible and define \(a=\lVert F'(x_0)^{-1}\rVert\), \(b=\lVert F(x_0)\rVert\), and a local derivative Lipschitz constant \(L\). Under scalar residual scaling \(G=cF\), where \(c\ne0\), the corresponding constants satisfy \(a_G=|c|^{-1}a\), \(b_G=|c|b\), and \(L_G=|c|L\). Thus the individual constants are scaling-sensitive, whereas \(a_Gb_G=ab\), \(a_GL_G=aL\), and the Newton correction \(G'(x_0)^{-1}G(x_0)=F'(x_0)^{-1}F(x_0)\) are invariant. General coordinate transformations can change norm-based bounds unless norms are transported with the transformation.
assumptions_latex: \(F\in C^1(U;Y)\), \(F'(x_0)\) is invertible, and \(\lVert F'(x)-F'(y)\rVert\le L\lVert x-y\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of raw Kantorovich constants on residual and coordinate scaling.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The scalar-scaling formulas are internally consistent and fit Scaling Sensitivity, but the record supplies no source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton local convergence family for square residual systems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(F:D\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(x_*\in D\) satisfy \(F(x_*)=0\). Write \(J(x)=F'(x)\) and \(e_k=x_k-x_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, deterministic, local theory for square smooth residual systems. Globalization and singular-root modifications are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Newton local convergence family consists of iterations \[x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\qquad B_ks_k=-F(x_k)+r_k,\] where \(B_k\) is nonsingular near \(x_*\), \(r_k\) is a linear-solve residual, and the exact Newton member is obtained from \(B_k=J(x_k)\) and \(r_k=0\). A member is locally convergent to \(x_*\) if there is \(\delta>0\) such that every \(x_0\in B_\delta(x_*)\) generates a well-defined sequence contained in \(D\) with \(x_k\to x_*\). Its local rate is q-linear when \(\limsup_k\|e_{k+1}\|/\|e_k\|<1\), q-superlinear when this ratio tends to zero, and q-quadratic when \(\|e_{k+1}\|\le C\|e_k\|^2\) eventually.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family comprises local residual-solving iterations formed by solving a Newton or Newton-like linear model, possibly with an approximate derivative and a nonzero linear-solve residual. Local convergence means that every sufficiently close initial point produces well-defined iterates converging to the specified root. Linear, superlinear, and quadratic members are distinguished by their successive-error ratios.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For the exact member, \(s_k=-J(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\).
The q-superlinear condition is \(\|e_{k+1}\|=o(\|e_k\|)\).
special_cases_latex: Exact Newton: \(B_k=J(x_k)\), \(r_k=0\).
Inexact Newton: \(B_k=J(x_k)\), \(\|r_k\|\le\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\).
Frozen-derivative Newton: \(B_k=J(\bar x)\) for a fixed base point \(\bar x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A q-quadratically convergent member is q-superlinear whenever \(e_k\ne0\) eventually.
boundary_notes: The definition classifies local behavior; it does not assert that any listed member converges under the ambient assumptions alone.
Rectangular least-squares residuals require Gauss–Newton or related normal-equation models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local superlinear and quadratic convergence of exact Newton
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convergence-rate theorem for exact Newton iteration near a nondegenerate root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be continuously differentiable on a convex open set $\mathcal D$, and let $x^*\in\mathcal D$ be a nondegenerate solution of $r(x)=0$, meaning that $J(x^*)$ is nonsingular. Let $\{x_k\}$ be generated by exact Newton iteration. Whenever $x_k\in\mathcal D$ is sufficiently close to $x^*$, $$\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|=o(\|x_k-x^*\|),$$ giving local Q-superlinear convergence. If, additionally, $J$ is Lipschitz continuous near $x^*$, then for all sufficiently close $x_k$, $$\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|=O(\|x_k-x^*\|^2),$$ giving local Q-quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a root whose Jacobian is nonsingular, exact Newton iteration for a continuously differentiable square residual system is locally Q-superlinear. If the Jacobian is also locally Lipschitz, the local rate is Q-quadratic.
assumptions_latex: r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is continuously differentiable on a convex open set }\mathcal D
x^*\in\mathcal D,\quad r(x^*)=0,\quad J(x^*)\text{ is nonsingular}
\{x_k\}\text{ is generated by exact Newton iteration}
x_k\in\mathcal D\text{ is sufficiently close to }x^*
J\text{ is Lipschitz continuous near }x^*\text{ for the quadratic-rate conclusion}

knowledge_statements.title: Regular-Root Newton Convergence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a zero with nonsingular Jacobian and locally Lipschitz derivative, Newton’s method is well defined and converges quadratically to that zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(F(x_*)=0\), and suppose \(F'(x_*)\) is nonsingular. If \(F'\) is Lipschitz continuous on a neighborhood of \(x_*\), then some radius \(r>0\) exists such that every \(x_0\in B_r(x_*)\) generates well-defined Newton iterates \(x_{k+1}=x_k-F'(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\), all iterates remain in \(B_r(x_*)\), and \(x_k\to x_*\). Moreover, for some constant \(C>0\), \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_*\rVert\le C\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert^2\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to x_*\) and \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_*\rVert\le C\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert^2\) locally.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic convergence at a nonsingular zero in finite dimensions.
