knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular root and its Newton convergence neighborhood
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable on an open set and let \(x_*\in D\) satisfy \(F(x_*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Newton iteration at an isolated regular root in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The point \(x_*\) is a regular root when \(J_*:=F'(x_*)\) is nonsingular. Newton convergence at this regular root means that there is \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(x_0\in B_\delta(x_*)\), \[x_{k+1}=x_k-F'(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\] is well defined and converges to \(x_*\). If, additionally, \(F'\) is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(x_*\), the regular-root convergence is locally q-quadratic: there is \(C>0\) such that \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\le C\|x_k-x_*\|^2\) for all generated iterates in a sufficiently small neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular root is a zero at which the square Jacobian is invertible. Regular-root Newton convergence means that every sufficiently close starting point yields well-defined exact Newton iterates converging to that root. A locally Lipschitz Jacobian gives the canonical quadratic error estimate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In finite dimensions, regularity is equivalent to \(\ker F'(x_*)=\{0\}\).
It is also equivalent to the existence of \(F'(x_*)^{-1}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), regularity is \(F'(x_*)\ne0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A regular root is locally isolated.
The Newton error ratio \(\|e_{k+1}\|/\|e_k\|\) tends to zero under the quadratic estimate.
boundary_notes: Nonsingularity alone does not specify a convergence radius.
At a singular root, the quadratic estimate generally need not hold.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton Convergence under Weakened Smoothness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder-continuous Jacobian with exponent alpha yields local Newton convergence of order at least one plus alpha at a regular zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, with \(F(x_*)=0\) and nonsingular \(F'(x_*)\). Suppose that for some \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), \(L>0\), and a neighborhood \(V\) of \(x_*\), one has \(\lVert F'(x)-F'(y)\rVert\le L\lVert x-y\rVert^\alpha\) for all \(x,y\in V\). Then Newton’s iteration is well defined for all sufficiently close starting points and converges to \(x_*\) with order at least \(1+\alpha\): \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_*\rVert\le C\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert^{1+\alpha}\) for some local constant \(C>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_*\rVert\le C\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert^{1+\alpha}\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Newton rate when the Jacobian is Hölder rather than Lipschitz continuous.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The Hölder-Jacobian rate statement is standard and appropriately classified as a theorem, but no source or theorem-level locator is supplied for the order-1+alpha result.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton convergence controlled by a Jacobian modulus of continuity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be differentiable near a regular root \(x_*\), and let \(\omega:[0,\rho]\to[0,\infty)\) be nondecreasing with \(\omega(t)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact local Newton theory with continuity weaker than a Lipschitz Jacobian; finite-dimensional square systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Newton convergence under weakened smoothness is the regime in which \(F'(x_*)\) is nonsingular and \[\|F'(x)-F'(x_*)\|\le\omega(\|x-x_*\|)\] near \(x_*\), rather than requiring \(\omega(t)=Lt\). The associated local Newton family is defined by \(x_{k+1}=x_k-F'(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\), with its rate controlled by \[\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\le C\,\omega(\|x_k-x_*\|)\|x_k-x_*\|\] eventually. Thus continuity of the Jacobian corresponds to superlinear convergence, while a Hölder modulus \(\omega(t)=Lt^\alpha\), \(0<\alpha\le1\), corresponds to q-order at least \(1+\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime replaces local Lipschitz continuity of the Jacobian by an explicit modulus of continuity at a regular root. The Newton error is bounded by the current error multiplied by that modulus. Ordinary continuity yields a superlinear asymptotic ratio, and Hölder continuity yields the corresponding fractional convergence order.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Superlinear convergence follows from \(\omega(\|e_k\|)\to0\).
special_cases_latex: \(\alpha=1\) recovers the Lipschitz-Jacobian quadratic regime.
For \(0<\alpha<1\), the canonical order is \(1+\alpha\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The weakened-smoothness family separates invertibility at the root from the regularity governing the rate.
boundary_notes: A source supporting the full modulus-of-continuity formulation and the displayed rate was not located in the supplied materials.
Semismooth Newton theory is a distinct nonsmooth framework and is not included.

Inexact Newton Local Convergence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly bounded forcing terms give local linear convergence; vanishing terms give superlinear convergence, and residual-proportional terms recover quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy the regular-root and local Lipschitz-Jacobian assumptions at \(x_*\). Suppose \(s_k\) satisfies \(F'(x_k)s_k=-F(x_k)+r_k\), with \(\lVert r_k\rVert\le\eta_k\lVert F(x_k)\rVert\), and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). For sufficiently close \(x_0\), if \(0\le\eta_k\le\bar\eta<1\), the iterates converge locally at least linearly. If \(\eta_k\to0\), convergence is superlinear. If \(\eta_k=O(\lVert F(x_k)\rVert)\), convergence is quadratic.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x_*)=0\), \(F'(x_*)\) is nonsingular, and \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_k\eta_k<1\) gives local linear convergence; \(\eta_k\to0\) gives superlinear convergence; \(\eta_k=O(\lVert F(x_k)\rVert)\) gives quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-controlled inexact Newton convergence near a regular zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inexact Newton step and forcing sequence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable near a stationary point \(x_*\), with \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\) positive definite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional unconstrained-optimization specialization of inexact Newton local convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An inexact Newton iteration is \[x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k,\qquad r_k=
abla^2f(x_k)p_k+
abla f(x_k),\qquad \|r_k\|\le\eta_k\|
abla f(x_k)\|,\] where \(0\le\eta_k<1\) is the forcing parameter. The sequence \(\{\eta_k\}\) is the forcing sequence. Local convergence is obtained when the starting point is sufficiently close and \(\eta_k\le ar\eta<1\); the convergence becomes superlinear when \(\eta_k	o0\), and under a Lipschitz Hessian it is quadratic when \(\eta_k=O(\|
abla f(x_k)\|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact Newton step solves the Newton linear system only to a residual tolerance proportional to the current gradient norm. The proportionality factors form the forcing sequence. Uniformly keeping them below one gives the local contraction regime, driving them to zero gives superlinear behavior, and making them comparable to the gradient norm preserves quadratic behavior under a Lipschitz Hessian.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(\nabla^2f(x_k)p_k=-\nabla f(x_k)+r_k\) gives the same residual condition.
special_cases_latex: \(\eta_k=0\) gives the exact Newton step.
A constant forcing bound \(\eta_k\le\bar\eta<1\) gives the canonical local linear regime.
immediate_consequences_latex: The accuracy required of the inner linear solver can be relaxed far from the limiting point and tightened asymptotically.
boundary_notes: The cited formulation concerns optimization; for a nonlinear system, replace the Hessian and gradient by \(F'(x_k)\) and \(F(x_k)\).
The definition does not prescribe a particular iterative linear solver.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convergence orders of residual-controlled inexact Newton
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies local Q-convergence according to the forcing sequence near a nondegenerate root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be convex and open, let \(r:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(x^*\in\mathcal D\) satisfy \(r(x^*)=0\) with \(J(x^*)\) nonsingular. Let \(\{x_k\}\) be generated by the inexact Newton framework with \(0\leq\eta_k\leq\eta<1\) and \(\|r_k+J_kp_k\|\leq\eta_k\|r_k\|\). When \(x_k\in\mathcal D\) is sufficiently close to \(x^*\): (i) if \(\eta\) is sufficiently small, convergence to \(x^*\) is Q-linear; (ii) if \(\eta_k\to0\), convergence is Q-superlinear; and (iii) if, additionally, \(J\) is Lipschitz continuous near \(x^*\) and \(\eta_k=O(\|r_k\|)\), convergence is Q-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a nondegenerate root of a continuously differentiable residual mapping, inexact Newton converges Q-linearly when the uniform forcing bound is sufficiently small. If the forcing parameters tend to zero, convergence is Q-superlinear. If the Jacobian is also locally Lipschitz and eta_k is of the order of the residual norm, convergence is Q-quadratic.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex and open}
x^*\in\mathcal D,\quad r(x^*)=0,\quad J(x^*)\text{ is nonsingular}
x_k\in\mathcal D\text{ is sufficiently close to }x^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta\text{ sufficiently small}\Rightarrow Q\text{-linear};\quad \eta_k\to0\Rightarrow Q\text{-superlinear};\quad J\text{ locally Lipschitz and }\eta_k=O(\|r_k\|)\Rightarrow Q\text{-quadratic}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Frozen-Jacobian Newton or chord iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be differentiable, let \(x_*\) be a root, and choose a base point \(\bar x\in D\) such that \(A:=F'(\bar x)\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residual evaluations with a derivative matrix held fixed over all iterations or over a prescribed block of iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The fully frozen-derivative Newton iteration is \[x_{k+1}=x_k-A^{-1}F(x_k),\qquad A=F'(\bar x).\] More generally, a block-frozen member chooses refresh indices \(0=t_0<t_1<\cdots\) and uses \[A_j=F'(x_{t_j}),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-A_j^{-1}F(x_k),\quad t_j\le k<t_{j+1}.\] Local convergence means that a neighborhood of \(x_*\) exists in which all required frozen matrices are nonsingular and the resulting iterates converge to \(x_*\). For the fully frozen map \(G(x)=x-A^{-1}F(x)\), the linearized local factor is governed by \(G'(x_*)=I-A^{-1}F'(x_*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A frozen-derivative Newton method reuses one Jacobian factorization for multiple residual corrections. The chord method freezes the derivative permanently at a base point; block-frozen variants refresh it only at selected indices. Its local linear behavior is determined by the derivative of the resulting fixed-point map at the root.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Each step solves \(As_k=-F(x_k)\) with the same coefficient matrix within a refresh block.
special_cases_latex: Taking \(t_j=j\) recovers exact Newton.
Taking only \(t_0=0\) gives the classical chord iteration.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\|I-A^{-1}F'(x_*)\|<1\), the linearization is contractive.
boundary_notes: No supplied source was found that supports the complete block-refresh definition and local factor statement.
Finite-difference Newton methods are not necessarily frozen-derivative methods.
review_flags: Needs a precise source for the chord and block-frozen family.
knowledge_statements.title: Frozen-Jacobian Newton or chord iteration
Chord Local Convergence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A frozen-Jacobian iteration converges linearly when its error-propagation operator is uniformly contractive near the root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable with \(F(x_*)=0\), and fix an invertible matrix \(B\). Assume a closed ball \(D\) about \(x_*\) satisfies \(\sup_{x\in D}\lVert I-B^{-1}F'(x)\rVert\le q<1\). Then the chord iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-B^{-1}F(x_k)\) is a contraction on any invariant sub-ball of \(D\). Every starting point in that sub-ball produces iterates converging to \(x_*\), with \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_*\rVert\le q\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert\). In the classical chord method, \(B=F'(x_0)\).
assumptions_latex: \(\sup_{x\in D}\lVert I-B^{-1}F'(x)\rVert\le q<1\), with the chosen ball invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear convergence with one Jacobian frozen at the initial point.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Newton Local Convergence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-difference Jacobian error adds a scale-times-error term; vanishing scales give superlinear convergence, and error-proportional scales give quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) have a regular zero \(x_*\) and a locally Lipschitz Jacobian. Let \(B_k\) be a finite-difference Jacobian at \(x_k\) with differencing scale \(h_k\), satisfying \(\lVert B_k-F'(x_k)\rVert\le C_hh_k\), and define \(x_{k+1}=x_k-B_k^{-1}F(x_k)\). For sufficiently close \(x_0\) and sufficiently small \(h_k\), the matrices \(B_k\) remain invertible and \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_*\rVert\le C(\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert^2+h_k\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert)\). Hence \(h_k\to0\) gives superlinear convergence, while \(h_k=O(\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert)\) gives quadratic convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x_*)=0\), \(F'(x_*)\) is nonsingular, and \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_*\rVert\le C(\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert^2+h_k\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert)\), with the stated rate consequences.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-difference Newton convergence with iteration-dependent differencing scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Reuse Effects
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusing one Jacobian for m corrections yields outer-cycle order m plus one near a regular root, trading more solves for fewer factorizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) have a regular zero \(x_*\), with a locally Lipschitz Jacobian. For a fixed integer \(m\ge1\), set \(y_{k,0}=x_k\), factor \(F'(x_k)\) once, compute \(y_{k,j+1}=y_{k,j}-F'(x_k)^{-1}F(y_{k,j})\) for \(j=0,\ldots,m-1\), and put \(x_{k+1}=y_{k,m}\). For sufficiently close \(x_0\), the outer iterates converge locally with \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_*\rVert\le C\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert^{m+1}\). Thus reuse reduces Jacobian factorizations while increasing the outer-cycle order from two to \(m+1\), although intermediate corrections use stale derivative information.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x_*)=0\), \(F'(x_*)\) is nonsingular, and \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz.
\(m\ge1\) is fixed and every inner correction uses \(F'(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer-cycle convergence order for repeated corrections using one Jacobian factorization.

notation.meaning: number of corrections per derivative evaluation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Secant and multisecant residual-solving models
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), and define \(s_i=x_{i+1}-x_i\) and \(y_i=F(x_{i+1})-F(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional derivative-free or quasi-Newton local models for square nonlinear systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A secant iteration has the form \[B_ks_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\] where the next Jacobian approximation satisfies at least the newest secant equation \(B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\). A depth-\(m_k\) multisecant model forms \[S_k=[s_{k-m_k},\ldots,s_{k-1}],\qquad Y_k=[y_{k-m_k},\ldots,y_{k-1}]\] and requires \(B_kS_k=Y_k\), or, for an inverse model \(H_k\), requires \(H_kY_k=S_k\). Local secant-multisecant theory studies well-definedness and convergence when \(x_k\to x_*\), \(F(x_*)=0\), and \(F'(x_*)\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A secant method replaces the current Jacobian by a matrix that reproduces one observed residual difference along one step. A multisecant method simultaneously reproduces several stored step–residual differences. Either a direct Jacobian model or an inverse model may be used, and local theory concerns their behavior near a regular root.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For one stored pair, the multisecant equation reduces to \(B_ks_{k-1}=y_{k-1}\).
special_cases_latex: Broyden's rank-one update is a single-secant member.
When the stored columns are linearly dependent, the multisecant constraints may be redundant or inconsistent after regularization.
immediate_consequences_latex: The equations prescribe the action of the model only on the span of the stored steps or residual differences.
boundary_notes: The definition does not choose a unique update when the secant constraints underdetermine the matrix.
Anderson acceleration requires additional coefficient and residual conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Broyden Local Convergence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Good Broyden iterates initialized near a regular root with an accurate nonsingular Jacobian approximation converge locally superlinearly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) have a regular zero \(x_*\), and suppose \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz. Define \(s_k=-B_k^{-1}F(x_k)\), \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\), and \(B_{k+1}=B_k+(y_k-B_ks_k)s_k^{\mathsf T}/(s_k^{\mathsf T}s_k)\). If \(x_0\) is sufficiently close to \(x_*\) and the nonsingular \(B_0\) is sufficiently close to \(F'(x_*)\), then all updates are well defined, \(x_k\to x_*\), and \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_*\rVert/\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert\to0\).
assumptions_latex: \(F(x_*)=0\), \(F'(x_*)\) is nonsingular, and \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz.
\(x_0\) and \(B_0\) are sufficiently close to \(x_*\) and \(F'(x_*)\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local superlinear convergence of the good Broyden Jacobian update.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Good Broyden iteration and its local convergence regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), let \(F(x_*)=0\), and set \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\), \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Good Broyden rank-one Jacobian update near a regular root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Broyden's method is \[B_ks_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\qquad B_{k+1}=B_k+\frac{(y_k-B_ks_k)s_k^T}{s_k^Ts_k}.\] The update is the minimum-Frobenius-norm change to \(B_k\) satisfying \(B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\). Its local convergence regime consists of continuously differentiable residual maps with a nonsingular \(F'(x_*)\), a locally Lipschitz Jacobian, and initial data \(x_0\) and \(B_0\) sufficiently close to \(x_*\) and \(F'(x_*)\), respectively; in that regime the iterates are well defined and converge q-superlinearly to \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Good Broyden updates a Jacobian approximation by the smallest Frobenius-norm rank-one correction that enforces the newest secant equation. Near a regular root with a Lipschitz Jacobian, sufficiently accurate initial point and matrix data define the standard local superlinear regime.
special_cases_latex: For affine \(F\), the exact Jacobian satisfies every secant equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Each correction has rank at most one.
The update need not converge to the full Jacobian in matrix norm for the iterates to converge superlinearly.
boundary_notes: The inverse-Broyden update is a distinct formula.
The local statement requires closeness of both the initial point and initial Jacobian approximation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual–Error Norm Equivalence Along Convergent Broyden Iterates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence-level local equivalence used in the surrounding Broyden convergence discussion; the extract does not independently establish a general neighborhood theorem for every nearby point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose $r(x^*)=0$, $x_k\to x^*$, $r(x_k)=J(x^*)(x_k-x^*)+o\!\left(\|x_k-x^*\|\right)$, and $J(x^*)$ is nonsingular. Then there exist $c,C>0$ and $K$ such that $c\|x_k-x^*\|\leq\|r(x_k)\|\leq C\|x_k-x^*\|$ for all $k\geq K$.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists c,C>0\;\exists K\;\forall k\geq K:\quad c\|x_k-x^*\|\leq\|r(x_k)\|\leq C\|x_k-x^*\|

knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear Secant Convergence Principles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally convergent quasi-Newton method is superlinear precisely when its Jacobian error vanishes along the generated step directions, subject to standard boundedness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable near a regular zero \(x_*\), with \(F'\) locally Lipschitz. Consider \(x_{k+1}=x_k-B_k^{-1}F(x_k)\), where \(B_k\) and \(B_k^{-1}\) remain uniformly bounded and \(x_k\to x_*\) with nonzero steps \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\). Then the Dennis–Moré condition \(\lVert(B_k-F'(x_*))s_k\rVert/\lVert s_k\rVert\to0\) implies \(q\)-superlinear convergence. Under the stated boundedness and local convergence hypotheses, this directional approximation condition is also necessary for \(q\)-superlinear convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x_*)=0\), \(F'(x_*)\) is nonsingular, and \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz.
\(x_k\to x_*\), while \(B_k\) and \(B_k^{-1}\) are uniformly bounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dennis–Moré directional consistency condition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(F(x_*)=0\), let \(F'(x_*)\) be nonsingular, and consider \(x_{k+1}=x_k-B_k^{-1}F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergent quasi-Newton sequences near a regular root; no claim of global convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence \(x_k\to x_*\) with \(x_k\ne x_*\), define \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\). The superlinear secant consistency condition is \[\frac{\|(B_k-F'(x_*))s_k\|}{\|s_k\|}\longrightarrow0.\] Under the stated regular-root assumptions and nonsingularity of the matrices \(B_k\), this condition is equivalent to q-superlinear convergence, \[\frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|}{\|x_k-x_*\|}\longrightarrow0.\] The condition requires asymptotic correctness only along the realized step directions, not convergence of \(B_k\) to \(F'(x_*)\) in matrix norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The central superlinear secant principle is directional consistency: the derivative-model error applied to the actual step must be negligible compared with the step. For an already convergent quasi-Newton sequence at a regular root, this is equivalent to a vanishing successive-error ratio. Full matrix convergence is unnecessary.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The left condition is \((B_k-F'(x_*))s_k=o(\|s_k\|)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\|B_k-F'(x_*)\|\to0\), the directional condition follows whenever \(s_k\ne0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Superlinear convergence can occur even when the model remains inaccurate on directions not sampled by the steps.
boundary_notes: Convergence of \(x_k\) is an explicit premise of the equivalence.
The condition alone does not guarantee that every \(B_k\) is nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x^*$ be a strict local minimum. The iterates have the stated superlinear rate if, for every $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n$ sufficiently close to $x^*$, there exist $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and a constant $C>0$ such that, for every $k\ge N$, \[\lVert x_{k+1}-x^*\rVert\le C\,\lVert x_k-x^*\rVert\,\lVert x_{k-n}-x^*\rVert.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a strict local minimum, every sufficiently close initial point produces iterates whose next error is eventually bounded by a constant times the product of the current error and the error from n iterations earlier.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Anderson mixing as an inverse multisecant step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), define the fixed-point residual \(f(x)=g(x)-x\), and set \(\Delta x_i=x_{i+1}-x_i\), \(\Delta f_i=f(x_{i+1})-f(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Type-II Anderson acceleration with an unconstrained least-squares coefficient problem and finite memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For memory \(m_k\), define \[X_k=[\Delta x_{k-m_k},\ldots,\Delta x_{k-1}],\qquad F_k=[\Delta f_{k-m_k},\ldots,\Delta f_{k-1}].\] Type-II Anderson acceleration chooses \(\gamma_k\in\arg\min_\gamma\|f(x_k)-F_k\gamma\|_2\) and sets \[x_{k+1}=x_k+f(x_k)-(X_k+F_k)\gamma_k.\] When \(F_k\) has full column rank, define \(H_k=-I+(X_k+F_k)(F_k^TF_k)^{-1}F_k^T\). Then \(H_kF_k=X_k\) and the same step is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-H_kf(x_k)\). This identity is the local multisecant–Anderson correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Type-II Anderson acceleration fits the current fixed-point residual by stored residual differences and corrects the unaccelerated step using the same coefficients. With independent stored residual differences, the resulting step equals an inverse quasi-Newton step whose inverse model satisfies all stored multisecant equations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the Moore–Penrose inverse gives \(H_k=-I+(X_k+F_k)F_k^\dagger\) under the corresponding least-squares convention.
special_cases_latex: With one stored pair, the model satisfies a single inverse secant equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Anderson acceleration can be analyzed locally through an inverse multisecant model.
boundary_notes: No supplied source was located for the exact sign convention and matrix identity used here.
Other Anderson variants use constrained affine coefficients, damping, regularization, or different residual signs.
review_flags: Needs a source matching the precise Type-II Anderson convention and induced inverse multisecant matrix.

Multisecant Local Theory
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-rank residual-difference history determines the minimum-change inverse-Jacobian update satisfying all stored secant equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_k=[s_{k-m+1},\ldots,s_k]\) and \(Y_k=[y_{k-m+1},\ldots,y_k]\), where \(s_i=x_{i+1}-x_i\) and \(y_i=F(x_{i+1})-F(x_i)\). If \(Y_k\) has full column rank, the unique matrix minimizing \(\lVert H-H_{k-1}\rVert_F\) subject to the multisecant equations \(HY_k=S_k\) is \(H_k=H_{k-1}+(S_k-H_{k-1}Y_k)Y_k^\dagger\). The associated residual-system step is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-H_kF(x_k)\). Local superlinear convergence requires, in addition to regularity and boundedness, that the approximation error vanish along the generated step subspaces.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and the stored step and residual-difference matrices are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_k=H_{k-1}+(S_k-H_{k-1}Y_k)Y_k^\dagger\) uniquely minimizes the Frobenius change subject to \(H_kY_k=S_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-change inverse-Jacobian representation satisfying multiple secant equations.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The minimum-change multisecant formula is coherent and the representation content kind fits, but no source supports it, and the appended superlinear-convergence sentence does not specify a complete theorem or precise step-subspace condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Anderson Local Theory
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safeguarded Anderson acceleration of a locally contractive fixed-point map converges locally at least linearly when its mixing coefficients remain bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable near a fixed point \(x_*\), and suppose \(\sup_{x\in V}\lVert g'(x)\rVert\le\kappa<1\) on a neighborhood \(V\). At iteration \(k\), choose coefficients \(\alpha_i^{(k)}\) over the retained indices with \(\sum_i\alpha_i^{(k)}=1\), bounded \(\ell_1\)-norm, and minimizing the norm of the affine combination of residuals \(f(x_i)=g(x_i)-x_i\); set \(x_{k+1}=\sum_i\alpha_i^{(k)}g(x_i)\). If a safeguard keeps iterates in \(V\) and accepts the unaccelerated step whenever acceleration fails sufficient residual decrease, then all sufficiently close starts converge locally to \(x_*\) at least linearly.
assumptions_latex: A safeguard retains iterates in \(V\) and falls back to \(g(x_k)\) when necessary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every sufficiently close safeguarded Anderson sequence converges to \(x_*\) at least linearly.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded local convergence for Anderson acceleration of a contractive fixed-point map.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem depends on an undefined sufficient-residual-decrease safeguard and gives no quantitative acceptance condition from which the asserted linear rate follows. A source identifying the exact Anderson variant, safeguard, and rate theorem is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Depth Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory depth is the number of retained residual-step pairs; standard regimes are fixed, bounded variable, full, restarted, and zero memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For iteration index \(k\), let \(m_k\) be the number of previous residual-step pairs used to compute the new multisecant model or Anderson coefficients. The method has depth \(m\) if \(m_k=\min\{m,k\}\); it has bounded variable depth if \(0\le m_k\le m_{\max}<\infty\); it has full memory if \(m_k=k\); and it has restarted memory if indices \(0=k_0<k_1<\cdots\) exist such that \(m_k=k-k_j\) for \(k_j\le k<k_{j+1}\). Depth zero denotes the unaccelerated fixed-point iteration.
assumptions_latex: Each retained pair is generated by an accepted preceding iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_k\) determines the fixed, bounded-variable, full-memory, restarted, or unaccelerated regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies multisecant and Anderson iterations by the number of retained residual-step pairs.

notation.meaning: number of retained pairs at iteration k

review_flags: Exact Anderson–multisecant terminology and admissibility conventions require a dedicated source.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Memory-Depth Regimes leaf and is internally coherent, but Anderson and multisecant depth-counting and restart conventions vary. An authoritative source with a precise locator is required before selecting these conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convergence framework for nonlinear least squares
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), usually \(m\ge n\), and define \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\) and \(J(x)=R'(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares near a stationary local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonlinear least-squares solution is a point \(x_*\in D\) locally minimizing \(\phi\); every differentiable such point satisfies \[J(x_*)^TR(x_*)=0.\] Since \[
abla\phi(x)=J(x)^TR(x),\qquad 
abla^2\phi(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+S(x),\qquad S(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mR_i(x)
abla^2R_i(x),\] local convergence theory classifies iterations \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\) by how their model approximates these two Hessian terms and by whether \(R(x_*)\) is zero, small, or nonzero. Local convergence means that all sufficiently close initial points produce well-defined iterates converging to \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear least squares minimizes one half of the squared residual norm. Its first-order condition is orthogonality of the residual to the Jacobian range. The Hessian splits into a Gauss–Newton term and a residual-weighted second-derivative term, and local convergence regimes are distinguished by the relative importance of these terms and by residual magnitude at the solution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x_*\) is stationary exactly when \(R(x_*)\perp\operatorname{range}J(x_*)\).
special_cases_latex: A zero-residual solution satisfies \(R(x_*)=0\), hence \(S(x_*)=0\).
When \(m=n\) and \(R(x_*)=0\), the problem includes solving a square nonlinear system.
immediate_consequences_latex: Gauss–Newton omits \(S(x)\), whereas full Newton retains it.
boundary_notes: Stationarity alone does not ensure local minimality.
Nonsmooth robust-loss least squares is outside this definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-magnitude regimes for Gauss–Newton
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\), let \(J(x)=R'(x)\), and let \(x_*\) satisfy \(J(x_*)^TR(x_*)=0\) with \(J(x_*)\) of full column rank.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undamped local Gauss–Newton iteration for smooth overdetermined least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Gauss–Newton step is defined by \[J(x_k)^TJ(x_k)p_k=-J(x_k)^TR(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k.\] The residual-magnitude regimes are determined by \(R(x_*)\) and the omitted Hessian term \(S(x_*)=\sum_iR_i(x_*)\nabla^2R_i(x_*)\). The problem is zero-residual when \(R(x_*)=0\), small-residual when the dimensionless quantity \[\rho_*:=\|(J_*^TJ_*)^{-1}S(x_*)\|\] is substantially below one, and large-residual for local Gauss–Newton purposes when this omitted-term measure is not contractive. Zero residual eliminates \(S(x_*)\) and gives the canonical quadratic regime; a nonzero but contractively small omitted term gives a linear leading rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauss–Newton solves the linearized least-squares problem at each iteration. Its local regimes depend not merely on the numerical residual norm but on the size of the residual-weighted second-order Hessian term relative to the Gauss–Newton matrix. Zero residual removes that term, while a small nonzero relative term produces a leading linear contraction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Gauss–Newton step minimizes \(\tfrac12\|R(x_k)+J(x_k)p\|_2^2\).
special_cases_latex: If every residual component is affine, then \(S(x)=0\) identically.
immediate_consequences_latex: Residual magnitude affects the rate through curvature-weighted residuals, not through \(\|R(x_*)\|\) alone.
boundary_notes: The labels small and large are model-relative rather than universal numerical thresholds.
Rank deficiency invalidates the displayed inverse and requires a pseudoinverse or regularization.

notation.meaning: relative magnitude of the omitted Hessian term

knowledge_statements.title: Gauss–Newton Zero-Residual Theory
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a zero-residual solution with a Lipschitz, full-column-rank Jacobian, undamped Gauss–Newton is locally quadratically convergent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), let its Jacobian \(J\) be locally Lipschitz, and suppose \(F(x_*)=0\) and \(J(x_*)\) has full column rank. For \(x_k\) sufficiently close to \(x_*\), define the Gauss–Newton step by \(J(x_k)^{\mathsf T}J(x_k)s_k=-J(x_k)^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\) and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). Then the step is uniquely defined, the iterates remain local, and constants \(C>0\) and \(\delta>0\) exist such that \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\le C\|x_k-x_*\|^2\) whenever \(\|x_k-x_*\|\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-column-rank, zero-residual local convergence for nonlinear least squares.

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4 Gauss-Newton Method p. 138

knowledge_statements.title: Gauss–Newton Small-Residual Theory
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a full-column-rank stationary point, Gauss–Newton has a local error bound consisting of a linear term proportional to the terminal residual and a quadratic term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), and let \(J(x)=DF(x)\). Suppose \(J(x_*)^{\mathsf T}F(x_*)=0\), \(J(x_*)\) has full column rank, and \(J\) is locally Lipschitz. For the undamped Gauss–Newton iteration, constants \(C_1,C_2,\delta>0\) exist such that, whenever \(\|x_k-x_*\|\le\delta\), \[\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\le C_1\|F(x_*)\|\,\|x_k-x_*\|+C_2\|x_k-x_*\|^2.\] Consequently, if \(C_1\|F(x_*)\|<1\), the iteration is locally convergent, with its linear term bounded in proportion to the residual magnitude.
assumptions_latex: \(J(x_*)^{\mathsf T}F(x_*)=0\) and \(J(x_*)\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(e_k=x_k-x_*\), one has \(\|e_{k+1}\|\le C_1\|F(x_*)\|\|e_k\|+C_2\|e_k\|^2\) locally, and local convergence follows if \(C_1\|F(x_*)\|<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local error recurrence showing linear residual influence plus a quadratic error term.

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4 Gauss-Newton Method p. 138

knowledge_statements.title: Gauss–Newton Residual Transition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauss–Newton appears quadratic above the residual-dependent crossover scale, but nonzero terminal residual generally leaves a linear asymptotic term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the small-residual recurrence \(\|e_{k+1}\|\le \rho\|e_k\|+C_2\|e_k\|^2\), where \(\rho=C_1\|F(x_*)\|<1\), the quadratic contribution dominates while \(C_2\|e_k\|\ge\rho\), whereas the residual-controlled linear contribution dominates when \(C_2\|e_k\|\le\rho\). Thus the crossover error scale is \(\|e_k\|\asymp \rho/C_2\). If \(F(x_*)=0\), then \(\rho=0\) and the asymptotic regime is quadratic; for nonzero residual, the asymptotic upper-bound regime is linear unless additional cancellation removes the linearization term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The crossover occurs at \(\|e_k\|\asymp\rho/C_2\); zero residual eliminates the linear term.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the crossover between quadratic and residual-controlled linear behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton local error factor and the quadratic boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local unit-step behavior governed by the residual-weighted Hessian term, without identifying its vanishing solely with zero residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2, write \nabla^2f(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+H(x), and let e_k=x_k-x^*. If x^* is stationary, J is uniformly full column rank near x^*, and the smoothness required for the local expansion holds, including Lipschitz continuity of H near x^*, then a unit Gauss\text{--}Newton step satisfies \|x_k+p_k^{\mathrm{GN}}-x^*\|\le\int_0^1\|[J(x_k)^TJ(x_k)]^{-1}H(x^*+te_k)\|\,\|e_k\|\,dt+O(\|e_k\|^2). Consequently, with \rho_*=\|[J(x^*)^TJ(x^*)]^{-1}H(x^*)\|, the leading local factor is \rho_*; if H(x^*)=0, the linear term vanishes and the local convergence is quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a stationary solution with a uniformly full-rank Jacobian, the leading error factor of a unit Gauss–Newton step is governed by the residual-weighted part of the true Hessian. A small factor predicts rapid local convergence. If that omitted curvature term vanishes, including but not only in zero-residual regimes, the linear error term disappears and convergence is quadratic.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauss–Newton Nonzero-Residual Theory
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonzero-residual stationary point with a full-column-rank Jacobian, Gauss–Newton converges locally linearly when the residual-weighted curvature is sufficiently small relative to the normal matrix in the chosen induced norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), define \(J_*=DF(x_*)\), and suppose \(F(x_*)\ne0\), \(J_*^{\mathsf T}F(x_*)=0\), and \(J_*\) has full column rank. Define \(B_*=J_*^{\mathsf T}J_*\), \(S_*=\sum_{i=1}^m F_i(x_*)\nabla^2F_i(x_*)\), and \(\rho=\|B_*^{-1}S_*\|\) in a fixed compatible induced norm. If \(\rho<1\), then, for every \(q\) satisfying \(\rho<q<1\), a neighborhood of \(x_*\) exists in which the undamped Gauss–Newton map satisfies \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\le q\|x_k-x_*\|\). Hence sufficiently close initial points generate iterates converging q-linearly to \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(q\in(\rho,1)\), the undamped Gauss–Newton iteration is locally contractive with \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\le q\|x_k-x_*\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative criterion for local convergence at a nonzero-residual stationary point.

notation.meaning: norm of the derivative of the Gauss–Newton map at x_*

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonzero-residual Gauss–Newton contraction regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice continuously differentiable and let \(x_*\in D\) satisfy \(J_*^TR(x_*)=0\), where \(J_*=R'(x_*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local undamped Gauss–Newton with a full-column-rank limiting Jacobian and nonzero residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonzero-residual Gauss–Newton regime is defined by \(R(x_*)\ne0\), \(\lambda:=\lambda_{\min}(J_*^TJ_*)>0\), and a constant \(\sigma\ge0\) satisfying \[\|(J(x)-J_*)^TR(x_*)\|_2\le\sigma\|x-x_*\|_2\] locally, with \(\sigma<\lambda\). For every \(c\in(1,\lambda/\sigma)\), sufficiently close initial points generate well-defined Gauss–Newton iterates obeying \[\|e_{k+1}\|_2\le\frac{c\sigma}{\lambda}\|e_k\|_2+\frac{c\alpha\gamma}{2\lambda}\|e_k\|_2^2,\] where \(\|J(x)\|_2\le\alpha\) and \(J\) has Lipschitz constant \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonzero-residual stationary solution, Gauss–Newton has a linear leading error term caused by the interaction between the residual and Jacobian variation. The canonical local contraction condition requires that interaction constant to be smaller than the least eigenvalue of the Gauss–Newton matrix.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Full column rank of \(J_*\) is equivalent to \(\lambda_{\min}(J_*^TJ_*)>0\).
special_cases_latex: When \(R(x_*)=0\), one may take \(\sigma=0\), recovering the zero-residual quadratic regime.
immediate_consequences_latex: The asymptotic linear factor can be made arbitrarily close to \(\sigma/\lambda\) through the choice of \(c>1\).
boundary_notes: If \(\sigma\ge\lambda\), this local contraction statement supplies no convergence guarantee.
Nonzero residual does not by itself preclude convergence; its curvature interaction must be measured.

notation.meaning: smallest eigenvalue of the limiting Gauss–Newton matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Levenberg–Marquardt Local Theory
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a full-rank zero-residual solution, Levenberg–Marquardt is quadratic when damping vanishes at least proportionally to the residual; persistent damping generally yields linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) have a locally Lipschitz Jacobian near \(x_*\), with \(F(x_*)=0\) and \(J(x_*)\) of full column rank. Define \(s_k\) by \((J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k+\lambda_k I)s_k=-J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\), where \(\lambda_k\ge0\), and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). If \(\lambda_k\le c\|F(x_k)\|\) locally, then sufficiently close initial points produce well-defined iterates converging quadratically to \(x_*\). If merely \(\lambda_k\to\bar\lambda>0\), the damping term generally leaves only linear local convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\le C\|x_k-x_*\|^2\) for sufficiently large local iterates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing-damping local convergence in the full-rank zero-residual regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Levenberg–Marquardt regularized least-squares step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\), with residual \(r_k=R(x_k)\), Jacobian \(J_k=R'(x_k)\), and trust-region radius \(\Delta_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares using the Gauss–Newton trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Levenberg–Marquardt step is a solution of \[\min_p\ \tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|p\|_2\le\Delta_k.\] Equivalently, a feasible \(p_k\) is a solution exactly when there exists \(\lambda_k\ge0\) such that \[(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)p_k=-J_k^Tr_k,\qquad \lambda_k(\Delta_k-\|p_k\|_2)=0.\] Local Levenberg–Marquardt theory studies accepted iterates \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\) near a stationary solution. When the trust region eventually becomes inactive, \(\lambda_k=0\) and the method takes Gauss–Newton steps, inheriting the corresponding zero- or nonzero-residual local rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Levenberg–Marquardt minimizes the norm of the linearized residual inside a trust region. Its step is equivalently characterized by a nonnegative diagonal regularization parameter and a complementarity condition. Once the trust region is inactive near a solution, the step becomes the ordinary Gauss–Newton step.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The regularized step minimizes \(\|J_kp+r_k\|_2^2+\lambda_k\|p\|_2^2\) for fixed \(\lambda_k\ge0\).
special_cases_latex: If the Gauss–Newton step lies strictly inside the trust region, then \(\lambda_k=0\).
If \(J_k\) is rank deficient and \(\lambda_k>0\), the regularized coefficient matrix is positive definite.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive regularization makes the step uniquely defined even when \(J_k^TJ_k\) is singular.
boundary_notes: The step definition alone does not specify the acceptance ratio or radius-update rule.
Damped formulations that prescribe \(\lambda_k\) directly are nearby variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Least-Squares Local Theory
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under constant rank and zero residual, pseudoinverse Gauss–Newton reduces the distance to the local solution manifold quadratically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), let \(F(x_*)=0\), and suppose \(J(x)\) has constant rank \(r<n\) throughout a neighborhood of \(x_*\). Then the local solution set \(S=\{x:F(x)=0\}\) is a smooth manifold of dimension \(n-r\). For the minimum-norm Gauss–Newton iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-J(x_k)^\dagger F(x_k)\), constants \(C,\delta>0\) exist such that \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\le C\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^2\) whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is locally an \((n-r)\)-dimensional manifold and \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\le C\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-rank, zero-residual convergence of the minimum-norm Gauss–Newton correction.
review_flags: A dedicated constant-rank Gauss–Newton source is required to confirm the stated manifold-distance estimate.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The constant-rank manifold conclusion is standard, but the quadratic pseudoinverse Gauss–Newton distance estimate requires a dedicated source. The estimate must also explicitly restrict x_k to a neighborhood of x_*, since small distance to S alone does not ensure that the iterate lies where the local constant-rank assumptions hold.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(J_k=R'(x_k)\), and suppose \(\operatorname{rank}J_k=r_k<n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linearized least-squares geometry when the Jacobian lacks full column rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rank-deficient Gauss–Newton step set is \[\mathcal P_k:=\arg\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\|J_kp+R(x_k)\|_2.\] It is generally non-singleton and equals \[\mathcal P_k=-J_k^\dagger R(x_k)+\ker J_k.\] The canonical minimum-norm step is \(p_k^{\min}=-J_k^\dagger R(x_k)\), characterized by \(p_k^{\min}\perp\ker J_k\). Rank-deficient local theory must therefore distinguish convergence to a particular solution from convergence to a solution set and must replace inversion of \(J_k^TJ_k\) by a pseudoinverse, rank-revealing factorization, or positive regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the residual Jacobian loses column rank, the linearized least-squares subproblem still has solutions but normally has infinitely many. Every solution is the minimum-norm pseudoinverse step plus an arbitrary null-space vector. Selecting the orthogonal minimum-norm member provides a canonical step, while local convergence may naturally be measured relative to a solution manifold.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The minimum-norm step satisfies \(J_k^T(J_kp_k^{\min}+R(x_k))=0\) and \(p_k^{\min}\in\operatorname{range}J_k^T\).
special_cases_latex: If \(J_k\) has full column rank, \(J_k^\dagger=(J_k^TJ_k)^{-1}J_k^T\).
Levenberg–Marquardt regularization replaces \(J_k^TJ_k\) by \(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The unregularized normal equations do not uniquely determine a step when \(J_k\) is column-rank deficient.
boundary_notes: Constant-rank and error-bound assumptions are needed for specific local convergence rates.
A numerical rank threshold is algorithm-dependent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-to-solution error bound at a singular root
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(S:=\{x\in D:F(x)=0\}\), and let \(x_*\in S\) be singular in the sense that \(F'(x_*)\) is not invertible as a square linear map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local residual error bounds near singular or nonisolated solutions; no particular iterative method is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local Hölder residual error bound of exponent \(\theta\in(0,1]\) holds at \(x_*\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|F(x)\|^\theta\qquad\text{for every }x\in B_\delta(x_*)\cap D.\] The case \(\theta=1\) is a local Lipschitz error bound, also called metric subregularity of the residual mapping at \((x_*,0)\). For an isolated solution, \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\|x-x_*\|\) after shrinking the neighborhood. Singular-root error-bound theory uses this inequality as the replacement for the inverse-Jacobian estimate unavailable at a singular root.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular-root error bound controls distance to the local solution set by a power of the residual norm. The exponent one gives the Lipschitz form associated with metric subregularity; smaller exponents allow weaker Hölder control. For an isolated root, distance to the solution set reduces locally to ordinary error relative to that root.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an isolated root, the bound is \(\|x-x_*\|\le\kappa\|F(x)\|^\theta\).
special_cases_latex: \(\theta=1\) gives a Lipschitz residual error bound.
For a nonisolated solution, distance must be measured to the set \(S\), not to one selected point.
immediate_consequences_latex: A residual stopping tolerance \(\|F(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) implies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\varepsilon^\theta\) inside the error-bound neighborhood.
boundary_notes: No supplied authoritative locator was found for this singular-root error-bound definition.
An error bound does not by itself specify a Newton-type iteration or its convergence rate.

Convergence Degradation at Multiple Roots
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton's method becomes linearly convergent at a root of multiplicity m, with asymptotic factor (m−1)/m instead of a quadratic rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=(x-a)^m h(x)\), where \(m\ge2\), \(h\) is continuously differentiable near \(a\), and \(h(a)\ne0\). For ordinary Newton iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\), with \(e_k=x_k-a\), one has \(e_{k+1}=((m-1)/m)e_k+O(e_k^2)\). Hence the simple-root quadratic rate degrades to q-linear convergence with asymptotic factor \((m-1)/m\). The factor approaches one as \(m\) increases, quantifying worsening local convergence at increasingly multiple roots.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar Newton convergence at a root of known multiplicity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of quadratic Newton convergence at a scalar multiple root
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:I\subseteq\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be sufficiently differentiable near \(x_*\), and suppose \(x_*\) is a root of multiplicity \(m\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical scalar exact Newton iteration at an isolated multiple root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Multiplicity \(m\) means that locally \[f(x)=(x-x_*)^m g(x),\qquad g(x_*)\ne0.\] For the unmodified Newton iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\), convergence degradation at the multiple root is the replacement of the simple-root quadratic rate by the asymptotic q-linear relation \[x_{k+1}-x_*=\frac{m-1}{m}(x_k-x_*)+O((x_k-x_*)^2).\] Equivalently, for a convergent sequence not terminating finitely, \[\frac{|x_{k+1}-x_*|}{|x_k-x_*|}\longrightarrow\frac{m-1}{m}.\] The singularity \(f'(x_*)=0\) is therefore the mechanism that invalidates the regular-root quadratic estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar root has multiplicity at least two when the function factors into the corresponding power of the root displacement times a nonzero local factor. Standard Newton iteration then loses the simple-root quadratic rate and becomes asymptotically linear, with contraction factor determined by the multiplicity.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Multiplicity \(m\) is equivalently characterized by \(f(x_*)=f'(x_*)=\cdots=f^{(m-1)}(x_*)=0\) and \(f^{(m)}(x_*)\ne0\), when these derivatives exist.
special_cases_latex: For a double root, the asymptotic factor is \(1/2\).
For \(m=1\), the displayed degradation factor is zero and the simple-root quadratic regime is recovered under standard smoothness.
immediate_consequences_latex: As \(m\) increases, the factor \((m-1)/m\) approaches one and the unmodified iteration becomes progressively slower.
boundary_notes: The inspected source explicitly supports linear degradation at a multiple root but does not state the full multiplicity-factor formula at the cited passage.
Multivariate multiplicity and singular Jacobians require additional algebraic or geometric definitions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplicity-Resolving Reformulation of a Singular Residual System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(x_*\in U\) satisfy \(F(x_*)=0\), and suppose \(F'(x_*)\) is rank deficient. Let \(S=F^{-1}(0)\), and let \(Z\) be a finite-dimensional auxiliary space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, exact, local residual equations. The definition covers augmentation, deflation, lifting, or multiplicity-aware transformations through their common projection and regularity properties; it does not prescribe one construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local multiplicity-resolution method for \(F(x)=0\) at \(x_*\) is a construction of a residual map \(\Phi:V\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times Z\to\mathbb R^{n+\dim Z}\) and a point \(z_*\in Z\) such that \(\Phi(x_*,z_*)=0\), the projected transformed zero set agrees locally with the original zero set, \[\pi_x\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(0)\cap V_0\bigr)=S\cap U_0,\] for neighborhoods \(V_0\) of \((x_*,z_*)\) and \(U_0\) of \(x_*\), and the transformed root is regular, \[D\Phi(x_*,z_*):\mathbb R^n\times Z\to\mathbb R^{n+\dim Z}\quad\text{is nonsingular}.\] A multiplicity-resolution method family is a collection of such constructions indexed by admissible auxiliary data, with every transformed solution projecting to an original solution and every original solution sufficiently near \(x_*\) admitting at least one local lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplicity-resolution method replaces a singular residual equation by an augmented local equation whose zeros project exactly onto the nearby zeros of the original equation. The augmented residual vanishes at a lift of the target root and has a nonsingular derivative there. Thus ordinary regular-root solvers may be applied in the lifted variables without introducing spurious projected roots locally. Different choices of auxiliary variables or equations constitute different members of the family.
equivalent_formulations_latex: When the local lift is unique, there is a map \(z=z(x)\) on \(S\cap U_0\) such that \(\Phi^{-1}(0)\cap V_0=\{(x,z(x)):x\in S\cap U_0\}\).
special_cases_latex: For an isolated scalar root, multiplicity correction may be represented without auxiliary variables by a transformed scalar residual having a nonzero derivative at the root.
Deflation methods are included when auxiliary null-vector or derivative constraints reduce the nullity until the final augmented Jacobian is nonsingular.
immediate_consequences_latex: The inverse function theorem applies to the square transformed residual at \((x_*,z_*)\).
Any sufficiently accurate transformed solution has a projection belonging to the original local solution set.
boundary_notes: The stated regularity condition excludes transformations that merely rescale the residual while leaving the augmented Jacobian singular.

For a positive-dimensional solution manifold, a square nonsingular augmentation generally selects or parametrizes a local lift; additional geometric conditions are needed to preserve the entire manifold.
No inspected source in the supplied corpus established this exact umbrella definition across all multiplicity-resolution constructions.

Deflation Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiate a scalar function m−1 times to turn a multiplicity-m root into a simple root, then apply Newton's method with standard stopping tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a scalar function \(f\), an initial point \(x_0\), and a known multiplicity \(m\ge2\) of a nearby root \(a\). Form the derivative-deflated function \(g=f^{(m-1)}\). Provided \(f\) is \(m+1\) times continuously differentiable and \(f^{(m)}(a)\ne0\), the root \(a\) is simple for \(g\). Iterate \(x_{k+1}=x_k-g(x_k)/g'(x_k)\) while \(|g(x_k)|>\varepsilon_g\) and \(|x_{k+1}-x_k|>\varepsilon_x\); otherwise output \(x_{k+1}\). For sufficiently close \(x_0\), this deflated Newton iteration converges quadratically to \(a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Newton iteration on \(g=f^{(m-1)}\) converges quadratically to the simple root \(a\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative deflation for a scalar root whose multiplicity is known.

A source covering derivative and system-level deflation families should be added.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity-Correction Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying the Newton correction by the known root multiplicity restores quadratic local convergence for a sufficiently smooth scalar problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a differentiable scalar function \(f\), an initial point \(x_0\), and the known multiplicity \(m\ge2\) of a nearby root \(a\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(x_{k+1}=x_k-m f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\). Stop and output \(x_{k+1}\) when both \(|f(x_{k+1})|\le\varepsilon_f\) and \(|x_{k+1}-x_k|\le\varepsilon_x\). If \(f(x)=(x-a)^m h(x)\), with \(h(a)\ne0\) and sufficient smoothness, then for \(x_0\) sufficiently close to \(a\), the corrected iteration satisfies \(|x_{k+1}-a|\le C|x_k-a|^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Correction Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sufficiently smooth scalar multiple-root problem, using the wrong multiplicity leaves linear convergence inside the contraction interval, loses guaranteed contraction at twice the true multiplicity, and makes the root repelling beyond that boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=(x-a)^m h(x)\), where \(m\ge2\), \(h\) is continuously differentiable near \(a\), and \(h(a)\ne0\). Apply the correction \(x_{k+1}=x_k-qf(x_k)/f'(x_k)\) with a fixed estimate \(q>0\), and define \(e_k=x_k-a\). Then \(e_{k+1}=(1-q/m)e_k+O(e_k^2)\). Quadratic convergence occurs when \(q=m\). If \(0<q<2m\) and \(q\ne m\), the iteration is locally q-linear with asymptotic factor \(|1-q/m|\). If \(q=2m\), the leading factor is \(-1\), so local contraction is not guaranteed; if \(q>2m\), the root is locally repelling.
assumptions_latex: The correction uses a fixed estimate \(q>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local factor is \(1-q/m\); contraction requires \(0<q<2m\), and quadratic cancellation occurs when \(q=m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar boundary for Newton correction using an incorrect multiplicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Theory near Nonisolated Solutions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-rank nonisolated zero lies on a smooth solution manifold, and the residual locally bounds distance to that manifold, not to a unique point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), with \(F(x_*)=0\), and suppose \(J(x)\) has constant rank \(r<n\) on a neighborhood of \(x_*\). Then, after restricting the neighborhood if necessary, the zero set \(S=\{x:F(x)=0\}\) is a continuously differentiable embedded manifold of dimension \(n-r\). Moreover, constants \(\kappa,\delta>0\) exist such that \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|F(x)\|\) whenever \(\|x-x_*\|\le\delta\). Thus residual decay controls distance to the solution set, but does not select a unique solution point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-rank manifold structure and residual error bound near a nonisolated zero.
review_flags: The constant-rank manifold claim is standard, but the residual error bound needs an exact authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Solution-Set Framework at a Nonisolated Zero
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed, let \(F:X\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuous, and let \(S=\{x\in X:F(x)=0\}\). Fix \(\bar x\in S\) that is nonisolated, meaning every neighborhood of \(\bar x\) contains a point of \(S\setminus\{\bar x\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local theory in which error and convergence are measured relative to the full solution set rather than to a distinguished isolated solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local solution-set theory near the nonisolated solution \(\bar x\) uses the set distance \[d_S(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\inf_{z\in S}\|x-z\|\] as its primal error and a residual \(r(x)\ge 0\) satisfying \(r(x)=0\iff x\in S\) locally. It has a Lipschitz residual-to-solution bound at \(\bar x\) when there exist \(\delta>0\) and \(\kappa>0\) such that \[\|x-\bar x\|\le\delta,\ x\in X\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r(x).\] For the equation residual, \(r(x)=\|F(x)\|\). More generally, for a set-valued residual \(\Psi\) with \(S=\Psi^{-1}(0)\), take \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\Psi(x))\); the displayed condition is metric subregularity at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a nonisolated solution, distance to one selected solution is not the intrinsic error because iterates may approach another nearby member of the solution set. The local theory therefore measures error by distance to the whole zero set. A residual is locally adequate when small residual forces small distance to that set through a uniform Lipschitz inequality. For a set-valued equation this property is metric subregularity at the reference solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|F(x)\|\) for every \(x\in X\cap\mathbb B(\bar x,\delta)\) in the residual-bounded regime.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(S=\Psi^{-1}(0)\), the condition is \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\Psi^{-1}(0))\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\Psi(x))\) locally at \(\bar x\).
If a sequence satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\to0\), its convergence is to the solution set even when \(x_k\) does not converge to the selected reference point \(\bar x\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\bar x\) is isolated in \(S\), then locally \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\|x-\bar x\|\), recovering the usual pointwise error measure.
If \(S\) is a smooth solution manifold, \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) measures the normal error and ignores harmless tangential displacement along the manifold.
immediate_consequences_latex: A stopping test based on \(r(x)\) certifies proximity to some local solution, not necessarily to \(\bar x\).
Any estimate \(r(x_{k+1})\le q r(x_k)\) with \(q<1\), together with the error bound, yields a corresponding residual-controlled estimate for distance to \(S\).
boundary_notes: Metric subregularity does not imply local uniqueness of the solution.
Pointwise convergence of iterates requires additional control of tangential motion along a nonisolated solution set.
The definition does not assert differentiability or manifold structure of \(S\).

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-to-Solution Error Bounds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a solution, distance to the zero set is bounded by a constant times a power of the residual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(S=F^{-1}(0)\), and let \(\bar x\in S\). A local residual-to-solution error bound of order \(\theta\in(0,1]\) holds at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq \kappa\lVert F(x)\rVert^{\theta}
\quad\text{whenever}\quad \lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\delta.
\]
The case \(\theta=1\) is a local Lipschitz error bound; \(\theta<1\) permits the weaker behavior typical near singular roots.
assumptions_latex: Distance and residual are measured using fixed finite-dimensional norms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-to-Solution Error Bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(S\subseteq T\) be a nonempty target solution set, and define \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\inf_{z\in S}\|x-z\|\). Let \(r_S:T\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfy \(r_S(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic error bounds. Both Lipschitz and Hölder residual bounds are distinguished, and locality may be defined by residual size or by proximity to a reference solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The residual \(r_S\) defines a residual-to-solution Lipschitz error bound for \(S\) relative to \(T\) if there is \(c>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c\,r_S(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in T.\] It is a local error bound in the residual sense if the same inequality holds on \(T_\varepsilon=\{x\in T:r_S(x)\le\varepsilon\}\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\). At a reference point \(\bar x\in S\), it is local in the neighborhood sense if there are \(c,\delta>0\) such that the inequality holds for every \(x\in T\cap\mathbb B(\bar x,\delta)\). A Hölder error bound of exponent \(\theta\in(0,1]\) replaces the right-hand side by \(c\,r_S(x)^\theta\). For a residual equation \(F(x)=0\), the canonical choice is \(S=F^{-1}(0)\) and \(r_S(x)=\|F(x)\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual-to-solution error bound is an inequality that turns a computable residual into an upper bound on the generally unknown distance to the solution set. A global bound holds throughout the test set. A local bound holds either where the residual is sufficiently small or in a neighborhood of a reference solution. The linear power gives a Lipschitz error bound; a fractional power gives a Hölder error bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c\,r_S(x)\) on the specified test region, or \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c\,r_S(x)^\theta\) in the Hölder variant.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(S=F^{-1}(0)\), the Lipschitz form is \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(0))\le c\|F(x)\|\).
For a set-valued mapping \(\Psi\), take \(r_S(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\Psi(x))\) and \(S=\Psi^{-1}(0)\).
special_cases_latex: When \(S=\{x_*\}\) locally, the bound becomes \(\|x-x_*\|\le c\,r_S(x)\).
For an affine system \(Ax=b\), a suitable constant gives \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\{z:Az=b\})\le c\|Ax-b\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(r_S(x_k)\to0\) and the iterates remain in the bound's region, then \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\to0\).
A residual termination threshold \(r_S(x)\le\tau\) certifies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c\tau\) in the Lipschitz case.
boundary_notes: The reverse inequality is not part of the definition.
An error bound does not by itself guarantee existence or uniqueness of a nearest solution.
The numerical size of the modulus \(c\) matters for certification even when existence of some modulus is known.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Structured Nonlinear Least-Squares Method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice continuously differentiable and define \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\). Let \(J(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be the residual Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth, finite-dimensional, unconstrained nonlinear least squares. Constrained least-squares variants are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonlinear least-squares method is residual-structured if, at each iterate \(x_k\), it constructs a step from \(r_k=r(x_k)\), \(J_k=J(x_k)\), and optionally approximations to the residual-curvature term \[S(x_k)=\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x_k)
abla^2r_i(x_k),\] exploiting \[
abla f(x_k)=J_k^Tr_k,\qquad 
abla^2f(x_k)=J_k^TJ_k+S(x_k).\] Its local model has the form \[m_k(p)=	frac12\|r_k\|^2+p^TJ_k^Tr_k+	frac12p^T igl(J_k^TJ_k+C_k igr)p,\] where \(C_k=0\) gives Gauss–Newton or Levenberg–Marquardt structure, \(C_k=S(x_k)\) gives full Newton structure, and an updated \(C_k\approx S(x_k)\) gives a structured quasi-Newton method. A method family is determined by the rule for \(C_k\), the step constraint or regularization, the inner linear least-squares solve, and the acceptance mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear least-squares methods minimize one half of the squared norm of a smooth residual vector. Their defining feature is use of the exact gradient and the decomposition of the Hessian into the positive-semidefinite Gauss–Newton term plus a residual-weighted second-derivative term. The principal families omit, retain, or approximate the latter term and combine the resulting model with line-search, trust-region, damping, or regularization controls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method model uses \(J_k^Tr_k\) as its linear term and \(J_k^TJ_k+C_k\) as its residual-structured curvature matrix.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Gauss–Newton model is exactly \(m_k(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|^2\).
The stationarity residual for the least-squares objective is \(\|J(x)^Tr(x)\|\).
special_cases_latex: If every \(r_i\) is affine, then \(S(x)=0\) and the Gauss–Newton curvature equals the exact Hessian.
If \(r(x_*)=0\), then \(S(x_*)=0\) even when the residual components are nonlinear.
immediate_consequences_latex: The matrix-vector product \(J_k^TJ_kv\) can be evaluated as \(J_k^T(J_kv)\) without explicitly forming the normal matrix.
Residual structure permits linear least-squares solvers to compute Gauss–Newton-type steps.
boundary_notes: This definition does not include nonsmooth robust losses that are not expressed as ordinary squared residuals.
Bounds or nonlinear constraints require a constrained optimization framework.
Derivative-free residual methods require separate models because \(J_k\) is unavailable.

notation.meaning: Residual-weighted second-derivative contribution to the Hessian.
Exact or approximate correction to Gauss–Newton curvature.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hybrid and Structured Quasi-Newton Constructions for Large-Residual Least Squares
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the omitted-curvature failure boundary, a residual-regime switching construction, and the Dennis–Gay–Welsch structured secant update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2$, $\nabla^2f(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m r_j(x)\nabla^2r_j(x)$. When the residual-weighted second-order term is significant, the Gauss–Newton model omits significant curvature and Gauss–Newton or Levenberg–Marquardt has only linear asymptotic convergence in the described large-residual regime. A switching construction accepts a sufficiently successful Gauss–Newton step and resets $B_k$ to $J_k^TJ_k$; otherwise it computes a step from $B_k$ with a line search, after which a BFGS-like update is applied in either case. The construction eventually takes Gauss–Newton steps in the zero-residual case and eventually reduces to BFGS in the nonzero-residual case. A structured alternative sets $B_k=J_k^TJ_k+S_k$ and imposes $S_{k+1}s=y^\sharp$, where $s=x_{k+1}-x_k$ and $y^\sharp=J_{k+1}^Tr_{k+1}-J_k^Tr_{k+1}$. With $y=J_{k+1}^Tr_{k+1}-J_k^Tr_k$, the displayed symmetric update is $S_{k+1}=S_k+\frac{(y^\sharp-S_ks)y^T+y(y^\sharp-S_ks)^T}{y^Ts}-\frac{(y^\sharp-S_ks)^Ts}{(y^Ts)^2}yy^T$. To prevent the correction from interfering near a zero-residual solution, replace $S_k$ on the right-hand side by $\tau_kS_k$, where $\tau_k=\min\!\left(1,\frac{|s^Ty^\sharp|}{|s^TS_ks|}\right)$, and omit the correction when the Gauss–Newton model produces a sufficiently good step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large residuals can make the Hessian term omitted by Gauss–Newton significant, limiting the residual-structured methods to linear asymptotic convergence. One hybrid switches between successful Gauss–Newton steps and BFGS-like steps. A structured alternative approximates only the omitted Hessian term with a symmetric secant update, scales that correction near zero-residual solutions, and suppresses it when the Gauss–Newton model is already adequate.
assumptions_latex: y^Ts\neq0\text{ for the displayed structured update}
s^TS_ks\neq0\text{ when the displayed scaling ratio is evaluated}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{k+1}s=y^\sharp,\qquad B_k=J_k^TJ_k+S_k;\quad \text{the switching construction eventually uses Gauss--Newton in the zero-residual case and BFGS in the nonzero-residual case}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth nonlinear least-squares objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a smooth nonlinear least-squares objective. The condition m at least n is a standing assumption of the source chapter, not an intrinsic requirement of nonlinear least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $r_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be smooth for $j=1,\ldots,m$. A nonlinear least-squares objective has the form
\[
f(x)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^m r_j(x)^2,
\]
where each $r_j$ is called a residual. In the setting of this source chapter, $m\ge n$ is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth nonlinear least-squares objective is one half the sum of the squares of smooth scalar residual functions. Each scalar function is called a residual. The source chapter additionally assumes that the number of residuals is at least the number of variables.
assumptions_latex: r_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is smooth for }j=1,\ldots,m
m\ge n\text{ is the source chapter's standing assumption}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton Method Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\), and write \(r_k=r(x_k)\) and \(J_k=J(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth, finite-dimensional, unconstrained nonlinear least squares. The family permits exact or approximate solution of the linearized least-squares subproblem and separate global step control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Gauss–Newton method generates a trial direction \(p_k\) by minimizing, exactly or approximately, the linearized residual model \[\ell_k(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|_2^2.\] An exact minimizer satisfies the normal equations \[J_k^TJ_kp_k=-J_k^Tr_k.\] The next iterate is formed as \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), where \(s_k\) is either \(p_k\), a line-search scaling \(\alpha_kp_k\), or a controlled approximation obtained from a trust region or regularized version of \(\ell_k\). The family is characterized by replacing the exact Hessian \(J_k^TJ_k+\sum_i r_i(x_k)\nabla^2r_i(x_k)\) with the Gauss–Newton matrix \(J_k^TJ_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gauss–Newton family minimizes a nonlinear sum of squares by repeatedly solving the linear least-squares problem obtained from the first-order model of the residual vector. Its curvature approximation is the Jacobian Gram matrix. Exact normal-equation, QR, SVD, iterative, line-search, trust-region, and damped implementations belong to the family when they retain this linearized-residual model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p}\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|^2\), equivalently \(J_k^T(J_kp_k+r_k)=0\), for an exact Gauss–Newton direction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exact direction solves \(J_k^TJ_kp_k=-J_k^Tr_k\).
The quadratic model is \(f(x_k)+p^T\nabla f(x_k)+\tfrac12p^TJ_k^TJ_kp\).
special_cases_latex: If \(J_k\) has full column rank, the exact Gauss–Newton direction is unique.
If \(J_k\) is rank deficient, the linearized least-squares problem remains solvable but may have multiple minimizers; the minimum-norm minimizer is \(-J_k^\dagger r_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For an exact direction, \(p_k^T\nabla f(x_k)=-\|J_kp_k\|^2\le0\).
The step can be computed without explicitly forming \(J_k^TJ_k\).
boundary_notes: The family omits the residual-curvature term and therefore differs from full Newton least squares.
A raw full step need not be globally convergent; acceptance control is a separate component.
Normal equations can square the condition number, so the defining equations do not prescribe their direct numerical solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Model Decrease
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the improvement available from the model within a ball centered at the current point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{E}_1\to\mathbb{R} and \psi:\mathbb{E}_1\times\mathbb{E}_1\to\mathbb{R}. For x\in\mathbb{E}_1 and r>0, define
\Delta_r(x)=f(x)-\min\left\{\psi(x;y):y\in\mathbb{E}_1,\ \lVert y-x\rVert\leq r\right\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local model decrease at a point and radius is the current objective value minus the minimum model value attainable within the closed radius-r ball around that point.
