knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tail estimates for the modified Gauss–Newton process
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For the iterates and quantities defined by the modified Gauss–Newton algorithm under Assumption 4.4.2.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(k\ge 0\) and \(r>0\), the modified Gauss--Newton iterates satisfy
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\ge \frac{L_0}{2}\sum_{i=k}^{\infty}r_{M_i}^2(x_i)\ge \frac{L_0}{2}\sum_{i=k}^{\infty}r_{2L}^2(x_i),
\]
and
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\ge r^2\sum_{i=k}^{\infty}M_i\chi\!\left(\frac{\Delta_r(x_i)}{M_i r^2}\right)\ge 2Lr^2\sum_{i=k}^{\infty}\chi\!\left(\frac{\Delta_r(x_i)}{2Lr^2}\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every iterate and for every positive radius, the objective gap bounds two tails of modified Gauss–Newton residual and progress measures, including their uniform-parameter counterparts.

\(F\), \(f\), \(L_0\), \(L\), \(M_i\), \(r_M\), \(\Delta_r\), and \(\chi\) satisfy the definitions and Assumption 4.4.2 used by the process.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratically Regularized Modified Gauss–Newton Iterate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the iterate and associated radius, regularized model value, and decrement for the modified Gauss–Newton construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let M>0 and x\in\mathcal{F}. Choose
V_M(x)\in\operatorname*{Argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{E}_1}\left\{\psi(x;y)+\frac{M}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\},
where the auxiliary objective is convex in y and \operatorname*{Argmin} denotes its global minimizers. Define
r_M(x)=\lVert V_M(x)-x\rVert,\qquad
f_M(x)=\psi(x;V_M(x))+\frac{M}{2}r_M^2(x),\qquad
\delta_M(x)=f(x)-f_M(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive regularization parameter and a feasible point, a modified Gauss–Newton iterate is any global minimizer of the convex Gauss–Newton model plus a quadratic displacement penalty. Its step radius, regularized model value, and model decrement are defined by the displayed formulas.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local quadratic contraction of the modified Gauss–Newton update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convergence near a nondegenerate zero-residual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^*\in\mathcal L(f(x_0))\) satisfy \(F(x^*)=0\) and
\[
\sigma:=\sigma_{\min}(F'(x^*))>0.
\]
If \(x_k\in\mathcal L(f(x_0))\) and
\[
\|x_k-x^*\|\le \frac{2}{L}\frac{\sigma\gamma_\phi}{3+5\gamma_\phi},
\]
then the modified Gauss--Newton update obeys \(x_{k+1}\in\mathcal L(f(x_0))\) and
\[
\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|\le \frac{3(1+\gamma_\phi)L\|x_k-x^*\|^2}{2\gamma_\phi\bigl(\sigma-L\|x_k-x^*\|\bigr)}\le \|x_k-x^*\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within the stated neighborhood of a nondegenerate zero-residual solution, one modified Gauss–Newton update remains in the initial level set and contracts the error with an explicit quadratic bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_\phi\) is as defined for the modified Gauss--Newton process.
\(x_{k+1}\) is produced by Algorithm 4.4.1 under Assumption 4.4.2 and the cited process definitions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic regularity and limit points of modified Gauss–Newton iterates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence consequences for the sequence generated by the modified Gauss–Newton process under its standing assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\{x_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\) is generated by Algorithm 4.4.1 under its standing assumptions, then
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}\|x_k-x_{k+1}\|=0,\qquad \lim_{k\to\infty}\Delta_r(x_k)=0.
\]
Consequently, the set \(X^*\) of limit points of \(\{x_k\}\) is connected, and every \(\bar x\in X^*\) satisfies \(\Delta_r(\bar x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modified Gauss–Newton iterates are asymptotically regular, their progress measure tends to zero, their limit-point set is connected, and every limit point has zero progress measure.
assumptions_latex: \(\{x_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\) is generated by the modified Gauss--Newton Algorithm 4.4.1.
The standing definitions and Assumption 4.4.2 of the process hold.
\(X^*\) denotes the set of limit points of \(\{x_k\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-iteration global rate for Algorithm 4.4.1 under its three stated assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Assumptions 4.4.1--4.4.3 hold, and let \(\{x_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\) be generated by Algorithm 4.4.1. For every \(k\), if \(f(x_k)\ge \frac{\sigma^2}{2L}\gamma_\phi^2\), then \(f(x_{k+1})\le f(x_k)-\frac{\sigma^2}{4L}\gamma_\phi^2\); otherwise, \(f(x_{k+1})\le \frac{L}{\sigma^2\gamma_\phi^2}f(x_k)^2\le \frac12 f(x_k)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity of the Regularized Model Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes how the optimal regularized model value and the selected step radius vary with the positive regularization parameter at a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed x, let
f_M(x)=\min_{y\in\mathbb{E}_1}\left\{\psi(x;y)+\frac{M}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\},\qquad M>0.
Then M\mapsto f_M(x) is concave. Moreover,
\frac{d}{dM}f_M(x)=\frac12 r_M^2(x),
and hence M\mapsto \frac12 r_M^2(x) is decreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed point, the minimum regularized model value is concave in the positive quadratic-regularization parameter. Its derivative is one half of the squared modified Gauss–Newton step radius, so that squared radius decreases as the parameter increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\mapsto f_M(x)\text{ is concave},\qquad \frac{d}{dM}f_M(x)=\frac12 r_M^2(x),\qquad M\mapsto\frac12r_M^2(x)\text{ is decreasing}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global stationarity of line-search Gauss–Newton
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of the nonlinear least-squares gradient to zero under uniform full rank and Wolfe step lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2 and \mathcal L=\{x\mid f(x)\le f(x_0)\}. Suppose \mathcal L is bounded, every r_j is Lipschitz continuously differentiable on a neighborhood \mathcal N of \mathcal L, and there is \gamma>0 such that \|J(x)z\|\ge\gamma\|z\| for all x\in\mathcal N and z\in\mathbb R^n. If x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}, where J_k^TJ_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}=-J_k^Tr_k and \alpha_k satisfies the Wolfe conditions, then \lim_{k\to\infty}J_k^Tr_k=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the initial level set is bounded, the residuals have Lipschitz-continuous derivatives nearby, the Jacobian remains uniformly full column rank there, and Gauss–Newton uses Wolfe line-search steps, then the gradients J-transpose-r converge to zero.
assumptions_latex: f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2,\quad \mathcal L=\{x\mid f(x)\le f(x_0)\}\text{ is bounded}
\alpha_k\text{ satisfies the Wolfe conditions denoted by (3.6)}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity condition for global-rate analysis of the modified Gauss–Newton process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-Model Lower Bound for the Regularized Decrement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the modified Gauss–Newton decrement using the best model decrease in an arbitrary positive-radius neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every x\in\mathbb{E}_1, r>0, and M>0,
\delta_M(x)\geq Mr^2\,\chi\!\left(\frac{\Delta_r(x)}{Mr^2}\right),
where
\chi(t)=\begin{cases}t-\frac12,&t\geq1,\\[2pt]\frac12t^2,&0\leq t\leq1.\end{cases}
For fixed x and r, the right-hand side is a decreasing function of M.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any point, positive radius, and positive regularization parameter, the modified Gauss–Newton decrement is bounded below by the stated piecewise function of the normalized local model decrease. With the point and radius fixed, this lower bound decreases as the regularization parameter increases.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solvability bound from dual nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general finite-dimensional linear-operator result used in the Gauss–Newton analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2\) be linear and suppose \(\sigma_{\min}(A^*)>0\). Then, for every \(b\in\mathbb E_2\), there exists \(x(b)\in\mathbb E_1\) such that
\[
Ax(b)=b,\qquad \|x(b)\|\le \frac{\|b\|}{\sigma_{\min}(A^*)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the adjoint of a linear operator has positive smallest singular value, every right-hand side is attainable, with a solution norm bounded by the reciprocal singular value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton direction from a linearized residual model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a generalized Gauss–Newton search direction using the first-order residual model and a properly chosen local-neighborhood constraint.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize every residual at the current point and minimize the merit function of the linearized residual vector over increments whose trial point lies in a properly chosen neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composite residual merit objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a residual-composite minimization model and records the standard squared-Euclidean merit choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For residual functions \(f_i:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\) and a merit function \(\phi:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\phi(u)\ge 0\) and \(\phi(u)=0\iff u=0\), define \(f(x)=\phi(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x))\) and consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb E}f(x)\). A standard choice is \(\phi(u)=\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^m(u^{(i)})^2\), whose squared form supports a smoother objective than the unsquared norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual problem may minimize a nonnegative merit function of the residual vector, where the merit vanishes exactly when all residuals vanish. The standard squared Euclidean merit is the sum of squared residuals and is chosen for its favorable smoothness.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Gauss–Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration minimizes the linearized residual in least squares and takes the resulting full step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a continuously differentiable residual \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), minimize \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\). From \(x_0\), at iteration \(k\) form \(J_k=F'(x_k)\) and compute any minimizer
\[
p_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in\mathbb{R}^n}\tfrac12\lVert F(x_k)+J_kp\rVert_2^2.
\]
If \(J_k\) has full column rank, this is equivalently \((J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k)p_k=-J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\). Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\), and stop when a prescribed residual, gradient, or step tolerance is met.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the iterates.
The linearized least-squares subproblem has a selected minimizer at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undamped Gauss–Newton iteration for smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of F at the current iterate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Line-Search Gauss–Newton Iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\) with continuously differentiable \(r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\). At \(x_k\), set \(r_k=r(x_k)\), \(J_k=J(x_k)\), and assume \(J_k\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical deterministic Gauss–Newton with an exact direction and line-search step length; trust-region, regularized, and inexact-inner-solve variants are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The classical Gauss–Newton method computes the unique direction \(p_k^{GN}\) from \[J_k^TJ_kp_k^{GN}=-J_k^Tr_k\] and updates \[x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k^{GN},\qquad \alpha_k\in(0,1].\] The step length is selected by a standard line search applied to \(f\), commonly to satisfy Armijo decrease or Wolfe conditions. Because \(J_k\) has full column rank, \(J_k^TJ_k\) is positive definite; whenever \(J_k^Tr_k\ne0\), \[(p_k^{GN})^T\nabla f(x_k)=-\|J_kp_k^{GN}\|^2<0,\] so the direction is a strict descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical method solves the Gauss–Newton normal equations exactly and globalizes the resulting descent direction with a scalar line search. Full column rank makes the direction unique. A unit step is allowed when accepted by the line search, while shorter steps protect the iteration away from a local solution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p_k^{GN}=\operatorname*{argmin}_p\|J_kp+r_k\|^2\).
A QR factorization of \(J_k\) may solve the same exact linear least-squares subproblem without forming \(J_k^TJ_k\).
special_cases_latex: With \(\alpha_k=1\), the iteration is the undamped classical Gauss–Newton method.
For a square nonsingular \(J_k\), the direction also satisfies \(J_kp_k^{GN}=-r_k\), coinciding with the Newton step for the residual equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: An Armijo backtracking line search is well-defined whenever the direction is strict descent.
The iteration terminates at a first-order stationary point when \(J_k^Tr_k=0\).
boundary_notes: Rank-deficient Jacobians fall outside this classical unique-direction definition.
The line search controls only the outer step; it does not define an inexact inner solve.
The method does not include Levenberg–Marquardt regularization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Gauss–Newton step and its least-squares representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Gauss–Newton for smooth nonlinear least squares, including its model, descent condition, and standard computational realizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For f(x)=	frac12\|r(x)\|^2 with Jacobian J(x), the Gauss	ext{--}Newton direction p_k^{\mathrm{GN}} satisfies J_k^T J_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}=-J_k^Tr_k and equivalently minimizes 	frac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2. It replaces 
abla^2f(x_k)=J_k^TJ_k+\sum_{j=1}^m r_j(x_k)
abla^2r_j(x_k) by J_k^TJ_k. If \operatorname{rank}J_k=n and 
abla f_k
e0, then (p_k^{\mathrm{GN}})^T
abla f_k=-\|J_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}\|^2<0. The subproblem may be solved directly from J_k by QR, SVD, or iterative products with J_k and J_k^T; when m is large, J^TJ and J^Tr may instead be accumulated residual by residual. A line search commonly selects \alpha_k using Armijo or Wolfe conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gauss–Newton step minimizes the squared norm of the linearized residual, or equivalently solves its normal equations. Its matrix is the Hessian approximation J-transpose-J, which omits the residual-weighted second derivatives and is especially accurate when residuals are small or nearly affine. With a full-column-rank Jacobian and nonzero gradient, the step is a strict descent direction. It can be computed by direct or iterative least-squares methods, with residual-wise accumulation available when storing a large Jacobian is undesirable, and is commonly globalized by an Armijo or Wolfe line search.
assumptions_latex: r_j\in C^1;\text{ second-order comparison additionally requires }r_j\in C^2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k^{\mathrm{GN}}\in\arg\min_p\tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2,\quad J_k^TJ_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}=-J_k^Tr_k,\quad (p_k^{\mathrm{GN}})^T\nabla f_k=-\|J_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}\|^2<0\text{ under the stated rank and nonstationarity conditions}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Step-Controlled Gauss–Newton Method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\), and let \(\ell_k(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|^2\) be the Gauss–Newton model at \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained least squares. The definition concerns outer-step magnitude and acceptance, independently of how accurately the linearized subproblem is solved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Gauss–Newton step-control method chooses a trial step from the Gauss–Newton model and restricts or scales it before acceptance. In a line-search member, \[p_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_p\ell_k(p),\qquad s_k=\alpha_kp_k,\quad \alpha_k\in(0,1],\] with \(\alpha_k\) satisfying a prescribed sufficient-decrease or curvature condition for \(f\). In a trust-region member, \[s_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|p\|\le\Delta_k}\ell_k(p),\qquad \Delta_k>0,\] and acceptance is governed by the ratio \[\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)}{\ell_k(0)-\ell_k(s_k)}.\] The iterate is \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) when the trial is accepted and remains \(x_k\) otherwise; the control parameter is updated from the acceptance information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family retains the Gauss–Newton residual model while controlling how far the outer iteration moves. Line-search methods scale an unconstrained direction. Trust-region methods constrain the step while solving the model. In both cases acceptance compares predicted behavior with the actual nonlinear objective, separating step control from the choice of inner linear algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted displacement is either \(s_k=\alpha_kp_k\) for a line search or a minimizer of \(\ell_k\) over \(\|p\|\le\Delta_k\) for a trust region.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a spherical trust region, a solution satisfies \((J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_k I)s_k=-J_k^Tr_k\), \(\lambda_k\ge0\), and \(\lambda_k(\Delta_k-\|s_k\|)=0\).
special_cases_latex: The full-step method is obtained when \(\alpha_k=1\) is accepted.
Levenberg–Marquardt trust-region steps are the spherical trust-region specialization.
immediate_consequences_latex: Step control can reject or shorten a direction even when the linearized subproblem is solved exactly.
When the unconstrained Gauss–Newton step lies inside an inactive trust region, the trust-region step equals that unconstrained step.
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe Armijo, Wolfe, or trust-region thresholds numerically.
Regularization imposed for inverse-problem stability is distinct from globalization-only damping.
Accuracy conditions for iterative inner solves belong to the inner-solve family.

notation.meaning: Ratio of actual to predicted reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Damped Gauss–Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gauss–Newton direction is shortened by a positive damping factor and accepted only under a specified safeguard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\), choose \(x_0\). At iteration \(k\), compute a Gauss–Newton direction \(p_k\) satisfying \(J_k^{\mathsf T}J_kp_k=-J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\), or equivalently minimizing the linearized residual. Select a damping factor \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) by a prescribed acceptance rule and set
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k.
\]
Terminate when the chosen residual, gradient, or step test holds. If \(p_k\) is not a descent direction for \(f\), the method must reject it or replace it with a safeguarded direction.
assumptions_latex: A Gauss–Newton direction or a safeguarded replacement can be computed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauss–Newton with a scalar damping factor applied to the computed direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search Gauss–Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtracking shortens a descent Gauss–Newton direction until the least-squares objective satisfies sufficient decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\) and \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\). Compute a direction \(p_k\) from the Gauss–Newton model, requiring \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\). Fix \(c\in(0,1)\) and \(\beta\in(0,1)\). Choose the smallest integer \(j_k\geq0\) for which
\[
f(x_k+\beta^{j_k}p_k)\leq f(x_k)+c\beta^{j_k}g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k.
\]
Set \(\alpha_k=\beta^{j_k}\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). Stop under a prescribed residual, gradient, or step tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the trial points.
The selected direction satisfies \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\) whenever \(g_k\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted step satisfies the Armijo inequality and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauss–Newton direction combined with Armijo backtracking on the least-squares objective.

notation.meaning: gradient of the least-squares objective at x_k

knowledge_statements.title: Step-Acceptance Safeguards
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonstationary iterate, a nonzero trial direction must make a uniformly acute angle with the negative gradient, and its step length is accepted only after it produces sufficient objective decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\), let \(g_k=F'(x_k)^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\), and let \(p_k\neq0\) be a trial direction at an iterate for which \(g_k\neq0\). Fix \(\sigma\in(0,1]\) and \(c\in(0,1)\). A descent-angle safeguard requires
\[
g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\leq-\sigma\lVert g_k\rVert_2\lVert p_k\rVert_2.
\]
A step length \(\alpha_k>0\) is accepted only if
\[
f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\leq f(x_k)+c\alpha_k g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k.
\]
If either test fails, the trial is shortened, rejected, or replaced by a nonzero direction satisfying the descent-angle test.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable at the current iterate and at every trial point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted trial satisfies \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\leq-\sigma\lVert g_k\rVert_2\lVert p_k\rVert_2\) and \(f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\leq f(x_k)+c\alpha_k g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent-angle and sufficient-decrease safeguards for a trial Gauss–Newton step.

notation.meaning: least-squares gradient at the current iterate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact and Inexact Gauss–Newton Inner Solves
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At an outer iterate \(x_k\), let \(r_k\in\mathbb R^m\), \(J_k\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(g_k=J_k^Tr_k\). The Gauss–Newton inner problem is \(\min_p\tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inner linear algebra for Gauss–Newton models, including rank-aware direct solvers and residual-controlled iterative solvers; outer acceptance is not specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Gauss–Newton inner-solve method returns \(p_k\) satisfying either the exact optimality condition \[J_k^T(J_kp_k+r_k)=0\] or an inexact condition \[\|J_k^T(J_kp_k+r_k)\|\le\eta_k\|g_k\|,\qquad 0\le\eta_k<1.\] Direct members compute an exact or rank-revealing minimizer using QR or SVD. Normal-equation members solve \(J_k^TJ_kp=-g_k\). Matrix-free iterative members access \(J_kv\) and \(J_k^Tw\) and stop when the displayed forcing condition is met. If the exact minimizer is nonunique, the canonical rank-aware selection is the minimum-norm solution \(p_k=-J_k^\dagger r_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner-solve family consists of numerical methods for the linear least-squares model inside a Gauss–Newton iteration. Exact QR, SVD, and normal-equation methods satisfy the model optimality condition. Iterative methods may terminate early when the normal residual is small relative to the current gradient. Matrix-free variants need only products with the Jacobian and its transpose.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step satisfies \(\|J_k^T(J_kp_k+r_k)\|\le\eta_k\|J_k^Tr_k\|\), with \(\eta_k=0\) for an exact solve.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exact condition is the normal equation \(J_k^TJ_kp_k=-J_k^Tr_k\).
The augmented least-squares residual is \(J_kp_k+r_k\), whose orthogonality to \(\operatorname{range}(J_k)\) characterizes an exact minimizer.
special_cases_latex: QR avoids explicitly forming the normal matrix when \(J_k\) has full column rank.
SVD supplies a minimum-norm solution and rank information when \(J_k\) is deficient.
Krylov methods evaluate \(J_k^TJ_kv\) through successive products \(J_kv\) and \(J_k^T(J_kv)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The inner solver can be changed without altering the outer Gauss–Newton model.
A decreasing forcing sequence \(\eta_k\) demands progressively more accurate inner solutions.
boundary_notes: The forcing inequality alone does not define an outer globalization rule.
Direct normal equations may be less stable than QR or SVD for ill-conditioned Jacobians.
Preconditioning changes the inner numerical method but not the target linearized least-squares problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Gauss–Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal equations need only be solved until their residual is a controlled fraction of the outer gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\), set \(J_k=F'(x_k)\), \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\), and \(B_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k\). Choose a forcing number \(\eta_k\in[0,1)\) and compute \(p_k\) such that
\[
\lVert B_kp_k+g_k\rVert_2\leq\eta_k\lVert g_k\rVert_2.
\]
Apply the prescribed full-step or globalization rule to obtain \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\), where \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\). Stop when the outer residual, gradient, or step tolerance is met; the inner solve may terminate as soon as the displayed inequality holds.
assumptions_latex: An inner solver can produce a step satisfying the forcing inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauss–Newton iteration whose normal equations are solved only to a forcing tolerance.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard relative normal-equation residual formulation of inexact Gauss–Newton

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The relative normal-equation residual is a plausible and precise inexact Gauss–Newton forcing condition, and the algorithm fits the leaf, but no authoritative locator supports this particular residual criterion or its use as the inner stopping rule.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inexact Gauss–Newton construction for large sparse problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate Gauss–Newton system solution when exact Jacobian or normal-equation factorization is expensive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When n and m are large, J(x_k) is sparse, and exact factorization of J_k or J_k^TJ_k is expensive, an inexact Gauss\text{--}Newton variant is obtained by applying an inexact Newton construction with \nabla^2f(x_k) replaced by J_k^TJ_k. The approximation satisfies J_k^TJ_k\succeq0, which simplifies the resulting inexact algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For large sparse nonlinear least-squares problems, an inexact Gauss–Newton method applies the approximate-solve pattern of inexact Newton to the positive-semidefinite matrix J-transpose-J, avoiding the need to compute every step by exact factorization.
assumptions_latex: n\text{ and }m\text{ are large and }J(x_k)\text{ is sparse}
\text{exact factorization of }J_k\text{ or }J_k^TJ_k\text{ is comparatively expensive}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla^2f(x_k)\text{ in an inexact Newton construction is replaced by }J_k^TJ_k\succeq0\text{ to obtain an inexact Gauss\text{--}Newton variant}.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Gauss–Newton Solves
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An iterative linear solver computes the Gauss–Newton step from Jacobian and adjoint-Jacobian products, stopping at an outer-prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At outer iterate \(x_k\), define \(J_k=F'(x_k)\) and \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\). Starting from an inner guess \(p_k^{(0)}\), apply an iterative linear solver to
\[
J_k^{\mathsf T}J_kp=-g_k,
\]
using products \(v\mapsto J_kv\) and \(w\mapsto J_k^{\mathsf T}w\), optionally with a fixed positive-definite preconditioner. Terminate at the first inner index \(t_k\) satisfying the prescribed normal-equation residual tolerance, set \(p_k=p_k^{(t_k)}\), globalize if required, and output \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\).
assumptions_latex: The actions of \(J_k\) and \(J_k^{\mathsf T}\) are available.
The inner stopping rule is specified and attainable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted outer step uses the first inner iterate meeting the prescribed linear residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Krylov realization of a Gauss–Newton step using normal-operator products.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Krylov implementation of the Gauss–Newton normal equations

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The matrix-free iterative normal-equation realization is mathematically coherent and appropriately classified as an algorithm, but the record has no source for the Krylov implementation, preconditioning qualification, or first-iterate stopping convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Solve Accuracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner solves may use a fixed relative tolerance, a tolerance tending to zero, or one scaled to an outer optimality residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an inexact Gauss–Newton step satisfy
\[
\lVert J_k^{\mathsf T}J_kp_k+J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\rVert_2
\leq \eta_k\lVert J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\rVert_2.
\]
The inner accuracy is uniformly relative if \(0\leq\eta_k\leq\bar\eta<1\); asymptotically exact if \(\eta_k\to0\); and rate-matched of order \(q>0\) if \(\eta_k=O(\lVert J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\rVert_2^q)\). These predicates classify inner stopping policies independently of the particular iterative linear solver used to meet them.
assumptions_latex: The outer gradient \(J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\) is defined for every generated iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence \((\eta_k)\) belongs to the uniformly relative, asymptotically exact, or rate-matched regime according to the stated predicate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forcing-number regimes distinguishing fixed, vanishing, and rate-matched inner accuracy.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: forcing-sequence taxonomy adapted from inexact Newton-type methods

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The fixed, vanishing, and rate-matched forcing predicates are precise, but their presentation as Gauss–Newton inner-accuracy regimes—especially the rate-matched condition based on the least-squares gradient—requires an authoritative inexact Gauss–Newton source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Levenberg–Marquardt Method Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\) with differentiable \(r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\). At \(x_k\), write \(r_k=r(x_k)\), \(J_k=J(x_k)\), and choose \(\lambda_k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained nonlinear least squares with isotropic quadratic damping or its equivalent spherical trust-region formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Levenberg–Marquardt step \(p_k^{LM}\) satisfies \[(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_k I)p_k^{LM}=-J_k^Tr_k.\] Equivalently, for \(\lambda_k>0\), \[p_k^{LM}=\operatorname*{argmin}_p\left\{\tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2+\tfrac{\lambda_k}{2}\|p\|^2\right\}.\] In the trust-region interpretation, \(p_k^{LM}\) solves \[\min_{\|p\|\le\Delta_k}\tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2\] for a multiplier \(\lambda_k\ge0\) satisfying \(\lambda_k(\Delta_k-\|p_k^{LM}\|)=0\). A Levenberg–Marquardt method family specifies how \(\lambda_k\) or \(\Delta_k\) is selected and updated, how the regularized linear system is solved, and how the trial step is accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Levenberg–Marquardt adds a nonnegative multiple of the identity to the Gauss–Newton normal matrix. The same step minimizes a Tikhonov-regularized linearized residual and, with the appropriate multiplier, solves a spherical Gauss–Newton trust-region problem. Family members differ in parameter updates, inner solvers, scaling, and acceptance tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_k I)p_k^{LM}=-J_k^Tr_k\) with \(\lambda_k\ge0\), together with the parameter rule defining the family member.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p_k^{LM}\) minimizes \(\tfrac12\|[J_k;\sqrt{\lambda_k}I]p+[r_k;0]\|^2\).
For the trust-region form, \(\|p_k^{LM}\|\le\Delta_k\) and \(\lambda_k(\Delta_k-\|p_k^{LM}\|)=0\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\lambda_k=0\) and the unconstrained Gauss–Newton step is admissible, the method reduces to Gauss–Newton.
As \(\lambda_k\) becomes large, the step becomes small and approaches a scaled negative-gradient direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: For every \(\lambda_k>0\), the coefficient matrix is positive definite even when \(J_k\) is rank deficient.
The augmented least-squares formulation permits QR-based solution without explicitly forming \(J_k^TJ_k\).
boundary_notes: General diagonal scaling replaces \(\lambda_k I\) by \(\lambda_kD_k^TD_k\) and is a nearby variant.
A fixed damping parameter does not by itself specify a globally convergent algorithm.
Regularization for noisy inverse problems requires parameter rules beyond ordinary globalization.

notation.meaning: Levenberg–Marquardt damping parameter or trust-region multiplier.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block elimination for orthogonal-distance-regression LM steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exploits the diagonal perturbation blocks in the residual Jacobian to avoid solving the full $(n+m)$-variable normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For residuals
\[
r_j=w_j[\phi(x;t_j+\delta_j)-y_j],\quad j=1,\ldots,m,
\qquad r_{m+j}=d_j\delta_j,\quad j=1,\ldots,m,
\]
the Jacobian has the block form
\[
J(x,\delta)=\begin{bmatrix}\widehat J&V\\0&D\end{bmatrix},
\]
where $V,D\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ are diagonal and $\widehat J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$. The Levenberg–Marquardt normal equations are
\[
\begin{bmatrix}\widehat J^T\widehat J+\lambda I&\widehat J^TV\\V\widehat J&V^2+D^2+\lambda I\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}p_x\\p_\delta\end{bmatrix}
=-\begin{bmatrix}\widehat J^T\widehat r_1\\V\widehat r_1+D\widehat r_2\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Whenever $V^2+D^2+\lambda I$ is nonsingular, its diagonal structure permits direct elimination of $p_\delta$, leaving an $n\times n$ system for $p_x$; $p_\delta$ is then recovered by diagonal solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The orthogonal-distance residual Jacobian consists of a model-derivative block and diagonal blocks associated with observation perturbations. In a Gauss–Newton or Levenberg–Marquardt step, a nonsingular diagonal lower-right block can be eliminated directly, reducing the full normal equations to a system involving only the model-parameter step.
assumptions_latex: \phi\text{ is differentiable with respect to }x\text{ and }t
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{bmatrix}\widehat J^T\widehat J+\lambda I&\widehat J^TV\\V\widehat J&V^2+D^2+\lambda I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p_x\\p_\delta\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}\widehat J^T\widehat r_1\\V\widehat r_1+D\widehat r_2\end{bmatrix}\ \text{reduces by block elimination to an }n\times n\text{ system for }p_x.

knowledge_statements.title: Damped Gauss–Newton Interpretations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Levenberg–Marquardt damping is both quadratic step regularization and a positive diagonal shift of the Gauss–Newton normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), a point \(x\), its Jacobian \(J=F'(x)\), and \(\lambda>0\), the damped Gauss–Newton step is the unique vector
\[
p_\lambda=\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in\mathbb{R}^n}
\left\{\tfrac12\lVert F(x)+Jp\rVert_2^2+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert p\rVert_2^2\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, it is the unique solution of
\[
(J^{\mathsf T}J+\lambda I)p_\lambda=-J^{\mathsf T}F(x).
\]
Thus damping is simultaneously Tikhonov regularization of the linearized least-squares problem and a positive shift of the Gauss–Newton normal matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regularized least-squares minimizer equals the solution of \((J^{\mathsf T}J+\lambda I)p=-J^{\mathsf T}F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Levenberg–Marquardt step as regularized linearized least squares and a shifted normal-equation solve.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Damped Gauss–Newton Interpretations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r_k\in\mathbb R^m\), \(J_k\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(\lambda_k>0\). Define \(g_k=J_k^Tr_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact isotropic damping of a smooth Gauss–Newton model at one iteration; parameter-update algorithms are not fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The damped Gauss–Newton step is the unique vector \(p_k(\lambda_k)\) characterized by any of the equivalent conditions \[(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)p_k=-g_k,\] \[p_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_p\left\{\tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2+\tfrac{\lambda_k}{2}\|p\|^2\right\},\] or \[p_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_p\tfrac12\left\|\begin{bmatrix}J_k\\ \sqrt{\lambda_k}I\end{bmatrix}p+\begin{bmatrix}r_k\\0\end{bmatrix}\right\|^2.\] It is also the solution of a spherical Gauss–Newton trust-region problem with radius \(\Delta_k=\|p_k(\lambda_k)\|\) and active multiplier \(\lambda_k\). Thus damping may be interpreted as Hessian regularization, penalization of step norm, augmented linear least squares, or an implicit trust-region restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A damped Gauss–Newton step has four interchangeable mathematical views: a shifted normal equation, a quadratic penalty on step length, an augmented least-squares problem, and an active spherical trust-region solution. These interpretations define the same exact step for a positive damping parameter, although they suggest different parameter-selection and numerical-solution procedures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All displayed formulations have the same unique minimizer \(p_k(\lambda_k)\) when \(\lambda_k>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The trust-region KKT conditions are \((J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)p_k=-g_k\), \(\|p_k\|\le\Delta_k\), and \(\lambda_k(\Delta_k-\|p_k\|)=0\).
The shifted normal matrix equals the Gram matrix of the augmented operator: \(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI=[J_k;\sqrt{\lambda_k}I]^T[J_k;\sqrt{\lambda_k}I]\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\lambda_k=0\), the interpretations reduce to the undamped Gauss–Newton problem, but uniqueness can fail.
For large \(\lambda_k\), \(p_k(\lambda_k)\) approaches \(-g_k/\lambda_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive damping makes the inner quadratic strongly convex.
QR factorization of the augmented matrix avoids forming the shifted normal matrix explicitly.
boundary_notes: The equivalence is stated for isotropic Euclidean damping; scaled norms require replacing \(I\) appropriately.
The correspondence between \(\lambda_k\) and \(\Delta_k\) is iteration-specific.
Directly updating \(\lambda_k\) and updating \(\Delta_k\) are algorithmically different despite producing equivalent subproblem solutions when matched.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Levenberg–Marquardt Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A least-squares trust-region solution is exactly a damped Gauss–Newton step whose multiplier satisfies feasibility and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(r\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(\Delta>0\). A vector \(p_*\) solves
\[
\min_{\lVert p\rVert_2\leq\Delta}\tfrac12\lVert r+Jp\rVert_2^2
\]
if and only if there exists \(\lambda_*\geq0\) such that
\[
(J^{\mathsf T}J+\lambda_*I)p_*=-J^{\mathsf T}r,
\quad \lVert p_*\rVert_2\leq\Delta,
\quad \lambda_*(\lVert p_*\rVert_2-\Delta)=0.
\]
When \(\lambda_*>0\), the trust-region boundary is active and the step is a Levenberg–Marquardt step with damping parameter \(\lambda_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Trust-region optimality is equivalent to the shifted normal equations, feasibility, and multiplier complementarity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between the least-squares trust-region step and a Levenberg–Marquardt multiplier.

notation.meaning: trust-region multiplier and LM damping parameter

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trust-Region Levenberg–Marquardt Iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\), define the Gauss–Newton model \(m_k(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|^2\) and choose a radius \(\Delta_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained least squares with a spherical trust region and exact subproblem characterization; approximate subproblem solutions require separate accuracy conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region Levenberg–Marquardt method computes \[p_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|p\|\le\Delta_k}\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|^2.\] Equivalently, \(p_k\) is feasible and there exists \(\lambda_k\ge0\) such that \[(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)p_k=-J_k^Tr_k,\qquad \lambda_k(\Delta_k-\|p_k\|)=0.\] It evaluates the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio \[\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+p_k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(p_k)},\] accepts or rejects the trial according to fixed thresholds, and updates \(\Delta_k\) from \(\rho_k\) and whether the boundary was active. If the unconstrained Gauss–Newton minimizer lies inside the trust region, then \(\lambda_k=0\); otherwise \(\lambda_k>0\) and \(\|p_k\|=\Delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trust-region Levenberg–Marquardt method minimizes the linearized residual norm inside a ball. A nonnegative multiplier produces the familiar shifted Gauss–Newton system. The multiplier is zero for an interior Gauss–Newton step and positive for a boundary step. Acceptance and radius adjustment compare the nonlinear objective decrease with the model prediction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trial step satisfies the trust-region subproblem and its multiplier conditions, and the outer method uses \(\rho_k\) to accept the step and update \(\Delta_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The constrained subproblem and the shifted system with complementarity are equivalent exact characterizations.
For \(\lambda_k>0\), the step also minimizes \(\tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2+\tfrac{\lambda_k}{2}\|p\|^2\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\|p_k^{GN}\|<\Delta_k\), then \(p_k=p_k^{GN}\).
If \(J_k\) is rank deficient and \(\lambda_k>0\), the shifted system remains uniquely solvable.
immediate_consequences_latex: A rejected trial changes the radius without changing the iterate.
The trust-region radius controls step length indirectly through the multiplier.
boundary_notes: The precise acceptance and update thresholds are implementation parameters, not part of the mathematical subproblem.
Non-spherical trust regions yield scaled Levenberg–Marquardt systems.
Approximate subproblem minimizers must satisfy an explicit model-decrease condition to inherit standard convergence theory.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trust-region characterization of the Levenberg–Marquardt step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spherical trust-region formulation and shifted normal-equation characterization for nonlinear least squares, including the rank-deficient and boundary cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}, r\in\mathbb R^m, and \Delta>0, a trust-region Levenberg\text{--}Marquardt step solves \min_{\|p\|\le\Delta}\tfrac12\|Jp+r\|^2. A vector p solves this problem if and only if there is \lambda\ge0 such that (J^TJ+\lambda I)p=-J^Tr, \|p\|\le\Delta, and \lambda(\Delta-\|p\|)=0. Let d_{\mathrm{GN}}=\min\{\|q\|:J^TJq=-J^Tr\}. If d_{\mathrm{GN}}<\Delta, a minimum-norm Gauss\text{--}Newton solution is an interior trust-region solution with \lambda=0. If d_{\mathrm{GN}}>\Delta, every trust-region solution has \|p\|=\Delta and \lambda>0. At d_{\mathrm{GN}}=\Delta, a boundary Gauss\text{--}Newton solution with \lambda=0 is possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Levenberg–Marquardt minimizes the Gauss–Newton least-squares model inside a spherical trust region. An unconstrained Gauss–Newton minimizer that fits in the region remains optimal. If no unconstrained minimizer is feasible, the solution lies on the boundary and satisfies a positively shifted normal equation. Equality at the boundary can occur with zero shift, which matters when stating the case split precisely.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global First-Order Convergence of Inexact Trust-Region Levenberg–Marquardt
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives sufficient model-decrease and step-radius conditions under which approximate least-squares trust-region steps converge to first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the trust-region Levenberg–Marquardt scheme with $\eta\in(0,1/4)$. Suppose its level set $\mathcal L$ is bounded and the residual functions $r_j$, $j=1,\ldots,m$, are Lipschitz continuously differentiable on a neighborhood $N$ of $\mathcal L$. If every approximate subproblem step $p_k$ satisfies $m_k(0)-m_k(p_k)\geq c_1\|J_k^Tr_k\|\min\!\left(\Delta_k,\frac{\|J_k^Tr_k\|}{\|J_k^TJ_k\|}\right)$ for a constant $c_1>0$, and $\|p_k\|\leq\gamma\Delta_k$ for a constant $\gamma\geq1$, then $\lim_{k\to\infty}\nabla f(x_k)=\lim_{k\to\infty}J_k^Tr_k=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the trust-region Levenberg–Marquardt scheme with acceptance parameter between zero and one quarter, a bounded level set, and Lipschitz continuously differentiable residuals, approximate subproblem steps converge to first-order stationarity when they provide a uniform Cauchy-type model decrease and stay within a fixed multiple of the trust-region radius.
assumptions_latex: \{x_k,\Delta_k,p_k\}\text{ is generated by the trust-region Levenberg--Marquardt scheme}
r_j\in C^{1,1}(N)\quad(j=1,\ldots,m),\text{ where }N\text{ is a neighborhood of }\mathcal L

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reusable QR Factorization for Changing Levenberg–Marquardt Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the factorization construction, reuse rule, and arithmetic costs for dense tall Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $J=Q\begin{bmatrix}R\\0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\lambda>0$, apply $n(n+1)/2$ Givens rotations to $\begin{bmatrix}R\\0\\\sqrt{\lambda}I\end{bmatrix}$ to obtain $\begin{bmatrix}R_\lambda\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}$. Then $R_\lambda^TR_\lambda=J^TJ+\lambda I$. When $\lambda$ changes, reuse the Householder QR factorization of $J$ and recompute only the Givens transformations and $R_\lambda$, at cost $O(n^3)$ per value of $\lambda$ after an initial $O(mn^2)$ factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First compute a Householder QR factorization of the Jacobian. For each positive regularization parameter, triangularize the stacked matrix containing the old triangular factor and the scaled identity with Givens rotations. The resulting triangular factor factors the regularized normal matrix, while the expensive Jacobian factorization is reused as the parameter changes.
assumptions_latex: J=Q\begin{bmatrix}R\\0\end{bmatrix}\text{ is a Householder QR factorization}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix-Free Inexact Levenberg–Marquardt Method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r_k\in\mathbb R^m\), and suppose routines are available for \(v\mapsto J_kv\) and \(w\mapsto J_k^Tw\) without storing \(J_k\). Let \(g_k=J_k^Tr_k\), \(\lambda_k>0\), and \(0\le\eta_k\le\bar\eta<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Large-scale smooth nonlinear least squares with operator products, an iterative regularized inner solve, and residual-controlled inexactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalable matrix-free Levenberg–Marquardt method returns an approximate step \(\bar p_k\) satisfying \[\|(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)\bar p_k+g_k\|\le\eta_k\|g_k\|.\] The inner iteration evaluates the shifted normal operator only through \[v\longmapsto J_k^T(J_kv)+\lambda_kv,\] or solves the equivalent augmented least-squares problem using products with \(J_k\) and \(J_k^T\). No explicit Jacobian, normal matrix, or factorization is required. The outer method chooses \(\lambda_k\) from actual-versus-predicted reduction and accepts \(\bar p_k\) only when its model decrease and nonlinear decrease meet the prescribed tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-free Levenberg–Marquardt method computes an inexact regularized Gauss–Newton step using only Jacobian-vector and transpose-Jacobian-vector products. A relative linear residual controls inner accuracy. This avoids storing or factoring the Jacobian and makes Krylov or LSQR-type inner methods suitable for large sparse problems.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The augmented operator is \(A_k=[J_k;\sqrt{\lambda_k}I]\), so the inner problem is \(\min_p\tfrac12\|A_kp+[r_k;0]\|^2\).
special_cases_latex: With \(\eta_k=0\), the definition reduces to an exact Levenberg–Marquardt step.
Preconditioned Krylov methods remain matrix-free when the preconditioner can be applied without forming \(J_k^TJ_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Each normal-operator product requires one product with \(J_k\), one with \(J_k^T\), and a scaled vector addition.
Several candidate damping parameters may be explored by iterative regularized least-squares techniques without dense factorizations.
boundary_notes: Finite-difference approximations to operator products introduce an additional derivative error not represented by \(\eta_k\).
Matrix-free operation does not guarantee scalability if products with \(J_k\) or \(J_k^T\) are themselves expensive.
The outer acceptance rule remains necessary; a small linear residual alone does not certify nonlinear progress.

notation.meaning: Relative forcing parameter for the inner solve.

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Scale Levenberg–Marquardt
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large-scale LM uses an iterative preconditioned shifted solve and adjusts damping according to agreement between actual and predicted reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\), choose \(x_0\), damping \(\lambda_k>0\), and an inner tolerance. At iteration \(k\), approximately solve
\[
(J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k+\lambda_k I)p_k=-J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)
\]
with an iterative method, using a positive-definite preconditioner when available. Form the ratio \(\rho_k\) of actual reduction in \(f\) to reduction predicted by the regularized linearized model. Accept \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\) when \(\rho_k\) exceeds a fixed threshold; otherwise retain \(x_k\). Decrease damping after successful steps, increase it after unsuccessful steps, and stop at a prescribed outer tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Products with \(J_k\) and \(J_k^{\mathsf T}\), or an equivalent normal operator, are computable.
The inner solver returns a step meeting the prescribed residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method accepts or rejects \(p_k\) using \(\rho_k\) and updates \(\lambda_k\) according to step success.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inexact, preconditioned Levenberg–Marquardt iteration for problems where dense factorization is impractical.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inexact large-scale Levenberg–Marquardt step rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extraction specifies the inexact-step condition and acceptance mechanism but does not enumerate the assumptions required for its conditional stationary-point convergence claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonlinear least squares with residual $r_k$ and Jacobian $J_k$, choose a constant $\eta\in(0,1)$ and a forcing value $\eta_k\in[0,\eta]$. For a candidate damping parameter $\lambda_k$, compute an inexact step $\bar p_k$ satisfying
\[
\left\|(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_k I)\bar p_k+J_k^Tr_k\right\|\leq \eta_k\|J_k^Tr_k\|.
\]
Use the ratio of actual to predicted decrease to determine step acceptance. Approximate solutions may be computed for several candidate values of $\lambda_k$, with the actual step chosen from the smallest tested $\lambda_k$ whose decrease ratio is satisfactory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large-scale inexact Levenberg–Marquardt method accepts a relative-residual approximate solution of the damped normal equations. Candidate damping values are tested through the actual-to-predicted decrease ratio, and the selected step corresponds to the smallest tested damping value that gives a satisfactory ratio.
assumptions_latex: J_k\text{ is the Jacobian of }r\text{ at the current iterate}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left\|(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_k I)\bar p_k+J_k^Tr_k\right\|\leq\eta_k\|J_k^Tr_k\|,\quad\text{and the selected step uses the smallest tested }\lambda_k\text{ with a satisfactory actual-to-predicted decrease ratio.}

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Levenberg–Marquardt
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-free LM solves the shifted normal equations through Jacobian and adjoint products, without forming either the Jacobian or normal matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iterate \(x_k\), let \(r_k=F(x_k)\) and choose \(\lambda_k>0\). Apply a Krylov solver to the shifted normal equation without assembling \(J_k\) or \(J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k\). For any trial vector \(v\), evaluate the system action as
\[
v\longmapsto J_k^{\mathsf T}(J_kv)+\lambda_kv.
\]
The right-hand side is obtained as \(-J_k^{\mathsf T}r_k\). Stop the inner iteration at the prescribed linear residual tolerance, call the resulting vector \(p_k\), and pass \(p_k\) to the outer LM acceptance and damping-update rule. Output the accepted iterate or retain \(x_k\) after rejection.
assumptions_latex: The products \(J_kv\) and \(J_k^{\mathsf T}w\) are available for arbitrary vectors.
The outer method supplies \(\lambda_k>0\) and an inner stopping tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inner solve uses only the operator \(v\mapsto J_k^{\mathsf T}(J_kv)+\lambda_kv\) and the vector \(-J_k^{\mathsf T}r_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Levenberg–Marquardt implementation using Jacobian-vector and adjoint-Jacobian-vector products only.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard matrix-free Krylov realization of the shifted normal equations

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The operator formula correctly realizes the shifted normal equations using Jacobian-vector and adjoint-Jacobian-vector products, and the algorithm fits the matrix-free leaf. An authoritative source with a specific matrix-free Levenberg–Marquardt or Krylov locator is still required.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Access Requirements
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-free LM needs residual evaluations, Jacobian-vector products, adjoint-Jacobian products, and a Krylov solve for the regularized normal equation; it need not assemble the Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and let \(J(x)=Dr(x)\). At an iterate \(x_k\), a matrix-free Levenberg–Marquardt implementation requires evaluations of \(r(x_k)\), products \(v\mapsto J(x_k)v\), and adjoint products \(w\mapsto J(x_k)^{\mathsf T}w\). Given \(\lambda_k>0\), these oracles determine products with the regularized normal operator by \[v\mapsto J(x_k)^{\mathsf T}J(x_k)v+\lambda_k v.\] Consequently, a Krylov solver can approximately compute \(s_k\) satisfying \[(J(x_k)^{\mathsf T}J(x_k)+\lambda_k I)s_k=-J(x_k)^{\mathsf T}r(x_k)\] without forming or storing \(J(x_k)\) or its normal matrix.
assumptions_latex: The implementation supplies mutually consistent Jacobian and adjoint-Jacobian products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Levenberg–Marquardt step can be computed using operator products alone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal oracle interface for a matrix-free Levenberg–Marquardt step.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the terminal container, and the operator formula is mathematically standard. However, the cited general Levenberg–Marquardt section does not specifically establish the claimed matrix-free oracle interface or its minimality. Moreover, the conclusion says the step can be computed, while the statement only guarantees an approximate Krylov solution. A matrix-free LM source and a correction from necessary to sufficient operator access are required.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularizing Levenberg–Marquardt Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularizing LM damps ill-conditioned Jacobian directions and stops by a discrepancy rule once the residual reaches the noise scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given noisy data \(y^\delta\) with \(\lVert y^\delta-y\rVert\leq\delta\), an initial point \(x_0\), and \(\tau>1\), define \(r_k=F(x_k)-y^\delta\) and \(J_k=F'(x_k)\). While \(\lVert r_k\rVert>\tau\delta\), choose \(\lambda_k>0\), compute \[s_k=-(J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k+\lambda_k I)^{-1}J_k^{\mathsf T}r_k,\] and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). The parameter rule must prevent unstable inversion of small singular directions, and iteration stops at the first index \(k_\delta\) satisfying \(\lVert F(x_{k_\delta})-y^\delta\rVert\leq\tau\delta\); the output is \(x_{k_\delta}\).
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuously differentiable on the relevant level set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned iterate is the first discrepancy-admissible damped Gauss–Newton approximation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrepancy-controlled LM regularization for noisy nonlinear residual equations.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the forward map at the current iterate

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the method container, but the damping rule is described only by the qualitative requirement that it prevent unstable inversion. A regularizing LM algorithm requires a concrete parameter-selection condition and hypotheses connecting it with the discrepancy stopping rule. The cited optimization text is not adequate support for the inverse-problems regularization and discrepancy-principle claims.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularizing Levenberg–Marquardt Iteration for Noisy Equations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:X\to Y\) act between Hilbert spaces, let noisy data \(y^\delta\) satisfy \(\|y^\delta-y\|\le\delta\), and seek a solution of \(F(x)=y\). At \(x_k^\delta\), set \(R_k^\delta=F(x_k^\delta)-y^\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic nonlinear inverse problems with bounded data noise. Regularization is achieved jointly by positive damping, a noise-aware parameter rule, and early stopping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A regularizing Levenberg–Marquardt method computes \(s_k^\delta\) from \[\bigl(F'(x_k^\delta)^*F'(x_k^\delta)+\alpha_kI\bigr)s_k^\delta=-F'(x_k^\delta)^*R_k^\delta,\qquad \alpha_k>0,\] and sets \(x_{k+1}^\delta=x_k^\delta+s_k^\delta\). The parameter \(\alpha_k\) is chosen by a rule tied to the noise level or linearized residual, and the iteration is stopped at an index \(k(\delta)\), commonly the first index satisfying a discrepancy condition \[\|F(x_{k(\delta)}^\delta)-y^\delta\|\le\tau\delta,\qquad \tau>1.\] The method is called regularizing only when its parameter and stopping rules are designed so that noise is not fitted indefinitely and the terminal iterates converge to an exact-data solution as \(\delta\downarrow0\) under the method's stated local assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularizing Levenberg–Marquardt applies a positive shift to each linearized inverse problem and terminates according to the data-noise level. Damping stabilizes ill-conditioned inner equations, while early stopping prevents the outer iteration from fitting noise. The label regularizing therefore refers to the complete parameter-and-stopping mechanism, not merely to adding a positive diagonal shift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}^\delta=x_k^\delta-(F'(x_k^\delta)^*F'(x_k^\delta)+\alpha_kI)^{-1}F'(x_k^\delta)^*R_k^\delta\), terminated by a noise-dependent rule such as \(\|R_{k(\delta)}^\delta\|\le\tau\delta\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The step minimizes \(\tfrac12\|R_k^\delta+F'(x_k^\delta)s\|^2+\tfrac{\alpha_k}{2}\|s\|^2\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\delta=0\), the discrepancy stopping rule is replaced by an exact-data convergence or residual criterion.
In finite dimensions, \(F'(x_k)^*\) is the transpose of the residual Jacobian.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(\alpha_k>0\) makes the linearized normal operator boundedly invertible on a finite-dimensional parameter space.
The stopping index explicitly depends on the noise level.
boundary_notes: Positive damping used solely for globalization is not sufficient to establish regularization.
Convergence as \(\delta\downarrow0\) requires additional assumptions on \(F\), the starting point, and the parameter rule.
No inspected full-text source supplied the exact regularizing scheme and its defining parameter conditions.

notation.meaning: Known upper bound on the data error.
Regularization parameter at the inner linearized problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structured Second-Order Least-Squares Method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice continuously differentiable and \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\). Define \(S(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional unconstrained nonlinear least squares, especially nonzero- or large-residual regimes where Gauss–Newton curvature is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structured second-order least-squares method uses the decomposition \[\nabla^2f(x_k)=J_k^TJ_k+S(x_k)\] and forms a model \[m_k(p)=f(x_k)+p^TJ_k^Tr_k+\tfrac12p^T(J_k^TJ_k+C_k)p,\] where \(C_k\) is either the exact residual-curvature matrix \(S(x_k)\) or an approximation constructed specifically for \(S(x_k)\). A step is obtained by minimizing or approximately minimizing this model within a line-search or trust-region framework. The method is structured because the exactly available Gauss–Newton term \(J_k^TJ_k\) is retained separately rather than approximating the entire Hessian as an undifferentiated matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structured second-order least-squares methods retain the Jacobian Gram matrix and add an exact or approximate correction for the residual-weighted Hessians. They are designed for problems where residuals at the solution are not small enough for Gauss–Newton alone to represent curvature accurately. Full Newton and structured quasi-Newton methods are the principal members.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model curvature has the decomposed form \(B_k=J_k^TJ_k+C_k\) with \(C_k=S(x_k)\) or \(C_k\approx S(x_k)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The correction is \(S(x)=\nabla^2f(x)-J(x)^TJ(x)\).
special_cases_latex: Setting \(C_k=0\) recovers the Gauss–Newton model but leaves the structured second-order subclass.
Setting \(C_k=S(x_k)\) gives the full Newton least-squares model.
Updating \(C_k\) by a residual-specific secant equation gives a structured quasi-Newton member.
immediate_consequences_latex: At a zero-residual solution, \(S(x_*)=0\), so exact and Gauss–Newton curvature coincide at the solution.
For large residuals, retaining or approximating \(S(x_k)\) can represent curvature omitted by Gauss–Newton.
boundary_notes: An ordinary BFGS approximation to the full Hessian is not structured in this sense unless the \(J_k^TJ_k\) component is retained explicitly.
The matrix \(J_k^TJ_k+C_k\) need not be positive semidefinite.
Globalization is required when the structured model is indefinite or inaccurate far from a solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Newton Least-Squares Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-Newton least squares uses both the Gauss–Newton matrix and the residual-weighted second derivatives of all residual components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)\rVert_2^2\), define \(J_k=Dr(x_k)\), \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}r(x_k)\), and \[H_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x_k)\nabla^2 r_i(x_k).\] At iteration \(k\), solve \(H_k s_k=-g_k\), or a regularized version when \(H_k\) is singular or indefinite. Choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) by a globalization rule and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k s_k\). Stop when a prescribed stationarity test such as \(\lVert g_k\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) holds; the output is the final iterate.
assumptions_latex: The linear system or its regularized replacement is solved to the required accuracy.
The step acceptance rule ensures the chosen trial step is admissible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each unregularized step is a Newton step for the exact least-squares objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-Hessian Newton iteration for finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares.

notation.meaning: exact Hessian of the least-squares objective

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full Newton Method for Nonlinear Least Squares
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let each residual \(r_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable and define \(f(x)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2\). At \(x_k\), let \(g_k=J_k^Tr_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact second-order, finite-dimensional, smooth unconstrained nonlinear least squares. A globalization mechanism may modify or constrain the Newton step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The full Newton least-squares curvature is \[H_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)=J_k^TJ_k+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x_k)\nabla^2r_i(x_k).\] When \(H_k\) is nonsingular, the full Newton direction is defined by \[H_kp_k^N=-g_k.\] Equivalently, \(p_k^N\) is the stationary point of the exact second-order Taylor model \[q_k(p)=f(x_k)+g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TH_kp.\] A full-Newton least-squares method combines this exact curvature with a line search, a trust region, or a modification of \(H_k\) when necessary to obtain an acceptable trial step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full Newton least squares uses both parts of the exact Hessian: the Jacobian Gram matrix and the residual-weighted sum of individual residual Hessians. It therefore differs from Gauss–Newton precisely by retaining the second term. The Newton equation defines the local direction, while line-search or trust-region safeguards handle indefiniteness and poor behavior away from a solution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p_k^N\) is a stationary point of the quadratic Taylor model \(q_k\).
The full Hessian is \(J_k^TJ_k+S(x_k)\), with \(S(x_k)=\sum_i r_i(x_k)\nabla^2r_i(x_k)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(r(x_*)=0\), then the correction vanishes at \(x_*\).
If all residuals are affine, then \(H_k=J_k^TJ_k\) for every iterate and full Newton equals Gauss–Newton.
immediate_consequences_latex: The full Newton model captures curvature that can dominate in large-residual problems.
Computing the exact correction generally requires second derivatives of the individual residual functions.
boundary_notes: The exact Hessian can be indefinite, so the unmodified Newton direction need not be descent.
A singular \(H_k\) requires a generalized solve, modification, or trust-region subproblem.
Methods approximating the correction belong to structured quasi-Newton rather than full Newton.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Quasi-Newton Least-Squares Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method preserves the exact Gauss–Newton term and applies a safeguarded secant update only to the residual-weighted curvature correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)\rVert^2\), maintain a symmetric matrix \(B_k\) approximating \(S(x_k)=\sum_i r_i(x_k)\nabla^2r_i(x_k)\), while retaining \(J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k\) exactly. Compute \(s_k\) from \[(J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k+B_k)s_k=-J_k^{\mathsf T}r(x_k),\] globalize the step, and put \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k s_k\). With \(p_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\), update \(B_k\) by a symmetric secant formula satisfying \[B_{k+1}p_k=z_k,\qquad z_k=(g_{k+1}-g_k)-(J_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}J_{k+1})p_k,\] whenever the update safeguards accept the pair.
assumptions_latex: Accepted secant pairs satisfy the curvature conditions required by the chosen symmetric update.
The step system is nonsingular or suitably regularized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model matrix combines exact first-derivative least-squares structure with learned second-order residual curvature.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quasi-Newton approximation of only the residual-weighted Hessian correction.

notation.meaning: non-Gauss–Newton part of the exact Hessian
structured secant displacement and curvature vectors

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structured Quasi-Newton Correction for Least Squares
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\), let \(J_k=J(x_k)\), and let \(S(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x)\). Set \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth, finite-dimensional, unconstrained nonlinear least squares using an updated approximation only for the residual-curvature part of the Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structured quasi-Newton least-squares method maintains a symmetric matrix \(S_k\approx S(x_k)\) and uses the total curvature approximation \[B_k=J_k^TJ_k+S_k.\] After a step \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\), a residual-structured secant target is \[y_k^{\sharp}=J_{k+1}^Tr_{k+1}-J_k^Tr_{k+1},\] and the updated correction is required, exactly or approximately, to satisfy \[S_{k+1}s_k=y_k^{\sharp}.\] The update is selected from symmetric low-rank corrections, commonly by a least-change condition, and \(B_k\) is used in a line-search or trust-region model. Scaling or omission rules may suppress \(S_k\) when the Gauss–Newton model is already adequate or when a zero-residual solution is approached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structured quasi-Newton least-squares methods preserve the exact Jacobian Gram term and approximate only the residual-weighted second-order correction. Their secant equation uses the change in the Jacobian transpose while holding the new residual vector fixed, which targets the omitted residual curvature rather than the whole Hessian. Symmetry, least-change updates, and globalization complete a particular method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_k=J_k^TJ_k+S_k\) with a symmetric correction updated toward \(S_{k+1}s_k=y_k^{\sharp}\), where \(y_k^{\sharp}=J_{k+1}^Tr_{k+1}-J_k^Tr_{k+1}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The target vector can be written \(y_k^{\sharp}=(J_{k+1}-J_k)^Tr_{k+1}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S_k=0\), the model is Gauss–Newton.
The Dennis–Gay–Welsch update is a symmetric least-change member using the structured secant data.
A scaling \(S_k\leftarrow\tau_kS_k\) may force the correction to vanish appropriately near a zero-residual solution.
immediate_consequences_latex: Second derivatives of individual residuals are not required.
The readily computed term \(J_k^TJ_k\) is refreshed exactly at every outer iteration while only the correction is carried between iterations.
boundary_notes: The structured secant equation differs from the ordinary full-gradient secant equation \(B_{k+1}s_k=\nabla f(x_{k+1})-\nabla f(x_k)\).
The correction need not be positive semidefinite.
Safeguards are needed when a secant denominator is small or the resulting model is unreliable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Higher-Order Residual Model Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be \(q\)-times continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x\in\mathcal D\), where \(q\geq1\). For \(j\geq1\), write \(D^jR(x)[s]^j\) for the value of the symmetric \(j\)-linear derivative of \(R\) on \((s,\ldots,s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth residual maps; this definition describes exact Taylor residual models and permits approximate derivative tensors separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The order-\(p\) residual model at \(x\), for \(1\leq p\leq q\), is \[M_{x,p}(s)=R(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{1}{j!}D^jR(x)[s]^j.\] The higher-order residual model hierarchy is the indexed family \(\mathcal M_x^{(q)}=\{M_{x,p}:1\leq p\leq q\}\), ordered by truncation degree. An approximate hierarchy replaces \(D^jR(x)\) by symmetric multilinear maps \(T_{x,j}\), giving \(\widehat M_{x,p}(s)=R(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}(1/j!)T_{x,j}[s]^j\). A model-based step at level \(p\) is any admissible \(s\) selected by solving or approximately minimizing a declared residual measure \(\rho(\widehat M_{x,p}(s))\), possibly over a trust region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sufficiently smooth residual map, the hierarchy consists of its Taylor residual models of degrees one through q. The degree-p model retains derivatives through order p. An approximate hierarchy may substitute symmetric derivative-tensor approximations, and a level-p step is selected from the corresponding modeled residual problem.
special_cases_latex: If \(R\) is affine, every level \(p\geq1\) equals the exact residual \(R(x+s)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Successive exact levels satisfy \(M_{x,p+1}(s)-M_{x,p}(s)=D^{p+1}R(x)[s]^{p+1}/(p+1)!\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe how an approximate tensor is constructed, how a model subproblem is globalized, or which residual measure is used.
The inspected source discusses a quadratic tensor model but does not support the full arbitrary-order hierarchy stated here.

notation.meaning: The jth derivative tensor applied j times to the step s.
Exact residual Taylor model of degree p at x.

review_flags: No inspected source locator supports the complete arbitrary-order hierarchy and its approximate-tensor variant.
knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Residual Model Hierarchy
Tensor Residual Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tensor residual model retains the quadratic Taylor term of every residual component before taking the squared norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be twice continuously differentiable. At \(x_k\), the quadratic tensor residual model is \[M_k(s)=r(x_k)+J_k s+\tfrac12\mathcal{T}_k[s,s],\] where the vector \(\mathcal{T}_k[s,s]\in\mathbb{R}^m\) has component \((\mathcal{T}_k[s,s])_i=s^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2r_i(x_k)s\). The associated least-squares model is \(q_k(s)=\tfrac12\lVert M_k(s)\rVert_2^2\). For \(s\to0\), Taylor's formula gives \(r(x_k+s)=M_k(s)+o(\lVert s\rVert^2)\); under locally Lipschitz second derivatives, the remainder is \(O(\lVert s\rVert^3)\).
assumptions_latex: For a cubic remainder bound, each \(\nabla^2r_i\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_k\) is a second-order consistent vector model of the residual map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order vector-valued Taylor model of a nonlinear residual map.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the residual map at \(x_k\)
squared-norm objective induced by the tensor residual model

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Residual Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hierarchy truncates the residual’s Taylor expansion at order p and then minimizes the squared norm of that vector model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\geq1\) and let \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) possess derivatives through order \(p\) near \(x_k\). Its order-\(p\) residual model is \[M_{k,p}(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{p}\frac{1}{j!}D^jr(x_k)[s]^j,\] with \(D^0r(x_k)=r(x_k)\). The induced least-squares model is \(q_{k,p}(s)=\tfrac12\lVert M_{k,p}(s)\rVert_2^2\). If \(D^pr\) is locally Lipschitz, then \[\lVert r(x_k+s)-M_{k,p}(s)\rVert=O(\lVert s\rVert^{p+1})\] as \(s\to0\). Thus increasing \(p\) raises the local residual-model consistency order.
assumptions_latex: The order-\(p\) derivative is locally Lipschitz for the stated remainder bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual-model error has order \(p+1\) under the Lipschitz derivative assumption.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-p Taylor hierarchy for smooth vector-valued residual maps.

notation.meaning: order-j derivative applied j times to the step

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The representation is internally coherent and fits the higher-order residual-model container. The Taylor hierarchy and Lipschitz-derivative remainder are plausible standard mathematics, but the specialized use as a nonlinear least-squares residual-model hierarchy has no cited source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Order Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher order improves local model accuracy, but dense derivative tensors grow combinatorially and make evaluation and subproblem solution more expensive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the order-\(p\) model \(M_{k,p}\), locally Lipschitz \(D^pr\) yields residual error \(O(\lVert s\rVert^{p+1})\), whereas constructing a dense symmetric order-\(j\) derivative for one scalar residual requires \(\binom{n+j-1}{j}\) independent coefficients. Hence a dense order-\(p\) model for \(m\) residuals may store up to \[m\sum_{j=0}^{p}\binom{n+j-1}{j}\] coefficients. Raising \(p\) improves the asymptotic local error by one power per added order but increases derivative acquisition, storage, contraction, and subproblem-solution costs; an advantageous order must balance this extra work against fewer or more reliable outer iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) has locally Lipschitz derivatives through the modeled order.
Derivative tensors are represented densely and symmetrically.
Cost comparison uses independent tensor coefficients as the storage measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Higher model order trades an additional power of local consistency for combinatorial dense-tensor growth.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy-versus-cost comparison within the residual Taylor-model hierarchy.

notation.meaning: number of independent entries in a symmetric order-j tensor

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the tradeoff container, and the symmetric-tensor coefficient count is appropriate for dense storage. However, a higher-order big-O bound does not by itself guarantee that the actual error improves by exactly one power, since lower-order models may already have higher accuracy through cancellation. The dense-cost model and a properly qualified accuracy comparison require a dedicated source.

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Residual Correction Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large-residual methods correct Gauss–Newton with an approximation to residual-weighted second-order curvature, which need not be small near a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)\rVert^2\), define \(G_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k\) and \(S_k=\sum_i r_i(x_k)\nabla^2r_i(x_k)\). Choose a computable symmetric approximation \(C_k\approx S_k\), possibly from directional second derivatives or secant information, and compute a safeguarded step from \[(G_k+C_k+\lambda_k I)s_k=-J_k^{\mathsf T}r(x_k),\qquad \lambda_k\geq0.\] Accept the step using a line-search or trust-region ratio and update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) when accepted. Setting \(C_k=0\) recovers Gauss–Newton; setting \(C_k=S_k\) gives the full Newton model.
assumptions_latex: The corrected matrix is nonsingular after any regularization.
A globalization test controls acceptance of the corrected step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The step model interpolates between Gauss–Newton and full Newton through \(C_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order correction of Gauss–Newton when residual-weighted curvature is nonnegligible.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and Hessian decomposition fit the large-residual correction container. No source is supplied, however, and the record permits any computable symmetric C_k approximating S_k without specifying a recognized correction construction or its safeguards. A dedicated large-residual nonlinear least-squares reference is needed to determine a reliable algorithmic statement.
