knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Difference Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate every Jacobian column by coordinate finite differences, solve the resulting approximate Newton equation, optionally globalize the correction by a line search, and stop when the nonlinear residual reaches the stated tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), an initial point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and a tolerance \(\tau>0\), choose nonzero increments \(h_{k,j}\) at iteration \(k\) and define the finite-difference matrix by \((B_k)_{:,j}=[F(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j)-F(x_k)]/h_{k,j}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\), where \(e_j\) is the \(j\)-th coordinate vector. Solve \(B_ks_k=-F(x_k)\). Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) for the full-step method, or choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) using a specified line-search acceptance rule and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_ks_k\). Select or adapt the increments to account for truncation and function-evaluation errors. Stop successfully when \(\lVert F(x_k)\rVert_2\le\tau\), and report breakdown if \(B_k\) is unusable or the prescribed line search cannot accept a step.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuously differentiable near all evaluated points.
Every perturbed point \(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j\) required by the difference formula is feasible to evaluate.
Each matrix \(B_k\) used to compute a correction is nonsingular.
For the line-search variant, the acceptance rule and its failure condition are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed procedure is a coordinate finite-difference Newton method for solving \(F(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-step or line-search Newton root iteration using coordinate finite differences to approximate the Jacobian.

notation.meaning: Coordinate finite-difference approximation to the Jacobian at iteration k.
Nonzero finite-difference increment for coordinate j at iteration k.
The j-th coordinate unit vector in R^n.
Accepted line-search step length when globalization is used.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, refine or select a discrete residual model, solve its Newton equation using an approximate derivative, and stop only when residual and discretization errors are acceptable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given discretized residual maps \(F_h:\mathbb{R}^{n_h}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_h}\), choose resolutions \(h_k\downarrow0\), transfer the current iterate to the \(h_k\)-space when necessary, and select a derivative model \(B_k\) for \(F_{h_k}'(x_k)\). Compute \(s_k\) from \(B_k s_k=-F_{h_k}(x_k)\), set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), and stop when both \(\|F_{h_k}(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\) and a prescribed discretization-error estimate is at most \(\varepsilon_h\). The method returns the final discrete iterate together with its resolution.
assumptions_latex: \(B_k\) is nonsingular whenever a step is accepted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton iteration applied to a sequence of finite-dimensional or discretized residual models.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4.3 Discrete Newton Method p. 79

knowledge_statements.title: Difference-Quality Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a nonsingular root with a Lipschitz Jacobian, a sufficiently small uniform derivative-model error gives local linear convergence; vanishing derivative error along the computed steps gives superlinear convergence; and derivative-model error proportional to the current iterate error gives quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable near a root \(x_*\), let \(J=F'\) be Lipschitz continuous there, and suppose \(J(x_*)\) is nonsingular. Consider steps satisfying \(B_k s_k=-F(x_k)\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). There exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\) and a constant \(\delta>0\) such that, if \(x_0\in U\), every \(B_k\) is nonsingular, and \(\|B_k-J(x_k)\|\leq\delta\), then the iteration is locally linearly convergent. If additionally \(\|(B_k-J(x_k))s_k\|/\|s_k\|\to0\) for nonzero steps, the convergence is superlinear. If instead \(\|B_k-J(x_k)\|=O(\|x_k-x_*\|)\), the convergence is quadratic.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is Lipschitz continuous in a neighborhood of \(x_*\).
\(x_0\) is sufficiently close to \(x_*\), and every matrix \(B_k\) used in a step is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convergence regimes determined by the quality of a derivative approximation.

notation.meaning: sufficiently small uniform derivative-model error threshold

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Newton Equation Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a nonnegative shift to the Newton matrix, solve the stabilized equation, and adapt the shift according to trial-point residual decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), an iterate \(x_k\), and \(\lambda_k\geq0\), choose \(\lambda_k\) so that \(J(x_k)+\lambda_k I\) is acceptably conditioned. Solve \((J(x_k)+\lambda_k I)s_k=-F(x_k)\), test the trial point \(x_k+s_k\) with a residual merit function, and accept it when the prescribed decrease test holds. Otherwise increase \(\lambda_k\) and recompute the step; after successful steps, \(\lambda_k\) may be decreased. Stop when the residual or step tolerance is met.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood containing all trial points.
\(J(x_k)+\lambda_k I\) is nonsingular for every computed step.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton equation stabilized by an additive regularization parameter.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits the container, but the cited generic Newton-like-method chapter does not establish this residual-equation shift-and-acceptance framework. For a nonsymmetric Jacobian, a nonnegative scalar shift is not inherently stabilizing, so a source specific to regularized nonlinear-equation Newton methods is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additively regularized Newton equation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable with Jacobian \(J\). For each iteration choose \(\lambda_k\geq0\) and a regularization matrix \(R_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth root finding. The defining mechanism regularizes the Newton linear equation by an additive matrix term; trust-region and normal-equation regularizations are nearby variants unless they reduce to this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An additively regularized Newton equation method defines \(s_k\) by \[(J(x_k)+\lambda_kR_k)s_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\] subject to nonsingularity of \(J(x_k)+\lambda_kR_k\). A genuine regularization iteration has \(\lambda_kR_k\ne0\); allowing \(\lambda_k=0\) makes exact Newton a limiting special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family replaces the possibly singular, ill-conditioned, or otherwise unsuitable Newton matrix by \(J(x_k)+\lambda_kR_k\). It solves the resulting regularized equation for \(s_k\) and updates \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). The parameter is nonnegative, and the modified matrix must be nonsingular for the step to be uniquely defined.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[s_k=-(J(x_k)+\lambda_kR_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\] whenever the inverse exists.
special_cases_latex: Scalar shifting uses \(R_k=I\), giving \((J(x_k)+\lambda_kI)s_k=-F(x_k)\).
Setting \(\lambda_k=0\) recovers the exact Newton equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: The unregularized Newton residual satisfies \(J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)=-\lambda_kR_ks_k\).
Regularization changes the defining linear model unless \(\lambda_kR_ks_k=0\).
boundary_notes: For nonsymmetric Jacobians, a positive scalar shift does not by itself guarantee nonsingularity or desirable conditioning.
Levenberg–Marquardt equations based on \(J(x_k)^TJ(x_k)+\lambda_kI\) are normal-equation regularizations and are not automatically identical to this additive-Jacobian definition.
No rule for choosing \(\lambda_k\) or accepting the step is included.
review_flags: The supplied sources did not provide a precise root-equation locator supporting this general additive-Jacobian regularization definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accelerated Process toward the Quadratic-Convergence Region
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a fixed-length accelerated cubic-Newton restart process intended to reach a local quadratic-convergence region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma_3(f)>0\), and let \(\mathcal A_k(x)\) denote the point produced after \(k\) iterations of the specified accelerated cubic-Newton method initialized at \(x\). Given \(x_0\), set \(m=\left\lfloor(24e/\gamma_3(f))^{1/3}\right\rfloor\) and \(y_0=x_0\). For every \(k\ge0\), set \(y_{k+1}=\mathcal A_m(y_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run the accelerated cubic-Newton method for the prescribed fixed number of iterations and repeatedly restart it from the previous stage output.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A_k(x)\text{ denotes the }k\text{-th point of the specified accelerated cubic-Newton method started at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-controlled Newton–Krylov iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(J_k=J(x_k)\), and let \(\mathcal K_m(J_k,r_0)=\operatorname{span}\{r_0,J_kr_0,\ldots,J_k^{m-1}r_0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth root finding with an iterative Krylov solution of each Newton equation. The outer method is inexact because the inner linear residual need not vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact Newton–Krylov method chooses \(0\leq\eta_k<1\) and computes a correction \(s_k\) by a Krylov subspace linear solver such that \[r_k^{\mathrm{lin}}=J_ks_k+F(x_k),\qquad \|r_k^{\mathrm{lin}}\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|,\] then sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), possibly after an independently specified globalization. For a zero initial inner guess, the computed step lies in a Krylov space generated by \(J_k\) and \(-F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each outer iterate, an inexact Newton–Krylov method applies a Krylov linear solver to the Newton equation. The inner solve stops when the linear residual \(J_ks_k+F(x_k)\) is no larger than a forcing fraction \(\eta_k\) of the nonlinear residual norm. The resulting correction, rather than the exact Newton correction, defines the next outer iterate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(e_k\) with \(\|e_k\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\) such that \[J_ks_k=-F(x_k)+e_k.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(\eta_k=0\) and the Krylov process reaches an exact solution, the outer step is exact Newton.
GMRES, MINRES, and CG are possible inner solvers only when their respective algebraic requirements match the Newton matrix.
immediate_consequences_latex: The forcing term separates the permitted linear-solve error from the nonlinear residual scale.
No explicit factorization of \(J_k\) is required by the family definition.
boundary_notes: Krylov membership depends on the initial inner guess and changes under left or right preconditioning.
The definition does not require Jacobian-free products; explicitly assembled Jacobians are allowed.
A convergence rate requires additional regularity and forcing-sequence hypotheses.

notation.meaning: residual of the inexact Newton linear equation
Krylov subspace of dimension at most m

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-controlled Newton–Krylov iteration
Inexact Newton Forcing Strategies
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forcing term bounds the relative residual of each approximate Newton solve; constant, vanishing, and residual-proportional choices target linear, superlinear, and quadratic local convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iterate \(x_k\), an inexact Newton step \(s_k\) has linear residual \(r_k=J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\) and must satisfy \(\|r_k\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\), where \(0\leq\eta_k<1\). A fixed bound \(\eta_k\leq\bar\eta<1\) defines a linear forcing regime; \(\eta_k\to0\) defines a superlinear forcing regime; and \(\eta_k=O(\|F(x_k)\|)\) defines a quadratic forcing regime under the usual nonsingular-root and Lipschitz-Jacobian hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based accuracy conditions for approximate Newton equation solves.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The forcing condition and convergence regimes are standard and fit the condition container, but no citation is supplied for the quantitative condition or the linear, superlinear, and quadratic regime claims.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forcing strategy for an inexact Newton equation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable. At iteration \(k\), an inexact Newton step has linear residual \(r_k^{\mathrm{lin}}=J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic relative-residual stopping strategies for inner Newton solves. This definition specifies admissible forcing values, not a convergence theorem or a particular adaptive formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact Newton forcing strategy is a rule \(\Phi_k\) that, from information available through iteration \(k\), chooses \[\eta_k=\Phi_k(x_0,\ldots,x_k,F(x_0),\ldots,F(x_k),\ldots)\in[0,\eta_{\max}],\qquad \eta_{\max}<1,\] and terminates the inner solve only after \[\|J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|.\] Smaller \(\eta_k\) requests a more accurate Newton equation solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forcing strategy is the rule that chooses the relative inner tolerance \(\eta_k\). The selected value lies between zero and a fixed bound below one, may depend only on information already available, and controls termination through \(\|J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(F(x_k)\ne0\), the admissibility test is \[\frac{\|J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\|}{\|F(x_k)\|}\leq\eta_k.\]
special_cases_latex: A constant forcing strategy sets \(\eta_k\equiv\bar\eta\) with \(0\leq\bar\eta<1\).
A tightening strategy has \(\eta_k\to0\) as the nonlinear residual approaches zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: At an exact root \(F(x_k)=0\), the relative test forces \(J(x_k)s_k=0\); implementations normally terminate the outer iteration instead.
The forcing rule is independent of the particular Krylov recurrence used to meet its residual test.
boundary_notes: An absolute tolerance without normalization by \(\|F(x_k)\|\) is a different stopping convention.
The bound \(\eta_{\max}<1\) is part of this canonical admissibility definition; sharper rate conditions are not asserted.
Finite-precision stagnation may prevent a requested tolerance from being attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve each Newton equation with a structure-compatible Krylov method, terminating the inner iteration when the inexact Newton residual tolerance is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At outer iterate \(x_k\), approximately solve \(J(x_k)s=-F(x_k)\) in a Krylov subspace until \(\|J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\), then set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). GMRES or BiCGSTAB may be used for a general nonsymmetric Jacobian, MINRES for a symmetric Jacobian, and conjugate gradients only when the relevant operator is symmetric positive definite. The selected inner solver must preserve its stated structural assumptions, and the outer stopping test remains the inexact Newton residual condition.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable at each outer iterate.
The chosen Krylov solver's symmetry and definiteness requirements hold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection-defined Newton–Krylov solver variant
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At outer iteration \(k\), consider the Newton equation \(J_ks=-F_k\), where \(J_k=J(x_k)\), \(F_k=F(x_k)\), and an inner process builds trial and test spaces \(\mathcal V_{k,m},\mathcal W_{k,m}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear Krylov variants used as inner solvers. The distinguishing object is the projection or residual-optimality condition, not the outer Newton update or forcing rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Newton–Krylov solver variant is specified by nested Krylov trial spaces \(\mathcal V_{k,m}\), test spaces \(\mathcal W_{k,m}\), and an inner iterate \(s_{k,m}\in s_{k,0}+\mathcal V_{k,m}\) satisfying either the Petrov–Galerkin condition \[F_k+J_ks_{k,m}\perp\mathcal W_{k,m}\] or the minimum-residual condition \[s_{k,m}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{s\in s_{k,0}+\mathcal V_{k,m}}\|F_k+J_ks\|.\] The accepted \(s_k=s_{k,m_k}\) must also meet the outer forcing tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver variant chooses how a Krylov trial space is generated and how the approximate Newton correction is selected from it. The correction either makes the linear residual orthogonal to a test space or minimizes its norm over the trial affine space. The outer method accepts an inner iterate only after it satisfies the prescribed forcing condition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For zero initial guess, a standard unpreconditioned trial space is \[\mathcal V_{k,m}=\mathcal K_m(J_k,-F_k).\]
special_cases_latex: GMRES uses the minimum-residual condition for a general square matrix.
FOM uses a Galerkin condition with matching trial and test Krylov spaces.
CG requires an appropriate symmetric positive-definite linear system; MINRES requires symmetry.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different projection conditions can produce different corrections from the same Krylov space.
Restarted variants replace an indefinitely growing space by successive spaces of bounded dimension.
boundary_notes: Solver names alone do not guarantee applicability; matrix symmetry and definiteness requirements remain operative.
Preconditioning changes the operator and spaces and is defined separately.
Breakdown, stagnation, and finite-precision loss of orthogonality are not characterized here.

Jacobian-Free Newton–Krylov Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Krylov solver receives Jacobian-vector products from residual differences, avoiding explicit Jacobian assembly while retaining an inexact Newton stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x_k\), run a Krylov method for the Newton equation without forming \(J(x_k)\). Whenever the inner method requests a product with \(v\neq0\), return \(J(x_k)v\approx[F(x_k+\sigma_{k,v}v)-F(x_k)]/\sigma_{k,v}\), with a nonzero scale \(\sigma_{k,v}\) chosen to balance truncation and evaluation error. Stop the inner iteration when its computed linear residual satisfies the forcing tolerance, set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), and stop the outer iteration when \(\|F(x_k)\|\) meets the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable near all sampled points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free Newton–Krylov iteration using residual differences for Jacobian products.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobian-free Newton–Krylov iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable. A Krylov solver for \(J(x_k)s=-F(x_k)\) requires products of the current Jacobian with vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth root finding. Jacobian-free means that Krylov matrix–vector products are supplied without assembling or storing the full Jacobian; preconditioners may still contain derivative information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Jacobian-free Newton–Krylov method is an inexact Newton–Krylov method in which each requested product \(J(x_k)v\) is replaced by a matrix-free directional approximation, canonically \[\mathcal J_{k,\varepsilon}(v)=\frac{F(x_k+\varepsilon_{k,v}v)-F(x_k)}{\varepsilon_{k,v}},\qquad \varepsilon_{k,v}\ne0,\] with sampled points in \(D\). The Krylov process approximately solves the resulting Newton equation until its chosen residual test is met, and no full matrix \(J(x_k)\) is formed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This method applies an inexact Newton–Krylov iteration while supplying every Jacobian–vector product through residual evaluations, typically a directional finite difference. The full Jacobian is neither assembled nor stored. The inner solver uses these products to obtain a correction satisfying its forcing tolerance, after which the outer iterate is updated.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If the exact directional derivative is available without matrix assembly, one may use \[\mathcal J_k(v)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}F(x_k+tv)\right|_{t=0}.\]
special_cases_latex: Forward directional differencing uses one perturbed residual evaluation per requested product when \(F(x_k)\) is cached.
Centered directional differencing uses two perturbed evaluations and \([F(x_k+\varepsilon v)-F(x_k-\varepsilon v)]/(2\varepsilon)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Storage of a dense \(n\times n\) Jacobian is not required by the outer–inner iteration.
The finite-difference map \(v\mapsto\mathcal J_{k,\varepsilon}(v)\) may fail to be exactly linear when \(\varepsilon_{k,v}\) depends on \(v\) or arithmetic is finite.
boundary_notes: The perturbation must keep \(x_k+\varepsilon_{k,v}v\) in the domain.
Jacobian-free does not mean derivative-free in the mathematical limit, because the product approximates a directional derivative.
A separately assembled preconditioner is compatible with this definition.

notation.meaning: matrix-free approximation to the current Jacobian action

Newton–Krylov Preconditioning Interfaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preconditioning may act on the left, right, or both sides; right-preconditioned variables must be mapped back before updating the nonlinear iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Newton equation \(J_k s=-F_k\), an invertible left preconditioner \(M_k\) gives \(M_k^{-1}J_k s=-M_k^{-1}F_k\). An invertible right preconditioner gives \(J_kM_k^{-1}y=-F_k\) followed by \(s=M_k^{-1}y\). A split interface with \(M_k=M_{L,k}M_{R,k}\) gives \(M_{L,k}^{-1}J_kM_{R,k}^{-1}y=-M_{L,k}^{-1}F_k\) and \(s=M_{R,k}^{-1}y\). Right and split interfaces retain the original nonlinear residual for outer acceptance tests.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent left- and right-preconditioned interfaces for Newton–Krylov inner solves.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Left and right preconditioning interfaces for Newton–Krylov solves
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At outer iteration \(k\), let \(J_k=J(x_k)\), \(F_k=F(x_k)\), and let \(P_k:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be an invertible linear operator whose action or approximate inverse action is computationally available.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Newton–Krylov linear solves. The interface is algebraic and does not prescribe how the preconditioner is constructed or updated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A left-preconditioned interface presents the Krylov solver with \[P_k^{-1}J_ks=-P_k^{-1}F_k,\] and measures the transformed residual unless an additional true-residual test is imposed. A right-preconditioned interface solves \[J_kP_k^{-1}z=-F_k,\qquad s=P_k^{-1}z,\] so the residual in the original Newton equation is \(J_ks+F_k\). A split interface factors the transformation into compatible left and right operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton–Krylov preconditioning interface specifies how an invertible auxiliary operator is inserted into the Newton equation and which residual the inner solver exposes. Left preconditioning transforms both equation sides. Right preconditioning changes variables and recovers the physical Newton correction after the Krylov solve. Split preconditioning combines both transformations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For right preconditioning, \[J_kP_k^{-1}z+F_k=J_ks+F_k.\]
For left preconditioning, the displayed inner residual is \[P_k^{-1}(J_ks+F_k).\]
special_cases_latex: The identity choice \(P_k=I\) gives the unpreconditioned Newton equation.
A fixed preconditioner uses \(P_k=P\) for all outer iterations; a variable preconditioner permits dependence on \(k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Left and right preconditioning generally generate different Krylov spaces even with the same \(P_k\).
A small left-preconditioned residual does not automatically imply a small unpreconditioned residual without norm-control information for \(P_k\).
boundary_notes: Flexible Krylov methods may be required when the applied right-preconditioner action changes between inner iterations.
The definition assumes an invertible mathematical operator even if its inverse action is computed approximately.
Preconditioning does not alter the desired root of \(F(x)=0\), but it changes the inner linear iteration.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Secant quasi-Newton method for nonlinear equations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(x_k,x_{k+1}\in D\), and define \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\) and \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional square nonlinear equations. The family approximates the Jacobian or its inverse using secant data and does not require a fresh exact Jacobian at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direct secant quasi-Newton equation method maintains a nonsingular matrix \(B_k\), computes \[B_ks_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\] and selects the next approximation from the secant set \[B_{k+1}s_k=y_k.\] An inverse form maintains \(H_k\approx J(x_k)^{-1}\), uses \(s_k=-H_kF(x_k)\), and imposes \(H_{k+1}y_k=s_k\). Additional conditions are required because a single vector secant equation does not uniquely determine an \(n\times n\) matrix when \(n>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A secant quasi-Newton method replaces the current Jacobian or inverse Jacobian by an evolving matrix inferred from changes in iterates and residuals. The direct form solves with \(B_k\) and requires the new matrix to map the latest step \(s_k\) to the latest residual change \(y_k\). The inverse form requires the new inverse approximation to map \(y_k\) back to \(s_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The direct secant equation is equivalent to interpolation by the new affine model at the two consecutive iterates.
When \(B_{k+1}\) is invertible and \(H_{k+1}=B_{k+1}^{-1}\), \[B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\iff H_{k+1}y_k=s_k.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the direct secant equation uniquely gives \(B_{k+1}=y_k/s_k\) when \(s_k\ne0\).
Broyden methods choose a rank-one member of the direct or inverse secant set.
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(n>1\) and \(s_k\ne0\), the direct secant constraint alone leaves multiple admissible matrices.
The method requires no evaluation of \(J(x_{k+1})\) in its defining update.
boundary_notes: A finite-difference Jacobian reconstructed independently at each iterate is not a propagated secant update.
Nonsingularity of the updated matrix is not guaranteed by the secant equation alone.
Globalization and update-skipping rules are outside this definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Argmin Invariance Under Positive Squaring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of a strictly positive objective and its squared transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be closed and convex, let $f:Q\to\mathbb R_+$ be strictly positive on $Q$, and define $\widehat f(x)=\tfrac12 f(x)^2$. Then
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}f(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}\widehat f(x).
\]
Consequently, minimizing $f$ over $Q$ and minimizing $\widehat f$ over $Q$ are equivalent optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squaring a strictly positive objective and multiplying by one half does not change its minimizers, so the original and transformed minimization problems are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential relative-scale convergence bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-iterate and weighted-average guarantee for the stated adaptive-metric method applied to the quadratic transform of a strictly positive objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_0\succ0\) induce \(\|\cdot\|_{G_0}\), let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be strictly positive, and set \(\hat f(x)=\tfrac12f(x)^2\). Fix \(\delta\in(0,1)\), assume \(g(x)\in\partial\hat f(x)\) satisfies \(\|g(x)\|_{G_0}^*\le L\) for every \(x\in Q\), and let \(x^*\) be an optimal solution. For the best points \(x_k^*\) generated by the stated method and \(R=\|x_0-x^*\|_{G_0}\), every \(k\ge0\) satisfies \[(1-\delta)\hat f(x_k^*)\le\hat f(x^*)+\frac{L^2R^2}{2n\left(e^{\delta(k+1)/n}-1\right)}.\] The same bound holds with \(\hat f(\tilde x_{k+1})\) in place of \(\hat f(x_k^*)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Squared Transformation of a Strictly Positive Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-objective squaring and its induced subgradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be closed and convex and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R_{++}$. For the problem $\min_{x\in Q}f(x)$, define
\[
\widehat f(x)=\tfrac12 f(x)^2.
\]
For any $g(x)\in\partial f(x)$, define
\[
\widehat g(x)=f(x)g(x),
\]
so that $\widehat g(x)\in\partial\widehat f(x)$. When an optimum exists, write $x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}f(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly positive objective on a closed convex set, the squared transformed objective is one half of the objective squared. Multiplying any subgradient of the original objective by its positive function value gives a subgradient of the transformed objective.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(B_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\ne0\), and \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional square nonlinear equations. The family consists of rank-one direct updates satisfying the latest secant equation; the classical good Broyden update is its Euclidean least-change member.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direct rank-one Broyden-family update has the form \[B_{k+1}=B_k+(y_k-B_ks_k)v_k^T,\qquad v_k^Ts_k=1.\] The normalization makes \(B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\). The classical good Broyden choice is \(v_k=s_k/(s_k^Ts_k)\), giving \[B_{k+1}=B_k+\frac{(y_k-B_ks_k)s_k^T}{s_k^Ts_k}.\] The associated iteration solves \(B_ks_k=-F(x_k)\) before updating the matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Broyden's rank-one family corrects the current Jacobian approximation only in the direction needed to satisfy the newest secant equation. An arbitrary update vector \(v_k\) is normalized by \(v_k^Ts_k=1\). The classical good Broyden member chooses the normalized step itself, which is the minimum Frobenius-change direct update.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The correction \(B_{k+1}-B_k\) has rank at most one.
For the good Broyden choice, \[B_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{B s_k=y_k}\|B-B_k\|_F.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(y_k=B_ks_k\), every normalized choice yields the null update \(B_{k+1}=B_k\).
For \(n=1\), all admissible normalized choices coincide with the scalar secant update.
immediate_consequences_latex: The family preserves the action of \(B_k\) on every vector \(w\) satisfying \(v_k^Tw=0\).
The update does not by itself ensure that \(B_{k+1}\) is nonsingular.
boundary_notes: The term “Broyden family” is used here for direct rank-one secant updates, not for the unrelated symmetric Broyden class of Hessian updates in optimization.
Inverse-storage formulas and memory-management policies are separated into child topics.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Broyden Variants
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update the approximate Jacobian by a rank-one correction that enforces the newest secant equation; different admissible projection vectors define direct Broyden variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_k\) and a nonsingular direct approximation \(B_k\), solve \(B_ks_k=-F(x_k)\), set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), and define \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\). The choice \(w_k=s_k\) is the standard least-change direct Broyden update in the Frobenius norm.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(B_k\) be a direct approximation to \(J(x_k)\), and define \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\ne0\) and \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear equations with an explicitly stored direct Jacobian approximation. The definition is the classical good Broyden formula, with scaled variants obtained by changing the metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The classical direct Broyden method computes \[B_ks_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\] and updates the direct Jacobian approximation by \[B_{k+1}=B_k+\frac{(y_k-B_ks_k)s_k^T}{s_k^Ts_k}.\] It is the unique minimizer of \(\|B-B_k\|_F\) subject to the direct secant equation \(Bs_k=y_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The direct variant stores a Jacobian approximation, solves the quasi-Newton equation with it, and applies the classical good Broyden rank-one correction. The correction is the unique Frobenius-nearest matrix to the previous approximation that maps the latest step to the latest residual change.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[B_{k+1}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}}\{\|B-B_k\|_F:Bs_k=y_k\}.\]
The update leaves \(B_kw\) unchanged for every \(w\) with \(s_k^Tw=0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(y_k=B_ks_k\), then \(B_{k+1}=B_k\).
A diagonally scaled direct variant replaces \(s_k\) in the update covector by \(D^2s_k/(s_k^TD^2s_k)\) for a nonsingular diagonal scale \(D\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The update has rank at most one.
Only the most recent secant equation is guaranteed unless additional preservation conditions happen to hold.
boundary_notes: The denominator requires \(s_k\ne0\).
The update may produce a singular or ill-conditioned matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct-form Broyden iteration using an approximate Jacobian matrix. The extract refers to, but does not reproduce, update formula (11.28).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose $x_0$ and a nonsingular initial Jacobian approximation $B_0$. For $k=0,1,2,\ldots$, solve $B_kp_k=-r(x_k)$, choose $\alpha_k$ by a line search along $p_k$, set $x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k$, $s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k$, and $y_k=r(x_{k+1})-r(x_k)$, and obtain $B_{k+1}$ from the specified Broyden update (11.28).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with a point and a nonsingular approximate Jacobian. At each iteration, solve the approximate Newton equation, line-search along that direction, update the point, form the step and residual difference, and then apply the referenced direct Broyden update.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Direct Broyden method for nonlinear equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jacobian-free secant modeling and the rank-one direct Broyden update for a residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), form \(M_k(p)=r(x_k)+B_kp\). If \(B_k\) is nonsingular, take \(p_k=-B_k^{-1}r(x_k)\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\). Define \[s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k,\qquad y_k=r(x_{k+1})-r(x_k).\] For \(s_k\neq0\), the direct Broyden update is \[B_{k+1}=B_k+\frac{(y_k-B_ks_k)s_k^T}{s_k^Ts_k},\] which satisfies \(B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\). If \(r\) is continuously differentiable along the step segment, then \[y_k=\int_0^1J(x_k+ts_k)s_k\,dt.\] For \(n>1\), the secant equation alone does not uniquely determine all entries of \(B_{k+1}\); for \(n=1\), it yields the scalar secant construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Broyden's method replaces the true Jacobian by an updated approximation. A nonsingular approximation defines the step by zeroing the linear residual model, and the direct rank-one update enforces the secant equation for the observed step and residual change. In dimensions above one the secant equation alone is underdetermined; in one dimension it gives the scalar secant construction.
assumptions_latex: B_k\text{ is nonsingular when }p_k=-B_k^{-1}r(x_k)\text{ is used}
r\text{ is continuously differentiable along }\{x_k+ts_k:0\leq t\leq1\}\text{ for the integral identity}

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Broyden Variants
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update the inverse Jacobian approximation directly by a rank-one correction enforcing the newest inverse secant equation, avoiding a new linear solve for the step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an inverse approximation \(H_k\), compute \(s_k=-H_kF(x_k)\), set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), and define \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\). For any vector \(v_k\) with \(v_k^{T}y_k\neq0\), update \(H_{k+1}=H_k+(s_k-H_ky_k)v_k^{T}/(v_k^{T}y_k)\). This rank-one family satisfies \(H_{k+1}y_k=s_k\); the choice \(v_k=y_k\) gives the least-change inverse update in the Frobenius norm.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is evaluable at both endpoints of each step.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-one updates of an inverse Jacobian approximation satisfying the inverse secant equation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse implementation of the classical Broyden update
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(B_k\) be nonsingular, let \(H_k=B_k^{-1}\), and define nonzero \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\) and \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear equations. This slot defines the inverse-storage formula algebraically corresponding to the classical direct good Broyden rank-one update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Provided \(s_k^TH_ky_k\ne0\), the inverse form corresponding to the classical direct Broyden update is \[H_{k+1}=H_k+\frac{(s_k-H_ky_k)s_k^TH_k}{s_k^TH_ky_k}.\] The quasi-Newton step is computed without a linear factorization as \[s_k=-H_kF(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k.\] The updated matrix satisfies the inverse secant equation \(H_{k+1}y_k=s_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This variant stores the inverse of the direct Broyden Jacobian approximation. It obtains the correction by multiplying the residual by \(-H_k\), then applies the rank-one inverse update. The denominator must be nonzero. When the corresponding direct update is nonsingular, the formula produces its inverse and satisfies the inverse secant equation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(B_{k+1}=B_k+(y_k-B_ks_k)s_k^T/(s_k^Ts_k)\) is nonsingular, then \(H_{k+1}=B_{k+1}^{-1}\) has the displayed form.
special_cases_latex: If \(H_ky_k=s_k\), the inverse update is zero.
The scalar case reduces to \(H_{k+1}=s_k/y_k\) when \(y_k\ne0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The inverse update has rank at most one.
Applying \(H_k\) to a residual costs a matrix–vector multiplication when \(H_k\) is stored densely.
boundary_notes: The condition \(s_k^TH_ky_k\ne0\) is essential; a zero denominator signals failure of this inverse formula.
Direct inverse storage can obscure ill-conditioning compared with maintaining a factorization of the direct approximation.
Other inverse secant least-change formulas need not equal the inverse of the classical direct good Broyden update.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-memory and restarted Broyden representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Write a direct Broyden approximation as \(B_k=B_{\mathrm{base}}+\sum_{i\in I_k}u_iv_i^T\), where each retained pair represents a rank-one secant correction and \(I_k\) is an ordered active index set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear equations. The defining distinction is explicit control of retained Broyden update information; it does not specify a unique deletion, aggregation, or restart criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Broyden memory-management variant fixes a memory budget \(m\geq0\) and maintains an active set satisfying \(|I_k|\leq m\). After a new pair \((u_k,v_k)\) is generated, a management operator \(\mathcal M_k\) chooses \[B_{k+1}=B_{\mathrm{base},k+1}+\sum_{i\in I_{k+1}}u_iv_i^T,\qquad |I_{k+1}|\leq m.\] The operator may discard old pairs, aggregate them into a new base matrix, or restart by replacing the representation with a freshly formed \(B_{\mathrm{base},k+1}\) and setting \(I_{k+1}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A memory-managed Broyden method represents its Jacobian approximation by a base matrix plus retained rank-one corrections and enforces a fixed bound on the number of stored pairs. When a new correction would exceed the budget, the method discards, compresses, or absorbs information. A restart clears the active corrections and supplies a new base approximation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A full-memory method has \(I_k=\{0,\ldots,k-1\}\); a bounded-memory method replaces this growing set by one of cardinality at most \(m\).
special_cases_latex: A sliding-window policy retains only the \(m\) most recent correction pairs.
A periodic restart sets \(I_k=\varnothing\) at prescribed iterations.
Memoryless operation has \(m=0\) and uses only the current base matrix.
immediate_consequences_latex: Storing the correction representation requires \(O(mn)\) vector storage rather than an additional dense matrix when the base action is available implicitly.
Discarding a pair can destroy an older secant equation; only constraints deliberately preserved by the management operator remain guaranteed.
boundary_notes: The definition does not claim equivalence between truncated and full-memory Broyden iterates.
A restart base must be specified independently, for example by a fresh finite-difference Jacobian.
Limited-memory BFGS sources do not automatically establish corresponding Broyden root-method formulas.

notation.meaning: indices of active rank-one correction pairs

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-memory and restarted Broyden representations
Limited-Memory Broyden Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent the inverse approximation by a base operator plus at most m stored rank-one corrections, discarding the oldest correction when memory is full.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a memory limit \(m\geq1\) and a base inverse model \(\bar H_k\). Retain at most the newest \(m\) pairs of rank-one factors \((u_i,v_i)\) and apply \(H_kz=\bar H_kz+\sum_{i\in I_k}u_i(v_i^Tz)\), where \(|I_k|\leq m\). Compute \(s_k=-H_kF(x_k)\), form \(y_k=F(x_k+s_k)-F(x_k)\), append factors representing an admissible inverse Broyden correction, and discard the oldest pair if the memory limit is exceeded. Stop using the residual norm or step norm.
assumptions_latex: Every retained correction has a nonzero Broyden denominator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse Broyden iteration retaining at most a fixed number of rank-one corrections.

knowledge_statements.title: Restarted Broyden Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodically discard accumulated Broyden corrections and rebuild a base Jacobian or inverse model when an age, stability, conditioning, or progress test triggers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a restart rule and an initial direct or inverse model. Perform Broyden steps and rank-one updates until the restart rule fires, for example after \(r\) accepted updates, a small update denominator, excessive conditioning, or failed residual decrease. At a restart, discard the accumulated corrections and set \(B_k\) to a newly evaluated or differenced Jacobian model, or set \(H_k\) to a corresponding inverse or preconditioner. Resume Broyden updating and terminate when the residual or step criterion is satisfied.
assumptions_latex: The restart model is nonsingular or supports a well-defined step.
The restart rule is evaluated after each attempted or accepted update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{restart at }k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad B_k\leftarrow\widehat J_k\ \text{ or }\ H_k\leftarrow\widehat J_k^{-1}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Broyden iteration periodically replacing accumulated secant information by a fresh base model.

notation.meaning: maximum number of updates between scheduled restarts

knowledge_statements.title: Memory–Restart Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limited memory reduces storage and operator application to order nm; restarting similarly caps accumulated information but periodically pays to rebuild the base model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), a dense direct or inverse Broyden matrix requires \(O(n^2)\) storage and \(O(n^2)\) work per matrix-vector product; solving a dense unfactored direct system costs \(O(n^3)\). A limited-memory inverse representation with \(m\) stored rank-one corrections requires \(O(nm)\) storage and \(O(nm)\) work per application. Restarting every \(r\) updates caps retained secant information at \(r\) but additionally incurs the cost of rebuilding and, when required, factoring the restart model.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic costs use the dense real-RAM model.
Each stored rank-one factor is an \(n\)-vector.
No exploitable sparsity or special matrix structure is assumed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic and storage comparison for dense, limited-memory, and restarted Broyden representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Least-Change Secant Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A least-change update enforces the newest secant equation while minimizing a weighted distance from the previous Jacobian approximation; the unrestricted Frobenius solution is rank one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\neq0\), and \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\). Given a matrix norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{W}\) induced by a positive-definite weighting, a least-change secant update is any solution
\[
B_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{B\in\mathcal{M}}\tfrac12\lVert B-B_k\rVert_W^2
\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bs_k=y_k,
\]
where \(\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) specifies optional structure. If \(\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), the norm is Frobenius, and feasibility holds, the minimizer is the rank-one update
\[
B_{k+1}=B_k+\frac{(y_k-B_ks_k)s_k^{\mathsf T}}{s_k^{\mathsf T}s_k}.
\]
assumptions_latex: The structured constraint set is nonempty when \(\mathcal M\neq\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\) and \(B_{k+1}\) has minimum prescribed change from \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional matrix updates satisfying one new secant equation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Least-change projection onto a secant set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be an affine space of admissible derivative approximations, let \(B_k\in\mathcal A\), let \(s_k\ne0\), and let \(y_k^{\#}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) specify the desired secant action.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional direct secant updates. The matrix norm and admissible affine structure are part of the method specification; existence or uniqueness depends on their choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matrix norm \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathsf M}\), a least-change secant update is any solution \[B_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{B\in\mathcal A}\{\|B-B_k\|_{\mathsf M}:Bs_k=y_k^{\#}\}.\] Equivalently, it is a metric projection of \(B_k\) onto \(\mathcal A\cap Q(y_k^{\#},s_k)\), where \[Q(y,s)=\{B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:Bs=y\}.\] The update is defined only when the feasible intersection is nonempty and a minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A least-change secant method chooses the new derivative approximation by changing the old one as little as possible, in a specified matrix norm, while enforcing a secant equation and any required matrix structure. Thus the update is a projection onto the intersection of an admissible matrix space and a secant affine set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\mathcal A=\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and the Frobenius norm, \[B_{k+1}=B_k+\frac{(y_k^{\#}-B_ks_k)s_k^T}{s_k^Ts_k}.\]
special_cases_latex: The unstructured Frobenius projection is the classical direct good Broyden update.
Weighted Frobenius norms produce scaled least-change updates.
Choosing \(\mathcal A\) as the symmetric matrices yields a structured problem that may require compatibility conditions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict convexity of the metric on a nonempty convex feasible set gives uniqueness.
The latest secant equation holds exactly for every feasible least-change update.
boundary_notes: If \(\mathcal A\cap Q(y_k^{\#},s_k)=\varnothing\), a relaxed or projected secant condition must be defined separately.
Changing the norm generally changes the update.
The optimization problem defines the update but does not ensure nonsingularity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structured least-change secant update
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Suppose the derivative decomposes as \(J(x)=C(x)+A(x)\), where \(C(x)\) is available and \(A(x)\) belongs to a prescribed affine subspace \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) encoding structure such as sparsity, symmetry, fixed rows, or fixed columns.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structured derivative approximation. The family preserves membership in a specified affine matrix class while imposing a compatible secant action on the unknown component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\), \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\), and choose a structured secant target \(y_k^{\#}\), canonically \[y_k^{\#}=y_k-C(x_{k+1})s_k.\] A structure-preserving least-change secant update selects \[A_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{A\in\mathcal A}\{\|A-A_k\|_{\mathsf M}:As_k=y_k^{\#}\},\] and defines \(B_{k+1}=C(x_{k+1})+A_{k+1}\). Thus \(A_{k+1}\in\mathcal A\), and with the canonical target the complete approximation satisfies \(B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method separates a known derivative component from an unknown structured component. It updates only the unknown component, selecting the nearest matrix that remains in the prescribed structural class and satisfies an appropriate secant equation. With the default target obtained by subtracting the known component's action, the complete derivative approximation satisfies the ordinary secant equation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[A_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{A\in\mathcal A\cap Q(y_k^{\#},s_k)}\|A-A_k\|_{\mathsf M}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C\equiv0\) and \(\mathcal A\) is a fixed sparsity-pattern subspace, every approximation retains that sparsity pattern.
If selected rows of the derivative are known exactly, \(C\) may contain those rows while \(\mathcal A\) forces the corresponding rows of \(A\) to be zero.
With \(\mathcal A=\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), the definition reduces to an unstructured least-change secant update.
immediate_consequences_latex: The complete approximation interpolates the latest residual difference whenever the canonical target is feasible.
Structural constraints are maintained at every update by membership in \(\mathcal A\).
boundary_notes: The feasible intersection may be empty for an incompatible structure and secant target.
Preserving sparsity of a direct approximation does not imply sparsity of its inverse.
A nonlinear manifold of structured matrices is not covered by the affine-subspace formulation.

notation.meaning: secant target for the structured component
complete derivative approximation after combining known and updated components

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Secant Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse secant method solves with a sparse Jacobian approximation and updates it by the smallest pattern-preserving change satisfying the latest secant equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}^2\) be a prescribed sparsity pattern and define \(\mathcal S_E=\{B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}:B_{ij}=0\text{ for }(i,j)\notin E\}\). From \(x_k\), compute a step \(p_k\) by solving \(B_kp_k=-F(x_k)\), set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\), and form \(s_k=p_k\) and \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\). Update by
\[
B_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{B\in\mathcal S_E}\lVert B-B_k\rVert_F
\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bs_k=y_k.
\]
Stop when a prescribed residual or step tolerance is met; otherwise repeat, provided the constrained secant system remains feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is evaluable at each accepted iterate.
The constrained secant update is feasible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-change Jacobian updates constrained to a prescribed sparsity pattern.

notation.meaning: linear space of matrices supported on the pattern

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The pattern-constrained algorithm is mathematically coherent under its explicit feasibility assumption, and the algorithm content kind fits. However, the cited general structure and secant sections do not specifically establish this sparse least-change algorithm or its safeguards; a sparse-secant section, theorem, or page-level treatment is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Secant Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured secant update is the unique least-change matrix in a prescribed affine model that satisfies the new secant equation, whenever the constraints are feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the admissible Jacobian models form the affine space \(\mathcal A=B^{(0)}+\mathcal L\), where \(\mathcal L\subseteq\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is a linear subspace encoding structure such as symmetry, block form, or known matrix components. For a positive-definite matrix weighting \(W\), the structured least-change secant update is
\[
B_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{B\in\mathcal A}\tfrac12\lVert B-B_k\rVert_W^2
\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bs_k=y_k.
\]
Whenever \(B_k\in\mathcal A\), the norm is strictly convex on \(\mathcal L\), and the affine constraints are feasible, the minimizer is unique, remains in \(\mathcal A\), and satisfies the secant equation.
assumptions_latex: The weighted norm is strictly convex on \(\mathcal L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{k+1}\in\mathcal A\), \(B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\), and the constrained minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Secant updates restricted to an affine matrix model encoding known Jacobian structure.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The affine constrained least-change formulation fits the structured-secant leaf, but the exact weighted norm is not defined and the cited locators do not specifically support the general affine-model and uniqueness formulation. A source locator treating structured secant updates with the stated weighting and feasibility conditions is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Preservation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact structure preservation is possible precisely when the requested secant displacement lies in the action of the allowed matrix variations; otherwise one constraint must be relaxed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an affine structural model \(\mathcal A=B^{(0)}+\mathcal L\), a structure-preserving secant update for data \((s,y)\) exists exactly when
\[
y-B^{(0)}s\in\mathcal Ls:=\{Ls:L\in\mathcal L\}.
\]
Thus structure preservation can fail even when \(s\neq0\). For example, if \(\mathcal A\) is the set of diagonal matrices, \(s=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\), and \(y=(0,1)^{\mathsf T}\), every \(B\in\mathcal A\) has \(Bs=(B_{11},0)^{\mathsf T}\), so no structured matrix satisfies \(Bs=y\). Any update must then relax the secant equation, enlarge the structural model, or reject the pair.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A=B^{(0)}+\mathcal L\) is an affine matrix family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{B\in\mathcal A:Bs=y\}\neq\varnothing\) if and only if \(y-B^{(0)}s\in\mathcal Ls\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility boundary for simultaneously imposing a matrix structure and a secant equation.

notation.meaning: all changes in the matrix action on the step permitted by the structure

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The feasibility equivalence and diagonal counterexample are mathematically consistent, and failure_boundary is the correct role. The cited least-change section has not been shown to support this exact affine-image characterization, so a specific supporting locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Multisecant Equation Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multisecant method fits one Jacobian approximation to several recent step-difference equations, with dependent history removed or regularized before computing the next step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose a memory length \(m\ge1\). At iteration \(k\), retain \(q_k\le m\) step and residual-difference pairs and assemble \(S_k=[s_{k-q_k},\ldots,s_{k-1}]\) and \(Y_k=[y_{k-q_k},\ldots,y_{k-1}]\). Given \(B_k\), compute
\[
B_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{B}\lVert B-B_k\rVert_F
\quad\text{subject to}\quad BS_k=Y_k.
\]
If \(S_k\) has full column rank, the unique unrestricted solution is
\[
B_{k+1}=B_k+(Y_k-B_kS_k)(S_k^{\mathsf T}S_k)^{-1}S_k^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Use \(B_{k+1}p_{k+1}=-F(x_{k+1})\), discard or regularize dependent columns, and stop at the prescribed residual tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is evaluable at retained iterates.
\(S_k\) has full column rank for the displayed closed form.
The linear system defining the next step is solvable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-change Jacobian updates enforcing several recent secant equations simultaneously.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The displayed matrix is the unique Frobenius least-change solution when the retained step matrix has full column rank, and algorithm is an appropriate kind. However, the retained vectors s_i and y_i are not explicitly defined in the record, and the generic secant-method locator does not confirm the multisecant specialization, history handling, or regularization guidance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multisecant equation method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), let \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\), and define \(s_i=x_{i+1}-x_i\) and \(y_i=F(x_{i+1})-F(x_i)\). For an index set \(I_k=\{i_1,\ldots,i_m\}\), put \(S_k=[s_{i_1},\ldots,s_{i_m}]\) and \(Y_k=[y_{i_1},\ldots,y_{i_m}]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic methods for square nonlinear systems; both direct- and inverse-Jacobian formulations are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multisecant equation method is an iteration that constructs a matrix \(B_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) or \(H_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) satisfying, exactly or in a stated least-squares sense, \(B_kS_k=Y_k\) or \(H_kY_k=S_k\), respectively, for two or more stored secant pairs, and then computes \(p_k\) from \(B_kp_k=-F(x_k)\) or \(p_k=-H_kF(x_k)\), followed by \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\). An exact direct multisecant matrix exists precisely when \(S_kc=0\Rightarrow Y_kc=0\); an exact inverse multisecant matrix exists precisely when \(Y_kc=0\Rightarrow S_kc=0\). When exact equations are incompatible or underdetermine the matrix, the method must specify a least-change, regularized, or least-squares selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonlinear system, collect at least two displacement vectors and their residual differences into matrices \(S_k\) and \(Y_k\). A multisecant method chooses a Jacobian model satisfying \(B_kS_k=Y_k\), or an inverse model satisfying \(H_kY_k=S_k\), exactly or by an explicitly specified approximation rule, and uses that model to form the next equation-solving step.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(S_k\) has full column rank, every exact direct solution has the form \(B_k=Y_kS_k^\dagger+Z(I-S_kS_k^\dagger)\), with arbitrary \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
If \(Y_k\) has full column rank, every exact inverse solution has the form \(H_k=S_kY_k^\dagger+Z(I-Y_kY_k^\dagger)\).
special_cases_latex: With one stored pair, \(m=1\), the definition reduces to an ordinary one-secant quasi-Newton equation.
Choosing the feasible matrix nearest a reference matrix in a specified matrix norm gives a least-change multisecant update.
immediate_consequences_latex: For every retained column, the model reproduces the observed residual change: \(B_ks_i=y_i\), or maps it back to the observed displacement: \(H_ky_i=s_i\).
boundary_notes: The equations alone do not uniquely determine an update unless a selection rule is supplied.
No convergence or nonsingularity property follows merely from satisfying several secant equations.
review_flags: No inspected local source was found that supports the simultaneous multisecant definition and its exact consistency conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-point acceleration method family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(G:X\to X\), and define the fixed-point residual \(r(x)=G(x)-x\). Let \(m_k\geq0\) and let \(\mathcal H_k=(x_{k-m_k},\ldots,x_k;G(x_{k-m_k}),\ldots,G(x_k))\) denote the available history.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic acceleration of a prescribed fixed-point map; convergence is not included in the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed-point acceleration method for \(G\) is a family of history-dependent maps \(\mathcal A_k\) generating \(x_{k+1}=\mathcal A_k(\mathcal H_k)\in X\), where \(\mathcal A_k\) uses one or more past iterates, images, or residuals to replace the stationary update \(G(x_k)\). It is fixed-point preserving if, for every \(x_*\in X\) with \(G(x_*)=x_*\), a constant history at \(x_*\) satisfies \(\mathcal A_k(x_*,\ldots,x_*;x_*,\ldots,x_*)=x_*\). The family is an acceleration relative to the base iteration only after an additional performance criterion—such as a smaller local linear factor, a higher local order, or a reduced residual—is stated; fixed-point preservation alone defines the admissible transformed iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-point acceleration method replaces the update \(x_{k+1}=G(x_k)\) by a history-dependent update using past iterates, mapped points, or residuals. The transformed update must retain every fixed point of \(G\) when supplied a constant fixed-point history. Calling it an acceleration additionally requires a stated comparison criterion.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using \(r(x)=G(x)-x\), the stationary map is \(G(x)=x+r(x)\), so an acceleration may equivalently be represented as a history-dependent correction \(x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k(r_{k-m_k},\ldots,r_k,x_{k-m_k},\ldots,x_k)\).
special_cases_latex: The choice \(m_k=0\) and \(\mathcal A_k(x_k;G(x_k))=G(x_k)\) recovers stationary fixed-point iteration.
Affine mixing, Anderson acceleration, and nonlinear extrapolation arise from different restrictions on \(\mathcal A_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If the iteration reaches a fixed point and its history is reset to that point, all subsequent iterates remain there.
boundary_notes: The definition does not require monotone residual decrease.
A history-dependent map that changes the fixed-point set is not fixed-point preserving in this sense.

notation.meaning: Iteration history supplied to the update.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationary fixed-point iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty subset of a normed space and let \(G:X\to X\) be a single fixed map. A point \(x_*\in X\) solves the associated fixed-point problem when \(G(x_*)=x_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic iteration with an iteration map that does not vary with the iteration index or depend on stored history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The stationary fixed-point iteration generated by \(G\) from \(x_0\in X\) is the sequence \(\{x_k\}_{k\geq0}\) defined for every \(k\geq0\) by \(x_{k+1}=G(x_k)\). It is well-defined for all indices because \(G(X)\subseteq X\). The adjective stationary means that the same map \(G\) is applied at every iteration; there are no iteration-dependent parameters, history-dependent coefficients, or changing auxiliary maps in the defining recurrence. The residual at an iterate is \(r_k=G(x_k)-x_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\), and termination at an exact solution is characterized by \(r_k=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from \(x_0\in X\), stationary fixed-point iteration repeatedly applies one unchanged self-map: \(x_{k+1}=G(x_k)\). Its residual is the displacement \(G(x_k)-x_k\), which vanishes exactly at a fixed point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(r(x)=G(x)-x\), the recurrence is \(x_{k+1}=x_k+r(x_k)\), and the fixed-point equation is the residual equation \(r(x)=0\).
special_cases_latex: For an affine map \(G(x)=Mx+c\), the recurrence is the stationary linear iteration \(x_{k+1}=Mx_k+c\).
When \(G(x)=x-\alpha F(x)\) with fixed \(\alpha\), the recurrence is a fixed-step residual iteration for \(F(x)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(x_k=x_*\) and \(G(x_*)=x_*\), then \(x_j=x_*\) for every \(j\geq k\).
boundary_notes: Variable relaxation, adaptive maps, and history-based extrapolation are nonstationary variants.
The definition does not assert that the sequence converges.
review_flags: The mathematical definition is standard, but no exact inspected source locator was available for this slot.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationary fixed-point iteration
Picard Iterations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Picard iteration repeatedly applies the fixed-point map and returns an iterate when its residual, step, or iteration count meets the chosen stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be a nonempty subset of a normed space and let \(G:D\to D\). Given \(x_0\in D\), Picard iteration generates
\[
x_{k+1}=G(x_k),\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots.
\]
Equivalently, for the fixed-point residual \(r(x)=G(x)-x\), the update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k+r(x_k)\). Stop when \(\lVert r(x_k)\rVert\le\varepsilon_r\), when \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert\le\varepsilon_x\), or after a prescribed iteration limit; return the last iterate. Any limit \(x_*\in D\) at which \(G\) is continuous satisfies \(G(x_*)=x_*\).
assumptions_latex: Continuity at a limit point is assumed only for the fixed-point conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=G(x_k)\); if \(x_k\to x_*\) and \(G\) is continuous at \(x_*\), then \(G(x_*)=x_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unaccelerated iteration of a nonlinear self-map.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The Picard iteration and conditional fixed-point conclusion are standard and correctly scoped, and algorithm fits the container. No source or inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Fixed-Point Iterations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary fixed-point method repeatedly applies one unchanged map; a standard residual form uses the same nonsingular preconditioner at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be a nonempty subset of a normed space and fix a single map \(T:D\to D\). A stationary fixed-point iteration selects \(x_0\in D\) and generates
\[
x_{k+1}=T(x_k),
\]
using the same \(T\) for every \(k\). For a residual equation \(F(x)=0\) and a fixed nonsingular preconditioner \(M\), the stationary residual form is
\[
T(x)=x-M^{-1}F(x),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-M^{-1}F(x_k).
\]
Stop at a prescribed residual, step, or iteration threshold and return the last iterate. Stationarity excludes iteration-dependent maps, parameters, or preconditioners.
assumptions_latex: \(T:D\to D\) is fixed throughout the iteration.
In the residual form, \(M\) is fixed and nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) for every \(k\), with no iteration-dependent change to \(T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point schemes whose iteration map does not vary with the iteration index.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The stationary-map description fits the algorithm container, but no source is supplied. In addition, the residual specialization must require that x-M^{-1}F(x) belongs to D for every relevant x in D; nonsingularity of M alone does not make the displayed map a self-map.

knowledge_statements.title: Map-Contractivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-map with global Lipschitz constant below one has one fixed point, and Picard iteration converges to it geometrically from every point in its closed domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be a nonempty closed subset of a Banach space and let \(T:D\to D\). Suppose there exists \(q\in[0,1)\) such that
\[
\lVert T(x)-T(y)\rVert\le q\lVert x-y\rVert
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in D.
\]
Then \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x_*\in D\), and every Picard sequence \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) with \(x_0\in D\) converges to \(x_*\). Moreover,
\[
\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert\le q^k\lVert x_0-x_*\rVert
\]
and, for \(k\ge1\),
\[
\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert\le\frac{q}{1-q}\lVert x_k-x_{k-1}\rVert.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a nonempty closed subset of a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique \(x_*\in D\) with \(T(x_*)=x_*\), and \(x_k\to x_*\) at least \(q\)-linearly.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach contraction regime for stationary fixed-point convergence.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The contraction theorem, geometric estimate, and a posteriori estimate are correctly stated for a closed subset of a Banach space, and theorem is the appropriate content kind. No authoritative theorem, section, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relaxed fixed-point mixing
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(G:X\to X\), and let \(r(x)=G(x)-x\). Let \(\beta_k\in\mathbb R\) be a prescribed or adaptively selected mixing parameter for which the produced point remains in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step scalar mixing between the current iterate and its image; multi-history Anderson combinations are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalar fixed-point mixing iteration is defined by \(x_{k+1}=(1-\beta_k)x_k+\beta_kG(x_k)=x_k+\beta_kr(x_k)\). It is under-relaxed when \(0<\beta_k<1\), unrelaxed when \(\beta_k=1\), and over-relaxed when \(\beta_k>1\). If coefficients are allowed to vary but remain scalar and the update uses only \(x_k\) and \(G(x_k)\), the resulting methods form the variable-mixing family. Every fixed point of \(G\) is fixed by every member of this family because \(r(x_*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-point mixing forms the next iterate from the current point and its mapped point: \(x_{k+1}=(1-\beta_k)x_k+\beta_kG(x_k)\). Values below one under-relax the base update, one reproduces it, and values above one over-relax it.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The update is a residual correction \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\beta_kr_k\).
For \(0\leq\beta_k\leq1\), the new point is a convex combination of \(x_k\) and \(G(x_k)\).
special_cases_latex: \(\beta_k=1\) gives stationary fixed-point iteration.
A constant \(\beta_k\equiv\beta\) gives stationary relaxed mixing.
immediate_consequences_latex: For any \(x_*\) satisfying \(G(x_*)=x_*\), the mixed map also sends \(x_*\) to itself.
boundary_notes: For \(\beta_k\notin[0,1]\), convexity of \(X\) alone does not ensure \(x_{k+1}\in X\).
Mixing does not by itself imply residual decrease or convergence.
review_flags: No inspected source locator directly supported this fixed-point mixing taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed fixed-point mixing
Relaxation Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation scales the fixed-point residual before updating; parameters below one damp Picard iteration, one recovers it, and parameters above one extrapolate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G:D\to X\) be a fixed-point map on a vector space, and choose parameters \(\omega_k\) such that each update remains in \(D\). Starting from \(x_0\in D\), define
\[
x_{k+1}=(1-\omega_k)x_k+\omega_kG(x_k)
=x_k+\omega_k r(x_k),
\qquad r(x)=G(x)-x.
\]
Constant relaxation uses \(\omega_k\equiv\omega\); \(0<\omega<1\) is under-relaxation, \(\omega=1\) is Picard iteration, and \(\omega>1\) is over-relaxation. Stop at a prescribed residual, step, or iteration threshold. Fixed points are unchanged whenever \(\omega_k\neq0\), since the relaxed residual equals \(\omega_k r(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(D\) lies in a vector space and contains every generated affine combination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\omega_kr(x_k)\), and the relaxed map has the same fixed points as \(G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar relaxation of a fixed-point map, including under- and over-relaxation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The relaxation formula fits the algorithm leaf, but X is not introduced as the ambient vector space containing D. For variable omega_k, fixed-point preservation should be stated for each relaxed map rather than for an unspecified single relaxed map. No supporting source locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Averaging Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging forms a convex combination of the identity and a self-map, preserves its fixed points, and yields an averaged nonexpansive operator when the original map is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a normed space and let \(G:C\to C\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define the averaged map
\[
T_\alpha=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha G,
\qquad T_\alpha(x)=(1-\alpha)x+\alpha G(x).
\]
Then \(T_\alpha:C\to C\) and
\[
\operatorname{Fix}(T_\alpha)=\operatorname{Fix}(G).
\]
If \(G\) is nonexpansive, then \(T_\alpha\) is an \(\alpha\)-averaged nonexpansive operator. Iteration of \(T_\alpha\) is the constant under-relaxed scheme \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha(G(x_k)-x_k)\); variable averaging replaces \(\alpha\) by admissible \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\).
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is nonexpansive only for the averaged-nonexpansive conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\alpha:C\to C\), \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_\alpha)=\operatorname{Fix}(G)\), and nonexpansiveness of \(G\) makes \(T_\alpha\) averaged.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex averaging of the identity with a fixed-point map.

notation.meaning: set of fixed points of a map

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Regime Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxed linear iteration converges precisely when every relaxed eigenmode lies inside the unit disk; boundary modes need not decay, and exterior modes diverge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the affine map \(G(x)=Ax+b\), a constant relaxation parameter \(\omega\) gives the iteration matrix
\[
T_\omega=(1-\omega)I+\omega A.
\]
The iteration converges to the unique fixed point from every initial vector exactly when
\[
\rho(T_\omega)<1.
\]
For a real eigenmode \(Av=\lambda v\), its error multiplier is \(\mu_\omega(\lambda)=1-\omega+\omega\lambda\), so that mode is stable exactly when \(\lvert1-\\omega+\omega\lambda\rvert<1\). Equality permits nondecay, while a value exceeding one causes divergence for initial errors with a component along that mode. Consequently, \(0<\omega<1\) alone does not ensure convergence if \(G\) is expansive.
assumptions_latex: \(G(x)=Ax+b\) on a finite-dimensional complex or real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global convergence holds if and only if \(\rho((1-\omega)I+\omega A)<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar stability boundary for relaxed linear fixed-point modes.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The spectral-radius criterion is standard for finite-dimensional affine stationary iteration under the stated nonsingularity assumption, and failure_boundary fits. However, the eigenmode expression contains the malformed sequence \\omega where \omega is intended, and no source locator supports the claimed sharp boundary and mode behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Anderson acceleration by residual-minimizing affine combinations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), define \(r_i=G(x_i)-x_i\), choose a depth bound \(m\geq0\), and set \(m_k=\min\{m,k\}\) and \(I_k=\{k-m_k,\ldots,k\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, unregularized Anderson acceleration in its affine-coefficient form, with optional scalar damping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), Anderson acceleration chooses coefficients \(\alpha^{(k)}=(\alpha_i)_{i\in I_k}\) solving \(\min_{\alpha}\|\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i r_i\|_2\) subject to \(\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i=1\), and sets \(x_{k+1}=\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i\bigl((1-\beta_k)x_i+\beta_kG(x_i)\bigr)\), where \(\beta_k\neq0\) is the damping parameter. The undamped form uses \(\beta_k=1\), giving \(x_{k+1}=\sum_i\alpha_iG(x_i)\). If the constrained least-squares problem has multiple minimizers, the method must prescribe a selection, regularization, or rank-handling rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anderson acceleration forms an affine combination of recent residuals having minimum Euclidean norm, then applies the same coefficients to recent damped fixed-point images. In the undamped method the next point is the corresponding affine combination of \(G(x_i)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Eliminating one affine coefficient converts the constrained problem into an unconstrained least-squares problem in residual differences.
The coefficient form can be rewritten as a multisecant inverse-Jacobian correction when the same retained differences and compatible regularization are used.
special_cases_latex: Depth \(m=0\) gives damped fixed-point iteration \(x_{k+1}=(1-\beta_k)x_k+\beta_kG(x_k)\).
Setting \(\beta_k=1\) gives the conventional undamped affine-combination form.
immediate_consequences_latex: Because the coefficients sum to one, a constant history at a fixed point is mapped to that same fixed point.
boundary_notes: Rank deficiency may make the coefficient vector nonunique even though the minimized residual combination is unique.
Safeguards, restarts, and regularization are additional variants rather than part of this core definition.
review_flags: No inspected authoritative source directly supported the stated Anderson coefficient formulation.
