knowledge_statements.statement_title: Globalization and Safeguarding of a Local Residual Step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and let \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|W F(x)\|_2^2\), where \(W\) is fixed and nonsingular on the residual space. At iteration \(k\), let a local model produce a candidate direction or step.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-dimensional globalization of Newton, quasi-Newton, or residual-model steps through merit decrease or model-agreement tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A globalization-safeguarding calculus is a rule that maps \((x_k,F(x_k),J_k,\mathcal M_k,\mathcal S_k)\) to an accepted step \(s_k\) and updated safeguard state \(\mathcal S_{k+1}\), subject to an explicit acceptance test. In line-search form,
\[
s_k=\alpha_kp_k,\quad \alpha_k\in(0,1],\quad \phi(x_k+s_k)\le \phi(x_k)+c\alpha_k\nabla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k,
\]
with \(c\in(0,1)\). In trust-region form, \(s_k\) approximately minimizes a local model over \(\|D_ks\|\le\Delta_k\), and acceptance and radius updating use the ratio of actual to predicted reduction. Safeguards bound trial parameters, detect ill-conditioning or failed progress, and replace an unsafe local step by a controlled one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Globalization-safeguarding calculus is the collection of mathematical rules that embeds a fast local residual step in a globally controlled iteration. It supplies a scalar progress measure, an admissible trial-step set, an acceptance inequality, and a state update. A line search shortens a direction until the merit function decreases sufficiently. A trust-region method restricts model minimization to a neighborhood and changes that neighborhood according to model agreement. Safeguards keep interpolation, radii, conditioning, and step lengths within declared bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\qquad s_k\in\mathcal A_k:=\{s:\text{the selected acceptance and safeguard conditions hold}\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For equation solving with \(W=I\), \(\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^TF(x)\).

The global mechanism may be represented as a state transition \((x_k,\mathcal S_k)\mapsto(x_{k+1},\mathcal S_{k+1})\), where \(\mathcal S_k\) contains a step length, trust radius, scaling, and conditioning information.
special_cases_latex: Backtracking Newton uses \(p_k=-J_k^{-1}F(x_k)\) and varies only \(\alpha_k\).
A residual trust-region method minimizes \(\tfrac12\|F_k+J_ks\|_2^2\) over \(\|D_ks\|_2\le\Delta_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: When the full local step passes the acceptance test, the globalization mechanism may accept \(\alpha_k=1\) or an interior trust-region solution, preserving the intended local method.
boundary_notes: Globalization does not by itself guarantee convergence to a root; the merit function can have stationary points with nonzero residual.
The definition does not assert a convergence theorem or fix universal acceptance constants.

notation.meaning: Safeguard state, such as radius, scaling, bounds, and counters.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Merit-Function Globalization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular, and define \(\phi_W(x)=\tfrac12\|WF(x)\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional equation or least-squares residuals, using a fixed weighted Euclidean merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A merit-function globalization of a residual method is an iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) in which trial steps generated by a local equation or residual model are accepted, rejected, or shortened according to decrease in
\[
\phi_W(x)=\frac12F(x)^TW^TWF(x),\qquad \nabla\phi_W(x)=J(x)^TW^TWF(x).
\]
For a line search, a canonical sufficient-decrease condition is \(\phi_W(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le\phi_W(x_k)+c\alpha_k\nabla\phi_W(x_k)^Tp_k\), where \(c\in(0,1)\) and \(p_k\) is a descent direction. For a model-based method, acceptance may instead compare actual merit reduction with predicted model reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merit-function globalization converts residual reduction into scalar optimization. The weighted squared residual \(\phi_W(x)=\frac12\|WF(x)\|_2^2\) ranks trial points and supplies the gradient \(J(x)^TW^TWF(x)\). A residual step is globally controlled by requiring sufficient merit decrease or satisfactory agreement between actual and predicted merit reduction. The scalar merit rule is an acceptance device; it does not change the defining root equation \(F(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(x)=0\Longrightarrow\phi_W(x)=0,\qquad x_{k+1}\text{ is accepted only according to the declared reduction test for }\phi_W.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(W\) is nonsingular, \(\phi_W(x)=0\) if and only if \(F(x)=0\).
For \(W=I\), the merit function is \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\) and \(\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^TF(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For a square system with nonsingular \(J_k\), the Newton direction \(p_k=-J_k^{-1}F_k\) satisfies \(\nabla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k=-\|F_k\|_2^2<0\) whenever \(F_k\ne0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Any root is a global minimizer of the nonnegative merit function with value zero.
Stationarity \(J(x)^TW^TWF(x)=0\) need not imply root attainment.
boundary_notes: If \(W\) is singular, zero weighted merit need not imply \(F(x)=0\).
Nonsmooth residual norms require generalized derivatives and are outside this smooth definition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes solvability of a nonlinear system through the minimum value of its sharp-merit reformulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Norm Merit Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half the squared residual norm is nonnegative, vanishes exactly at roots, and converts residual reduction into an ordinary differentiable descent test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a continuously differentiable residual map \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), the residual-norm merit function is \[\phi(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2.\] It is nonnegative, satisfies \(\phi(x)=0\) if and only if \(F(x)=0\), and has gradient \(\nabla\phi(x)=J_F(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x)\). Thus a direction \(p\) is a strict descent direction exactly when \(F(x)^{\mathsf T}J_F(x)p<0\). For a Newton direction satisfying \(J_F(x)p=-F(x)\), one has \(\nabla\phi(x)^{\mathsf T}p=-\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\).
assumptions_latex: For the final identity, \(J_F(x)p=-F(x)\) is consistent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-squares merit function for globalizing a square or rectangular differentiable residual system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sum-of-squares residual merit function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition and root-to-minimizer implication, with the failure of the converse recorded explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For r=(r_1,\ldots,r_n), define f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^n r_i(x)^2. Every root x^* of r is a global minimizer of f with value zero. A local minimizer \bar x with f(\bar x)>0 is not a root, so local minimization of f does not by itself imply root attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum-of-squares residual merit function is one half of the squared Euclidean residual norm. Every root is a zero-valued global minimizer, but a positive-valued local minimizer is not a root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(x^*)=0\implies f(x^*)=0=\min_{x\in X}f(x),\qquad \bigl(\bar x\text{ is a local minimizer and }f(\bar x)>0\bigr)\implies r(\bar x)\ne0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaled and Weighted Residual Merit Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and let \(D_F=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\) with \(d_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive diagonal residual weighting in finite-dimensional smooth residual problems; variable-space scaling is distinguished from residual-space weighting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The diagonal scaling-weighting family of squared-residual merit functions is
\[
\phi_{D_F}(x)=\frac12\|D_FF(x)\|_2^2=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m d_i^2F_i(x)^2,
\]
with
\[
\nabla\phi_{D_F}(x)=J(x)^TD_F^2F(x),\qquad B_{\mathrm{GN}}(x)=J(x)^TD_F^2J(x).
\]
The weights are admissible when every \(d_i\) is finite and strictly positive, ensuring \(\phi_{D_F}(x)=0\iff F(x)=0\). A variable scaling \(D_x\succ0\) is a separate choice that measures steps by \(\|D_xs\|_2\) and changes scaled steepest-descent or trust-region geometry without deleting residual equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merit scaling assigns a positive scale to each residual component before forming its squared norm. The resulting objective is \(\frac12\sum_i d_i^2F_i(x)^2\), its gradient is \(J^TD_F^2F\), and its Gauss–Newton matrix is \(J^TD_F^2J\). Strictly positive finite weights preserve the zero set while changing the relative influence of residual components. Scaling the variables with \(D_x\) is related but distinct: it changes the geometry used to measure steps rather than the relative residual penalties.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(M=D_F^2\succ0\) gives \(\phi_M(x)=\tfrac12F(x)^TMF(x)\).
If typical residual magnitudes are \(r_i^{\mathrm{typ}}>0\), a common static normalization is \(d_i=1/r_i^{\mathrm{typ}}\).
special_cases_latex: Uniform weighting \(D_F=\gamma I\), \(\gamma>0\), rescales the merit value but does not change its stationary points.
Unweighted residual minimization is recovered with \(D_F=I\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The normal-equation stationarity condition becomes \(J(x)^TD_F^2F(x)=0\).
boundary_notes: Zero weights discard equations and therefore do not preserve the root set.
Dynamic or iteration-dependent weighting requires additional update and boundedness conditions not specified here.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Merit Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular equation scaling preserves all roots but changes the least-squares geometry and the relative influence of residual components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and let \(S\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular. The scaled residual merit function is \[\phi_S(x)=\tfrac12\lVert SF(x)\rVert_2^2=\tfrac12F(x)^{\mathsf T}S^{\mathsf T}SF(x).\] Its gradient is \(\nabla\phi_S(x)=J_F(x)^{\mathsf T}S^{\mathsf T}SF(x)\). Nonsingularity of \(S\) preserves the root set: \(\phi_S(x)=0\) if and only if \(F(x)=0\). Scaling changes the relative numerical magnitudes of residual components and therefore changes descent comparisons away from roots.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual merit after fixed nonsingular scaling of equations.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic statement is correct, but the cited locator identifies a general restricted-step chapter and has not been shown to support fixed nonsingular equation scaling or its merit-function interpretation. A source locator specifically addressing residual scaling or weighted least squares is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Merit Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite weight changes the residual metric and the influence of residual directions while preserving the roots; a merely semidefinite weight may not preserve them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be symmetric positive definite. The weighted residual merit function is \[\phi_W(x)=\tfrac12F(x)^{\mathsf T}WF(x)=\tfrac12\lVert W^{1/2}F(x)\rVert_2^2.\] Its gradient is \(\nabla\phi_W(x)=J_F(x)^{\mathsf T}WF(x)\), and \(\phi_W(x)=0\) if and only if \(F(x)=0\). The matrix \(W\) changes the metric and relative influence of residual directions without changing the root set. If \(W\) is only positive semidefinite, the zero-set equivalence need not hold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite weighted least-squares merit for residual systems.

notation.meaning: symmetric positive-definite square root of the weight

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5 Restricted Step Methods p. 95

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling–Weighting Interactions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling and weighting combine by congruence: their effect is completely represented by the positive-definite metric induced on the original residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a residual map \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), a nonsingular scaling \(S\), and a symmetric positive-definite weight \(W\), weighting the scaled residual gives \[\tfrac12(SF(x))^{\mathsf T}W(SF(x))=\tfrac12F(x)^{\mathsf T}(S^{\mathsf T}WS)F(x).\] Hence scaling followed by weighting is equivalent to the single original-coordinate weight \(M=S^{\mathsf T}WS\), which remains positive definite. Conversely, every positive-definite \(M\) admits such a factorization, for example \(M=S^{\mathsf T}S\) with \(S=M^{1/2}\). Thus only the induced metric determines the merit values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The combined residual metric is \(M=S^{\mathsf T}WS\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Congruence rule relating equation scaling to residual weighting.

notation.meaning: induced weight in original residual coordinates

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The congruence identity and positive-definiteness claim are correct, but the supplied restricted-step locator has not been shown to support the scaling–weighting interaction or the asserted metric equivalence. A specifically supporting locator is needed.

knowledge_statements.title: Merit Stationarity without Root Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Least-squares stationarity can occur at a nonzero residual; a simple rootless scalar equation has a stationary global merit minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\), stationarity means \(J_F(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x)=0\), which need not imply \(F(x)=0\). Concretely, for \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(F(x)=x^2+1\), one has \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12(x^2+1)^2\) and \(\phi'(x)=2x(x^2+1)\). Therefore \(x=0\) is stationary, indeed a global minimizer, but \(F(0)=1\). Root attainment follows from stationarity only under an additional condition excluding nonzero residuals from \(\ker J_F(x)^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spurious stationary points of squared-residual merit functions.

notation.meaning: null space of the transposed Jacobian

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonroot Stationary Point of a Residual Merit Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(W\) be nonsingular, and let \(\phi_W(x)=\tfrac12\|WF(x)\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional weighted least-squares merit functions; the definition distinguishes first-order stationarity from satisfaction of the original equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a merit-stationary nonroot when
\[
\nabla\phi_W(\bar x)=J(\bar x)^TW^TWF(\bar x)=0,
\qquad F(\bar x)\ne0.
\]
It is a nonroot local merit minimizer if, additionally, there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(\phi_W(\bar x)\le\phi_W(x)\) whenever \(\|x-\bar x\|_2<\varepsilon\). Such a point satisfies the normal-equation stationarity condition but not the original residual equation. Geometrically, the weighted residual \(W F(\bar x)\) is orthogonal to the weighted Jacobian range \(\operatorname{range}(WJ(\bar x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merit stationarity without root attainment occurs when the squared-residual merit gradient vanishes even though the residual is nonzero. Formally, \(J(\bar x)^TW^TWF(\bar x)=0\) while \(F(\bar x)\neq0\). A globalization method that minimizes the merit function can legitimately converge to such a stationary point, particularly to a nonroot local minimum, although it has failed to solve the original equations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The stationarity equation is equivalent to \(WF(\bar x)\perp\operatorname{range}(WJ(\bar x))\).
For \(W=I\), the condition reduces to \(J(\bar x)^TF(\bar x)=0\) with \(\|F(\bar x)\|_2>0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(m=n\) and \(J(\bar x)\) is nonsingular, merit stationarity forces \(F(\bar x)=0\); hence a nonroot stationary point requires rank deficiency of \(J(\bar x)\) in the square case.
immediate_consequences_latex: A stopping test based only on \(\|\nabla\phi_W(x)\|\) cannot distinguish a root from a nonroot merit-stationary point.
Residual norm and merit-gradient norm must be reported separately when diagnosing termination.
boundary_notes: Stationarity alone does not imply that \(\bar x\) is a local minimum; it may be a saddle or local maximum of the merit function.
The definition does not claim that every residual method can converge to every such point.

notation.meaning: Set of points where the merit gradient vanishes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-residual stationarity requires a singular Jacobian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded obstruction showing why stationarity of the squared-residual merit function is not necessarily a root certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n be differentiable, let J(x) be its Jacobian, and define f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2. If \nabla f(x^*)=J(x^*)^T r(x^*)=0 and r(x^*)\ne0, then J(x^*) is singular. Positive-residual local minima may attract merit-based iterations, so convergence to a stationary point of f alone does not certify a root.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a stationary point of the squared-residual merit function, the transposed Jacobian annihilates the residual. For a square residual system, a nonzero residual is therefore possible only when the Jacobian is singular. Stationary-point convergence alone is not a root certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Line Search for Residual Equations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, define \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\), and let \(p_k\) satisfy \(\nabla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional residual equations using a descent direction for squared residual norm and an inexact sufficient-decrease line search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A line-search residual method generates
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k,
\]
where \(p_k\) is produced by a Newton, quasi-Newton, Gauss–Newton, secant, or related residual model, and \(\alpha_k>0\) is selected along the ray \(x_k+\alpha p_k\) to satisfy a declared acceptance condition. A canonical condition is Armijo decrease,
\[
\phi(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le\phi(x_k)+c_1\alpha_k\nabla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k,
\qquad c_1\in(0,1).
\]
The search normally tests \(\alpha=1\) first and reduces or interpolates the step length only if the full local step is unacceptable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual line-search method chooses a residual-model direction and then searches only along that direction. The next iterate has the form \(x_k+\alpha_kp_k\), where the positive step length is required to pass an explicit merit-function test. With the squared residual merit, Armijo decrease compares the achieved value with a linear prediction based on \(J(x_k)^TF(x_k)\). Testing the full step first permits recovery of the local Newton-type behavior near a regular solution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(p_k=-J_k^{-1}F_k\) with nonsingular square \(J_k\), \(\nabla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k=-\|F_k\|_2^2\).
A geometric backtracking implementation restricts \(\alpha_k\) to \(\{1,\beta,\beta^2,\ldots\}\) for fixed \(\beta\in(0,1)\).
special_cases_latex: The unglobalized local method is recovered when the full step \(\alpha_k=1\) is accepted.
immediate_consequences_latex: Because \(p_k\) is a descent direction, sufficiently small positive step lengths satisfy strict local merit decrease.
boundary_notes: A direction that is not a merit descent direction may cause ordinary backtracking to fail.
The definition does not require exact one-dimensional minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Backtracking Newton Equation Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a Newton direction, backtrack geometrically until Armijo residual-merit decrease holds, update, and stop at a prescribed residual or step tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\), constants \(c\in(0,1)\), \(\beta\in(0,1)\), and \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\), at iteration \(k\) solve \(J_F(x_k)p_k=-F(x_k)\). If this equation is unsolvable or \(\nabla\phi(x_k)^{\mathsf T}p_k\ge0\), declare Newton-step failure or replace the direction by a specified descent safeguard. Otherwise choose the smallest integer \(j_k\ge0\) such that \[\phi(x_k+\beta^{j_k}p_k)\le\phi(x_k)+c\beta^{j_k}\nabla\phi(x_k)^{\mathsf T}p_k,\] set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\beta^{j_k}p_k\), and stop when the prescribed residual or step tolerance is met.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted step satisfies the stated Armijo decrease inequality for \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Armijo backtracking applied to Newton steps for nonlinear equations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Armijo-Backtracked Newton Method for Nonlinear Equations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(J_k=J(x_k)\) be nonsingular, and define \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth square nonlinear systems at iterates where a Newton direction can be computed; conditioning safeguards may replace the exact Newton direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A backtracking Newton equation method computes
\[
J_kp_k=-F(x_k)
\]
and chooses the first acceptable step length from \(\alpha=1\) followed by safeguarded reductions, for example \(\alpha\leftarrow\beta\alpha\) with \(\beta\in(0,1)\), until
\[
\phi(x_k+\alpha p_k)\le\phi(x_k)+c\alpha\nabla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k
=\phi(x_k)-c\alpha\|F(x_k)\|_2^2,
\]
where \(c\in(0,1)\). It then sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). Interpolation-based reductions are included when each proposed \(\alpha\) is clipped to declared lower and upper fractions of the previous trial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method solves the Newton linear system, tries the full Newton step, and repeatedly reduces the step length until the squared residual satisfies sufficient decrease. For an exact Newton direction, the merit directional derivative equals minus the squared residual norm, so it is strictly negative at every nonroot iterate with nonsingular Jacobian. Safeguarded quadratic or cubic interpolation may replace fixed-factor reduction, provided it cannot propose an arbitrarily small or insufficiently reduced trial in one update.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Since \(J_kp_k=-F_k\), \(\nabla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k=F_k^TJ_kp_k=-\|F_k\|_2^2\).
Fixed-factor backtracking uses \(\alpha_k=\beta^{j_k}\), where \(j_k\) is the smallest nonnegative integer satisfying the decrease test.
special_cases_latex: If \(\alpha=1\) satisfies the test, the iteration is the ordinary Newton step.
With residual scaling \(D_F\), replace \(\phi\) by \(\tfrac12\|D_FF\|_2^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: At a nonroot iterate with nonsingular \(J_k\), sufficiently small positive \(\alpha\) satisfy the Armijo condition.
boundary_notes: Near-singular Jacobians require a perturbed, regularized, or least-squares direction.
Finite-precision minimum-step termination may indicate a nonroot stationary point and must not be labeled root attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Residual Line Searches
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-memory reference maximum permits temporary residual-merit increases while retaining an Armijo decrease requirement relative to recent history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix memory \(M\ge1\), \(c,\beta\in(0,1)\), and \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\). At iteration \(k\), choose a direction \(p_k\) with \(\nabla\phi(x_k)^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\), define \(R_k=\max_{0\le i\le\min\{k,M-1\}}\phi(x_{k-i})\), and choose the smallest \(j_k\ge0\) satisfying \[\phi(x_k+\beta^{j_k}p_k)\le R_k+c\beta^{j_k}\nabla\phi(x_k)^{\mathsf T}p_k.\] Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\beta^{j_k}p_k\). Stop when the prescribed residual, stationarity, or step tolerance holds. Individual merit values may increase, but accepted values are controlled by the recent reference maximum.
assumptions_latex: Each search direction is a strict descent direction for \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted steps obey the nonmonotone Armijo inequality relative to \(R_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-memory nonmonotone Armijo search for a residual merit function.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The displayed finite-memory maximum rule is a recognizable nonmonotone Armijo variant, but no source is supplied for this exact reference sequence, memory convention, or acceptance rule. Variant-specific authoritative support is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Memory Nonmonotone Residual Line Search
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\), and let \(p_k\) satisfy \(\nabla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth residual minimization with finite-memory reference values; this definition does not cover stochastic acceptance rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an integer memory bound \(M\ge0\) and define \(m_k=\min\{k,M\}\) and
\[
R_k=\max_{0\le j\le m_k}\phi(x_{k-j}).
\]
A finite-memory nonmonotone residual line search chooses \(\alpha_k>0\) satisfying
\[
\phi(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le R_k+c\alpha_k\nabla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k,
\qquad c\in(0,1),
\]
and sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). Because \(R_k\ge\phi(x_k)\), an accepted step may increase the current merit value, but it must remain below a controlled recent reference after accounting for predicted descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmonotone residual line search replaces the current merit value in the Armijo test by a bounded-memory reference, commonly the maximum of the most recent merit values. This permits occasional increases in residual norm while still requiring sufficient decrease relative to the reference envelope. Memory zero gives the ordinary monotone Armijo search. The method remains a line search because every trial lies on \(x_k+\alpha p_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The reference sequence can be written \(R_k=\max\{\phi(x_i):\max(0,k-M)\le i\le k\}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(M=0\), \(R_k=\phi(x_k)\), recovering monotone Armijo decrease.
For \(M>0\), \(\phi(x_{k+1})>\phi(x_k)\) is admissible when the reference-envelope inequality still holds.
immediate_consequences_latex: The accepted merit sequence need not be monotone even though the finite-memory envelope controls increases.
boundary_notes: The inspected source mentioned nonmonotone algorithms but did not support this exact maximum-window acceptance formula.
Alternative averaged-reference and watchdog searches are distinct variants.

notation.meaning: Maximum number of previous merit values retained.

review_flags: A precise authoritative locator for the maximum-window residual acceptance rule was not established.

Safeguarded Secant Line Searches
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Secant interpolation proposes a step inside a bracket; clipping or replacement prevents endpoint stagnation and guarantees controlled bracket contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a descent direction \(p_k\), define \(g(\alpha)=\phi(x_k+\alpha p_k)\) and maintain a bracket \([a,b]\) containing acceptable trial lengths or a sign change of \(g'\). Form the secant trial \(\alpha_s=b-g'(b)(b-a)/(g'(b)-g'(a))\) when the denominator is nonzero. With safeguard \(\tau\in(0,1/2)\), replace \(\alpha_s\) by a prescribed interior trial whenever \(\alpha_s\notin[a+\tau(b-a),b-\tau(b-a)]\). Evaluate the merit conditions, update the bracket while retaining its invariant, and terminate at an accepted step or when the bracket-width tolerance is reached.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is continuously differentiable along the search ray.
The bracket update preserves its stated acceptance or derivative-sign invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every safeguarded trial lies in \([a+\tau(b-a),b-\tau(b-a)]\), unless an acceptable endpoint is returned.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bracketed secant interpolation safeguarded by interval contraction.

notation.meaning: merit function restricted to the search ray

The cited general inexact-line-search section must be inspected or replaced before the exact algorithm can be trusted.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Safeguarded Secant Step-Length Search
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\psi(\alpha)=\phi(x_k+\alpha p_k)\) be differentiable for \(\alpha\ge0\), with \(\psi'(0)<0\). Suppose two sampled step lengths \(a<b\) and their directional derivatives are available.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional derivative-based step selection along a fixed residual descent direction; the secant update is safeguarded inside a prescribed interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A safeguarded secant line search proposes a new trial by applying a secant update to the scalar stationarity equation \(\psi'(\alpha)=0\):
\[
\alpha^{\mathrm{sec}}=b-\psi'(b)\frac{b-a}{\psi'(b)-\psi'(a)},
\]
whenever the denominator is nonzero. Given safeguard fractions \(0<\tau_\ell<\tau_u<1\), the actual trial is clipped or replaced so that
\[
\alpha^{\mathrm{trial}}\in[a+\tau_\ell(b-a),\ a+\tau_u(b-a)].
\]
The interval is then updated using the declared sufficient-decrease and curvature or derivative-sign tests. Acceptance requires the chosen line-search conditions; a secant proposal alone is not an accepted step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A safeguarded secant line search treats the directional derivative along a fixed search ray as a scalar root-finding problem. It interpolates a zero of that derivative from two sampled points, but forces the next trial to lie strictly inside a controlled fraction of the current interval. Failed interpolation, a small denominator, or a proposal outside the safe interval triggers clipping or a fallback such as bisection. The final step must still pass the line-search acceptance conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The secant formula is the intersection with zero of the affine interpolant through \((a,\psi'(a))\) and \((b,\psi'(b))\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\alpha^{\mathrm{sec}}\) lies in the safeguard interval, it may be used unchanged.
If the secant denominator vanishes, a midpoint or another safeguarded interior trial is required.
immediate_consequences_latex: The safeguard prevents interpolation from proposing a trial arbitrarily close to an interval endpoint in one update.
boundary_notes: This definition concerns secant interpolation in the step length, not a multidimensional secant approximation of the Jacobian.
No inspected source supported the exact residual-specific safeguarded secant specification.

notation.meaning: Restriction of the merit function to the search line.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Trust-Region Method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable. At \(x_k\), set \(F_k=F(x_k)\), choose a Jacobian model \(J_k\), a nonsingular scaling \(D_k\), and a radius \(\Delta_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth residual equations or nonlinear least squares using a first-order residual model and a scaled trust region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A residual trust-region method computes an approximate solution of
\[
\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}^n}m_k(s):=\frac12\|F_k+J_ks\|_2^2
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|D_ks\|_2\le\Delta_k.
\]
For a trial \(s_k\) with positive predicted reduction, define
\[
\rho_k=\frac{\phi(x_k)-\phi(x_k+s_k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)},\qquad \phi(x)=\frac12\|F(x)\|_2^2.
\]
The step is accepted or rejected according to thresholds on \(\rho_k\), and \(\Delta_k\) is contracted after poor agreement and may be enlarged after good agreement, especially when the step reaches the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual trust-region method minimizes the norm of the linearized residual only inside a neighborhood where that model is considered reliable. The trial step solves or approximates \(\min\frac12\|F_k+J_ks\|^2\) subject to a scaled radius. Its acceptance ratio divides actual squared-residual reduction by the reduction predicted by the model. This ratio controls both acceptance and the next radius.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Expanding the model gives \(m_k(s)=\phi(x_k)+g_k^Ts+\tfrac12s^TB_ks\), where \(g_k=J_k^TF_k\) and \(B_k=J_k^TJ_k\).
For square nonsingular \(J_k\), if the Newton step \(-J_k^{-1}F_k\) lies inside the region, it is the unconstrained minimizer of the residual model.
special_cases_latex: With \(D_k=I\), the trust region is the Euclidean ball \(\|s\|_2\le\Delta_k\).
Dogleg and hook-step procedures are alternative subproblem solvers.
immediate_consequences_latex: A negative or very small \(\rho_k\) signals poor model agreement and calls for rejection or radius contraction.
boundary_notes: If predicted reduction is nonpositive, the ratio is not a valid acceptance statistic and a different step must be computed.
Exact subproblem solution is not required by the definition.

notation.meaning: Ratio of actual to predicted merit reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Hook-Step Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hook step minimizes the linearized residual within a ball and is characterized by a nonnegative regularization multiplier and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iterate \(x_k\), radius \(\Delta_k>0\), residual \(r_k=F(x_k)\), and Jacobian \(J_k=J_F(x_k)\), compute a hook step \(p_k\) solving \[\min_{\lVert p\rVert_2\le\Delta_k}\tfrac12\lVert r_k+J_kp\rVert_2^2.\] Equivalently, there exists \(\lambda_k\ge0\) such that \((J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k+\lambda_kI)p_k=-J_k^{\mathsf T}r_k\), together with \(\lambda_k(\lVert p_k\rVert_2-\Delta_k)=0\) and \(\lVert p_k\rVert_2\le\Delta_k\). Accept or reject the trial using actual-to-predicted merit reduction, update \(\Delta_k\), and stop at the prescribed residual or stationarity tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_k\) is a global minimizer of the stated linearized-residual trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region minimization of the linearized residual norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locally Constrained Optimal Hook Step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), where \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite, and let \(\Delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean trust-region quadratic models with positive-definite model Hessian; scaled variants replace the identity by a positive-definite metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hook step is a trust-region step of the shifted-system form
\[
s(\mu)=-(H+\mu I)^{-1}g,\qquad \mu\ge0,
\]
where \(\mu\) is chosen so that either \(\mu=0\) and \(\|s(0)\|_2\le\Delta\), or \(\mu>0\) and \(\|s(\mu)\|_2=\Delta\), up to a declared radius tolerance. The accepted trial is \(x_+=x_c+s(\mu)\). In a scaled norm \(\|Ds\|_2\le\Delta\), the corresponding shifted equation is \((H+\mu D^TD)s=-g\) with complementary boundary conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hook-step construction solves a family of shifted Newton systems. If the unshifted Newton step lies inside the trust region, it is used. Otherwise a positive shift is selected so that the shifted step reaches the trust-region boundary, within a stated tolerance. The shift regularizes and shortens the step while allowing its direction to curve from Newton-like toward gradient-like behavior.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For positive-definite \(H\), these conditions characterize the minimizer of \(g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\) over \(\|s\|_2\le\Delta\).
The scalar parameter may be found from \(\|s(\mu)\|_2^{-1}-\Delta^{-1}=0\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\|H^{-1}g\|_2\le\Delta\), \(\mu=0\) and the hook step is the full Newton step.
For residual models, \(g=J^TF\) and \(H=J^TJ\) when \(J\) has full column rank.
immediate_consequences_latex: Increasing a positive shift moves the step toward a shorter, regularized direction.
boundary_notes: Indefinite or singular \(H\) requires the general trust-region optimality conditions and hard-case safeguards.
Practical algorithms often accept a band around \(\Delta\) rather than exact boundary equality.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative trust-region shift or hook parameter.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dogleg Trust-Region Path
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(p)=f+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\), where \(B\) is symmetric positive definite, \(g\ne0\), and the trust region is \(\|p\|_2\le\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite quadratic trust-region models in the Euclidean norm; modified-Hessian variants are separate choices when the original Hessian is indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the unrestricted minimizer and the steepest-descent minimizer by
\[
p^B=-B^{-1}g,\qquad p^U=-\frac{g^Tg}{g^TBg}g.
\]
The dogleg path is the piecewise-linear curve
\[
\widetilde p(\tau)=
\begin{cases}
\tau p^U,&0\le\tau\le1,\\
p^U+(\tau-1)(p^B-p^U),&1\le\tau\le2.
\end{cases}
\]
The dogleg step is \(p^B\) if \(\|p^B\|_2\le\Delta\); otherwise it is the unique point on this path satisfying \(\|\widetilde p(\tau)\|_2=\Delta\). A double-dogleg variant inserts an additional point on the Newton direction before reaching \(p^B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dogleg method approximates the curved family of exact trust-region solutions by two straight segments. The first runs from zero to the unconstrained minimizer along the negative-gradient ray, and the second runs from that point to the full Newton or quasi-Newton model minimizer. If the full step is feasible it is selected; otherwise the selected step is the unique intersection of this polygonal path with the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p_{\mathrm{DL}}=p^B\text{ if }\|p^B\|_2\le\Delta;\quad p_{\mathrm{DL}}=\widetilde p(\tau_*)\text{ with }\|\widetilde p(\tau_*)\|_2=\Delta\text{ otherwise}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The boundary intersection on the second segment can be found from the positive root of \(\|p^U+t(p^B-p^U)\|_2^2=\Delta^2\), with \(t\in[0,1]\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\Delta\le\|p^U\|_2\), the dogleg step is a scaled negative-gradient step on the first segment.
If \(\Delta\ge\|p^B\|_2\), the step is the full model minimizer.
immediate_consequences_latex: The dogleg path lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{g,B^{-1}g\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dogleg Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the linearized residual model, the dogleg step follows the steepest-descent segment to the Cauchy point and then turns toward the Gauss–Newton step, returning the full Gauss–Newton step when feasible or the first trust-boundary intersection otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable. At an iterate \(x_k\), define \(r_k=F(x_k)\), \(J_k=J_F(x_k)\), \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}r_k\), and \(m_k(p)=\tfrac12\lVert r_k+J_kp\rVert_2^2\). For \(g_k\ne0\), define the Cauchy step \(p_k^C=-\alpha_kg_k\), where \(\alpha_k=\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2/\lVert J_kg_k\rVert_2^2\), and let the Gauss–Newton step \(p_k^N\) be the unique solution of \(J_k^{\mathsf T}J_kp=-g_k\). If \(\lVert p_k^N\rVert_2\le\Delta_k\), return \(p_k^N\). Otherwise return the first point satisfying \(\lVert p\rVert_2=\Delta_k\) along the piecewise-linear path from \(0\) to \(p_k^C\) and then to \(p_k^N\). Use the actual-to-predicted model-reduction ratio to accept or reject the trial and to update \(\Delta_k\).
assumptions_latex: \(J_k\) has full column rank, so \(J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k\) is positive definite and \(J_kg_k\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step lies on the dogleg path and satisfies \(\lVert p_k\rVert_2\le\Delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-segment trust-region path from the Cauchy step to the Gauss–Newton step for a linearized residual model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dogleg ingredients for a nonlinear residual model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cauchy and full Gauss–Newton steps defining the residual-equation dogleg path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
m_k(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|_2^2,
\]
the model Hessian $J_k^TJ_k$ is positive semidefinite. The Cauchy point is
\[
p_k^{\mathrm c}=-\tau_k\frac{\Delta_k}{\|J_k^Tr_k\|}J_k^Tr_k,
\qquad
\tau_k=\min\left\{1,\frac{\|J_k^Tr_k\|^3}{\Delta_k r_k^TJ_k(J_k^TJ_k)J_k^Tr_k}\right\},
\]
whenever these quotients are defined. If $J_k$ is nonsingular, the unconstrained model minimizer is unique and equals
\[
p_k^{\mathrm J}=-(J_k^TJ_k)^{-1}J_k^Tr_k=-J_k^{-1}r_k.
\]
The residual dogleg construction uses the piecewise-linear path joining $0$, $p_k^{\mathrm c}$, and $p_k^{\mathrm J}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a linearized residual least-squares model, J_k^T J_k is positive semidefinite, so no indefinite-model case is needed. The residual dogleg construction uses the origin, the Cauchy point, and the full Gauss–Newton point; when J_k is nonsingular, the full point is the unique unconstrained minimizer and equals -J_k^{-1}r_k.
assumptions_latex: J_k^Tr_k\neq0\text{ and the displayed denominator is nonzero when the quotient formula for }p_k^{\mathrm c}\text{ is used}
J_k\text{ is nonsingular for uniqueness and the displayed formulas for }p_k^{\mathrm J}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J_k^TJ_k\succeq0,\quad p_k^{\mathrm J}=-J_k^{-1}r_k\text{ when }J_k\text{ is nonsingular, and the residual dogleg construction uses }0\to p_k^{\mathrm c}\to p_k^{\mathrm J}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-equation dogleg step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection of a trust-region-feasible point on the Cauchy-to-Gauss–Newton segment for the residual least-squares model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Compute the residual-model Cauchy point $p_k^{\mathrm c}$. If $\|p_k^{\mathrm c}\|=\Delta_k$, set $p_k=p_k^{\mathrm c}$. Otherwise compute the unconstrained Gauss--Newton point $p_k^{\mathrm J}$ and set
\[
p_k=p_k^{\mathrm c}+\tau\bigl(p_k^{\mathrm J}-p_k^{\mathrm c}\bigr),
\qquad
\tau=\max\left\{t\in[0,1]:\left\|p_k^{\mathrm c}+t(p_k^{\mathrm J}-p_k^{\mathrm c})\right\|\leq\Delta_k\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute the residual-model Cauchy point. If it lies on the trust-region boundary, use it. Otherwise move from it toward the full Gauss–Newton point as far as possible along the segment while remaining in the trust region.
assumptions_latex: p_k^{\mathrm c}\text{ is the Cauchy point for }m_k(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|_2^2
p_k^{\mathrm J}\text{ exists and is computed when }\|p_k^{\mathrm c}\|<\Delta_k

knowledge_statements.title: Double-Dogleg Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double dogleg inserts a scaled Gauss–Newton point between the Cauchy and full Gauss–Newton steps, creating a three-segment trust-region path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m_k(p)=\tfrac12\lVert r_k+J_kp\rVert_2^2\), compute the Cauchy step \(p_k^C\) and Gauss–Newton step \(p_k^N\). Choose \(\gamma_k\in(0,1)\) so that the intermediate point \(p_k^I=\gamma_kp_k^N\) lies beyond \(p_k^C\) in norm and provides the prescribed model decrease. If \(\lVert p_k^N\rVert_2\le\Delta_k\), return \(p_k^N\); otherwise return the first trust-boundary intersection along the polygonal path \(0\to p_k^C\to p_k^I\to p_k^N\). Accept the trial by the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio and update \(\Delta_k\).
assumptions_latex: The Cauchy and Gauss–Newton steps are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step is the feasible full Gauss–Newton step or the first boundary point on \(0\to p_k^C\to p_k^I\to p_k^N\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-segment trust-region path using an intermediate scaled Gauss–Newton point.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The intermediate scaling parameter is constrained only by an informal “prescribed model decrease,” so the record does not define a reproducible double-dogleg algorithm. Because double-dogleg variants use specific intermediate-point rules, the exact formula and supporting locator must be confirmed before mathematical revision is reliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Dogleg Path Comparisons
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dogleg step is no worse than the feasible Cauchy step, equals the Gauss–Newton step when feasible, and otherwise can be selected on the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(p)=\tfrac12\|F+Jp\|^2\), \(g=J^{\mathsf T}F\), and \(\Delta>0\). Let \(p_C\) minimize \(m\) on \(\{-\alpha g:\alpha\geq0,\ \|\alpha g\|\leq\Delta\}\), and let \(p_N\) be a minimum-norm minimizer of \(\min_p\|F+Jp\|\). The dogleg path joins \(0\) to \(p_C\) and then \(p_C\) to \(p_N\). If \(p_D\) minimizes \(m\) over the portion of this path inside \(\|p\|\leq\Delta\), then \(m(0)-m(p_D)\geq m(0)-m(p_C)\). If \(\|p_N\|\leq\Delta\), then \(p_D=p_N\); otherwise a minimizing dogleg step may be chosen on \(\|p_D\|=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares residual-model decrease attained on the classical dogleg path with the Cauchy benchmark.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subspace-Restricted Trust-Region Solver
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(p)=f+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\), with symmetric \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), radius \(\Delta>0\), and a matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) whose columns form an orthonormal basis of a selected subspace \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional quadratic trust-region subproblems restricted to an explicitly selected low-dimensional or Krylov subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A trust-region subspace solver replaces the full problem by
\[
\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^r}\; g^TQy+\frac12y^T(Q^TBQ)y
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|y\|_2\le\Delta,
\]
and returns \(p=Qy\in\mathcal S\). The subspace must be chosen so that the reduced problem contains useful descent or curvature directions. In the classical two-dimensional positive-definite construction,
\[
\mathcal S=\operatorname{span}\{g,B^{-1}g\},
\]
so the Cauchy point and dogleg path are feasible. For indefinite models, the subspace may include an approximate negative-curvature eigenvector or be generated iteratively by Lanczos or conjugate-gradient recurrences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subspace trust-region solver searches only among steps represented by \(p=Qy\). It projects the gradient and model matrix into that subspace, solves the smaller trust-region problem there, and maps the reduced solution back to the full space. The two-dimensional gradient–Newton subspace extends dogleg search; Krylov subspaces support large sparse problems; negative-curvature directions allow indefinite models to be handled.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The reduced gradient and Hessian are \(g_r=Q^Tg\) and \(B_r=Q^TBQ\).
If \(Q\) spans all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the reduced problem is the original trust-region subproblem under an orthogonal change of coordinates.
special_cases_latex: For \(\mathcal S=\operatorname{span}\{g,B^{-1}g\}\) with \(B\succ0\), reduced minimization achieves at least the Cauchy decrease because the Cauchy point belongs to the subspace.
A one-dimensional subspace \(\operatorname{span}\{g\}\) yields the Cauchy step.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every reduced solution is feasible for the full trust-region problem when \(Q^TQ=I\).
boundary_notes: Subspace optimality is not full-space optimality unless the full solution lies in the selected subspace.
An indefinite model requires attention to negative curvature; a gradient–Newton space alone may omit it.

notation.meaning: Orthonormal basis matrix for the selected subspace.
Dimension of the reduced trust-region problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Trust-Region Solvers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An iterative inner solver returns a feasible step after residual accuracy, negative-curvature, or sufficient model-decrease termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), symmetric \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), radius \(\Delta>0\), and tolerances \(\eta,\kappa\in(0,1)\), initialize \(p_0=0\). Generate feasible iterates \(\|p_j\|\leq\Delta\) using matrix-vector products with \(B\), while decreasing \(q(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp\). Stop at the first iterate satisfying either \(\|g+Bp_j\|\leq\eta\|g\|\), a detected nonpositive-curvature direction followed to the boundary, or \(q(0)-q(p_j)\geq\kappa\|g\|\min\{\Delta,\|g\|/\max(1,\|B\|)\}\). Return that feasible iterate as the inexact trust-region step.
assumptions_latex: The iteration preserves \(\|p_j\|\leq\Delta\) and can evaluate products \(Bv\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned \(p\) satisfies \(\|p\|\leq\Delta\) and an explicit inexactness, curvature, or decrease condition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic inexact inner iteration for a quadratic trust-region subproblem.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the solver leaf, but the rule does not specify how feasible decreasing iterates are generated or establish that one of the stopping tests will be reached. The exact sufficient-decrease normalization also requires a supporting locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov Trust-Region Solvers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncated conjugate gradients searches successive Krylov subspaces and returns when the model-gradient residual is small, the boundary is crossed, or nonpositive curvature is detected and followed to the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(q(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp\), a radius \(\Delta>0\), and a tolerance \(\eta\in(0,1)\), set \(p_0=0\), \(r_0=g\), and \(d_0=-r_0\). At iteration \(j\), return \(p_j\) if \(\|r_j\|\leq\eta\|g\|\). If \(d_j^{\mathsf T}Bd_j\leq0\), return \(p_j+\tau_jd_j\), where \(\tau_j\geq0\) satisfies \(\|p_j+\tau_jd_j\|=\Delta\). Otherwise set \(\alpha_j=(r_j^{\mathsf T}r_j)/(d_j^{\mathsf T}Bd_j)\). If \(\|p_j+\alpha_jd_j\|\geq\Delta\), return \(p_j+\tau_jd_j\), where \(0<\tau_j\leq\alpha_j\) and \(\|p_j+\tau_jd_j\|=\Delta\). If the boundary is not crossed, set \(p_{j+1}=p_j+\alpha_jd_j\), \(r_{j+1}=r_j+\alpha_jBd_j\), \(\beta_{j+1}=(r_{j+1}^{\mathsf T}r_{j+1})/(r_j^{\mathsf T}r_j)\), and \(d_{j+1}=-r_{j+1}+\beta_{j+1}d_j\). With \(\mathcal K_\ell(B,g)=\operatorname{span}\{g,Bg,\ldots,B^{\ell-1}g\}\), each generated \(p_j\) lies in \(\mathcal K_j(B,g)\) for \(j\geq1\), and a boundary step returned during iteration \(j\) lies in \(\mathcal K_{j+1}(B,g)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step \(p\) satisfies \(\|p\|\leq\Delta\), belongs to a Krylov subspace generated by \(B\) and \(g\), and is returned because of residual convergence, boundary truncation, or detected nonpositive curvature.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated-conjugate-gradient solution of a Euclidean quadratic trust-region model.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Subspace Accuracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subspace solves range from sufficient decrease through approximate first-order KKT satisfaction to approximate second-order optimality; exact solution is the zero-tolerance endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp\), and let \(p\) satisfy \(\|p\|\leq\Delta\). A decrease regime requires \(q(0)-q(p)\geq\kappa\|g\|\min\{\Delta,\|g\|/\max(1,\|B\|)\}\). A first-order regime additionally requires a multiplier \(\lambda\geq0\) such that \(\|g+(B+\lambda I)p\|\leq\eta\|g\|\) and \(\lambda(\Delta-\|p\|)=0\). A second-order regime further requires \(v^{\mathsf T}(B+\lambda I)v\geq-\epsilon_H\|v\|^2\) for every vector \(v\) in the computed subspace. Exact subspace solution corresponds to zero residual and \(\epsilon_H=0\).
assumptions_latex: The computed subspace contains the returned step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed predicates define nested decrease, first-order, second-order, and exact subspace-accuracy regimes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested stopping regimes for approximate subspace solutions of quadratic trust-region problems.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the accuracy-regime leaf, but the full-space residual condition is stronger than the projected stationarity normally used for a subspace solve. The assertion that zero full residual and zero restricted curvature tolerance characterize an exact subspace solution therefore requires a precise source and clarification of the subspace optimality conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Trust-Region Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank deficiency is handled by a minimum-norm Gauss–Newton step when feasible or by positive trust-region regularization on the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F\in\mathbb R^m\), possibly rank-deficient \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(\Delta>0\), solve \(\min_{\|p\|\leq\Delta}\tfrac12\|F+Jp\|^2\). Choose \(\lambda\geq0\) and compute \(p(\lambda)\) from \((J^{\mathsf T}J+\lambda I)p=-J^{\mathsf T}F\). If \(\lambda>0\), select it so that \(\|p(\lambda)\|=\Delta\). If \(\lambda=0\), use the minimum-norm solution \(p(0)=-J^{\dagger}F\) when it is feasible. Return a pair satisfying \((J^{\mathsf T}J+\lambda I)p=-J^{\mathsf T}F\), \(\lambda(\Delta-\|p\|)=0\), and \(J^{\mathsf T}J+\lambda I\succeq0\).
assumptions_latex: The linearized residual subproblem is solved to its KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned \(p\) globally minimizes \(\tfrac12\|F+Jp\|^2\) over \(\|p\|\leq\Delta\), without requiring full column rank of \(J\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized linearized-residual step valid when the Jacobian lacks full rank.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The KKT system and pseudoinverse case are mathematically standard, and algorithm is a suitable kind for this method leaf. The supplied broad applications and part-level locators do not specifically support the rank-deficient least-squares specialization or its stated selection procedure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularized Trust-Region Method for Rank-Deficient Residual Models
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable. At \(x_k\), let \(J_k\) be rank deficient or numerically ill-conditioned and consider \(m_k(s)=\tfrac12\|F_k+J_ks\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional residual trust-region steps when the linearized residual has deficient or unreliable rank; the definition uses regularization or minimum-norm selection rather than an inverse Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A rank-deficient residual trust-region method defines its step without requiring \(J_k^{-1}\). One canonical form solves
\[
\min_{\|D_ks\|_2\le\Delta_k}\frac12\|F_k+J_ks\|_2^2,
\]
selecting the minimum-norm minimizer when it is nonunique. A regularized implementation computes
\[
(J_k^TJ_k+\mu_kD_k^TD_k)s_k=-J_k^TF_k,
\qquad \mu_k\ge0,
\]
with \(\|D_ks_k\|_2\le\Delta_k\) and \(\mu_k(\Delta_k-\|D_ks_k\|_2)=0\), or uses a rank-revealing factorization to obtain an equivalent stable step. Trial acceptance remains based on actual versus predicted residual reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the Jacobian is rank deficient, a Newton inverse and the normal equations may be singular or unstable. A rank-deficient trust-region method instead minimizes the linearized residual over a bounded step set, optionally choosing the minimum-norm solution. Regularization adds a positive scaled identity term, while QR with pivoting or an SVD can expose the numerical rank. The radius and regularization parameter control components that the linearized residual does not determine reliably.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|D_ks\|_2\le\Delta_k}\|F_k+J_ks\|_2,\quad\text{or equivalently satisfies a regularized shifted normal system with trust-region complementarity}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: With an SVD \(J_k=U\Sigma V^T\), the regularized step has filtered components \(-\frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2+\mu_k}u_i^TF_k\) along \(v_i\).
As \(\mu\downarrow0\), the regularized least-squares operator approaches the pseudoinverse on the resolved range under the usual minimum-norm convention.
special_cases_latex: If \(J_k\) has full column rank and the Gauss–Newton step is feasible, \(\mu_k=0\) and the ordinary step is recovered.
If \(J_k=0\), the linearized model is constant; no positive predicted reduction is available from that model.
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(\mu_k>0\) and nonsingular \(D_k\), the shifted normal matrix is positive definite even when \(J_k\) is rank deficient.
Nullspace components are suppressed by minimum-norm selection or positive regularization.
boundary_notes: Forming \(J_k^TJ_k\) explicitly can square the condition number; rank-revealing QR, SVD, or stable iterative solvers may be preferable.
Rank deficiency can also signal genuine nonisolated solutions, so regularization does not establish uniqueness of a root.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Merit Global Convergence Safeguard
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(J(x)=F'(x)\), and define \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\), so \(\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^TF(x)\). At iteration \(k\), let \(m_k(s)=\tfrac12\|F(x_k)+J(x_k)s\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic residual methods using a differentiable squared-residual merit function and either line-search or trust-region acceptance are covered.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
\[\mathcal S=(\mathcal P,\mathcal A,\mathcal U,\mathcal R)\] is a global convergence-safeguard system if, whenever \(
abla\phi(x_k)
e0\), it produces a primary trial \(p_k\), applies an acceptance test, updates its control parameter, and, after rejection or an undefined primary step, supplies a recovery trial. In the line-search form, \(
abla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k<0\) and an accepted \(s_k=\alpha_kp_k\) satisfies \[\phi(x_k+s_k)\leq\phi(x_k)+c_1\alpha_k
abla\phi(x_k)^Tp_k,\qquad c_1\in(0,1).\] In the trust-region form, \(\|s_k\|\leq\Delta_k\), \[ho_k= rac{\phi(x_k)-\phi(x_k+s_k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)},\] and acceptance requires positive predicted reduction and \(ho_k\geq\eta_1\) for fixed \(\eta_1\in(0,1)\). Rejection invokes \(\mathcal U\) or \(\mathcal R\) so that a smaller trial scale is generated unless a stated stopping condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global convergence-safeguard system for \(F(x)=0\) consists of a primary-step rule, acceptance test, control-parameter update, and recovery rule. It globalizes the residual merit function \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\). A line-search realization accepts a scaled descent step only after sufficient decrease. A trust-region realization accepts a bounded step only when its actual-to-predicted reduction ratio is at least a fixed positive threshold. Rejected or undefined primary steps cause contraction or a recovery trial rather than an uncontrolled update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \phi(x_{k+1})<\phi(x_k)\ \text{whenever the accepted step is nonzero and }\nabla\phi(x_k)\ne0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a nonsingular square Jacobian, the primary Newton direction is \(p_k=-J(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\), while the merit gradient remains \(J(x_k)^TF(x_k)\).
The trust-region model is equivalently \(m_k(s)=\tfrac12\|M_k(s)\|_2^2\) with \(M_k(s)=F(x_k)+J(x_k)s\).
special_cases_latex: A damped Newton method is obtained by choosing \(s_k=\alpha_kp_k\).
A residual trust-region method approximately minimizes \(m_k(s)\) over \(\|s\|\leq\Delta_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The safeguard separates local step construction from global acceptance.
A rejected full Newton step need not be discarded permanently; the same local model may be retried at a smaller scale.
boundary_notes: The definition does not by itself imply convergence to a root; convergence may be only to residual stationarity.
Nonsmooth residuals require generalized derivatives and are outside this scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Convergence to Roots
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual-stationary accumulation points are roots when the Jacobian is uniformly surjective; residual norms vanish, and uniqueness gives convergence of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable and \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|^2\). Suppose a trust-region residual method remains in a compact level set, every accumulation point \(x_*\) satisfies \(J(x_*)^{\mathsf T}F(x_*)=0\), and there exists \(\sigma>0\) such that \(\|J(x)^{\mathsf T}y\|\geq\sigma\|y\|\) for all \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) and all \(x\) in that level set. Then every accumulation point is a root of \(F\), and \(\|F(x_k)\|\to0\). If the root in the level set is unique, then \(x_k\to x_*\).
assumptions_latex: The iterate level set is compact.
Every accumulation point is stationary for \(\phi\).
The Jacobian satisfies the stated uniform surjectivity bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root convergence obtained by combining residual stationarity with uniform Jacobian surjectivity.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the residual mapping at x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Convergence of a Residual Iteration to the Root Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuous, let \(Z=\{x\in\mathcal D:F(x)=0\}\), and let an algorithm generate \(x_{k+1}=T_k(x_k)\) from every admissible \(x_0\in\mathcal D_0\subseteq\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a property of an algorithm relative to its declared starting set, not a claim that every residual method has the property. Both finite termination and infinite sequences are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The algorithm is globally convergent to roots on \(\mathcal D_0\) if, for every \(x_0\in\mathcal D_0\), its iteration is well defined until either it terminates at some \(x_K\in Z\), or it produces an infinite sequence satisfying \[\operatorname{dist}(x_k,Z)\longrightarrow0.\] It is globally residual-convergent to roots if the infinite-sequence condition is instead \[\|F(x_k)\|\longrightarrow0.\] When every relevant sublevel set is compact and \(Z\) is nonempty, residual convergence together with the condition that every accumulation point lies in \(\mathcal D\) implies that all accumulation points belong to \(Z\). Full point convergence is the stronger requirement that for every admissible start there exists \(x_*\in Z\) such that \(x_k\to x_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global convergence to roots is quantified over every admissible starting point. The iteration must either stop at a root or remain well defined and approach the root set. A commonly used residual form requires \(\|F(x_k)\|\to0\). If the iterates remain in a compact region and accumulation points stay in the domain, continuity of \(F\) makes every accumulation point a root. Convergence of the entire sequence to one root is stronger than merely approaching the root set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x_0\in\mathcal D_0:\quad x_K\in Z\ \text{for some finite }K\quad\text{or}\quad\operatorname{dist}(x_k,Z)\to0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(Z=\{x_*\}\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,Z)\to0\) is equivalent to \(x_k\to x_*\).

For continuous \(F\), bounded \(\{x_k\}\), and compact containment in \(\mathcal D\), the conditions \(\|F(x_k)\|\to0\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,Z)\to0\) are equivalent when the relevant zero set is compact.
special_cases_latex: For square systems with a nonsingular root, a safeguarded iteration may eventually accept full Newton steps while retaining its global root property.
immediate_consequences_latex: The adjective global refers to the starting set \(\mathcal D_0\), not to uniqueness of the attained root.
Different starting points may converge to different members of \(Z\).
boundary_notes: Residual stationarity \(J(x_k)^TF(x_k)\to0\) is weaker and does not define global convergence to roots.
Divergence, undefined steps, or convergence to a nonroot stationary point violates this definition.

notation.meaning: Distance from \(x\) to the root set.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Convergence to Residual Stationarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard smoothness, boundedness, acceptance, and Cauchy-decrease conditions, trust-region iterates approach stationarity of the squared-residual merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable and \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|^2\). Suppose the level set \(\{x:\phi(x)\leq\phi(x_0)\}\) is compact, \(\nabla\phi\) is Lipschitz continuous there, and model Hessians are uniformly bounded. Consider a trust-region method that accepts steps by the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio, updates the radius by standard bounded factors, and produces at least a fixed fraction of Cauchy decrease. Then \(\|\nabla\phi(x_k)\|=\|J(x_k)^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\|\to0\). Consequently every accumulation point \(x_*\) is residual-stationary: \(J(x_*)^{\mathsf T}F(x_*)=0\).
assumptions_latex: The relevant level set is compact and \(\nabla\phi\) is Lipschitz continuous there.
Trial steps achieve a uniform fraction of Cauchy decrease under standard ratio-based radius updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|J(x_k)^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\|\to0\), and each accumulation point is stationary for \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order global convergence of a standard trust-region method applied to squared residuals.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the stationarity leaf, but phrases such as standard bounded factors do not state the acceptance and radius-update hypotheses needed to distinguish a liminf result from full convergence of the gradient norm. The exact theorem and hypotheses must be checked against the cited section.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Convergence to First-Order Residual Stationarity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable and set \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\). Then \(\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^TF(x)\), where \(J(x)=F'(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns smooth finite-dimensional least-residual stationarity. It intentionally does not identify stationary points with roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm is globally convergent to residual stationarity on \(\mathcal D_0\subseteq\mathcal D\) if, for every \(x_0\in\mathcal D_0\), it either terminates at a point \(x_K\) satisfying \[J(x_K)^TF(x_K)=0,\] or generates an infinite well-defined sequence for which \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\|J(x_k)^TF(x_k)\|=0.\] A weaker subsequential form requires only \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|J(x_k)^TF(x_k)\|=0.\] If the sequence is bounded, \(J^TF\) is continuous on a neighborhood of its accumulation set, and the full limit is zero, then every accumulation point \(\bar x\) is residual-stationary: \(J(\bar x)^TF(\bar x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global convergence to residual stationarity means that every admissible run either stops where the gradient of the squared-residual merit function is zero or makes that gradient converge to zero. Since \(\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^TF(x)\), the defining residual-stationarity measure is \(\|J(x_k)^TF(x_k)\|\). The liminf condition is a weaker version. With bounded iterates and continuity, full convergence of the measure makes every accumulation point stationary for \(\phi\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Residual stationarity is equivalent to first-order stationarity of \(\min_x\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\).
If \(J(\bar x)\) has full row rank, then \(J(\bar x)^TF(\bar x)=0\) implies \(F(\bar x)=0\).
special_cases_latex: For a square nonsingular \(J(\bar x)\), residual stationarity at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to \(F(\bar x)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonroot stationary point must have \(F(\bar x)\ne0\) and a rank-deficient Jacobian transpose on the residual direction.
A global stationarity result is not automatically a global root-convergence result.
boundary_notes: Stationarity does not distinguish local minima, saddles, and local maxima of \(\phi\).
Nonsmooth residual mappings require a subdifferential stationarity notion.

notation.meaning: Gradient of the squared-residual merit function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recovery-Step Family for Failed Residual Trials
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\), and \(m_k(s)=\tfrac12\|F(x_k)+J_k s\|_2^2\). Let \(p_k\) denote a primary Newton, quasi-Newton, or model step.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition covers deterministic fallback steps activated by rejection, singularity, model failure, or inability to compute the primary step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A recovery-step method is a rule \(\mathcal R_k\) that is invoked when the primary trial is inadmissible or fails the globalization test and returns \(r_k\) satisfying \[x_k+r_k\in\mathcal D,\qquad \|r_k\|\leq\Delta_k,\qquad m_k(0)-m_k(r_k)>0.\] For a trust-region recovery family, a standard quantitative requirement is Cauchy comparability: for a fixed \(\kappa_R\in(0,1]\), \[m_k(0)-m_k(r_k)\geq\kappa_R\bigl(m_k(0)-m_k(s_k^C)\bigr),\] where \(s_k^C\) minimizes \(m_k\) along the projected negative-gradient ray within \(\|s\|\leq\Delta_k\). The recovered trial is accepted only if its actual reduction is positive and its ratio \[\rho_k^R=\frac{\phi(x_k)-\phi(x_k+r_k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(r_k)}\] meets the declared threshold; otherwise the control radius is contracted and recovery is retried or a failure status is returned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recovery-step method supplies a bounded alternative whenever the primary residual step is undefined, inadmissible, or rejected. The recovery step stays in the domain, predicts a strict decrease in the linearized residual model, and achieves a fixed fraction of the Cauchy-step decrease. It is accepted only after actual residual-merit decrease agrees sufficiently with the prediction. Failure causes a smaller recovery scale or an explicit termination status.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A line-search recovery family may instead choose a direction \(d_k^R\) with \(\nabla\phi(x_k)^Td_k^R<0\) and backtrack until sufficient decrease holds.
special_cases_latex: The scaled steepest-residual direction \(-J_k^TF_k\) is a recovery direction whenever it is nonzero.
A regularized step \((J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)r_k=-J_k^TF_k\) is a common trust-region-compatible member.
immediate_consequences_latex: Recovery remains distinct from accepting an unsuccessful primary step.
Cauchy comparability prevents the recovery rule from returning arbitrarily ineffective model steps.
boundary_notes: No inspected source supplied an exact canonical definition under the title “Recovery-Step Method Family.”
Restoration methods for nonlinear constraints may use a different feasibility measure and are not identified with this residual-only definition.

notation.meaning: Cauchy step for the residual model.

review_flags: Exact source support is needed for the recovery-family terminology and Cauchy-comparability contract.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovery-Step Family for Failed Residual Trials
Restoration Step Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration mode approximately minimizes residual infeasibility and accepts a step only when actual reduction agrees sufficiently with predicted reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an iterate \(x_k\), define \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|^2\). Given a restoration radius \(\Delta_k^R>0\), construct a model \(r_k(s)\) of \(\phi(x_k+s)\) and compute \(s_k^R\) with \(\|s_k^R\|\leq\Delta_k^R\) satisfying \(r_k(0)-r_k(s_k^R)\geq\kappa_R\bigl(r_k(0)-r_k(s_k^C)\bigr)\), where \(s_k^C\) is the restoration-model Cauchy step and \(\kappa_R\in(0,1]\). Accept the step when \(\phi(x_k)-\phi(x_k+s_k^R)\geq\eta_R\bigl(r_k(0)-r_k(s_k^R)\bigr)\); otherwise reduce \(\Delta_k^R\) and repeat. Return the accepted point to the primary mode.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and a locally consistent restoration model are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted restoration step produces certified positive reduction of \(\phi\) relative to its predicted restoration decrease.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery steps devoted to reducing residual infeasibility when the primary model is unreliable.

notation.meaning: Cauchy step for the restoration model

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the restoration-family leaf, but this specific ratio-tested Cauchy-decrease restoration scheme has no cited source. Its relationship to residual restoration, rather than a generic trust-region minimization step, cannot be established from standard-field rationale alone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Small-Step Safeguards for Line-Search Interior-Point Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded method-specific safeguard and its asymptotic diagnostic justification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a line-search primal-dual interior-point iteration, monitor the primal and dual step lengths \(\alpha_s\) and \(\alpha_z\). If they fall below a prescribed threshold, replace the primal-dual step by one guaranteeing progress toward feasibility and, preferably, optimality: a filter method may invoke a feasibility-restoration step, while a trust-region implementation may substitute a trust-region step. This safeguard detects the stated failure regime because convergence of the line-search iterates to a nonstationary point implies \(\alpha_s\to0\) and \(\alpha_z\to0\). Constraint penalization is another possible modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A modified line-search interior-point method monitors its primal and dual step lengths and replaces an excessively short primal-dual step with a feasibility-restoration or trust-region step. This is theoretically motivated because convergence to a nonstationary point forces both monitored step lengths to zero; constraint penalization is another possible remedy.
assumptions_latex: \text{A line-search primal-dual interior-point iteration produces step lengths }\alpha_s,\alpha_z.
\text{A prescribed small-step threshold and a restoration or trust-region mechanism are available.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(x_k\to\bar x\ \text{with }\bar x\text{ nonstationary}\bigr)\Rightarrow\alpha_{s,k}\to0\ \text{and}\ \alpha_{z,k}\to0,\quad\text{so small steps can trigger a feasibility-progress replacement step.}

knowledge_statements.title: Fallback Step Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the primary trial fails, a symmetric positive-definite scaling of the negative residual gradient, combined with trust-region and Armijo safeguards, supplies a feasible descent fallback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_k=F(x_k)\), \(J_k=J(x_k)\), \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|^2\), and \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}F_k=\nabla\phi(x_k)\). If the primary step cannot be computed or fails its acceptance test and \(g_k\neq0\), choose a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(D_k\) and set \(d_k=-D_k^{-1}g_k\). Select \(\alpha_k=\beta^{j_k}\), where \(j_k\) is the smallest nonnegative integer such that \(\alpha_k\|d_k\|\leq\Delta_k\) and \(\phi(x_k+\alpha_kd_k)\leq\phi(x_k)+c\alpha_kg_k^{\mathsf T}d_k\), with \(c,\beta\in(0,1)\). Return \(s_k^F=\alpha_kd_k\). If \(g_k=0\), terminate with residual stationarity rather than requesting a descent fallback.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(g_k\neq0\), the backtracking search terminates and the returned \(s_k^F\) satisfies \(\|s_k^F\|\leq\Delta_k\) and \(\phi(x_k+s_k^F)\leq\phi(x_k)+c\alpha_kg_k^{\mathsf T}d_k<\phi(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded residual-descent steps used when a primary Newton-type trial is unavailable or rejected.

notation.meaning: gradient of the squared-residual merit function at the current iterate
