knowledge_statements.title: Least-Squares Parameter Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondegenerate least-squares minimizer changes with parameters by solving the differentiated stationarity system; the exact Hessian includes residual-weighted second derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi(x,p)=\tfrac12\|r(x,p)\|_2^2\), where \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^q\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is twice continuously differentiable. Suppose \(x_*\) is stationary at \(p_*\), so \(g(x_*,p_*)=0\) for \(g=r_x^{\mathsf T}r\), and suppose \(H=g_x(x_*,p_*)\) is nonsingular. The local stationary branch satisfies
\[
D_px(p_*)=-H^{-1}g_p(x_*,p_*),
\qquad
H=r_x^{\mathsf T}r_x+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i\nabla_{xx}^2r_i.
\]
If \(H\) is positive definite, this branch consists locally of strict minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative of an isolated nondegenerate nonlinear least-squares minimizer with respect to model parameters.

notation.meaning: stationarity residual r_x transposed times r
Jacobian of g with respect to x, equivalently the exact objective Hessian

knowledge_statements.statement_title: SVD-Resolved Least-Squares Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(m\geq n\), have full column rank, and let \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Consider \(x_*\in\arg\min_x\|Jx-y\|_2\), and write the thin singular-value decomposition \(J=U_1\Sigma V^T\), where \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n)\) and \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition covers unconstrained Euclidean linear least squares with full column rank. Rank-deficient, weighted, constrained, and nonlinear least-squares sensitivities require modified formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The least-squares parameter sensitivity to perturbations of the observation vector is the linear operator \(S_y=J^\dagger=V\Sigma^{-1}U_1^T\), since \(x_*=J^\dagger y=\sum_{i=1}^n (u_i^Ty/\sigma_i)v_i\). The absolute observation-to-parameter condition number is \(\chi_y=\|J^\dagger\|_2=1/\sigma_n\). Directionally, a perturbation \(\delta y\) changes the parameter by \(\delta x=\sum_{i=1}^n(u_i^T\delta y/\sigma_i)v_i\). Thus components of the data in left-singular directions associated with small singular values are strongly amplified. The matrix condition number is \(\kappa_2(J)=\sigma_1/\sigma_n\), while the normal-equations matrix satisfies \(\kappa_2(J^TJ)=\kappa_2(J)^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For full-rank linear least squares, the pseudoinverse maps observation perturbations to parameter perturbations. Its norm equals the reciprocal of the smallest singular value. Data components aligned with left singular vectors belonging to small singular values are amplified most strongly, and forming normal equations squares the spectral condition number.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The solution also satisfies the normal equations \(J^TJx_*=J^Ty\).
special_cases_latex: If the columns of \(J\) are orthonormal, then \(J^\dagger=J^T\) and \(\chi_y=1\).
If \(J\) is rank deficient, replacing reciprocals of zero singular values by zero defines the minimum-norm pseudoinverse solution, but uniqueness is lost.
immediate_consequences_latex: QR or SVD solution avoids the unnecessary squaring of conditioning incurred by explicitly solving normal equations.
Truncating contributions associated with very small singular values trades exact least-squares fitting for reduced sensitivity.
boundary_notes: Perturbations in \(J\) require additional terms and are not represented solely by \(J^\dagger\delta y\).
Relative condition numbers require explicit scaling by the sizes of \(x_*\) and \(y\).

notation.meaning: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the full-column-rank design matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Backward-Error Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative residual is a verifiable perturbation making an approximate root exact, and its norm is the minimal constant-additive backward error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and let \(\widehat x\) be an approximate root. Consider constant additive perturbations \(h\in\mathbb{R}^m\), so the perturbed problem is \(F(x)+h=0\). The vector
\[
h_*=-F(\widehat x)
\]
is a directly verifiable certificate that \(\widehat x\) is an exact root of the perturbed problem. Moreover, under the normwise measure
\[
\eta(\widehat x)=\inf\{\|h\|:F(\widehat x)+h=0\},
\]
one has \(\eta(\widehat x)=\|F(\widehat x)\|\). Scaled backward error is obtained by measuring \(D_Fh\) instead.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\widehat x)\) is evaluable in the chosen arithmetic.
Backward perturbations are restricted to constant additive residual vectors.
A norm is fixed on residual space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_*=-F(\widehat x)\) certifies exactness and \(\eta(\widehat x)=\|F(\widehat x)\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact normwise backward error for an approximate root under constant additive residual perturbations.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact residual-based backward error under explicitly restricted perturbations
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The certificate is correct for the explicitly restricted class of constant additive residual perturbations and fits the leaf. No authoritative backward-error source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normwise Backward-Error Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a numerical problem be represented by data \(d\in\mathcal{D}\), an exact solution relation \(\mathcal{S}(d)\), and a computed output \(\widehat{x}\). Let \(\rho\) be a nonnegative relative perturbation measure on admissible data pairs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition is deterministic and normwise unless a different perturbation measure is explicitly chosen. It applies to equations and optimization outputs through their exact solution relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The backward error of \(\widehat{x}\) is \(\eta(\widehat{x};d)=\inf\{\rho(d,\widetilde d):\widetilde d\in\mathcal{D},\ \widehat{x}\in\mathcal{S}(\widetilde d)\}\). A backward-error certificate is a computable number \(\overline\eta\) together with a specified admissible perturbation model such that \(\eta(\widehat{x};d)\leq\overline\eta\). For \(Ax=b\), one normwise model permits \((A+\Delta A)\widehat{x}=b+\Delta b\) with \(\|\Delta A\|\leq\epsilon\|A\|\) and \(\|\Delta b\|\leq\epsilon\|b\|\); the certificate is the least such \(\epsilon\), or a verified upper bound on it. If only \(b\) may change, the residual \(r=b-A\widehat{x}\) gives \(\Delta b=-r\) and relative backward error \(\|r\|/\|b\|\) when \(b\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backward error is the smallest admissible relative change to the input data that makes the computed output an exact solution. A certificate supplies a verified upper bound and states exactly which data may be perturbed and how perturbation size is measured.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta(\widehat{x};d)=\inf\{\rho(d,\widetilde d):\widehat{x}\in\mathcal{S}(\widetilde d)\}\), and a valid certificate satisfies \(\eta\leq\overline\eta\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A backward-stable algorithm produces outputs whose backward errors are bounded at the scale required by the adopted arithmetic and perturbation model.
special_cases_latex: For a nonlinear equation \(F(x)=0\) with additive output-independent residual perturbations, \(\widetilde F=F-F(\widehat{x})\) makes \(\widehat{x}\) exact, though the size of a function perturbation requires a chosen function-space norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: A small residual is a backward-error certificate only after residual size has been related to an explicitly permitted data perturbation.
Backward accuracy does not imply forward accuracy for an ill-conditioned problem.
boundary_notes: The infimum need not be attained without closedness or compactness assumptions.
Componentwise, structured, and probabilistic backward errors use different admissible perturbation sets.

notation.meaning: set of exact solutions for data d
relative size of an admissible data perturbation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Condition-Guided Local Forward-Error Estimate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(x_*\) satisfy \(F(x_*)=0\), and let \(\widehat{x}\) be an approximation. Set \(J=F'(\widehat{x})\) and \(r=F(\widehat{x})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition addresses local smooth square systems with a nonsingular approximate Jacobian. A rigorous certificate additionally needs a validated neighborhood and a bound on Jacobian variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A condition-guided forward-error estimate is a quantity \(\mathcal{E}(\widehat{x})\) formed from a backward-error measure and a local inverse-Jacobian sensitivity bound, with the intended assertion \(\|\widehat{x}-x_*\|\leq\mathcal{E}(\widehat{x})\). Its first-order form is \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{lin}}=\|J^{-1}r\|\), while the coarser normwise form is \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cond}}=\|J^{-1}\|\,\|r\|\). A rigorous version specifies a set \(X\ni\widehat{x}\), proves existence of a root \(x_*\in X\), and supplies a remainder factor \(\gamma<1\) such that \(\|\widehat{x}-x_*\|\leq\|J^{-1}r\|/(1-\gamma)\). The estimate is called condition-guided because amplification is controlled by \(J^{-1}\), not by residual size alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The estimate converts residual or backward error into distance from the approximate point to a root by using inverse-Jacobian sensitivity. The Newton correction is the directional first-order estimate; multiplying the residual norm by the inverse-Jacobian norm gives a coarser bound. Rigorous use requires control of nonlinear remainder terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{lin}}=\|F'(\widehat{x})^{-1}F(\widehat{x})\|\), with a rigorous inflated bound \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{lin}}/(1-\gamma)\) only when the stated neighborhood conditions hold.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a linear system \(F(x)=Ax-b\), the nonlinear remainder vanishes and \(\widehat{x}-x_*=A^{-1}F(\widehat{x})\) exactly.
special_cases_latex: If \(\|J^{-1}\|\leq M\), then \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cond}}\leq M\|r\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The same residual norm can correspond to very different forward errors when inverse-Jacobian norms differ.
A Newton-step norm is an estimator, not automatically a validated error bound.
boundary_notes: The constant \(\gamma\) depends on a specific nonlinear validation theorem and is not defined by pointwise data alone.
No inspected source supplies this exact nonlinear certificate formulation.
review_flags: A source is needed for the exact nonlinear remainder hypothesis defining gamma and the resulting rigorous bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Condition-Guided Local Forward-Error Estimate
Forward-Error Estimates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance to a root is bounded by the residual times an inverse bound for the Jacobian averaged along the connecting segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable on a convex set containing a root \(x_*\) and an approximation \(\widehat x\). Define
\[
A=\int_0^1F'\bigl(x_*+t(\widehat x-x_*)\bigr)\,dt.
\]
If \(A\) is nonsingular and \(\|A^{-1}\|\le K\), then
\[
\|\widehat x-x_*\|
=\|A^{-1}F(\widehat x)\|
\le K\|F(\widehat x)\|.
\]
Thus a residual becomes a forward-error bound only after multiplication by a valid inverse-sensitivity bound for the averaged Jacobian between the approximation and the root.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a convex set containing \(x_*\) and \(\widehat x\), with \(F(x_*)=0\).
A certified bound \(\|A^{-1}\|\le K\) is available.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-to-root forward bound using the averaged Jacobian along the root-error segment.

notation.meaning: Jacobian averaged over the segment from the root to the approximation
upper bound for the inverse averaged-Jacobian norm

knowledge_statements.title: Condition Estimates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear solves yield lower inverse-norm estimates, while an approximate inverse with verified defect below one yields a rigorous upper estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular. Any nonzero probe \(v\) and computed exact solution \(z=J^{-1}v\) give the lower estimate
\[
\|J^{-1}\|\ge \frac{\|z\|}{\|v\|}.
\]
For an approximate inverse \(R\), if a verified induced-norm bound \(\delta=\|I-RJ\|<1\) is available, then \(R\) is nonsingular and
\[
\|J^{-1}\|\le\frac{\|R\|}{1-\delta}.
\]
Together these inequalities bracket the absolute root condition factor without explicitly forming \(J^{-1}\), provided the solve and defect bounds account for numerical error.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is nonsingular and all norms are compatible induced norms.
The relation \(Jz=v\) and the bound on \(\delta=\|I-RJ\|\) are verified, including numerical error.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable lower and upper certificates for the inverse norm of a nonsingular root Jacobian.

notation.meaning: probe vector and corresponding solution of Jz=v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: induced-norm definition and Neumann-series inverse bound
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The probe lower bound and verified-defect upper certificate are mathematically consistent and appropriate for condition estimates. An authoritative source with a specific locator is still required.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Error Interpretation from Conditioning
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a simple root, forward error is approximately backward error multiplied by inverse-Jacobian conditioning; a small residual can be misleading for an ill-conditioned root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_*\) be a simple root of a continuously differentiable map \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\widehat x\to x_*\). With \(J_*=F'(x_*)\) nonsingular and backward error \(\eta(\widehat x)=\|F(\widehat x)\|\), Taylor expansion gives
\[
\widehat x-x_*=J_*^{-1}F(\widehat x)+o(\|\widehat x-x_*\|).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\|\widehat x-x_*\|\le
\|J_*^{-1}\|\,\eta(\widehat x)+o(\eta(\widehat x)).
\]
A small residual therefore implies small forward error only when the relevant root is locally well conditioned; residual size alone is not a forward-accuracy certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near a simple root \(x_*\).
Residual and variable norms are fixed and compatible with the induced operator norm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local interpretation of residual backward error through the root condition number.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: first-order conditioning relation between backward and forward error
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The local forward-versus-backward error interpretation is appropriate for the principle leaf and correctly restricts the claim to approximations approaching a simple root. No authoritative source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validated Certificate for a Smooth-System Root
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(X\subseteq D\) be a nonempty compact box or other explicitly represented set, and let all interval or enclosure operations use outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The object is a finite-dimensional certificate for a general smooth square system. Polynomial-specific algebraic certificates and unvalidated floating-point heuristics are outside the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A validated root certificate for \((F,X)\) is finite, machine-checkable enclosure data \(\mathcal{C}\) together with a predicate \(P\in\{P_{\mathrm{exist}},P_{\mathrm{unique}},P_{\mathrm{exclude}}\}\) whose verified semantics are respectively \(P_{\mathrm{exist}}:\exists x\in X,\ F(x)=0\); \(P_{\mathrm{unique}}:\exists!x\in X,\ F(x)=0\); and \(P_{\mathrm{exclude}}:\nexists x\in X,\ F(x)=0\). Every real quantity entering the predicate must be enclosed by certified arithmetic, and every derivative enclosure must contain \(F'(x)\) for all \(x\in X\). A certificate may be conditional on stated regularity assumptions, but its outcome predicate must follow from the enclosed data rather than from an unverified approximate solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validated root certificate is checkable enclosure data that rigorously establishes existence, uniqueness, or absence of a zero in a specified set. Outward-rounded enclosures must cover every real value used by the certificate, including all Jacobians over the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate's verified outcome is exactly one stated predicate among existence, unique existence, or exclusion of roots in \(X\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A unique-existence certificate can be represented by any verified self-map or contraction criterion whose hypotheses and set inclusions are enclosed.
special_cases_latex: Interval Newton and Krawczyk inclusions are two operator-based realizations of unique-existence predicates.
If one residual component has an interval enclosure excluding zero on \(X\), this can provide an exclusion certificate.
immediate_consequences_latex: A small floating-point residual without enclosure data is not a validated certificate.
Uniqueness in \(X\) does not imply that \(F\) has no roots outside \(X\).
boundary_notes: Existence and uniqueness predicates must not be inferred from solver termination status alone.
No inspected supplied source gives this exact abstract certificate definition.

notation.meaning: finite enclosure data supporting the outcome predicate

review_flags: An authoritative interval-analysis source is required for the abstract certificate semantics and enclosure requirements.
knowledge_statements.title: Validated Certificate for a Smooth-System Root
Interval Newton Certification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the verified interval Newton image lies strictly inside the starting box and all enclosed Jacobians are nonsingular, the box contains exactly one root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a compact interval box, choose \(x_0\in X\), and let \(F\) be continuously differentiable on \(X\). Let \(\mathcal J(X)\) be an interval enclosure of every \(F'(x)\) for \(x\in X\), and let \(N(x_0,X)\) be an outward-rounded enclosure of
\[
\{x_0-A^{-1}F(x_0):A\in\mathcal J(X)\}.
\]
If every \(A\in\mathcal J(X)\) is nonsingular and
\[
N(x_0,X)\subset\operatorname{int}(X),
\]
then \(F\) has exactly one zero in \(X\). The strict inclusion and verified interval evaluations constitute the certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on the compact interval box \(X\).
\(\mathcal J(X)\) outwardly encloses \(F'(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), and every enclosed matrix is nonsingular.
All interval evaluations use inclusion-preserving outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(x_0,X)\subset\operatorname{int}(X)\) certifies existence and uniqueness of a zero of \(F\) in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence-and-uniqueness certificate from strict inclusion of an interval Newton image in a box.

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of the Jacobian range on X

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The certificate fits the interval Newton leaf, but the precise set-valued inverse construction, interval-enclosure semantics, and existence-and-uniqueness implication require confirmation from an authoritative interval-analysis theorem with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interval Newton Operator and Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(X\subseteq D\) be a closed interval box, choose \(x_0\in X\), and let \([J](X)\) be an interval matrix satisfying \(F'(x)\in[J](X)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition uses a square smooth system and interval arithmetic with outward rounding. The set-valued linear solve must enclose every solution associated with point matrices in the interval Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interval Newton image is \(N(F,X,x_0)=x_0-[J](X)^{-1}F(x_0)\), interpreted as a verified enclosure of all vectors \(x_0-A^{-1}F(x_0)\) for admissible nonsingular \(A\in[J](X)\), or computed through an equivalent verified interval linear solver. An interval Newton existence-and-uniqueness certificate is the strict inclusion \(N(F,X,x_0)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\), subject to the regularity conditions of the adopted interval Newton theorem. An exclusion certificate is \(N(F,X,x_0)\cap X=\varnothing\). The contracted box is \(X^+=X\cap N(F,X,x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interval Newton operator encloses Newton corrections obtained from every Jacobian represented over a box. Strict inclusion of its image in the box certifies a unique root under the standard regularity hypotheses; disjointness certifies that the box contains no root. Intersecting the image with the box contracts the search region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(F,X,x_0)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\) is the defining inclusion certificate, while \(N(F,X,x_0)\cap X=\varnothing\) is the defining exclusion test.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A preconditioned interval linear system may be used to enclose the same Newton image without explicitly forming an interval-matrix inverse.
special_cases_latex: In one dimension, \(N=x_0-F(x_0)/F'(X)\) when interval division is defined.
immediate_consequences_latex: Successful inclusion provides both a root enclosure and a uniqueness assertion in \(X\).
Failure of the inclusion test is inconclusive and is not a certificate of nonexistence.
boundary_notes: If the interval Jacobian contains singular matrices, naive interval inversion may be undefined or excessively wide.
The inspected source set did not provide a precise theorem locator supporting these exact inclusion predicates.

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of all Jacobians over X

review_flags: A precise interval-Newton theorem source is required, especially for uniqueness and exclusion hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Newton Operator and Certificate
Krawczyk-Operator Certification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict inclusion of the verified Krawczyk image inside the box certifies a root and, under the stated square-system assumptions, its uniqueness in that box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a compact interval box, let \(x_0\in X\), and let \(F\) be continuously differentiable on \(X\). Let \(\mathcal J(X)\) enclose all Jacobians on \(X\), and choose a nonsingular point matrix \(C\). Define the outward-rounded Krawczyk enclosure
\[
K(x_0,X)=x_0-CF(x_0)+\bigl(I-C\mathcal J(X)\bigr)(X-x_0).
\]
If
\[
K(x_0,X)\subset\operatorname{int}(X),
\]
then \(F\) has a zero in \(X\), and that zero is unique in \(X\). The data \((X,x_0,C,\mathcal J(X))\) and the verified strict inclusion form a checkable certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuously differentiable on the compact box \(X\).
\(\mathcal J(X)\) inclusion-wise encloses every Jacobian on \(X\), and \(C\) is nonsingular.
All interval operations are inclusion preserving and outward rounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(x_0,X)\subset\operatorname{int}(X)\) certifies existence and uniqueness of a zero of \(F\) in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validated root certificate from strict self-inclusion of the Krawczyk operator.

notation.meaning: nonsingular approximate inverse of the midpoint Jacobian

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The Krawczyk enclosure and strict-inclusion certificate fit the leaf. The exact hypotheses needed for existence and uniqueness in the entire box, including the roles of the preconditioner and interval Jacobian enclosure, require an authoritative theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Krawczyk Operator and Inclusion Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(X\subseteq D\) be an interval box with center or base point \(x_0\in X\), let \([J](X)\) enclose \(F'(x)\) on \(X\), and choose a nonsingular point matrix \(C\) approximating \(F'(x_0)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the standard finite-dimensional smooth square-system operator. All products and inclusions involving interval quantities are evaluated with outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Krawczyk operator is \(K(F,X,x_0,C)=x_0-CF(x_0)+(I-C[J](X))(X-x_0)\). A Krawczyk inclusion certificate is the verified relation \(K(F,X,x_0,C)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\); under the standard Krawczyk regularity hypotheses it certifies a root in \(X\) and the associated uniqueness conclusion of that theorem. A verified disjointness relation \(K(F,X,x_0,C)\cap X=\varnothing\) is an exclusion certificate. The operator is preconditioned by the point matrix \(C\), so it avoids direct inversion of the interval Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Krawczyk operator combines a point Newton correction with an interval bound for the remaining linearization error. Strict containment in the interior of the box supplies the standard existence and uniqueness certificate, while disjointness supplies exclusion. A point inverse approximation acts as a preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=x_0-CF(x_0)+(I-C[J](X))(X-x_0)\), with strict inclusion \(K\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)\) defining the positive Krawczyk certificate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(X=x_0+Z\) gives \(K=x_0-CF(x_0)+(I-C[J](X))Z\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=F'(x_0)^{-1}\), the center term is the ordinary Newton iterate and the remaining interval term bounds Jacobian variation.
For an affine map \(F(x)=Ax-b\) with \(C=A^{-1}\), the interval remainder term vanishes.
immediate_consequences_latex: A tighter enclosure of \([J](X)\) generally produces a tighter Krawczyk image.
Failure of strict inclusion is inconclusive and may be addressed by subdivision or improved preconditioning.
boundary_notes: Uniqueness may be stated relative to \(X\) or to a larger domain depending on the precise theorem version; the intended convention must be sourced.
No inspected source provided an exact Krawczyk theorem locator.

notation.meaning: point preconditioner approximating the inverse Jacobian

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Typed Root Outcome Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(X\subseteq D\) be a specified validation region, and let \(Z_X=\{x\in X:F(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The system classifies logically verified outcomes for one stated region. It does not classify heuristic solver messages or claims about unsearched regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A root outcome certificate is a pair \((\tau,\mathcal{C})\), where \(\mathcal{C}\) is verified enclosure data and the type \(\tau\) belongs to \(\{\mathrm{EXCLUDE},\mathrm{EXIST},\mathrm{UNIQUE},\mathrm{MULTIPLE},\mathrm{UNRESOLVED}\}\). Its semantics are \(\mathrm{EXCLUDE}:|Z_X|=0\), \(\mathrm{EXIST}:|Z_X|\geq1\), \(\mathrm{UNIQUE}:|Z_X|=1\), and \(\mathrm{MULTIPLE}:|Z_X|\geq2\), where a MULTIPLE certificate must distinguish at least two roots by disjoint certified enclosures or an equivalent verified count. UNRESOLVED asserts no root predicate and records only that the available tests failed to decide. A positive certificate must identify the exact region, arithmetic enclosure convention, and predicate established by its verification rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A typed outcome certificate reports exclusion, existence, uniqueness, multiplicity, or an explicitly unresolved result for roots in one fixed region. Each positive type has a precise cardinality meaning. An unresolved outcome makes no mathematical claim about whether roots exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The outcome type determines a cardinality predicate for \(Z_X\), except that \(\mathrm{UNRESOLVED}\) carries no cardinality assertion.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A collection of pairwise disjoint unique-root boxes contained in \(X\) certifies at least that many distinct roots in \(X\).
special_cases_latex: An interval Newton or Krawczyk interior inclusion can instantiate \(\mathrm{UNIQUE}\).
An interval range test satisfying \(0\notin[F_i](X)\) for some component \(i\) can instantiate \(\mathrm{EXCLUDE}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Root Uniqueness Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly self-mapping interval-Newton enclosure with a regular interval Jacobian certifies exactly one root in the box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a compact interval box, let \(x_0\in X\), and let \(F\) be continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X\). Suppose \([JF](X)\) encloses every Jacobian \(JF(x)\) for \(x\in X\), every matrix in \([JF](X)\) is nonsingular, and the validated interval-Newton image \(N(x_0,X)=x_0-[JF](X)^{-1}F(x_0)\) satisfies \(N(x_0,X)\subset\operatorname{int}X\). The inclusion and regularity data certify that \(F(x)=0\) has exactly one solution in \(X\).

\(JF(x)\in[JF](X)\) for every \(x\in X\), and all matrices in \([JF](X)\) are nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.title: Root Exclusion Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a validated enclosure of the residual range omits zero, the entire box contains no root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty compact box and let \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}^n\). A validated range enclosure \([F](X)\) satisfies \(F(X)\subseteq[F](X)\). If interval evaluation verifies \(0\notin[F](X)\), then no point of \(X\) can solve \(F(x)=0\). Equivalently, it suffices to verify that some component enclosure \([F_i](X)\) excludes zero. The enclosure and the zero-exclusion test form a directly checkable root-exclusion certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Outcome Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate tests are sufficient, not converses: a failed test yields an inconclusive outcome rather than the opposite root claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a verification region \(X\), the certified outcomes obey strict logical boundaries: an existence certificate establishes \(Z_X\ne\varnothing\); a uniqueness certificate establishes \(|Z_X|=1\); and an exclusion certificate establishes \(Z_X=\varnothing\), where \(Z_X=\{x\in X:F(x)=0\}\). Failure of a sufficient certificate test implies none of the opposite outcomes. Thus \(0\in[F](X)\) does not prove existence, failure of interval-Newton inclusion does not prove nonexistence or multiplicity, and an existence certificate alone does not prove uniqueness. When no sufficient test succeeds, the only sound outcome is inconclusive.
assumptions_latex: Each reported certificate has been validated under its own hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z_X\ne\varnothing\), \(|Z_X|=1\), and \(Z_X=\varnothing\) require their respective certificates; failure of a test alone certifies none of them.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundaries separating existence, uniqueness, exclusion, and inconclusive validated outcomes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Q- and R-Convergence Rate Families
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(x_k\to x_*\), and define \(e_k=\|x_k-x_*\|\). Assume \(e_k>0\) whenever a quotient is formed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition classifies asymptotic iterate errors. Residual rates coincide with iterate rates only under additional local error-bound conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convergence is Q-linear if there exist \(q\in(0,1)\) and \(k_0\) such that \(e_{k+1}\leq q e_k\) for all \(k\geq k_0\). It is Q-superlinear if \(e_{k+1}/e_k\to0\). It has Q-order at least \(p>1\) if there exist \(M>0\) and \(k_0\) such that \(e_{k+1}\leq M e_k^p\) for all \(k\geq k_0\); \(p=2\) is Q-quadratic convergence. It is R-linear if there is a nonnegative sequence \(v_k\) with \(e_k\leq v_k\) and \(v_k\) converging Q-linearly to zero. R-superlinear and R-order-\(p\) convergence are defined analogously through a dominating scalar sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Q-rates constrain successive actual errors: linear convergence contracts by a fixed factor, superlinear convergence has a vanishing error ratio, and order p bounds the next error by a constant times the current error to power p. R-rates are weaker because only a dominating scalar sequence must have the corresponding Q-rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rate family is determined by asymptotic inequalities for \(e_{k+1}\) relative to \(e_k\), or by a dominating sequence for R-rates.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Q-linear convergence is equivalently an eventual uniform bound \(\sup_{k\geq k_0}e_{k+1}/e_k\leq q<1\).
special_cases_latex: Q-quadratic convergence is Q-superlinear whenever \(e_k\to0\).
Every Q-linear sequence is R-linear by taking \(v_k=e_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: R-linear convergence can permit occasional increases in the actual error.
A finite collection of observed ratios does not establish an asymptotic rate.
boundary_notes: Some authors define exact Q-order by a positive finite limit rather than an upper bound; this record uses the at-least-order convention.
Rates of objective values, residuals, steps, and iterates are distinct unless linked by additional assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Q-linear convergence means that every sufficiently late error is at most a fixed fraction, strictly below one, of the preceding error; when late errors are positive, this is equivalent to the successive-error limsup being below one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space, let \(x_k\to x^*\), and define \(e_k=\|x_k-x^*\|\). The sequence converges Q-linearly to \(x^*\) if there exist \(q\in(0,1)\) and \(k_0\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(e_{k+1}\le q e_k\) for every \(k\ge k_0\). Consequently, \(e_k\le q^{k-k_0}e_{k_0}\) for every \(k\ge k_0\). If \(e_k>0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), this definition is equivalent to \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}e_{k+1}/e_k<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists q\in(0,1),\exists k_0\in\mathbb{N},\forall k\ge k_0:\ e_{k+1}\le q e_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic Q-linear convergence of iterates in a normed space.

knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear-Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Superlinear convergence means either finite termination at the limit or, for a nonterminating sequence, that the successive-error ratio tends to zero; it does not require a fixed order greater than one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space, let \(x_k\to x^*\), and set \(e_k=\|x_k-x^*\|\). The convergence is Q-superlinear if either the sequence terminates at \(x^*\), meaning that \(x_k=x^*\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), or \(e_k>0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\) and \(\lim_{k\to\infty}e_{k+1}/e_k=0\). In the nonterminating case, for every \(q\in(0,1)\) there exists \(k_q\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(e_{k+1}\le q e_k\) for all \(k\ge k_q\). Q-superlinear convergence need not have a fixed Q-order greater than one.
assumptions_latex: \(x_k\to x^*\), with eventual positivity of \(e_k=\|x_k-x^*\|\) in the nonterminating case.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic Q-superlinear convergence measured by successive norm errors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: High-Order Q-Convergence Regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x_k\to x_*\) in a normed finite-dimensional space, and put \(e_k=\|x_k-x_*\|\). Let \(p>1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition is asymptotic and local. It classifies the sequence itself, independently of the algorithmic mechanism that generated it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence is in a high-order Q-convergence regime of order at least \(p\) if there exist constants \(M>0\) and \(k_0\) such that \(e_{k+1}\leq M e_k^p\) for every \(k\geq k_0\). The regime is quadratic when \(p=2\), cubic when \(p=3\), and of higher integer order when \(p>3\). Exact Q-order \(p\) may be specified by the stronger condition \(\lim_{k\to\infty}e_{k+1}/e_k^p=\mu\) with \(0<\mu<\infty\). Because \(p>1\) and \(e_k\to0\), every such at-least-order regime is Q-superlinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: High-order Q-convergence means that, eventually, the next error is bounded by a constant times a power greater than one of the current error. Power two is quadratic, power three is cubic, and a positive finite normalized-error limit identifies exact order under the stronger convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_{k+1}\leq M e_k^p\) eventually for some \(p>1\); exact order uses \(e_{k+1}/e_k^p\to\mu\in(0,\infty)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For exact Q-order \(p\), \(\log e_{k+1}=p\log e_k+\log\mu+o(1)\).
special_cases_latex: Newton's method under its standard regularity and Lipschitz-Jacobian assumptions is a canonical quadratic regime.
An error recurrence \(e_{k+1}\leq M e_k^3\) is cubic and therefore also superlinear.
immediate_consequences_latex: For sufficiently small errors, a higher exponent produces faster asymptotic decay than a linear recurrence.
The constant \(M\) need not be less than one for order greater than one.
boundary_notes: The definition does not imply that the iterates ever enter the asymptotic neighborhood.
Finite-precision stagnation can terminate the observable high-order regime.

notation.meaning: asymptotic error constant for exact Q-order

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic convergence means that the next error is eventually bounded by a constant times the square of the current error; for a nonterminating sequence, this implies superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space, let \(x_k\to x^*\), and define \(e_k=\|x_k-x^*\|\). The convergence is Q-quadratic if there exist \(C>0\) and \(k_0\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(e_{k+1}\le C e_k^2\) for every \(k\ge k_0\). If \(e_k>0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), this is equivalent to \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}e_{k+1}/e_k^2<\infty\), and it implies \(e_{k+1}/e_k\to0\). Thus every nonterminating Q-quadratically convergent sequence is Q-superlinear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C>0,\exists k_0\in\mathbb{N},\forall k\ge k_0:\ e_{k+1}\le C e_k^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Q-quadratic convergence expressed through a uniform squared-error bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Recurrence, Onset Condition, and Double-Logarithmic Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General local quadratic-rate recurrence, with the onset condition needed for the stated fast-regime guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c>0\), and let \((r_k)\) be a nonnegative error sequence satisfying \(r_{k+1}\le cr_k^2\) for all \(k\ge k_0\). If \(cr_{k_0}<1\), then, from this fixed onset iterate, the additional iteration complexity for reaching \(r_k\le\epsilon\) is \(O(\ln\ln(1/\epsilon))\) as \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). Moreover, whenever \(cr_k\le\tfrac12\), one has \(r_{k+1}\le\tfrac12r_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative error sequence obeying a quadratic recurrence, entry into a regime where c times the error is below one guarantees quadratic decay, with double-logarithmic asymptotic dependence on the requested accuracy from that fixed onset. If c times an error is at most one half, the next error is at most half as large.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order convergence has an eventual error-power bound with exponent above two; exact order additionally requires a finite positive limiting error ratio for an eventually nonzero sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space, let \(x_k\to x^*\), define \(e_k=\|x_k-x^*\|\), and fix \(p>2\). The convergence has Q-order at least \(p\) if there exist \(C>0\) and \(k_0\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(e_{k+1}\le C e_k^p\) for every \(k\ge k_0\). If \(e_k>0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), the convergence has exact Q-order \(p\) when \(e_{k+1}/e_k^p\to\mu\) for some \(\mu\in(0,\infty)\). Because \(p>2\) and \(e_k\to0\), every sequence of Q-order at least \(p\) also satisfies an eventual Q-quadratic bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Q-order convergence with a fixed exponent strictly greater than two.

knowledge_statements.title: Observed-Order Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logarithmic ratios of three successive errors estimate local order and reveal transitions when the estimates stabilize at different levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let positive errors \(e_{k-1},e_k,e_{k+1}\) be available and satisfy \(e_{k-1}\ne e_k\). The local observed order is represented by \(\widehat p_k=\log(e_{k+1}/e_k)/\log(e_k/e_{k-1})\). If \(e_{k+1}=\mu e_k^p(1+o(1))\) with \(\mu\in(0,\infty)\), then \(\widehat p_k\to p\). A transition from order \(p_1\) to order \(p_2\) is empirically indicated by successive index ranges on which \(\widehat p_k\) stabilizes near \(p_1\) and then near \(p_2\). The estimator is undefined or unreliable when errors coincide or reach a noise floor.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-error estimator for detecting transitions between empirical convergence orders.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Convergence-Rate Degradation Descriptor
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(e_k>0\) be an error sequence converging to zero. Let \(p_{\mathrm{nom}}>1\) be a nominal local order and define the observed quotient \(q_k=e_{k+1}/e_k\) and order indicator \(p_k=\log(e_{k+1}/e_k)/\log(e_k/e_{k-1})\) whenever these expressions are defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The taxonomy describes asymptotic error behavior, not its cause. Error must refer consistently to iterates, residuals, objectives, or another declared quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convergence-rate degradation relative to a nominal order \(p_{\mathrm{nom}}\) is classified as: order degradation when the established or limiting order satisfies \(1<p<p_{\mathrm{nom}}\); linearization when \(q_k\to q\in(0,1)\); sublinearization when \(q_k\to1\) while \(e_k\to0\); stagnation when \(\liminf e_k>0\) or the error reaches a nonzero computational floor; and irregular or R-only behavior when a dominating sequence has a stated rate but successive actual errors fail the corresponding Q-condition. The descriptor must state the reference error, nominal regime, asymptotic criterion, and whether the classification is proved or merely observed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rate degradation means that the actual asymptotic error behavior is slower than a declared nominal regime. It may remain superlinear at a lower order, become linear, become sublinear, stagnate at a nonzero floor, or satisfy only a weaker R-rate because actual errors behave irregularly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degradation label is assigned from the asymptotic behavior of \(e_k\), \(q_k\), and any supported order indicator relative to \(p_{\mathrm{nom}}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Linearization can be expressed by eventual bounds \(e_{k+1}\leq q e_k\) with \(q<1\) when a limit is unavailable.
special_cases_latex: An inexact Newton method with forcing terms bounded away from zero may display linear rather than superlinear convergence.
Rounding error can produce stagnation after an initially quadratic phase.
immediate_consequences_latex: A poor finite sample of observed orders is not an asymptotic classification.
Changing from iterate error to residual norm can change the apparent degradation label.
boundary_notes: The order indicator is unstable when errors are noisy, zero, or nearly unchanged.
The inspected source defines Q- and R-rates but does not state this exact degradation taxonomy.
review_flags: A source is required for the combined degradation categories and the empirical-order formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Convergence-Rate Degradation Descriptor
Rate Degradation under Inexactness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact Newton steps are linear for fixed forcing accuracy, superlinear when forcing vanishes, and quadratic when forcing decreases proportionally to the residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable near a root \(x^*\), with \(JF(x^*)\) nonsingular and locally Lipschitz Jacobian. Suppose \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) and \(JF(x_k)s_k=-F(x_k)+r_k\), where \(\|r_k\|\le\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\) and \(0\le\eta_k<1\). Locally, a uniform bound \(\eta_k\le\bar\eta<1\) permits Q-linear convergence; \(\eta_k\to0\) permits Q-superlinear convergence; and \(\eta_k=O(\|F(x_k)\|)\) preserves Q-quadratic convergence. Thus nonvanishing forcing terms degrade the exact-Newton quadratic regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local inexact-Newton rates controlled by the forcing sequence.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The forcing-term rate hierarchy is a standard inexact-Newton property and fits the leaf, but it is a nontrivial local theorem. No source is supplied to verify the required starting neighborhood, norm conventions, admissible forcing bound, and the exact hypotheses for the linear, superlinear, and quadratic conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rate Degradation under Noise
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the crossover scale, the additive noise term is as large as the nominal high-order term in the upper error bound, so that bound alone no longer certifies noiseless order or convergence to zero; it does not by itself prove a positive error floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let nonnegative errors satisfy \(e_{k+1}\le C e_k^p+D\delta\), where \(p>1\), \(C,D>0\), and \(\delta>0\). The two terms in this upper bound are comparable at the crossover scale \(e_k=(D\delta/C)^{1/p}\). When \(e_k\le(D\delta/C)^{1/p}\), the bound gives \(C e_k^p\le D\delta\), so the additive noise contribution is at least as large as the nominal power term in the available estimate. Consequently, this recurrence alone does not certify the noiseless relation \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k^p)\) or convergence of \(e_k\) to zero. Additional lower bounds or dynamical assumptions are required to establish an actual positive accuracy floor or convergence to a noise-dependent neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k\le(D\delta/C)^{1/p}\Rightarrow C e_k^p\le D\delta\), and the stated recurrence alone does not certify \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k^p)\) or \(e_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noise-floor boundary for a nominal power-order upper error recurrence.

notation.meaning: crossover error scale in the upper bound

knowledge_statements.title: Rate Degradation under Singularity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton's method converges only linearly to a scalar root of multiplicity at least two, with factor one minus the reciprocal multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(m\ge2\), consider \(F(x)=(x-x^*)^m\). The root \(x^*\) has multiplicity \(m\), and \(F'(x^*)=0\). For every \(x_k\ne x^*\), the ordinary Newton update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-F(x_k)/F'(x_k)=x^*+(1-1/m)(x_k-x^*)\). Hence \(e_{k+1}=(1-1/m)e_k\): convergence is exactly Q-linear, with factor \(1-1/m\), rather than Q-quadratic. This family isolates Jacobian singularity at a multiple root as a mechanism degrading the standard simple-root Newton rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_{k+1}=(1-1/m)e_k\), so the convergence is Q-linear and not Q-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar multiple roots showing loss of Newton's quadratic convergence.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The scalar multiple-root family is mathematically correct, and counterexample is the appropriate content kind for this singularity-induced degradation leaf. An authoritative source with a specific locator is still required for candidate-review evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Degradation Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed inexactness, noise, and ill-conditioning preserve the ideal order only when their combined error is no larger than the ideal local error term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) have a root \(x_*\), and write \(e_k=\lVert x_k-x_*\rVert\). A mixed degradation regime is described locally by \[e_{k+1}\le C\bigl(e_k^p+\eta_k e_k+\delta_k+\kappa_k\delta_k\bigr),\] where \(p>1\) is the ideal local order, \(0\le\eta_k<1\) is an inexact-solve factor, \(\delta_k\ge0\) bounds evaluation noise, and \(\kappa_k\ge1\) measures Jacobian sensitivity. Ideal order \(p\) persists only when \(\eta_k e_k+\kappa_k\delta_k=O(e_k^p)\); otherwise the largest perturbation term determines the attainable rate or error floor.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x_*)=0\) and the stated recurrence holds in a neighborhood of \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_k e_k+\kappa_k\delta_k=O(e_k^p)\) is sufficient within the recurrence for retention of order \(p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solver Work-Unit Taxonomy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a deterministic solver run on an instance of dimension parameters \((m,n)\) until a declared termination event. Let primitive operation classes be residual evaluation, derivative evaluation, model construction, factorization, linear solve, vector operation, communication, and storage.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition provides navigation by work unit and does not itself assert an iteration- or evaluation-complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The computational-work descriptor of a run is the vector \(W=(N_F,N_J,N_{\mathrm{fac}},N_{\mathrm{sol}},N_{\mathrm{it}},A,M,S)\). The integer counts record residual evaluations, Jacobian or derivative evaluations, matrix factorizations, linear-system solves, and outer iterations. The quantities \(A\), \(M\), and \(S\) record arithmetic work, data movement or communication, and peak storage in declared units. A scalar cost may be formed only after choosing nonnegative weights \(c\), as \(C_c=c^TW\). An asymptotic work classification additionally specifies which dimensions and tolerance parameters vary, but the taxonomy itself is the choice and separate reporting of work coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver work is represented by separate counts for residuals, derivatives, factorizations, solves, and iterations, together with arithmetic, communication, and storage measures. Combining them into one cost requires explicit weights. The taxonomy names work units but contains no complexity bound by itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=(N_F,N_J,N_{\mathrm{fac}},N_{\mathrm{sol}},N_{\mathrm{it}},A,M,S)\), and any scalarized cost is \(C_c=c^TW\) for declared weights \(c\geq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A hardware-specific runtime model may be written as a weighted or nonlinear function of \(W\), but it is not intrinsic to the algorithm.
special_cases_latex: When function evaluations dominate, reporting \((N_F,N_J)\) can be more informative than elapsed time.
For matrix-free methods, \(N_J\) may be replaced by counts of Jacobian-vector and transpose-Jacobian-vector products.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two methods with equal iteration counts can have different computational work.
Equivalent-function-evaluation counts require a declared conversion rule and should not replace separate totals when derivative costs differ.
boundary_notes: Wall-clock time depends on hardware and implementation and is not a machine-independent work unit.
The extended communication and storage coordinates go beyond the inspected source's explicit evaluation and arithmetic measures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual–Jacobian Evaluation Work Pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be the residual map used by a numerical run, and let \(J_F\) denote its Jacobian or a requested derivative representation. Fix a termination event and a counting convention before the run.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The pair measures oracle-like evaluations and remains distinct from linear-algebra work. Cached, batched, partial, and matrix-free derivative requests must be assigned explicit counting rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The residual–Jacobian evaluation work pair is \(W_{FJ}=(N_F,N_J)\in\mathbb{N}_0^2\), where \(N_F\) counts calls that return a newly evaluated residual \(F(x)\), and \(N_J\) counts calls that return a newly evaluated Jacobian \(J_F(x)\) or the declared derivative object. Reuse of a cached value does not increase the corresponding count. If a Jacobian is formed by forward differences using residual calls, those calls increase \(N_F\); \(N_J\) is increased only if the convention counts the assembled finite-difference Jacobian as a derivative evaluation. A scalar equivalent-evaluation count \(N_{m eq}=N_F+c_JN_J\) is meaningful only after declaring the relative cost \(c_J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The work pair separately counts new residual and Jacobian evaluations. Cached reuse is not counted again, finite-difference residual calls remain residual evaluations, and any conversion to a single equivalent count requires a declared Jacobian cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_{FJ}=(N_F,N_J)\), with optional scalarization \(N_{\rm eq}=N_F+c_JN_J\) only for a declared \(c_J\geq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an objective-gradient interface, the analogous pair is \((N_f,N_{\nabla f})\).
special_cases_latex: A derivative-free run has \(N_J=0\), although its residual count may be large.
For a matrix-free method, the derivative coordinate may be refined into \((N_{Jv},N_{J^Tv})\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Separate reporting remains comparable when residual and derivative costs vary across applications.
Iteration count cannot reconstruct \((N_F,N_J)\) when globalization performs a variable number of trial evaluations.
boundary_notes: Simultaneous residual-and-Jacobian calls require a stated allocation rule.
The pair excludes factorization, solve, communication, and storage costs.

notation.meaning: count of newly computed residual values
count of newly computed Jacobian objects

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Evaluation Work
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual evaluation work counts newly computed residual values and sums the cost charged to those computations. If every such computation has uniformly bounded cost, cumulative residual work is bounded by that cost times the evaluation count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(T\in\mathbb{N}_0\), and let \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) for \(k=0,\ldots,T\) be residual-query points. Define \(I_k=1\) if \(F(x_k)\) is newly evaluated and \(I_k=0\) if the required value is obtained without a new residual evaluation. The residual-evaluation count and attributed work are \[N_F(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{T}I_k,\qquad W_F(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{T}I_kc_F(x_k),\] where \(c_F(x_k)\ge0\) is the work charged to a new evaluation of \(F(x_k)\). If \(c_F(x_k)\le\bar c_F\) for every \(k=0,\ldots,T\), then \[W_F(T)\le\bar c_FN_F(T).\] Cache retrievals and work outside the residual-evaluation routine are excluded unless the accounting model explicitly charges them.
assumptions_latex: Each query is classified unambiguously as a new evaluation or as reuse without a new residual evaluation.
\(c_F(x_k)\ge0\) includes all work assigned by the accounting model to the residual-evaluation routine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting convention for calls that compute the nonlinear residual and for their attributed work.

notation.meaning: indicator of a new residual evaluation at query index k
number of new residual evaluations through index T
work charged to a new residual evaluation at x_k

knowledge_statements.title: Jacobian Evaluation Work
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jacobian evaluation work counts and prices newly formed Jacobian matrices. Uniformly bounded formation cost bounds total work by the formation count, and matrix-free Jacobian-vector products remain a separate operation unless the cost model says otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable at query points \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) for \(k=0,\ldots,T\), where \(T\in\mathbb{N}_0\), and let \(J(x)=F'(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). Define \(I_k^J=1\) if \(J(x_k)\) is newly formed and \(I_k^J=0\) otherwise. The Jacobian-formation count and work are \[N_J(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{T}I_k^J,\qquad W_J(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{T}I_k^Jc_J(x_k),\] where \(c_J(x_k)\ge0\) is the work charged to forming \(J(x_k)\). If \(c_J(x_k)\le\bar c_J\) for every \(k=0,ldots,T\), then \(W_J(T)\le\bar c_JN_J(T)\). A Jacobian-vector product is not counted as full Jacobian formation unless the selected accounting model explicitly identifies the two operations.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is differentiable at each \(x_k\), where \(k=0,\ldots,T\) and \(T\in\mathbb{N}_0\).
The accounting model distinguishes new Jacobian formation, reuse, and Jacobian-vector products.
\(c_J(x_k)\ge0\) includes all work assigned to forming \(J(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting convention for explicit or oracle-based formation of residual Jacobians.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the residual map at x

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Evaluation Reuse
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint residual-Jacobian routine saves work when its cost is below the sum of the corresponding separate costs. Savings may be summed over finitely many joint queries only when the reused intermediates remain valid for each requested computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(J(x)=F'(x)\). Suppose separate evaluations of \(F(x)\) and \(J(x)\) have nonnegative costs \(c_F(x)\) and \(c_J(x)\), while a joint routine returning mathematically equivalent values has cost \(c_{F,J}(x)\ge0\). Joint evaluation gives a strict work saving at \(x\) exactly when \[c_{F,J}(x)<c_F(x)+c_J(x).\] For a finite set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) of joint-query points, define \[S(Q)=\sum_{x\in Q}\bigl(c_F(x)+c_J(x)-c_{F,J}(x)\bigr).\] If \(c_{F,J}(x)\le c_F(x)+c_J(x)\) for every \(x\in Q\), then \(S(Q)\ge0\). Reuse is credited only when the cached intermediates match the point, model state, precision, and derivative convention required by the consuming computation.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is differentiable at every point under consideration.
The joint and separate routines return mathematically equivalent residual and Jacobian values.
\(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is finite, and cache validity includes point, model state, precision, and derivative convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost reduction obtained when residual and Jacobian evaluations share valid cached intermediates.

notation.meaning: cost of a joint residual-Jacobian evaluation at x
finite set of points receiving joint evaluations
total work saved through joint evaluation over Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Algebra Work Descriptor
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider a residual-system solver whose iteration forms or accesses matrices and computes steps through direct or iterative linear algebra. Let \(n\) be the variable dimension, \(m\) the residual dimension, and let all counts refer to one declared run.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The taxonomy classifies linear-algebra work without imposing dense-matrix complexity assumptions. Sparse, structured, matrix-free, parallel, and mixed-precision realizations retain separate descriptors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear-algebra work descriptor is \(W_{\rm LA}=(N_{\rm fact},N_{\rm solve},N_{\rm mv},N_{\rm prec},N_{\rm kry},A_{\rm LA},M_{\rm LA},S_{\rm LA})\). Its coordinates count matrix factorizations, triangular or equivalent solves, matrix-vector products, preconditioner constructions or applications, and Krylov iterations, and measure arithmetic operations, data movement, and peak storage attributable to linear algebra. Each factorization is labeled by type, such as Cholesky, QR, LU, or SVD, and each matrix-vector product is labeled by its operator, such as \(Jv\), \(J^Tv\), or \((J^TJ)v\). Comparisons must state whether symbolic analysis, ordering, and reusable factors are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear-algebra work is described by separate counts of factorizations, solves, products, preconditioner operations, and Krylov iterations, together with arithmetic, data movement, and storage. Factorization and operator types must be identified, and reused setup work must be accounted for explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_{\rm LA}=(N_{\rm fact},N_{\rm solve},N_{\rm mv},N_{\rm prec},N_{\rm kry},A_{\rm LA},M_{\rm LA},S_{\rm LA})\) with every coordinate tied to a declared primitive operation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a fixed dense direct method, arithmetic work may be summarized asymptotically in \((m,n)\), but this scalar summary does not replace the operation labels.
special_cases_latex: Solving full-rank least squares by normal equations records formation of \(J^TJ\), a Cholesky factorization, and two triangular solves.
A QR route records orthogonal-factorization work and a triangular solve; an SVD route records singular-value decomposition work.
A matrix-free Krylov route may have \(N_{\rm fact}=0\) but nonzero product and preconditioner counts.
immediate_consequences_latex: Methods with identical residual-evaluation counts can have substantially different linear-algebra costs.
The normal-equations route can be cheaper in some regimes while squaring the spectral condition number.
boundary_notes: Dense \(O(n^3)\) or \(O(n^2)\) summaries are not valid for every sparse or structured implementation.
The full descriptor extends beyond the inspected sources' less formal work discussion.

notation.meaning: arithmetic work attributable to linear algebra

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Factorization Work
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense pivoted LU factorization costs cubic arithmetic and quadratic storage, and each additional right-hand side costs quadratic work. Sparse-factorization complexity is governed instead by fill and elimination structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be dense and nonsingular, where \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting computes factors satisfying \(PA=LU\), with permutation matrix \(P\), using \(\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(n^2)\) floating-point operations and \(O(n^2)\) storage. For each right-hand side \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), solving \(Ax_i=b_i\) from the stored factors by forward and backward substitution costs \(2n^2+O(n)\) operations. Hence, for \(r\in\mathbb{N}\) right-hand sides sharing the same factorization, the total work is \[W_{LU}(n,r)=\frac{2}{3}n^3+2rn^2+O(n^2+rn),\] with \(O(n^2)\) storage. Sparse-factorization work depends on fill and elimination structure, so this dense bound is not a sparse-complexity estimate.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is dense and nonsingular, with \(n\in\mathbb{N}\).
\(r\in\mathbb{N}\) right-hand sides \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\) use the same stored factorization.
Arithmetic cost counts scalar floating-point operations under the stated convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense arithmetic and storage bounds for factorization-based linear solves arising in residual-system methods.

notation.meaning: permutation, unit lower-triangular, and upper-triangular factors satisfying PA=LU

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov Iteration Work
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Krylov work consists of matrix actions, preconditioner applications, and vector operations. Uniformly bounded short recurrences give work linear in the iteration count, whereas full orthogonalization can produce quadratic vector work and linear-in-iterations basis storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}\). Consider a Krylov method for \(As=b\) that produces \(s_m\in\mathbb{R}^n\) after \(m\) iterations and stops when \[\lVert b-As_m\rVert\le\eta\lVert b\rVert,\qquad 0\le\eta<1.\] Suppose iteration \(j\) uses one multiplication by \(A\), one preconditioner application, and at most \(q_j\in\mathbb{N}_0\) length-\(n\) vector operations, whose total cost is \(O(nq_j)\). If a matrix action and a preconditioner application cost \(c_A\ge0\) and \(c_P\ge0\), respectively, then \[W_K(m)\le m(c_A+c_P)+O\!\left(n\sum_{j=1}^{m}q_j\right).\] If \(q_j=O(1)\) uniformly, then \(W_K(m)=O(m(c_A+c_P+n))\). A method using full orthogonalization can instead require \(O(m^2n)\) vector work and \(O(mn)\) basis storage.
assumptions_latex: Each iteration uses one matrix action, one preconditioner application, and at most \(q_j\) length-\(n\) vector operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_K(m)=O(m(c_A+c_P+n))\) when \(q_j=O(1)\) uniformly, while full orthogonalization can require \(O(m^2n)\) vector work and \(O(mn)\) basis storage.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation and storage accounting for an iterative Krylov linear solve.

notation.meaning: costs of one matrix action and one preconditioner application
number of length-n vector operations at iteration j
total attributed Krylov work through iteration m

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioner Setup Work
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preconditioner work equals setup work plus application work. Reuse amortizes a setup cost only over the positive number of applications for which that preconditioner remains valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let constructing a preconditioner \(P\) cost \(W_{\mathrm{set}}\ge0\), and let each application of \(P^{-1}\) cost \(c_P\ge0\). If the same valid preconditioner is used for \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) Krylov iterations across one or more linear solves, then its attributed work is \[W_P(m)=W_{\mathrm{set}}+mc_P,\] and its amortized work per application is \[\frac{W_P(m)}{m}=c_P+\frac{W_{\mathrm{set}}}{m}.\] More generally, if rebuilds occur at indices in a finite set \(R\), rebuild \(r\in R\) costs \(W_{\mathrm{set},r}\ge0\), and every application has the same cost \(c_P\), then \[W_P=\sum_{r\in R}W_{\mathrm{set},r}+N_Pc_P,\] where \(N_P\in\mathbb{N}_0\) is the total number of applications. Setup work is amortized only over applications performed before the corresponding preconditioner becomes invalid or is replaced.
assumptions_latex: Setup and application work are accounted for separately.
A preconditioner is reused only while its stated validity criterion holds.
For the rebuild formula, \(R\) is finite and each application has the common cost \(c_P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amortized accounting for constructing and applying a reusable preconditioner.

notation.meaning: finite set of preconditioner rebuild indices

knowledge_statements.title: Inner–Outer Accuracy Balance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner solve should reduce its linear residual relative to the nonlinear residual; decreasing forcing terms recover superlinear or near-quadratic outer convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), an inexact Newton step \(s_k\) satisfies the inner–outer balance condition when \[\lVert F(x_k)+J(x_k)s_k\rVert\le\eta_k\lVert F(x_k)\rVert,\qquad 0\le\eta_k\le\bar\eta<1.\] Near a root with nonsingular Jacobian, a fixed upper bound \(\bar\eta<1\) supports local linear convergence. Requiring \(\eta_k\to0\) supports superlinear convergence; if \(J\) is locally Lipschitz and \(\eta_k=O(\lVert F(x_k)\rVert^\alpha)\) for \(0<\alpha\le1\), the local order is at least \(1+\alpha\), capped at the quadratic order of exact Newton iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near a root \(x_*\), with \(J(x_*)\) nonsingular.
For the order claim, \(J\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_k\to0\) yields superlinear local convergence, and \(\eta_k=O(\lVert F(x_k)\rVert^\alpha)\) yields order at least \(1+\alpha\) under the stated assumptions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forcing-term condition balancing an inexact Newton solve against current nonlinear residual accuracy.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The forcing condition fits the container, but the asserted linear, superlinear, and order-(1+alpha) convergence conclusions are theorem-level claims with no citation. An authoritative inexact-Newton theorem and precise locator are required before the hypotheses and order conclusion can be trusted.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative inner–outer accuracy balance
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(J_k=F'(x_k)\), and suppose an outer iteration computes a step \(s_k\) by approximately solving a linearized system \(A_ks=b_k\). Write \(q_k=A_ks_k-b_k\) for its inner residual and \(R_k\ge 0\) for the outer residual or stationarity measure used at iteration \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic residual methods with an iterative inner linear or regularized subproblem solve. The definition specifies an accuracy policy, not a convergence theorem or a work-optimal forcing sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inner–outer accuracy balance is a forcing sequence \((\eta_k)_{k\ge0}\subset[0,\bar\eta]\), with \(0\le\bar\eta<1\), together with the acceptance requirement \[\|q_k\|\le \eta_k R_k\quad\text{for every accepted outer step }k.\] It is asymptotically exact when \(\eta_k\to0\), uniformly relative when \(\eta_k\le\bar\eta<1\), and absolute-relative when tolerances \(\delta_k\ge0\) are also allowed and \[\|q_k\|\le \delta_k+\eta_kR_k.\] A work-based balance additionally declares inner oversolving at iteration \(k\) when the achieved inner residual is materially below the required bound without changing outer acceptance or the requested outer accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner–outer accuracy balance assigns each outer iteration a forcing tolerance between zero and a fixed number below one. The computed inner-system residual must not exceed that tolerance times the current outer residual. The balance is asymptotically exact if the forcing tolerances tend to zero, uniformly relative if they remain uniformly below one, and absolute-relative if an additive absolute tolerance is permitted. Oversolving means reducing the inner residual substantially beyond the accepted requirement without affecting outer acceptance or requested accuracy.
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(R_k=\|b_k\|\) and \(\delta_k=0\), the balance is the relative residual condition \(\|A_ks_k-b_k\|/\|b_k\|\le\eta_k\) whenever \(b_k\ne0\).
For an inexact Newton equation \(J_ks_k=-F(x_k)\), it becomes \(\|F(x_k)+J_ks_k\|\le\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\).
special_cases_latex: Exact inner solution corresponds to \(\eta_k=\delta_k=0\).
A fixed inner relative tolerance corresponds to \(\eta_k\equiv\eta\in[0,1)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The policy distinguishes inner termination from the outer stopping test \(R_k\le\varepsilon\).
Decreasing \(\eta_k\) imposes progressively more accurate local models without requiring an exact solve at every early iteration.
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert that every admissible forcing sequence preserves global or superlinear convergence.
Different norms or preconditioned residuals require the same norm to be used consistently in the stated acceptance inequality.

notation.meaning: Residual of the inner linearized or regularized solve.
Nonnegative outer residual or stationarity measure.
Relative and absolute inner accuracy tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative inner–outer accuracy balance
Globalization Evaluation-Complexity Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Globalization evaluation cost separates accepted iterations, rejected trials, and derivative refreshes; caching makes rejected trials primarily residual-evaluation expenses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a globalization method performs \(N_{\mathrm{acc}}\) accepted outer iterations and \(N_{\mathrm{rej}}\) rejected trial evaluations. If each trial point requires at most one new residual evaluation, and a Jacobian is formed only at the initial point and after accepted steps, then \[N_F\le1+N_{\mathrm{acc}}+N_{\mathrm{rej}},\qquad N_J\le1+N_{\mathrm{acc}}.\] Therefore \[W_{\mathrm{eval}}\le \bar c_F(1+N_{\mathrm{acc}}+N_{\mathrm{rej}})+\bar c_J(1+N_{\mathrm{acc}}).\] Different globalization families are distinguished by how they bound rejected trials, model updates, and derivative refreshes; the displayed bound applies only under the stated caching policy.
assumptions_latex: Every trial point requires at most one newly computed residual.
Jacobians are formed initially and only after accepted steps.
Residual and Jacobian costs are bounded by \(\bar c_F\) and \(\bar c_J\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation accounting shared by line-search and trust-region globalization schemes.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The displayed count follows from the stated caching policy, but no source supports that policy across the claimed globalization families. Line-search and trust-region methods differ in trial evaluations, model updates, and derivative refresh rules, so a method-specific or family-level source is required.
