knowledge_statements.statement_title: Evaluation-complexity family for globalization mechanisms
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider an algorithm for reducing a merit or residual measure \(M(x)\), with termination condition \(\mathcal{R}(x)\le\varepsilon\). During accepted and rejected trials it may evaluate the residual \(F\), Jacobian \(J\), merit function \(M\), or derivative information. Let \(N_F,N_J,N_M,N_D\) denote their cumulative counts up to termination.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case finite-dimensional deterministic evaluation accounting. Arithmetic and linear-algebra costs are excluded unless explicitly added as separate coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A globalization evaluation-complexity family is a collection \[\mathfrak{C}=\{(N_F(\varepsilon),N_J(\varepsilon),N_M(\varepsilon),N_D(\varepsilon)):0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0\}\] associated with a specified globalization rule and problem class, where each coordinate is the supremum, over admissible problem instances and starts, of the number of the indicated evaluations performed before the first iterate satisfying \(\mathcal{R}(x_k)\le\varepsilon\). A line-search family counts all backtracking trials; a trust-region family counts accepted and rejected trial points; and a regularization family counts unsuccessful parameter updates. A claimed order \(N_i(\varepsilon)=O(g_i(\varepsilon))\) means that constants \(C_i>0\) and \(\varepsilon_i>0\), independent of \(\varepsilon\), exist such that \(N_i(\varepsilon)\le C_ig_i(\varepsilon)\) for every \(0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A globalization evaluation-complexity family records, as functions of the requested tolerance, the worst-case numbers of residual, Jacobian, merit, and derivative evaluations required to reach the specified termination measure. Counts include unsuccessful globalization trials: backtracking points for line search, rejected trial points for trust regions, and unsuccessful parameter changes for regularization. A big-O evaluation bound requires constants uniform in sufficiently small tolerances and over the declared problem class.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A scalarized evaluation count is \(N_w(\varepsilon)=w_FN_F+w_JN_J+w_MN_M+w_DN_D\) for fixed nonnegative weights, but it retains less information than the vector family.
Separate successful and unsuccessful counts may be represented by replacing each coordinate with an ordered pair.
special_cases_latex: If residual and merit values are returned by one oracle call, one may impose \(N_M\le N_F\) under the declared oracle convention.
If every accepted iteration uses one Jacobian and rejected trials reuse it, \(N_J\) may be smaller than the number of trial evaluations.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two globalization schemes are evaluation-equivalent only relative to the same stopping measure, oracle convention, and problem class.
An iteration-complexity bound alone does not determine \(N_F\) when an iteration can contain arbitrarily many rejected trials.
boundary_notes: The definition is not a floating-point operation count and does not price factorizations or Krylov iterations.
Average-case, probabilistic, and data-access complexities require different quantifiers.

notation.meaning: Worst-case count of evaluation type i at tolerance epsilon.

review_flags: The supplied hints do not establish this vector-valued taxonomy and its oracle-counting conventions.
A source supporting the exact complexity-family definition and treatment of rejected trials is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-complexity family for globalization mechanisms
Continuation Condition-Length Complexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified continuation requires a number of steps proportional to condition length when step size is inversely proportional to local conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x:[0,S]\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be an arc-length-parameterized regular solution path, and let \(\kappa(s)\ge1\) be its local condition measure. Define its condition length by \[L_\kappa=\int_0^S\kappa(s)\,ds.\] Suppose a certified continuation method chooses steps \(h_i\) satisfying \(\theta\rho/\kappa(s_i)\le h_i\le\rho/\kappa(s_i)\), with fixed \(0<\theta\le1\), and the condition measure varies by at most the certification constant within each step. Then the number \(N\) of continuation steps satisfies \[N\le1+\left\lceil C_{\mathrm{var}}L_\kappa/(\theta\rho)\right\rceil,\] where \(C_{\mathrm{var}}\ge1\) is the within-step condition-variation factor.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a regular solution path parameterized by arc length.
Within each step, condition variation is bounded by \(C_{\mathrm{var}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Step-count bound for certified continuation measured by path condition length.

notation.meaning: condition length of the solution path

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits, but the step-count theorem has no cited source and the phrase describing within-step condition variation does not specify the exact inequality needed to derive the displayed constant. Certification and condition-length conventions are model dependent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Condition length of a regular continuation path
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H:\mathbb{R}^n\times[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable and let \(z:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be an absolutely continuous regular solution path satisfying \(H(z(t),t)=0\) and \(H_z(z(t),t)\) nonsingular for every \(t\). Let \(\mu(z,t)>0\) be a declared local condition measure and let \(\|\cdot\|_*\) be a norm on the product-space tangent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional regular homotopy paths. Singular endpoints, bifurcations, and path jumping are outside the defining regular regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The continuation condition length of \((z(t),t)\) is \[L_\mu(z)=\int_0^1\mu(z(t),t)\,\|(\dot z(t),1)\|_*\,dt.\] More generally, for a parameterization \(\gamma(s)=(z(s),t(s))\), it is \(L_\mu(\gamma)=\int\mu(\gamma(s))\|\dot\gamma(s)\|_*ds\). A continuation method has condition-length complexity \(N(\gamma)\le C_0+C_1L_\mu(\gamma)\) on a declared path class when constants \(C_0,C_1\) are uniform over that class and \(N\) counts accepted predictor-corrector steps or another explicitly named continuation operation. The measure is parameterization invariant under orientation-preserving absolutely continuous reparameterizations when \(\mu\) depends only on the path point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Condition length is the arc length of a regular solution path weighted pointwise by a chosen condition measure. A continuation algorithm has condition-length complexity when its counted number of continuation operations is bounded by an affine function of that weighted path length, with constants uniform over the declared path class. Under the stated dependence of the condition measure, orientation-preserving reparameterization does not change the length.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using condition arclength \(d\ell_\mu=\mu(\gamma(s))\|\dot\gamma(s)\|_*ds\), one has \(L_\mu(\gamma)=\int_\gamma d\ell_\mu\).
For an arclength parameter \(s\) with \(\|\dot\gamma(s)\|_*=1\), the length reduces to \(\int\mu(\gamma(s))ds\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\mu\equiv1\), condition length equals ordinary product-space arc length.
For \(\mu(z,t)=\|H_z(z,t)^{-1}\|\), approaching a singular Jacobian can make the weighted length large or infinite.
immediate_consequences_latex: Ordinary path length and conditioning contribute multiplicatively to local condition arclength.
A finite parameter interval does not imply finite condition length.
boundary_notes: A particular normalization of the condition number and product norm must be declared before numerical complexity constants can be compared.
The definition alone supplies no step bound near points where \(H_z\) is singular.

notation.meaning: Condition-weighted length of the continuation path.
Parameterized solution path in state-parameter space.

review_flags: No inspected source was available for the exact condition-length normalization and complexity convention.
The hinted interior-point continuation material is not cited because its support for this general homotopy definition was not established.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set-valued failure diagnosis and method selection system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a solver-state space whose elements contain an iterate, residual, Jacobian diagnostics, step data, globalization data, and accuracy indicators. Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a finite family of failure labels and \(\mathcal{M}\) a finite family of recovery mechanisms or solver methods.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A mathematical decision system for residual-based nonlinear solvers. It formalizes diagnosis and admissible responses without asserting that observed finite data uniquely identify the underlying cause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A failure-diagnosis method-selection system is a triple \((D,A,S)\) with a set-valued diagnostic map \(D:\mathcal{S}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{F}\), an admissibility relation \(A\subseteq\mathcal{F}\times\mathcal{M}\), and a selector \(S:\mathcal{S}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{M}\) satisfying \[S(\sigma)\subseteq\bigcap_{f\in D(\sigma)}A(f),\qquad A(f)=\{m\in\mathcal{M}:(f,m)\in A\}.\] A state is diagnostically ambiguous when \(|D(\sigma)|>1\), recoverable when the displayed intersection is nonempty, and conflicted when it is empty. A diagnostic label may be activated only by its declared predicate \(P_f(\sigma)\); thus \(D(\sigma)=\{f:P_f(\sigma)=1\}\). Regularization, globalization, rank management, accuracy refinement, and continuation are distinct mechanism classes in \(\mathcal{M}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The system maps an observed solver state to all failure labels whose declared predicates are active, relates each label to admissible recovery mechanisms, and selects only methods admissible for every active diagnosis. Multiple active labels represent ambiguity or coupled failure. A state is recoverable if at least one method is jointly admissible and conflicted otherwise. The formalism does not treat a diagnostic label as proof of a unique physical cause.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The relation \(A\) may be represented by a binary incidence matrix \(B\), where \(B_{fm}=1\) exactly when method \(m\) is admissible for failure \(f\).
A priority-weighted selector may minimize \(c(m,\sigma)\) over the common admissible set without changing the diagnostic map.
special_cases_latex: If \(D(\sigma)=\{f\}\), then \(S(\sigma)\subseteq A(f)\).
If \(D(\sigma)=\varnothing\), the selector may retain the current method under an explicitly declared default convention.
immediate_consequences_latex: Overlapping diagnostic predicates can encode coupled rank, scaling, globalization, and accuracy failures.
An empty common admissible set signals the need for escalation or additional diagnostics rather than an arbitrary method choice.
boundary_notes: The system is descriptive unless predicates and admissibility relations are validated for a specified solver and problem class.
Recovery mechanisms can alter several diagnostics simultaneously; the relation need not be one-to-one.
review_flags: This system-level formalization is synthesized from the node blueprint and lacks an inspected authoritative source.
Source support is needed for treating the taxonomy as a set-valued diagnostic-selection object.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact and numerical Jacobian rank-failure taxonomy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable at \(x\), let \(J=F'(x)\), and let \(p=\min\{m,n\}\). Write \(\sigma_1(J)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_p(J)\ge0\) for its singular values. Fix an absolute-relative rank threshold \(\tau(J)=\tau_a+\tau_r\sigma_1(J)\), where \(\tau_a,\tau_r\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean Jacobians. Exact algebraic rank and threshold-dependent numerical rank are explicitly separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The numerical rank at threshold \(\tau\) is \[r_\tau(J)=\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:\sigma_i(J)>\tau(J)\}.\] The Jacobian is exactly rank deficient when \(\operatorname{rank}J<p\), numerically rank deficient when \(r_\tau(J)<p\), and full-rank but ill-conditioned when \(\sigma_p(J)>\tau(J)\) while \(\kappa_2(J)=\sigma_1(J)/\sigma_p(J)\) exceeds a declared conditioning threshold. Rank failure is persistent on a set \(U\) when the same deficiency holds for every \(x\in U\), isolated when it holds only at an isolated point, and scaling-sensitive when admissible diagonal scalings change \(r_\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The taxonomy first defines numerical rank by counting singular values above a declared absolute-relative threshold. Exact rank deficiency means algebraic rank below the maximum possible rank. Numerical rank deficiency means at least one singular value fails the threshold even if it is nonzero. A matrix may instead be full numerical rank but ill-conditioned. Deficiency can further be persistent, isolated, or sensitive to scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal{R}_{\tau}(J)\in\{\text{exactly deficient},\text{numerically deficient},\text{full-rank ill-conditioned},\text{well-conditioned full rank}\}\] with membership determined by \(\operatorname{rank}J\), \(r_\tau(J)\), and \(\kappa_2(J)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Numerical deficiency is equivalent to \(\sigma_p(J)\le\tau(J)\).
For full column rank with \(m\ge n\), exact deficiency is equivalent to singularity of \(J^TJ\).
special_cases_latex: For a square Jacobian, exact rank deficiency is equivalent to \(\det J=0\).
With \(\tau_a=0\), the numerical-rank decision is invariant under uniform nonzero scalar multiplication of \(J\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The numerical rank is not intrinsic until the norm, scaling, and threshold are fixed.
Exact and numerical rank failure may disagree in floating-point computation.
boundary_notes: A small singular value diagnoses sensitivity but does not by itself determine whether the nonlinear problem has no solution, multiple solutions, or a nonisolated solution.
Sparse rank-revealing factorizations may use operational thresholds different from the singular-value definition.

notation.meaning: Spectral condition number when the smallest singular value is positive.

review_flags: No inspected source supports the complete exact, numerical, persistent, isolated, and scaling-sensitive taxonomy.
A precise numerical-linear-algebra source locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobian singularity regimes at a residual-system point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), set \(J_*=F'(x_*)\), and let \(p=\min\{m,n\}\). When \(m=n\), call \(x_*\) a root if \(F(x_*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local finite-dimensional singularity classification based on the derivative and nearby rank. It does not classify higher-order singularities beyond nullity and rank persistence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Jacobian singularity regime at \(x_*\) is described by the tuple \[\mathscr{S}(x_*)= igl(
u_R,
u_L,r_*,r_{\mathrm{near}},ho_* igr),\] where \(r_*=\operatorname{rank}J_*<p\), \(
u_R=n-r_*\), \(
u_L=m-r_*\), \(r_{\mathrm{near}}=\sup_{x\in U}\operatorname{rank}F'(x)\) for sufficiently small neighborhoods \(U\), and \(ho_*=\|F(x_*)\|\). The singularity is constant-rank when \(\operatorname{rank}F'(x)=r_*\) throughout some neighborhood, rank-dropping when \(r_*<r_{\mathrm{near}}\), root-singular when \(ho_*=0\), and nonroot-singular when \(ho_*>0\). For square systems, simple roots are excluded because they have \(r_*=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Jacobian singularity regime records the derivative rank, right and left nullities, the largest nearby rank, and the residual norm. Constant-rank singularities retain the same rank locally, whereas rank-dropping singularities have lower rank at the point than arbitrarily nearby. A singular point may be a root or a nonroot according to whether its residual vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_*\in\mathcal{S}_{r_*}\iff \operatorname{rank}F'(x_*)=r_*<p,\] with subregimes determined by \(r_{\mathrm{near}}=r_*\) or \(r_{\mathrm{near}}>r_*\) and by \(\|F(x_*)\|=0\) or \(\|F(x_*)\|>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a square system, singularity is equivalent to \(\det F'(x_*)=0\).
Right nullity \(\nu_R>0\) is equivalent to the existence of a nonzero direction \(d\) with \(J_*d=0\).
special_cases_latex: A corank-one square singularity has \(\nu_R=\nu_L=1\).
A constant-rank underdetermined system may have a local solution manifold rather than an isolated solution.
immediate_consequences_latex: A Newton equation at a singular point need not have a unique step.
Nullity and residual status distinguish derivative degeneracy from failure merely to reach a root.
boundary_notes: The tuple does not distinguish folds, cusps, or multiplicity; those require higher derivatives and transversality conditions.
The nearby-rank component is a local exact-arithmetic notion, not a floating-point rank estimate.

notation.meaning: Right and left nullities of the Jacobian.
Maximum rank attained arbitrarily near the point.
Residual norm at the singular point.

review_flags: No inspected source supports this exact tuple-valued regime family.
Higher-order singularity terminology and neighborhood quantifiers require authoritative source validation.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobian singularity regimes at a residual-system point
Singular Jacobian Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square Jacobian is singular exactly when it loses rank, has zero smallest singular value, and possesses a nonzero null direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable at \(x\), with Jacobian \(J(x)=F'(x)\). The point \(x\) lies in the singular Jacobian regime exactly when \[\operatorname{rank}J(x)<n.\] Equivalently, \(\det J(x)=0\), the smallest singular value satisfies \(\sigma_{\min}(J(x))=0\), and there exists a nonzero direction \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(J(x)v=0\). In this regime the classical Newton equation may have no solution or multiple solutions, and the inverse-based local Newton model is undefined without regularization, generalized inverses, or a reformulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rank-loss condition for a square residual Jacobian.

notation.meaning: smallest singular value of the Jacobian

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate and nondegenerate roots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies a root of a continuously differentiable square residual system by singularity of its Jacobian at the root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n and let r:D\to\mathbb{R}^n be continuously differentiable, so its Jacobian J(x) exists and is continuous on D. If x^*\in D satisfies r(x^*)=0, then x^* is a degenerate solution if J(x^*) is singular and is a nondegenerate solution otherwise, equivalently when J(x^*) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable square residual mapping, a root is degenerate exactly when the Jacobian at that root is singular; otherwise the root is nondegenerate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is degenerate}\iff J(x^*)\text{ is singular},\qquad x^*\text{ is nondegenerate}\iff J(x^*)\text{ is nonsingular}.

knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Singular Jacobian Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular Jacobian is nearly singular when its spectral condition number exceeds a chosen threshold, indicating strong amplification of perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, and fix an operational threshold \(\tau>1\). The point \(x\) lies in the nearly singular Jacobian regime at threshold \(\tau\) when \[\kappa_2(J(x))=\frac{\sigma_{\max}(J(x))}{\sigma_{\min}(J(x))}\ge\tau.\] Equivalently, \(0<\sigma_{\min}(J(x))\le\sigma_{\max}(J(x))/\tau\). Under normwise relative perturbations, a large \(\kappa_2(J(x))\) indicates amplification of data or arithmetic errors in the Newton step. Near singularity is therefore threshold-dependent, unlike exact singularity, and the selected \(\tau\) must reflect working precision and application tolerances.
assumptions_latex: The condition measure is the spectral-norm condition number.
\(\tau>1\) is fixed by the numerical accuracy policy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Thresholded ill-conditioning condition for an invertible square residual Jacobian.

notation.meaning: spectral condition number of the Jacobian

knowledge_statements.title: Transition to Rank Loss
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the Jacobian has constant positive rank r before a limiting parameter value, rank is lost there exactly when the rth singular value becomes zero; that singular value approaches zero along the preceding path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\ge 1\), let \(q=\min\{m,n\}\), let \(r\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\), and let \(J:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be continuous. Suppose that \(t_*\in(0,T]\) and \(\operatorname{rank}J(t)=r\) for every \(t\in[0,t_*)\). Then \(t_*\) is a transition to rank loss precisely when \(\operatorname{rank}J(t_*)<r\). Under these assumptions this is equivalent to \(\sigma_r(J(t_*))=0\), and continuity of singular values gives \(\sigma_r(J(t))\to0\) as \(t\uparrow t_*\). When \(r<q\), one also has \(\sigma_{r+1}(J(t))=0\) for every \(t<t_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}J(t_*)<r\iff\sigma_r(J(t_*))=0\), and in that case \(\sigma_r(J(t))\to0\) as \(t\uparrow t_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the first singular-value collapse along a continuous Jacobian family.

notation.meaning: The ith singular value in nonincreasing order.
The limiting parameter value at which the preceding rank may be lost.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dynamic exact and numerical rank-change regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be a continuous matrix path, such as \(J(t)=F'(x(t))\) along an iteration or continuation path. Let \(r(t)=\operatorname{rank}J(t)\) and, for a declared threshold \(\tau(t)\ge0\), let \(r_\tau(t)=\#\{i:\sigma_i(J(t))>\tau(t)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional matrix paths. Exact rank events and threshold-dependent numerical rank events are kept separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dynamic rank-change event occurs at \(t_*\in(a,b)\) when either exact rank or declared numerical rank is not locally constant at \(t_*\). It is an exact rank drop when \[r(t_*)<\limsup_{t\to t_*}r(t),\] a numerical rank loss when \(r_\tau(t_*)<\limsup_{t\to t_*}r_\tau(t)\), and a numerical rank recovery when \(r_\tau(t_*)>\liminf_{t\to t_*}r_\tau(t)\). A chattering regime on an interval is present when \(r_\tau\) changes infinitely often there or, for a discrete path, changes on an unbounded number of consecutive indices. A stable-rank regime is an interval on which the selected rank is constant and its active singular values remain separated from the threshold by a positive margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a continuous or discrete Jacobian path, a dynamic rank-change event is a point where exact or thresholded rank is not locally constant. Exact drops, numerical losses, and numerical recoveries are distinguished. Repeated threshold crossings constitute rank chattering. Stable rank requires both constant selected rank and a positive singular-value gap from the rank threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal{E}_\tau=\{t\in(a,b):r_\tau\text{ is not locally constant at }t\},\] with drop, recovery, chattering, and stable-rank subregimes defined by the one-sided rank behavior and threshold gap.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A numerical event occurs when at least one singular-value curve crosses the threshold \(\tau(t)\), provided crossings are interpreted with the strict inequality in \(r_\tau\).
For discrete iterates, the event set is \(\{k:r_{\tau,k+1}\ne r_{\tau,k}\}\).
special_cases_latex: For a square continuous path, an exact rank loss can occur only where the determinant vanishes.
With a fixed relative threshold, uniform rescaling of every \(J(t)\) leaves \(r_\tau(t)\) unchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: Near-threshold singular values can cause numerical rank changes without any exact rank change.
Rank chattering can repeatedly alter projected or truncated steps.
boundary_notes: A continuous matrix path may have discontinuous exact rank because rank is not a continuous integer-valued function.
Noise-induced changes cannot be distinguished from structural changes without a perturbation model.

notation.meaning: Exact rank along the matrix path.
Threshold-dependent numerical rank along the path.

review_flags: The dynamic event and chattering taxonomy lacks an inspected supporting source.
A source must validate the threshold-crossing and stability-margin conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic exact and numerical rank-change regimes
Iteration-Induced Rank Changes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive iterates change thresholded numerical rank only when a singular value crosses the chosen threshold; a spectral-norm Lipschitz bound identifies which singular values can cross.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), let \(J_k=J(x_k)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(q=\min\{m,n\}\), and fix an absolute singular-value threshold \(\tau>0\). Define \(r_k=\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}:\sigma_i(J_k)>\tau\}\). An iteration-induced numerical-rank change occurs at step \(k\) precisely when \(r_{k+1}\ne r_k\). If \(\|J(x)-J(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2\) for points on the step segment, then \(|\sigma_i(J_{k+1})-\sigma_i(J_k)|\le L\|s_k\|_2\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Consequently, a rank change can occur only if at least one singular value of \(J_k\) lies within \(L\|s_k\|_2\) of \(\tau\).
assumptions_latex: \(\|J(x)-J(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2\) for points on the step segment.
Numerical rank uses the fixed threshold \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines numerical-rank changes observed between successive nonlinear-solver iterates.

notation.meaning: Thresholded numerical rank of the kth Jacobian.
The solver step from iterate k to iterate k+1.
A spectral-norm Lipschitz constant for the Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Induced Rank Changes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a continuous path, rank cannot fall below r near a point where the rth singular value is positive. Rank gain above a reference rank r occurs exactly where the next singular value becomes positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(J:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be continuous, define \(A(t)=J(x(t))\), and let \(q=\min\{m,n\}\). Fix \(t_*\in[a,b]\) and \(r\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). If \(\sigma_r(A(t_*))>0\), then there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(\operatorname{rank}A(t)\ge r\) for every \(t\in[a,b]\) satisfying \(|t-t_*|<\delta\). Equivalently, if a sequence \(t_j\to t_*\) satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}A(t_j)<r\), then \(\sigma_r(A(t_*))=0\). If \(\operatorname{rank}A(t_*)=r<q\), then a nearby point \(t\) has rank greater than \(r\) exactly when \(\sigma_{r+1}(A(t))>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes Jacobian rank changes along a continuously parameterized solution or continuation path.

notation.meaning: The Jacobian evaluated along the parameterized path.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Change Detection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Thresholded numerical rank is stable when every singular value is farther than epsilon from the cutoff. With a strict cutoff, ambiguity occupies a band whose lower endpoint is excluded and whose upper endpoint is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(q=\min\{m,n\}\), fix \(\tau>0\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and define \(r_\tau(A)=\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}:\sigma_i(A)>\tau\}\). If \(|\sigma_i(A)-\tau|>\varepsilon\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\), then \(r_\tau(A+E)=r_\tau(A)\) for every \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with \(\|E\|_2\le\varepsilon\). Under unstructured spectral-norm perturbations and the strict threshold convention, differing admissible rank decisions exist precisely when some singular value satisfies \(\tau-\varepsilon<\sigma_i(A)\le\tau+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives perturbation margins separating stable numerical-rank decisions from ambiguous ones.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaling-sensitive numerical-rank instability
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and let \(\mathcal{D}_m\) and \(\mathcal{D}_n\) be declared sets of nonsingular positive diagonal row and column scalings. For \((D_r,D_c)\in\mathcal{D}_m\times\mathcal{D}_n\), set \(J_{D}=D_rJD_c\) and compute its numerical rank using a fixed rule \(r_\tau(J_D)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional numerical rank under admissible diagonal changes of units or equilibration. Exact rank is invariant and is not classified as scaling-unstable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The scaling–rank instability set of \(J\) is \[\mathcal{R}_\tau(J;\mathcal{D})=\{r_\tau(D_rJD_c):(D_r,D_c)\in\mathcal{D}_m\times\mathcal{D}_n\}.\] Scaling and rank are coupled at \(J\) when this set has more than one element. Its rank-variation index is \(\Delta r_\tau(J)=\max\mathcal{R}_\tau-\min\mathcal{R}_\tau\). Its conditioning variation is \[\Gamma_\kappa(J)=\frac{\sup_{D}\kappa_2(D_rJD_c)}{\inf_D\kappa_2(D_rJD_c)},\] whenever the denominator is finite and positive. A scaling-rank instability regime is a family of Jacobians for which \(\Delta r_\tau>0\), or for which selected singular values approach the rank threshold under admissible scalings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling and numerical rank are coupled when admissible positive diagonal row or column scalings cause the rank reported by a fixed threshold rule to change. The rank-variation index measures the range of reported ranks. A separate conditioning-variation ratio measures how strongly the condition number changes over the scaling family. Exact algebraic rank does not change under nonsingular scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Delta r_\tau(J)>0\iff\exists D,D'\text{ admissible such that }r_\tau(D_rJD_c)\ne r_\tau(D'_rJD'_c).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Coupling is equivalently the failure of the map \(D\mapsto r_\tau(D_rJD_c)\) to be constant on the admissible scaling family.
For an absolute threshold, uniform scalar rescaling can itself change numerical rank; for a purely relative threshold, uniform scalar rescaling does not.
special_cases_latex: If \(D_r\) and \(D_c\) are restricted to identity matrices, then \(\Delta r_\tau=0\).
Exact rank satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}(D_rJD_c)=\operatorname{rank}J\) for every admissible nonsingular scaling.
immediate_consequences_latex: A rank diagnosis based on unscaled units may reverse after equilibration.
Reported null spaces can change discontinuously when a scaled singular value crosses the numerical threshold.
boundary_notes: The result depends on the admissible scaling family and numerical-rank rule; unrestricted scaling can make the diagnostic uninformative.
Condition-number improvement does not necessarily preserve a thresholded rank decision.

notation.meaning: Set of numerical ranks produced by admissible scalings.

Ill-Scaled Jacobian Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Jacobian is ill-scaled when its nonzero row or column norms differ by at least a prescribed large factor, although exact rank remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have no zero row or column, and fix \(\gamma>1\). The Jacobian is \(\gamma\)-ill-scaled when at least one of the ratios \(\max_i\|e_i^{\mathsf T}J\|_2/\min_i\|e_i^{\mathsf T}J\|_2\) and \(\max_j\|Je_j\|_2/\min_j\|Je_j\|_2\) is at least \(\gamma\). This condition concerns representation-dependent magnitude imbalance, not exact rank: multiplication by nonsingular diagonal row and column scalings preserves \(\operatorname{rank}J\) while potentially changing its condition number and thresholded numerical rank.
assumptions_latex: \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has no zero row or column.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J\) is \(\gamma\)-ill-scaled exactly when the row-norm or column-norm ratio is at least \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines severe row or column magnitude imbalance using a prescribed scaling ratio.

notation.meaning: A standard coordinate vector of the appropriate dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Numerical Rank Decisions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical-rank decision is unstable if two admissible perturbations yield different thresholded ranks. For a strict cutoff, the instability band excludes its lower endpoint and includes its upper endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(q=\min\{m,n\}\), fix \(\tau>0\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and define \(r_\tau(A)=\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}:\sigma_i(A)>\tau\}\). The numerical-rank decision is unstable when there exist \(E_1,E_2\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(\|E_1\|_2\le\varepsilon\) and \(\|E_2\|_2\le\varepsilon\) such that \(r_\tau(J+E_1)\ne r_\tau(J+E_2)\). Under unstructured spectral-norm perturbations, this occurs precisely when there is an \(i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\) such that \(\tau-\varepsilon<\sigma_i(J)\le\tau+\varepsilon\). The lower endpoint is excluded because reaching \(\tau\) from below does not cross a strict threshold.
assumptions_latex: Numerical rank counts singular values strictly exceeding \(\tau\).
Unstructured perturbations are bounded by \(\varepsilon\) in spectral norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Sensitive Rank Thresholds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular diagonal scaling can change absolute-threshold numerical rank even though it cannot change exact rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\delta<\tau<1\) and let \(J=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\). With \(r_\tau(A)=\#\{i:\sigma_i(A)>\tau\}\), one has \(r_\tau(J)=1\). For the nonsingular row scaling \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta^{-1})\), however, \(DJ=I_2\) and hence \(r_\tau(DJ)=2\). Exact rank is unchanged because \(D\) is nonsingular, but the fixed absolute threshold yields different numerical ranks. Therefore scaling must be fixed or incorporated into a relative, scale-aware tolerance before rank classifications are compared.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Model and objective-landscape failure taxonomy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be twice continuously differentiable and let \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\). Write \(J(x)=r'(x)\), \(g(x)=J(x)^Tr(x)\), and \(H(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares. The taxonomy concerns properties of the model and landscape, rather than arithmetic, implementation, or stopping-test failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A model-landscape failure label at \(x\) is assigned by declared tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_r,\varepsilon_\sigma\) and predicates: nonroot stationarity when \(\|g(x)\|\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\|r(x)\|>\varepsilon_r\); local nonidentifiability when \(\sigma_{\min}(J(x))\le\varepsilon_\sigma\); large-residual model mismatch when the omitted curvature \(S(x)=\sum_i r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x)\) is not negligible relative to \(J(x)^TJ(x)\); attraction failure when the solver limit belongs to an undesirable stationary component; and residual misspecification when the attainable residual infimum remains above a declared adequacy threshold. The taxonomy is set-valued, so several labels may hold simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The taxonomy classifies smooth nonlinear least-squares failures using explicit predicates. Its principal classes are nonroot stationarity, local nonidentifiability, large-residual failure of the Gauss–Newton model, attraction to an undesirable stationary component, and residual misspecification indicated by an unattainable adequacy target. Labels may overlap because one observed outcome can have several landscape causes.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The taxonomy may be represented as a vector of indicator predicates rather than a single mutually exclusive label.
At an exact stationary point, nonroot stationarity is \(J(x)^Tr(x)=0\) together with \(r(x)\ne0\).
special_cases_latex: For an affine residual map, \(S(x)=0\), so the large-residual curvature-mismatch label is absent.
If \(r(x_*)=0\), then \(x_*\) cannot be a nonroot stationary outcome.
immediate_consequences_latex: Termination based only on \(\|g(x)\|\) cannot distinguish a root from a nonroot stationary point.
Rank deficiency and attraction failure can coexist at the same limit point.
boundary_notes: Tolerance-dependent predicates are operational diagnoses, not exact structural statements unless tolerances are zero.
Noise contamination and deterministic model misspecification may be observationally indistinguishable without additional assumptions.

notation.meaning: Residual-weighted second-derivative term omitted by the Gauss–Newton model.
Declared predicate for failure label ell.

The set-valued combination of failure classes requires a supporting source or explicit editorial standard.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary between root attainment and nonroot stationarity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and define \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\), \(J(x)=r'(x)\), and \(g(x)=J(x)^Tr(x)\). Fix residual and stationarity tolerances \(\varepsilon_r,\varepsilon_g\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares. The definition distinguishes solving the residual equation from merely satisfying first-order stationarity for the least-squares objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact nonroot outcome set is \[\mathcal{N}=\{x:J(x)^Tr(x)=0,\ \|r(x)\|>0\}.\] The operational nonroot outcome region is \[\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_r}=\{x:\|J(x)^Tr(x)\|\le\varepsilon_g,\ \|r(x)\|>\varepsilon_r\}.\] The root-success region is \(\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon_r}=\{x:\|r(x)\|\le\varepsilon_r\}\). Thus the nonroot outcome failure boundary is the joint threshold surface separating residual acceptance from stationarity-only acceptance, namely points where \(\|r(x)\|=\varepsilon_r\) or \(\|g(x)\|=\varepsilon_g\), interpreted relative to the two regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonroot outcome is a stationary point of the least-squares objective whose residual is nonzero. With tolerances, it is a point passing the stationarity test but failing the residual test. The failure boundary consists of the residual and stationarity threshold surfaces that separate root acceptance from stationarity-only acceptance. Consequently, a small gradient is not by itself evidence that the residual equation has been solved.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Since \(\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^Tr(x)\), exact nonroot stationarity is equivalently \(\nabla\phi(x)=0\) and \(\phi(x)>0\).
At exact tolerances, root and nonroot stationary outcomes are separated by whether \(\phi(x)=0\) or \(\phi(x)>0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(J(x)\) has full row rank, then \(J(x)^Tr(x)=0\) implies \(r(x)=0\), so exact nonroot stationary outcomes are excluded at that point.
For overdetermined problems, a positive least-squares minimum may be a legitimate best fit even though it is a failure as a root-finding outcome.
immediate_consequences_latex: A solver report must identify whether termination was triggered by the residual test or the stationarity test.
The same point can be successful for least-squares minimization and unsuccessful for residual-equation solution.
boundary_notes: The classification depends on the declared objective and norms.
A nonroot stationary point need not be a local minimum; it may be a saddle or local maximum.
review_flags: The mathematical distinction is standard, but no supplied locator was inspected to support this exact tolerance-based boundary definition.
A precise nonlinear least-squares source locator is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary between root attainment and nonroot stationarity
Inconsistent Residual Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual system is inconsistent if no feasible point is an exact root; strong inconsistency additionally requires a strictly positive best residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be a residual map on a nonempty feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). The residual system \(F(x)=0\) is inconsistent on \(X\) when \(F^{-1}(\{0\})\cap X=\varnothing\), equivalently when every feasible point has \(\|F(x)\|_2>0\). It is strongly inconsistent when \(\inf_{x\in X}\|F(x)\|_2>0\). Inconsistency alone does not imply a positive gap: the infimum may be zero without being attained when \(X\) is noncompact or the image \(F(X)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines residual equations having no exact root and distinguishes a positive residual gap.

notation.meaning: The feasible domain of the residual equations.
The set of exact roots of the residual map.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Nonroot Outcomes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary nonroot has zero least-squares gradient but nonzero residual, so solver stationarity does not imply that the residual equations were solved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(J(x)=DF(x)\), and define \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\). A point \(x_*\) is a stationary nonroot outcome when \(J(x_*)^{\mathsf T}F(x_*)=0\) and \(F(x_*)\ne0\). The first equality is exactly \(\nabla\phi(x_*)=0\), whereas the second excludes a residual root. Such a point may be a local minimizer, maximizer, or saddle of \(\phi\); first-order stationarity alone does not classify it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*\) is a stationary nonroot iff \(J(x_*)^{\mathsf T}F(x_*)=0\) and \(\|F(x_*)\|_2>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines stationary points of nonlinear least squares that do not solve the residual equations.

notation.meaning: The Jacobian of the residual map.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonroot–Root Discrimination
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual size distinguishes roots from nonroots; a small normal-equation residual additionally identifies an approximately stationary nonroot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable and \(J=DF\). In exact arithmetic, \(x\) is a root exactly when \(\|F(x)\|_2=0\); it is a stationary nonroot when \(\|J(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x)\|_2=0\) but \(\|F(x)\|_2>0\). With certified error bounds \(|\widehat r-\|F(x)\|_2|\le\eta_r\) and \(|\widehat g-\|J(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x)\|_2|\le\eta_g\), the inequality \(\widehat r-\eta_r>0\) certifies nonroot status, while \(\widehat g+\eta_g\le\tau_g\) additionally certifies approximate stationarity at tolerance \(\tau_g\).
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is differentiable at the tested point.
The reported residual and gradient norms have certified absolute error bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat r-\eta_r>0\) certifies \(F(x)\ne0\); together with \(\widehat g+\eta_g\le\tau_g\), it certifies a tolerance-stationary nonroot.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides exact and tolerance-aware tests separating residual roots from stationary nonroots.

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Residual Gauss–Newton Breakdown
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When residual-weighted curvature is large, Gauss–Newton may ignore decisive curvature and stop at a stationary nonroot that is even a strict local maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\), the exact Hessian is \(\nabla^2\phi(x)=J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m F_i(x)\nabla^2F_i(x)\), while Gauss–Newton retains only \(J^{\mathsf T}J\). The omission need not be small at a large-residual point. Concretely, for \(F(x)=(x,c-x^2)^{\mathsf T}\) with \(c>\tfrac12\), one has \(F(0)=(0,c)^{\mathsf T}\), \(J(0)^{\mathsf T}F(0)=0\), and the Gauss–Newton step at \(0\) is zero, although \(\phi''(0)=1-2c<0\). Thus the method can stop at a nonroot strict local maximum.
assumptions_latex: The Gauss–Newton step solves \(J^{\mathsf T}Jp=-J^{\mathsf T}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(F(x)=(x,c-x^2)^{\mathsf T}\), Gauss–Newton returns \(p=0\) at \(x=0\) although \(F(0)\ne0\) and \(\phi''(0)<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits failure when the residual-weighted second-order term omitted by Gauss–Newton dominates.

notation.meaning: A positive residual-size parameter exceeding one half.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Large-residual Gauss–Newton model-breakdown regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be twice continuously differentiable and let \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\). Define \(J=r'(x)\), \(G(x)=J^TJ\), and \(S(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x)\), so that \(\nabla^2\phi(x)=G(x)+S(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares. Breakdown means loss of adequacy of the Gauss–Newton curvature approximation, not necessarily divergence of every safeguarded Gauss–Newton algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a declared relative threshold \(\theta>0\), the large-residual Gauss–Newton breakdown regime is \[\mathcal{B}_\theta=\{x:\|S(x)\|>\theta\max\{\|G(x)\|,\gamma\}\},\] where \(\gamma>0\) is an optional normalization floor. Directionally, breakdown for a proposed step \(s\ne0\) occurs when \[|s^TS(x)s|>\theta\max\{s^TG(x)s,\gamma\|s\|^2\}.\] These predicates formalize that residual-weighted second derivatives omitted by the Gauss–Newton model are not negligible relative to retained curvature. A large residual norm alone is only a warning indicator; membership requires a curvature comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauss–Newton retains the Jacobian Gram matrix in the objective Hessian and omits the residual-weighted second-derivative term. Large-residual model breakdown occurs when the omitted term is larger than a declared fraction of the retained curvature, either in operator norm or along the proposed step. A large residual by itself does not satisfy this definition, because nearly affine residuals can have a zero omitted term.
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(G(x)\) is positive definite, a scale-invariant comparison is \(\|G(x)^{-1/2}S(x)G(x)^{-1/2}\|>\theta\).
The directional predicate compares the exact and Gauss–Newton quadratic-model curvatures along the same step.
special_cases_latex: For affine residuals, \(S(x)=0\), so this breakdown regime is empty regardless of residual magnitude.
At a zero-residual point, \(S(x)=0\), and the exact Hessian equals the Gauss–Newton matrix.
immediate_consequences_latex: A corrected Gauss–Newton, Newton, regularized, or trust-region model may be indicated when the breakdown predicate is active.
Residual size and residual nonlinearity must both be considered when diagnosing model inadequacy.
boundary_notes: The threshold \(\theta\), norm, and floor \(\gamma\) are diagnostic conventions rather than universal constants.
The definition does not claim that an active predicate forces algorithmic failure under globalization.
review_flags: Several supplied books likely discuss the Gauss–Newton Hessian decomposition, but no locator was inspected for this exact thresholded breakdown definition.
The normalization floor and directional variant require explicit source support or editorial qualification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local and practical identifiability geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be a continuously differentiable parameter-to-observation map, let \(\theta_*\in\operatorname{int}\Theta\), and let \(J_*=h'(\theta_*)\). Define the exact observation fiber \(\mathcal{F}_*=\{\theta\in\Theta:h(\theta)=h(\theta_*)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-dimensional local identifiability. Statistical identifiability of probability laws and global identifiability over arbitrary parameter domains are nearby but distinct notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The parameter is locally identifiable at \(\theta_*\) when some neighborhood \(U\) satisfies \(\mathcal{F}_*\cap U=\{\theta_*\}\). It is locally nonidentifiable when every neighborhood contains a distinct point of \(\mathcal{F}_*\). Its first-order identifiable tangent space is \(\ker(J_*)^\perp\), and its first-order unidentifiable directions form \(\ker J_*\). For a noise or resolution scale \(\delta>0\), the practical ambiguity set is \[\mathcal{A}_\delta(\theta_*)=\{\theta\in\Theta:\|h(\theta)-h(\theta_*)\|\le\delta\}.\] Practical weak identifiability occurs when this set has large diameter locally or when \(\sigma_{\min}(J_*)\) is below a declared resolution threshold, even if the exact fiber is locally a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local identifiability means that no distinct nearby parameter produces exactly the same observation. Local nonidentifiability means that every neighborhood contains an observationally equivalent parameter. The Jacobian null space supplies the first-order unidentifiable directions. Practical identifiability uses a nonzero observation tolerance: parameters are weakly identifiable when the corresponding ambiguity set is large or the smallest Jacobian singular value falls below the declared resolution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Local identifiability is local injectivity of \(h\) at the observation value in the stated fiber sense.
First-order nonidentifiability is equivalent to the existence of \(d\ne0\) satisfying \(J_*d=0\).
special_cases_latex: Full column rank of \(J_*\) supplies a standard regular local-identifiability regime when the relevant inverse or immersion hypotheses apply.
A symmetry orbit contained in \(\mathcal{F}_*\) produces structural nonidentifiability.
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact local identifiability does not guarantee good numerical conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Local and practical identifiability geometry
Structural Nonidentifiability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural nonidentifiability means distinct parameters produce identical ideal observations; locally, indistinguishable parameters occur arbitrarily near the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a parameter domain and let \(G:\Theta\to\mathcal{Y}\) map parameters to ideal, noise-free observations. The model is globally structurally identifiable on \(\Theta\) when \(G\) is injective; it is structurally nonidentifiable when there exist distinct \(\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta\) with \(G(\theta_1)=G(\theta_2)\). It is locally structurally nonidentifiable at \(\theta_*\) when every neighborhood of \(\theta_*\) contains a distinct \(\theta\) satisfying \(G(\theta)=G(\theta_*)\). This property belongs to the exact model and persists independently of measurement noise or sample precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is structurally nonidentifiable iff \(\exists\theta_1\ne\theta_2\) in \(\Theta\) such that \(G(\theta_1)=G(\theta_2)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines noise-independent failure of uniqueness in the parameter-to-observation map.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The global and local definitions are plausible and fit the structural-nonidentifiability leaf, but no evidence record or inspectable source locator is supplied. An authoritative structural-identifiability source is required before candidate review can pass.

knowledge_statements.title: Practical Nonidentifiability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structurally unique parameter is practically nonidentifiable when some scaled parameter direction changes the residual by no more than the prescribed noise-resolution level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r:\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable, let \(W\succ0\), and fix \(\theta_*\in\operatorname{int}\Theta\). With \(J_*=Dr(\theta_*)\), parameter scaling \(S\succ0\), noise scale \(\sigma>0\), and resolution threshold \(\tau>0\), the model is practically nonidentifiable at \(\theta_*\) if it is locally structurally identifiable there but
\[\lambda_{\min}\!\left(S^{\mathsf T}J_*^{\mathsf T}WJ_*S\right)\le \tau\sigma^2.\]
Equivalently, some scaled unit direction \(v\) satisfies \(\|W^{1/2}J_*Sv\|_2\le\sigma\sqrt{\tau}\), so admissible parameter displacement along \(Sv\) produces locally unresolved residual change.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local numerical identifiability relative to specified noise, scaling, and resolution thresholds.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Valley Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat valley has one or more low-curvature directions separated by a spectral gap from directions of appreciably stronger local growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(\theta)=\tfrac12\|W^{1/2}r(\theta)\|_2^2\) be twice continuously differentiable near a stationary point \(\theta_*\), and let \(H_*=\nabla^2F(\theta_*)\succeq0\). For tolerances \(0\le\varepsilon<\gamma\), the landscape has an \((\varepsilon,\gamma)\)-flat valley of dimension \(q\ge1\) at \(\theta_*\) when \(H_*\) has an orthogonal decomposition \(\mathbb{R}^p=V\oplus V^\perp\), with \(\dim V=q\), such that
\[v^{\mathsf T}H_*v\le\varepsilon\|v\|_2^2\quad(v\in V),\qquad w^{\mathsf T}H_*w\ge\gamma\|w\|_2^2\quad(w\in V^\perp).\]
Thus second-order growth is weak along \(V\) and uniformly stronger transverse to \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{R}^p=V\oplus V^\perp\) with curvature at most \(\varepsilon\) on \(V\) and at least \(\gamma\) on \(V^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local spectral criterion for flat directions in a smooth least-squares landscape.

knowledge_statements.title: Identifiable Subspaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The identifiable subspace is the row space of the residual Jacobian; its orthogonal complement is the nullspace of first-order invisible parameter directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r:\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable at \(\theta_*\), with Jacobian \(J_*=Dr(\theta_*)\), and let \(W\succ0\). The locally identifiable and unidentifiable parameter subspaces are
\[\mathcal I_*=\operatorname{range}(J_*^{\mathsf T}W)=\ker(J_*)^\perp,\qquad \mathcal N_*=\ker(J_*),\qquad \mathbb{R}^p=\mathcal I_*\oplus\mathcal N_*.\]
For every \(d=d_{\mathcal I}+d_{\mathcal N}\), the first-order residual change is \(J_*d=J_*d_{\mathcal I}\). Hence directions in \(\mathcal I_*\) are locally distinguishable to first order, whereas directions in \(\mathcal N_*\) are invisible to first order.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order decomposition of parameter space into residual-visible and residual-invisible directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attraction failure in a nonconvex residual landscape
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable and nonconvex, and let a deterministic solver generate \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\). For a fixed point or invariant stationary set \(C\), define its basin \(\mathcal{B}(C)=\{x_0:\operatorname{dist}(x_k,C)\to0\}\). Let \(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{acc}}\) be the declared family of acceptable terminal components.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic nonconvex iteration dynamics. Acceptability may encode residual quality, objective value, feasibility, or application-specific criteria and must be declared independently of attraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonconvex attraction landscape failure occurs from \(x_0\) when the generated orbit converges to, or has its limit set contained in, a stationary component \(C\notin\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{acc}}\). The failure-initialization set is \[\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fail}}=\bigcup_{C\notin\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{acc}}}\mathcal{B}(C).\] Basin ambiguity is present at a point lying on the common boundary of basins of two components with different acceptability labels. Attraction cycling is a failure when the omega-limit set is a nontrivial periodic or recurrent invariant set that does not satisfy the terminal criterion. Escape or divergence is classified separately when the orbit is unbounded or has no acceptable limit set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified solver map, each stationary component has a basin consisting of initial points whose iterates approach it. Attraction failure means that the initial point lies in the basin of an unacceptable stationary component, or that its limit set is an unacceptable cycle or recurrent set. Basin ambiguity occurs on a boundary separating acceptable and unacceptable basins. The definition separates the geometry of attraction from the external criterion declaring a terminal component acceptable.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For point attractors, \(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{fail}}=\{x_0:T^k(x_0)\to x_*\text{ for some unacceptable }x_*\}\).
The acceptable initialization region is the union of basins of components in \(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{acc}}\), up to nonconvergent and boundary points.
special_cases_latex: Convergence to a strict local minimizer with an objective value above a declared target is an attraction failure.
For a globally convex objective with a unique minimizer and a globally convergent map, this nonconvex basin-failure class is absent.
immediate_consequences_latex: Local convergence of a method does not imply that every initialization belongs to an acceptable basin.
Changing globalization or initialization can change basin membership without changing stationary points of the objective.
boundary_notes: Basins are method-dependent; they are not properties of the objective alone.
Finite termination observations do not establish asymptotic basin membership without additional guarantees.

Nonglobal Local Minima
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonglobal local minimum is optimal within some neighborhood but has strictly larger objective value than the best feasible value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}\). A point \(x_*\in X\) is a nonglobal local minimum if there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[F(x_*)\le F(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in X\cap B_\delta(x_*),\]
but
\[F(x_*)>\inf_{x\in X}F(x).\]
If the global infimum is attained, the second condition is equivalent to the existence of \(y\in X\) satisfying \(F(y)<F(x_*)\). The definition applies directly to residual objectives such as \(F(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local minimizers whose objective value exceeds the global infimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Basin-of-Attraction Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basin sensitivity means arbitrarily close starting points can converge to different attractors, or one can converge while the other does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:X\to X\) be an iteration map on a metric space \((X,d)\), and let \(a\) be an attracting fixed point with basin
\[\mathcal B(a)=\{x\in X:T^k(x)\to a\}.\]
The outcome is basin-sensitive at \(x_0\in\overline{\mathcal B(a)}\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(u,v\in X\) with \(d(u,x_0)<\varepsilon\) and \(d(v,x_0)<\varepsilon\) such that \(u\in\mathcal B(a)\) while \(v\in\mathcal B(b)\) for some attractor \(b\ne a\), or \(T^k(v)\) fails to converge. Thus no neighborhood of \(x_0\) has a unique asymptotic outcome.
assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) has an attracting fixed point \(a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every neighborhood of \(x_0\) contains initializations with distinct asymptotic outcomes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instability of an algorithmic attractor under arbitrarily small initialization perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Initialization-Dependent Outcomes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With data and solver settings fixed, different initial points produce different limits, or produce convergence for one run and failure for another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an algorithm with fixed data and fixed hyperparameters define iterates \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) on \(X\). Its outcome is initialization-dependent on \(D\subseteq X\) if there exist \(x_0,y_0\in D\) for which both limits exist and
\[x_\infty(x_0)=\lim_{k\to\infty}T^k(x_0),\qquad x_\infty(y_0)=\lim_{k\to\infty}T^k(y_0),\qquad x_\infty(x_0)\ne x_\infty(y_0),\]
or exactly one of the two sequences converges. If both limits are feasible stationary points with unequal objective values, initialization changes not only the returned point but also the attained solution quality.
assumptions_latex: The update map \(T\) and all noninitial inputs are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic outcome map is not constant on \(D\), or convergence status differs on \(D\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual contamination and model-misspecification boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let observations satisfy \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(h:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be a model family, and define \(r(\theta)=y-h(\theta)\). Let \(\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a declared contamination class and \(\mathcal{E}_\delta=\{e:\|e\|\le\delta\}\) an admissible ordinary-error set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic residual decomposition. The boundary is relative to specified contamination, noise, and model classes; without these classes contamination and misspecification are not identifiable from a residual alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The data are contamination-compatible at level \(\delta\) when \[\exists\theta\in\Theta,\ c\in\mathcal{C},\ e\in\mathcal{E}_\delta:\quad y=h(\theta)+c+e.\] They are clean-model compatible when the same condition holds with \(c=0\). They are misspecified relative to \((h,\mathcal{C},\delta)\) when \[d(y,\mathcal{H}+\mathcal{C})=\inf_{\theta,c}\|y-h(\theta)-c\|>\delta,\] where \(\mathcal{H}=h(\Theta)\). The contamination–misspecification boundary is the level set \(d(y,\mathcal{H}+\mathcal{C})=\delta\). Decompositional ambiguity occurs when both clean and nonzero-contamination representations exist or when distinct pairs \((\theta,c)\) fit within tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given explicit model, contamination, and ordinary-error classes, observations are contamination-compatible if they can be represented as a model prediction plus an allowed contamination vector and bounded ordinary error. They are misspecified if even the enlarged model-plus-contamination class cannot approach the data within tolerance. The boundary is the distance level set equal to the tolerance. Multiple admissible decompositions represent ambiguity rather than a uniquely diagnosed cause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y\text{ is misspecified}\iff d(y,\mathcal{H}+\mathcal{C})>\delta,\qquad y\text{ is on the boundary}\iff d(y,\mathcal{H}+\mathcal{C})=\delta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Compatibility is equivalent to \(y\in\mathcal{H}+\mathcal{C}+\mathcal{E}_\delta\).
For \(\delta=0\), exact contamination compatibility is membership in the Minkowski sum \(\mathcal{H}+\mathcal{C}\).
special_cases_latex: Sparse contamination uses \(\mathcal{C}=\{c:\|c\|_0\le s\}\) or a bounded version of that set.
With \(\mathcal{C}=\{0\}\), the boundary reduces to the ordinary model-adequacy boundary \(d(y,\mathcal{H})=\delta\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Residual magnitude alone cannot distinguish contamination from misspecification.
Enlarging \(\mathcal{C}\) weakens the misspecification diagnosis and can increase decomposition ambiguity.
boundary_notes: The definition is deterministic and does not assign probabilities to contamination or noise.
If the contamination class is unrestricted, every datum is contamination-compatible and the distinction becomes vacuous.

notation.meaning: Distance from the observations to the augmented model class.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual contamination and model-misspecification boundary
Outlier-Driven Residual Distortion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In least-squares location fitting, one arbitrarily large outlier moves the estimate without bound and induces nonzero residuals on every clean observation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For scalar location data \(y_1=\cdots=y_{n-1}=0\) and \(y_n=M\), consider the least-squares residual objective
\[F_M(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\theta)^2.\]
Its unique minimizer is \(\widehat\theta_M=M/n\). Therefore one contaminated observation drives \(|\widehat\theta_M|\to\infty\) as \(|M|\to\infty\), even though the uncontaminated observations remain fixed. At the minimizer, the ordinary residuals are \(-M/n\) for each clean observation and \(M(1-1/n)\) for the outlier, so contamination distorts both the estimate and the entire residual pattern.
assumptions_latex: The loss is unweighted squared residual loss.
Exactly one observation equals \(M\), while the others equal zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single-contamination family showing unbounded displacement under squared-residual fitting.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Model Misspecification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural misspecification with a positive approximation gap occurs when the true conditional mean remains a strictly positive L2 distance from every response available in the chosen model family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y=g_0(X)+\varepsilon\), where \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon^2]<\infty\), and let \(\mathcal G=\{g(\cdot;\theta):\theta\in\Theta\}\subset L^2(P_X)\) be the fitted response family. The model is structurally misspecified with a positive approximation gap for the conditional mean if
\[\delta_*^2:=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E\!\left[(g_0(X)-g(X;\theta))^2\right]>0.\]
If \(\theta_*\) attains this infimum, then the systematic residual component \(b(X)=g_0(X)-g(X;\theta_*)\) is nonzero in \(L^2(P_X)\). Consequently, neither increasing the sample size nor solving the fitting problem more accurately can eliminate the positive population approximation gap while the response family remains \(\mathcal G\).
assumptions_latex: \(g_0\) and every member of \(\mathcal G\) belong to \(L^2(P_X)\).
A parameter \(\theta_*\) attaining the infimum exists when \(b\) is invoked.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent population residual discrepancy caused by positive separation of the data-generating conditional mean from the model class.

notation.meaning: Systematic residual component at an attaining parameter

knowledge_statements.title: Contamination versus Misspecification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without additional restrictions, the observed residual cannot distinguish contamination from model discrepancy because the same residual component admits infinitely many allocations between those two causes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given design points \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), observations \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^n\), a data-generating response \(g_0\), and a fitted model \(g(x;\theta)\), define \(g_0^n=(g_0(x_i))_{i=1}^n\) and \(g_\theta=(g(x_i;\theta))_{i=1}^n\). Suppose
\[y=g_0^n+c+e,\]
where \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) is observation contamination and \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) is ordinary noise. The fitted residual is then
\[r(\theta)=y-g_\theta=c+b(\theta)+e,\qquad b(\theta)=g_0^n-g_\theta.\]
Without identifying restrictions on \(c\) and \(b(\theta)\), their allocation is not identifiable from the residual: for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[c+b(\theta)=(c+d)+(b(\theta)-d).\]
Consequently, separating contamination from misspecification requires additional assumptions, such as sparsity of \(c\), regularity or low complexity of \(b(\theta)\), and sufficient design information; residual magnitude alone cannot determine the cause.
assumptions_latex: No identifying restrictions are imposed on \(c\) and \(b(\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The allocation \((c,b(\theta))\) is not identifiable from \(r(\theta)\), because \((c+d,b(\theta)-d)\) gives the same sum for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An observational nonuniqueness boundary between sparse corruption and systematic model discrepancy.

notation.meaning: Data-generating response evaluated at the observed design points

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Taxonomy of iterative-update failures
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a nonlinear solver generate \(x_{k+1}=T_k(x_k)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with step \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\) and nonnegative target measure \(R_k=R(x_k)\). Fix tolerances \(\varepsilon_R,\varepsilon_s\ge0\), a stagnation window \(q\ge1\), and a boundedness region \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic iterations, including nonstationary update maps. The labels describe observed orbit behavior and may coexist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The iterative-update failure label set is defined by the following predicates: divergence when \(\sup_k\|x_k\|=\infty\) or \(R_k\to\infty\); nonconvergent cycling when the limit set contains more than one point and \(R_k\not\to0\); step stagnation when \(\max_{j=k-q+1,\ldots,k}\|s_j\|\le\varepsilon_s\) while \(R_k>\varepsilon_R\); residual stagnation when the relative reduction over the window is below a declared threshold while \(R_k>\varepsilon_R\); unstable amplification when nearby states or perturbations are expanded by the update dynamics; and update deterioration when an internal approximation loses a declared secant, conditioning, or regularity property. The taxonomy map returns every active label rather than forcing exclusivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The taxonomy assigns iterative-update failures using predicates on the generated orbit and its internal update model. Its classes include divergence, nonconvergent cycling, small-step stagnation away from the target, insufficient residual reduction, unstable amplification of perturbations, and deterioration of an internal secant or history approximation. More than one label may apply to the same run.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an autonomous map, a period-\(p\) cycle is a set of distinct points satisfying \(T^p(x)=x\) with \(p>1\).
Small-step stagnation is the joint condition of a small update and failure of the target measure, not merely \(\|s_k\|\) being small.
special_cases_latex: A convergent sequence with limit residual above \(\varepsilon_R\) is a non-solution stagnation outcome.
A bounded alternating two-cycle is cycling but not divergence.
immediate_consequences_latex: Step-size termination alone can incorrectly label a stagnated non-solution as successful.
Boundedness does not imply convergence because cycles and larger limit sets remain possible.
boundary_notes: Finite-window predicates are operational warnings and do not establish asymptotic behavior.
Randomized or noisy iterations require probabilistic versions of divergence, stagnation, and stability.
review_flags: The combined orbit and internal-model taxonomy has no inspected authoritative source.
Precise source support is needed for the coexistence and finite-window conventions.
